Its name comes from the golden appearance of its domes, which were once gilded.

A visit to Choto Sona Masjid feels like a journey back in time. The peaceful surroundings, historical importance, and stunning craftsmanship make it a must-visit destination for history lovers, architecture enthusiasts, and heritage travellers. It is truly a precious jewel of Sultanate-era Bengal.

Beautiful design, floral and geometric motif in the masjid.

Gaur was the capital of Bengal for several times. Hence a lot of infrastructures were built in this region. Many mosques, madrasah and other buildings were constructed particularly during Sultanate and Mughal periods, "Chhota Sona Mosjid" is one of them.

"Chhota Sona Mosjid" (Small Golden Mosque) a unique symbol of muslim architecture, is located at a distance of 36 kilometers north of chapai Nawabganj district town at Shahbajpur union, Singarhat Muja, Pirojpur village under Shibganj upazilla. It is a rectangular building measuring and inner measuring is. The mosque is built by thin bricks and outer of the wall is covered with stones. There are 11 arched entrances including five on the east and three on both north and south. Five highly ornate black stone mihrabs decorate the western wall of the prayer chamber. There is an ornate "Badshah-ka-takht" (Sultan or dignitaries place of prayer) or "Ladies Gallery" (Place of ladies prayer) in the north west corner of the mosque which is built on finely carved slender stone columns.

There are four octagonal miners or turrets on the four corners of the mosque and twelve half rounded and three chau-chala domes on the roof. The domes were once gilted thus the mosque is known as "Sona Mosjid" (Golden) Mosque). It is called "Chhota Sona Mosjid" (Small Golden Mosque) since it is smaller than "Large Golden Mosque" in Gaur (West Bengal in India).

The main attraction of this monument is its superb decoration. Specially outer surface of the walls are decorated with flower, rosette, hanging chain and bell motif, geometric design like those of terracotta plaques. Floor of the mosque and the courtyard were originally covered with beautiful glazed tiles decorated with highly artistic floral and geometric patterns. On the eastern side of the mosque, there is a stone gateway with beautiful arch. In terms of architectural and aesthetical beauty this mosque is regarded as the Gem of Gaur.

A stone inscription in Arabic, over the central entrance, records that the mosque was constructed by the Munsar Wali Muhammad between 1493 AD-1519 A.D during the reign of Sultan Alauddin Hossain Shah.

Chhota Sona Mosjid is the protected monument of the Department of Archaeology of Bangladesh.

The Choto Sona Mosque (Small Golden Mosque) is a 15th-century sultanate-era mosque in Chapai Nawabganj, Bangladesh, built between 1493 and 1519 during Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah's reign. Renowned for its 15 domes once gilded in gold, it features stone carvings, 5 arched entrances, and is protected by the Department of Archaeology.
Beautiful Bangladesh

Key Features and History
Location: Firozpur, near the Kotwali Gate, 35 km from Chapainawabganj town, located near the Indian border.
Architecture: A rectangular building built with brick and covered in black basalt stone, measuring 25.1m x 15.9m. It features 15 domes, including three central chauchala domes, and was famous for its gilded exterior, which no longer exists.
Interior: The interior features a central mihrab and a separate elevated ladies' gallery (Badshah-ka-Takht).
Builder: Built by Wali Muhammad during the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah.
Cultural Importance: The mosque is depicted on the Bangladeshi 20-taka note and is a popular heritage site.
Condition: Despite the 1897 earthquake damaging its southern side, it remains one of the best-preserved pre-Mughal monuments in Bengal.

review_text:
Chhot Sona Mosque, Chapai Nawabganj

Called the 'jewel of Sultanate architecture', it is located half a kilometer southeast of the Tahkhana Complex in the Firuzpur Quarter of Gaur-Lakhnauti, the capital of Bengal, and about three kilometers south of the Kotwali Darwaza. It is located along the western edge of the southern bank of a large pond. To the west of the mosque is a modern two-story guest house built a few years ago by the Department of Archaeology, Government of Bangladesh. A modern road runs north-south through the guest house and the mosque. It is believed that the road is of old times and once connected the southern suburbs of Gaur-Lakhnauti with the main city via Kotwali Darwaza.

According to an inscription placed above the main entrance, the mosque was built by one Majlis-e-Majalis, Majlis Mansur Wali Muhammad bin Ali. The letters indicating the exact date of construction in the inscription have been erased. However, it is clear from the mention of Sultan Alauddin Hossain Shah's name in it that the mosque was built sometime during his reign (A.H. 899-925/1493-1519 AD).

The Chota Sona Mosque is the best preserved example of the Sultanate monuments preserved by the Department of Archaeology, Government of Bangladesh. The gold gilt used in its decoration has given it the name Sona Mosque. Originally, there was an outer wall around the mosque compound. This outer wall, 42 meters long in the east-west direction and 43 meters long in the north-south direction, had a gate in the middle of its eastern side. The entire outer wall, except for the gate, has now been completely obliterated, but traces of it are still visible in places.

Choto Sona Mosque, located in the Chapainawabganj district of Bangladesh, is one of the finest examples of Sultanate-era architecture in the country. Situated in the historic city of Gaur, near the border with India, the mosque is a notable relic from the 15th century during the reign of the Bengal Sultanate.

The name "Choto Sona Mosque" means "Small Golden Mosque," believed to be derived from the gilded domes that once adorned the structure. Although the gold embellishments have not survived, the elegance and craftsmanship of the mosque remain striking. Built with finely dressed stone, the mosque originally had fifteen domes, five along each row, supported by stone pillars and pointed arches.

Its walls are adorned with delicate terracotta and stone carvings, showcasing floral, geometric, and arabesque patterns that reflect the artistry of the time. The main prayer hall is rectangular and features three beautifully decorated mihrabs on the western wall.

The mosque is a blend of Persian, Arab, and indigenous Bengali architectural influences. Despite centuries of weathering and historical changes, it stands as a symbol of the region's rich cultural and religious heritage. Choto Sona Mosque is not only a place of historical importance but also a major attraction for tourists and researchers interested in Islamic architecture and South Asian history.

review_text:
Chhoto Sona Mosque is one of the oldest mosques in Bangladesh. It is located in Shibganj sub-district of Chapainawabganj district in Rajshahi division. It was built between 1493 and 1519.

The mosque is one of the most beautiful landmarks of Gaura and pre-Mughal architectures. During the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah, a man named Wali Mohammad built the mosque. The outer sides, especially the domes of the mosque were painted in golden color. These golden domes glittered in the sunlight. Therefore it is known as Sona (gold) Mosque.
The mosque is mainly made of brick, which was covered in black (basalt) stones. The exquisite carving on these black stones made the mosque attractive. The inner and outer walls are covered with architectural design on stones. The Mihrab is also decorated with beautiful carvings.

There are 15 domes in the mosque. One of the remarkable features is that only the outer domes are visible among these domes. The mosque has a decorated room separate for women's prayer. It is thought that this room was built for local sultans or officials so they can offer their prayers safely. The entrance of the mosque is stunningly beautiful.

The Choto Sona Mosque is one of the most historically and architecturally significant monuments in the Chapai Nawabganj district. Given your interest in the region's history and landmarks, it is a site of immense cultural importance.
Here are the key details about this heritage site:
### Historical Significance
* **Era:** It was built during the period of the **Bengal Sultanate**, specifically between **1493 and 1519**, under the reign of Sultan Alauddin Husain Shah.
* **Founder:** The mosque was commissioned by Majlis Mansur Wali Muhammad bin Ali.
* **The Name:** It earned the name "Small Golden Mosque" because its fifteen domes were originally gilded, causing the building to shine in the light. While the gold has faded over the centuries, the name persists.
* **Status:** It is a protected monument under the Department of Archaeology and Museums of Bangladesh and is widely regarded as a "gem of Sultanate architecture."
### Architecture
* **Style:** The structure is a masterpiece of the Bengal Sultanate style, known for its thick stone walls, graceful arches, and intricate terracotta ornamentation.
* **Layout:** The mosque is rectangular, measuring 25.1 meters by 15.9 meters. It features five arched entrances on the eastern façade and three on both the north and south walls.
* **Interior:** The prayer hall is divided into three aisles by two rows of stone pillars. It features fifteen units covered by domes and *chauchala* (four-sided) vaults.
### Location and Nearby Interest
* **Geography:** It is situated in the Firozpur Quarter, approximately 3 kilometers south of the historic Kotwali Gate and southeast of the Mughal Tahakhana complex.
* **Notable Graves:** Within the mosque premises, there are graves believed to be those of the founder, Wali Muhammad, and his family. Additionally, the graves of the famous 1971 Liberation War heroes **Captain Mohiuddin Jahangir** and **Major Nazmul Haque Tulu** are located on the grounds.
### Visiting Tips
* **Conservation:** The site has undergone several restorations, particularly following damage from an earthquake in 1897. Because of its age and delicate terracotta work, it is a site where visitors are encouraged to be mindful of preservation efforts.
* **Atmosphere:** It is often noted for its serene, naturally cool interior, thanks to the thick stone construction, making it a peaceful location for those interested in exploring the medieval history of the region.

Sompur Mahavihara, also known as the Somapura Mahavihara, is a significant archaeological and historical site located in Paharpur, Bangladesh. This UNESCO World Heritage Site stands as a testament to the architectural and cultural achievements of the Pala Dynasty, which reigned from the 8th to the 12th centuries. Built by Emperor Dharmapala around the late 8th century, Sompur Mahavihara served as a premier center for Buddhist education and religious practices in the Indian subcontinent.

The site is renowned for its immense and intricate architectural design. The main structure of Sompur Mahavihara is a colossal quadrangular monastery, surrounded by a series of cells for monks, all enclosed within a high wall. The central shrine, a massive stupa, stands in the middle, embodying the essence of Buddhist stupas with its impressive height and elaborate carvings. The terracotta plaques that adorn the outer walls of the monastery are exquisite, depicting a variety of scenes from everyday life, mythological stories, and Buddhist iconography. These plaques are not only artistically significant but also provide valuable insights into the social and cultural milieu of the time.

Sompur Mahavihara was not merely an architectural marvel but also a thriving hub of intellectual activity. It attracted scholars and students from various regions, including China, Tibet, Nepal, and Southeast Asia, fostering a rich exchange of ideas and knowledge. The monastery's library was reputed to be vast, housing numerous manuscripts on diverse subjects, including philosophy, medicine, and science.

The decline of the Pala Dynasty and subsequent invasions led to the gradual abandonment and ruin of Sompur Mahavihara. Despite this, its legacy endured through the centuries, influencing the architecture of later Buddhist and Hindu temples in the region. The site was rediscovered and excavated in the early 20th century by British archaeologists, bringing to light its historical and cultural importance.

Today, Sompur Mahavihara is a popular tourist destination and a significant site for archaeological research. Its ruins continue to captivate visitors with their grandeur and historical depth. Efforts are ongoing to preserve and restore the site, ensuring that future generations can appreciate this remarkable monument of Bangladesh's rich heritage. Sompur Mahavihara stands as a powerful symbol of the region's historical connection to Buddhism and its enduring legacy in South Asian history.

Paharpur an important archaeological site in Bangladesh, situated in a village named Paharpur (Pahadpur) under the Badalgachhi Upazila of Naogaon district. The village is connected with the nearby Railway station Jamalganj, the district town Naogaon and Jaipurhat town by metalled roads. It is in the midst of alluvial flat plain of northern Bangladesh. In contrast to the monotonous level of the plain, stands the ruins of the lofty (about 24m high from the surrounding level) ancient temple which was covered with jungle, locally called Pahar or hill from which the palace got the name of Paharpur.

The site was first noticed by Buchanon Hamilton in course of his survey in Eastern India between 1807 and 1812. Westmacott next visited it. Sir Alexander Cunningham visited the place in 1879. Cunningham intended to carry out an extensive excavation in the mound. But he was prevented by zamindar of Balihar, the owner of the land. So he had to be satisfied with limited excavation in a small part of the monastic area and top of the central mound. In the latter area he 'discovered the ruins of a square tower of 6.70m (22 ft) side with a projection in the middle of each side'. The site was declared to be protected by the Archaeological Survey of India in 1919 under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904.

Upon arrival, you're greeted by the imposing sight of the Mahavihara's main stupa, which rises majestically above the surrounding landscape. The sheer scale of the structure is awe-inspiring, hinting at the grandeur that once characterized this thriving center of learning and spirituality.

As you explore the ruins, you can't help but marvel at the intricate terracotta carvings that adorn the walls, depicting scenes from Buddhist mythology, everyday life, and intricate geometric patterns. Each carving is a testament to the skill and craftsmanship of the artisans who labored to create them over a thousand years ago.

Walking through the sprawling complex, you come across the remains of monastic cells, meditation halls, and lecture rooms, each whispering tales of the monks and scholars who once called this place home. The tranquil atmosphere lends itself to contemplation and reflection, inviting you to imagine what life must have been like in this bustling center of intellectual and spiritual exchange.

One of the highlights of the visit is the museum adjacent to the site, which houses a remarkable collection of artifacts excavated from the Mahavihara complex. From intricately carved stone sculptures to ancient manuscripts and religious relics, the museum offers a fascinating glimpse into the daily lives and religious practices of the monks who once inhabited this sacred space.

Overall, visiting Somapura Mahavihara is a truly immersive experience that leaves a lasting impression on anyone fortunate enough to explore its ancient halls. It's a journey through time that offers profound insights into the rich tapestry of Bangladesh's cultural heritage and the enduring legacy of Buddhism in the region.

Paharpur Buddhist Vihara or Sompur Vihar or Sompur Mahavihar is an ancient Buddhist Vihara which is now destroyed. Sri Dharmapala Deva (781-821), the second king of the Palavansh dynasty, was building this vihara in the late 8th or 9th century. Sir Alexander Cunningham discovered this huge structure in 1879 AD.
Paharpur Vihara or Sompur Buddhist Vihara is the second largest Buddhist Vihara in Southern Himalayas according to UNESCO. In size it can be compared to the Nalanda Mahavihara in India. It was the most famous Buddhist teaching center for 300 years. Not only from different parts of the subcontinent, but Buddhists from countries like China, Tibet, Myanmar (now Brahmadesh), Malaysia, Indonesia etc. used to come here to acquire religious knowledge. Acharya of Bihar in 10th century AD was Atish Dipankar Srijnana. UNESCO recognized it as a World Heritage Site in 1985.

Hiuen Tsang came to Pundravardhana in the middle of the 7th century, but there is no mention of the monastery and temple at Sompur in his detailed account. Gopal's son Dharma Pal (781 - 822 AD) ascended the throne and ruled for a long time and expanded the kingdom beyond Bengali Bihar to Gandhara on the north-west border of Pakistan. Emperor Dharmapala was a very devout Buddhist and it was he who founded Vikramshila and Sompur Viharas. According to another view, the author of the famous Tibetan history book "Pag Sam Zon Zhang" very clearly mentions the huge monastery and lofty temple built at Sompur by Dharmapala's son Devapala (810-850)[2]. It is mentioned in various inscriptions that the monks of Sompur Vihar used to donate money and jewels to various Indian Buddhist pilgrimage sites like Nalanda, Buddha Gaya, etc., which indicates a prosperous condition in the 10th - 11th centuries. Apart from Sompur Bihar, Agrapur (Agradiguna of Rajshahi), Ushmpur, Gotpur, Etapur and Jagaddal (Jagadal of Rajshahi) Bihars are mentioned under the patronage of Pala kings till 9th century. In the late 9th century, Gurjara Raja I Bhoja and Mahendra Pala, inflicted particular damage on the Pala Empire. Later in the late 10th century, the Pala dynasty king Mahipala (995 - 1043) restored the empire and repaired Sompur Vihar. But after the death of Mahipala and his son Nayapala, the Pala dynasty started to decline again. On this occasion, Chedi Raja Karna of Central India, Chola Raja Rajendra and a native Kaivarta feudal lord named Dibbo successively attacked Varendrabhumi. The destruction of the Paharpur temple and Vihar at Nalanda is probably related to the invasion of this period. In the 11th century Rampala of the Pala dynasty restored Hritrajya. In the 12th century, the Sena kings from Karnataka in the Deccan occupied Bengal. Sompur lost royal patronage during the reign of those kings. At this time, the fall of Sompur began for the last time. About the vihara on the verge of collapse under Sen rule, one scholar wrote, "The remains of the vihara and matha at Paharpur bear no clear signs of large-scale destruction. The decline of this institution through the abandonment or destruction of the vihara must have been the effect of the widespread unrest and population displacement caused by the Muslim invasions."

review_text:
Somapura Mahavihara

The central temple and monastery of Paharpur is the highlight of this ancient centre of Buddhist learning.

The magnificent main temple dominates the Paharpur site, rising up 22 metres as a cruciform over three terraces. Entering through the central staircase on the north side, you can climb up to the second and third tiers of the temple and explore the different chambers up close. From here, you get a wonderful view of the vast monastery and its 177 monk cells, more stupas, and other archaeological structures.

The monastery is shaped as a square that forms the edges of a quadrangle with the temple in the centre. Each side is about six metres thick and contains the rooms the monks would once have lived in – 177 of them in total. There are also the remains of other buildings that would have been used for studying and daily life. Built like a fort, the large monastery has only one main gateway to enter, in the middle of the north wall.

The Somapura Mahavihara monastery was first built at the end of the 8th century. It was in use until the 12th century. The main temple and monastery buildings were gradually covered over and the site was not rediscovered until 1807. It took more than a century before proper excavations took place.

Since then, a lot of the artistic decoration on Paharpur has been painstakingly-restored. The outer wall of the temple is decorated with ornamental bricks and bands of terracotta plaques which depict fauna, flora, and figurines. At the intermediate level of the temple, about half of the terracotta plaques remain of what would once have been two bands of running around the full perimeter of the shrine, featuring artistic masterpieces combining Buddhist and Hindu influences.

The best time to visit the monastery complex is in the morning or late afternoon hours just before sunset. It takes about two hours to see the extensive site. English-speaking guides are available upon request at the ticket booth.

Credit: Paharpur Archaeological Museum Custodian - Mr. Tanveer

It was built by the King Dharmapal. It is one of the greatest archeological accomplishments in the lands lying south of the Himalayan Hill ranges. The architectural style of vihar complex evolved here influenced South-East Asian countries. The monument angkor "Wat" of Cambodia and "Borobudru Tample" of Java, Indonesia has quite resemblances with Paharpur Mahavihar.

The Vihar is situated with large area. After initial entrance it has quite pleasant space for Car & Bus Parking.

Then after the Main Gate with Ticket Counter it has big open space with the coverage of tree's shadows, bench facilities for sitting are also available. On the right side, it has Mosque, Food Court and different different Toilets for both Male and Female. And on the left side has Museum and walkway too as right side.

In third phase, has nice attracting garden. Then towards fourth phase it has a nice little bridge (made with wood). And from here the architectural structure starts. In this phase has also big open field towards the Main Structure. After climbing through the stairs you can visit round the main structure by walk. It's very amazing to look the whole vihar from the top of it.

From my personal opinion I would say, amazing place to enjoy with your families. But, Transportation facilities are not so good enough. Evidence of the rise of Mahayana Buddhism in Bengal from the 7th century onwards, Somapura Mahavira, or the Great Monastery, was a renowned intellectual centre until the 12th century. Its layout perfectly adapted to its religious function, this monastery-city represents a unique artistic achievement. With its simple, harmonious lines and its profusion of carved decoration, it influenced Buddhist architecture as far away as Cambodia. Paharpur Buddha bihar or Sompur Bihar: The most glorious place of interest in Badalgachhi Upazila, Naogaon District is Sompur Bihar or Paharpur Buddhist Monastery. Paharpur Buddha Bihar is located in Paharpur village under the present Paharpur Union Parishad. The name Paharpur is modern and the ancient name is Sompur. The Buddhist Pala dynasty was established in Bangladesh in the 7th century (770-810 AD). In the eighth and ninth centuries AD, Dharmapala, the second and third kings of the Pala dynasty, and his son Devpala established vast empires as far as Bengal, Bihar and Kannauj. This Paharpur monastery and temple were built in Bangladesh under their patronage in the era of extreme excellence of Buddhism. Although this monastery was reduced to rubble due to historical and geographical reasons, this magnificent monastery still stands proudly as the largest Buddhist monastery in Asia.

The Paharpur Buddhist monastery had 16 rooms for Buddhist monks. Paharpur Buddhist Monastery is located on a total land of 70.31 acres. At present, the Bangladesh Archaeological Department has built a museum, a rest house and several administrative buildings here. As a result of excavations up to 1934 AD, the Archaeological Department discovered the rooms and the entire ruins surrounding the Vita of Satyapir and the temple on the east side of the monastery. In the center of the main monastery and around it are 196 living rooms, wide entrances, numerous entertainment stupas, small temples and ponds. The temple is 358 feet long from north to south and 314 feet wide from east to west. The main monastery is located in the middle of it. The evening was the daughter of the king here. Paharpur Buddhist Monastery is today recognized as one of the oldest cultural heritages in the world due to its large size and historical significance. It has recently been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

63 idols can be seen in the stone gravel of Paharpur. Statues of many animals are also found in the temple. The height of the monastery from the mainland is about 72 feet. Paharpur can be identified as a mini version of the ancient Nalanda University. Every year many domestic and foreign tourists and common people gather here.

Kantajew Temple, also known as Kantanagar Temple, is one of the most famous historical and religious landmarks in Bangladesh. Located in Dinajpur, this magnificent temple is admired for its breathtaking terracotta artwork, rich history, and unique architectural beauty. It is dedicated to Lord Krishna and attracts thousands of visitors every year, including tourists, history lovers, photographers, and devotees. The peaceful surroundings and artistic excellence make it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in Bangladesh's cultural heritage.
The most remarkable feature of the temple is its beautiful terracotta panels. Almost every wall is decorated with detailed carvings that depict scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Krishna's life, and everyday village life of Bengal. These artworks demonstrate the extraordinary skill and creativity of the craftsmen who built the temple centuries ago. Even after many years, the intricate designs remain impressive and continue to fascinate visitors from around the world.
The temple was built in the eighteenth century by Maharaja Pran Nath and later completed by his adopted son, Maharaja Ram Nath. Originally, it had nine towers, but these were destroyed during the earthquake of 1897. Despite this loss, the temple still stands proudly as one of the finest examples of terracotta architecture in South Asia. The preservation efforts by the authorities have helped protect this valuable historical monument for future generations.
The environment around Kantajew Temple is calm, clean, and pleasant. Visitors can walk around the temple, admire its artistic details, and enjoy the peaceful atmosphere. During the annual Rash Mela festival, the temple becomes even more vibrant as thousands of devotees and tourists gather to celebrate with religious ceremonies, cultural programs, local handicrafts, and traditional foods. This festival adds a colorful and lively dimension to the overall experience.
One of the strengths of Kantajew Temple is its educational value. It offers visitors an opportunity to learn about the history, religion, architecture, and cultural traditions of Bangladesh. Students, researchers, and photographers can gain valuable knowledge while exploring the temple. The site also contributes to local tourism, creating business opportunities for nearby shops, guides, and small vendors.
However, there is still room for improvement. Additional information boards explaining the history and artwork would help visitors better understand the significance of the temple. Improved parking facilities, more seating areas, and enhanced visitor services would make the experience even more comfortable, especially during festivals and peak tourist seasons.
Overall, Kantajew Temple is an extraordinary destination that reflects the rich cultural and artistic heritage of Bangladesh. Its stunning terracotta decorations, historical importance, and peaceful surroundings create a memorable experience for every visitor. Whether someone visits for religious purposes, historical interest, or simple admiration of beautiful architecture, the temple leaves a lasting impression. I highly recommend visiting Kantajew Temple to appreciate one of Bangladesh's greatest architectural treasures and to experience the beauty, history, and traditions that have been preserved for generations. It is truly a national treasure worthy of admiration and protection.

Kantajew Temple, also known as Kantanagar Temple, stands in the Dinajpur district of Bangladesh as one of the finest examples of late medieval terracotta architecture. Built between 1704 and 1752 under the patronage of Maharaja Pran Nath and completed by his son Ramnath, the temple is dedicated to Lord Krishna, locally known as Kantaji.

What makes the Kantajew Temple remarkable is its intricate terracotta ornamentation covering almost every inch of its surface. Each panel tells a story—episodes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, and the life of Krishna—alongside scenes of everyday rural Bengal. The temple was originally a nine-spired (navaratna) structure, but the upper part was destroyed in an earthquake in the late 19th century. Despite this, its artistic splendor remains breathtaking.

Architecturally, the temple follows a three-tiered design resting on a slightly raised platform, built entirely of burnt brick. The use of terracotta plaques instead of stone showcases the local artisans’ mastery in creating detailed narrative art through clay.

Beyond its religious role, the Kantajew Temple reflects the cultural and artistic heritage of 18th-century Bengal. It stands not just as a place of devotion, but as a historical document carved in clay—preserving the artistic language, faith, and social life of a bygone era.

Must visit place in Dinajpur . Beautiful terracotta work in everywhere in the Temple .

Built in 1752 by Pran Nath, a renowned maharaja from Dinajpur, it is the country’s finest example of brick and terracotta style temple architecture. Its most remarkable feature, typical of mid-18th-century Hindu temples, is its superb surface decoration, with infinite panels of sculpted terracotta plaques depicting both figurative and floral motifs.
The 15-sq-m, three-storey edifice was originally crowned with nine ornamental two-storey towers, which collapsed during the great earthquake of 1897 and were never replaced. The building sits in a courtyard surrounded by offices and pilgrims’ quarters, all protected by a stout wall. Visitors can no longer go inside the inner sanctum of the temple, which houses a Krishna shrine, but the intricate detail of its exterior will keep you engaged.

Kantaji Temple, also known as the Kantanagar Temple, is located in the graceful heart of gorgeous countryside of Dinajpur. This is a stunning block of religious artwork, and is surely one of the most impressive Hindu monuments in Bangladesh.

Built in 1704-1752 A.D. by Maharaja  Pran Nath,  and his adopted son Ram Nath, it is the country’s finest example of brick and terracotta style. Its most remarkable feature, typical of late Mughal-era temples, is its superb surface decoration, with infinite panels of sculpted terracotta plaques.
This 15-sq-meter, three-story edifice was originally crowned with nine ornamental two-story towers, which collapsed during the great earthquake of 1897 and were never replaced. The temple is built on a high platform. This is a Nava-ratna temple. The roof of the ground floor and first floor each contains four sikharas or ratnas at their corners while the roof of second floor in its middle contains the ruins of the central sikhara.

The entire outer surface of the temple is exquisitely established with terracotta plaques which depict flora and fauna, geometric motifs, mythological scenes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, and the contemporary social scenes and favorite pastime. The idol of Kantaji is kept in the vagarious of the temple in its ground floor.
The department of Archaeology has been performing the necessary conservation and restoration works of Kantaji Temple since it was declared a protected monument by the Government in 1960. This is a UNESCO world heritage site.

“A fascinating journey into ancient Bengal—rich in history with some areas needing better upkeep.”

What I Loved:

Incredible historical depth — Mahasthangarh is the oldest known urban archaeological site in Bangladesh, dating back to at least the 3rd century BCE, and served as the capital of the ancient Pundravardhana kingdom .

Architectural highlights — Walking through the massive citadel walls (around 1.5 km by 1.3 km) truly evokes the grandeur of the ancient city .

Key landmarks — Highlights include Govinda Bhita (an ancient temple by the Karatoya River), the Mahasthangarh Museum (housing relics from multiple eras), and the Mazar of Shah Sultan Balkhi Mahisawar—a unique blend of Hindu, Buddhist, and Islamic history .

Scenic setting — The elevated terrain (~36 m above sea level) and its location by the once-wider-than-the-Gangetic Karatoya River combine to make the site both strategic and picturesque .

Final Thoughts:

Mahasthangarh is an astonishing window into ancient Bengal’s urban and cultural evolution. From its vast ramparts and sacred temples to relics spanning Hindu, Buddhist, and Islamic eras, a visit here is both an intellectual and aesthetic adventure. A bit more investment in conservation and interpretive signage would elevate the experience even further—but even as it stands, Mahasthangarh earned 4 stars from me. A must-visit for history lovers and explorers!

review_text:
Mahasthangarh is one of the earliest and most significant urban archaeological sites discovered in Bangladesh. Located on the western bank of the Karatoya River in Bogura, this ancient fortified city served as Pundranagara, the provincial capital of the Maurya, Gupta, Pala, and Sena dynasties from the 3rd century BCE to the 18th century CE.

The site spans an impressive elevated plateau, enclosed by massive earthen and brick ramparts. Key historical structures within and surrounding the citadel include the Gokul Medh (commonly referred to as Behula's Basantaghar), Bairagir Bhita, and the Govinda Bhita temple complex. Excavations at Mahasthangarh have unearthed a treasure trove of artifacts, including punch-marked ancient coins, terracotta plaques, ornamental bricks, and delicate stone sculptures.

Visiting Mahasthangarh offers an extraordinary journey into Bengal's ancient urban civilizational history. The site complex also houses a well-curated site museum displaying recovered pottery, inscriptions, and rare religious artifacts, surrounded by lush green landscapes.

Mahasthangarh is one of the earliest and most significant urban archaeological sites discovered in Bangladesh. Located on the western bank of the Karatoya River in Bogura, this ancient fortified city served as Pundranagara, the provincial capital of the Maurya, Gupta, Pala, and Sena dynasties from the 3rd century BCE to the 18th century CE.

The site spans an impressive elevated plateau, enclosed by massive earthen and brick ramparts. Key historical structures within and surrounding the citadel include the Gokul Medh (commonly referred to as Behula's Basantaghar), Bairagir Bhita, and the Govinda Bhita temple complex. Excavations at Mahasthangarh have unearthed a treasure trove of artifacts, including punch-marked ancient coins, terracotta plaques, ornamental bricks, and delicate stone sculptures.

Visiting Mahasthangarh offers an extraordinary journey into Bengal's ancient urban civilizational history. The site complex also houses a well-curated site museum displaying recovered pottery, inscriptions, and rare religious artifacts, surrounded by lush green landscapes.

review_text:
A unique witness to the ancient history and heritage of Bangladesh is Mahasthan Garh, which is located on the banks of the Karatoya River in Shibganj Upazila of Bogra district. It is the ruins of the oldest city in Bengal, which is also identified by many as ancient Pundranagar. The history of Mahasthan Garh extends to the third century BC, which proves that it was a very prosperous and developed town.

Upon entering Mahasthan Garh, the ancient architecture, archaeological remains and the dilapidated fort wall take the visitors back to the glorious history of the past. The inscriptions, terracotta plaques, coins, and idols of gods and goddesses found here prove that it was a religious, political and cultural center. The importance of Mahasthan Garh never diminished during the Buddhist, Hindu and Muslim reigns.

There is an archaeological museum for visitors, where ancient relics are preserved. In addition, various historical landmarks can be seen at places such as Govinda Bhita, Khodar Pathar Bhita, Basu Vihar, Munir Ghat, etc. Every brick, every broken wall speaks a silent commentary of history.

It is a wonderful destination for tourists. Coming here creates a unique opportunity to immerse oneself in the history of ancient Bengal. It is educational for students and a huge repository of research for researchers.

Overall, Mahasthan Garh is a symbol of the historical glory of Bangladesh. Initiatives to preserve such historical places and present them to tourists should be increased further, so that our future generations can get acquainted with this glorious chapter of history.

মহাস্থান গড়ে প্রবেশ করলে প্রাচীন স্থাপত্য, প্রত্নতাত্ত্বিক নিদর্শন এবং ভগ্নপ্রায় দুর্গ প্রাচীর দর্শকদের অতীতের গৌরবময় ইতিহাসে ফিরিয়ে নিয়ে যায়। এখানে প্রাপ্ত শিলালিপি, পোড়ামাটির ফলক, মুদ্রা, দেবদেবীর মূর্তি প্রমাণ করে এটি একটি ধর্মীয়, রাজনৈতিক ও সাংস্কৃতিক কেন্দ্র ছিল। বৌদ্ধ, হিন্দু ও মুসলিম শাসনামলে মহাস্থান গড়ের গুরুত্ব কখনোই হ্রাস পায়নি।

দর্শনার্থীদের জন্য এখানে রয়েছে একটি প্রত্নতাত্ত্বিক জাদুঘর, যেখানে প্রাচীন নিদর্শনসমূহ সংরক্ষিত আছে। পাশাপাশি গোবিন্দ ভিটা, খোদার পাথর ভিটা, বাসু বিহার, মুনির ঘাট ইত্যাদি স্থানে ঘুরে দেখা যায় নানা ঐতিহাসিক চিহ্ন। প্রতিটি ইট, প্রতিটি ভাঙা প্রাচীর যেন ইতিহাসের এক নীরব ভাষ্য বলে।

Mahasthan is located in Shibganj Upazila of Bogra district. Everyone knows this place as Mahasthangarh. Another name for it is Pundranagar. This town was the capital of ancient Bengal. Various folk tales, stories, and legends are heard around this place, among which are Behula Lakhindar, Jiyat Kund, Shila Devi Ghat, etc. It is known from history that a Muslim preacher named Shah Sultan Balkhi captured this town by defeating Chand Saudagar. Currently, Mahasthan has been transformed into a tourist attraction. There are ruins of the ancient palace, ruins of Behula Lakhindar's residence, Mahasthan Tourism Park, Mahasthan Archaeological Museum, Govinda Bhita, Jiyat Kund, etc. The popular food here is Katakti, Mahasthan's Katakti is popular all over the country.
Every day, countless people come here to visit the shrine. Many people come on educational tours. Also, a large crowd gathers on Fridays to offer prayers at the Mahasthan Mosque.

review_text: Tajhat Palace in Rangpur is a magnificent early 20th-century landmark built by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, who inherited the estate of Manna Lal Roy, a wealthy jeweller known for trading jewel-encrusted crowns from which the name Tajhat was derived. Inside, while the museum collection is relatively small and mostly features ancient manuscripts, stone inscriptions, and historical artifacts, the interior architecture remains exceptionally well-planned, elegant, and tastefully decorated with a striking grand marble staircase. The overall environment is quiet, spacious, and highly recommended for history lovers, families, and photographers, though visitors should strictly note that the toilet facilities on the premises are in very poor condition and need major improvement.

review_text:
Tajhat Zamindar Palace is located about 6 kilometers from Rangpur city, in the village of Tajhat in Mahiganj. In the late eighteenth century, a jeweler named Mannalal settled there and started the Tajhat zamindari. After his death, his adopted son Gopal Lal Roy Bahadur became the zamindar. In the early twentieth century, around 2,000 workers helped build the palace, and it was completed in 1917. At that time, the construction cost was about one and a half crore taka, which was a huge amount.
The palace is made of red brick, white stone, and limestone. It has four floors and looks similar to Ahsan Manzil in Dhaka, with a design influenced by Mughal architecture. On the third and fourth floors, you can find the personal items of Zamindar Gopal, along with bedrooms, bathrooms, and guest rooms. One of the main attractions is the large staircase made of Italian marble with 31 steps.
Around the palace, there are two ponds on each side, a big open field in front, and many trees such as mahogany, kamini, mango, and jackfruit, along with flower gardens. There was also a secret staircase at the back of the palace, but it is now closed.

How to go:
If you take a bus from Dhaka to Kurigram, you can get off in front of the Rangpur Museum(tajhate jamider bari) Besides this, from Rangpur Shapla Chattar you can reach the museum gate by rickshaw for around 20 taka.

In the early twentieth century, around 2,000 workers helped build the palace, and it was completed in 1917. At that time, the construction cost was about one and a half crore taka, which was a huge amount.
The palace is made of red brick, white stone, and limestone. It has four floors and looks similar to Ahsan Manzil in Dhaka, with a design influenced by Mughal architecture. On the third and fourth floors, you can find the personal items of Zamindar Gopal, along with bedrooms, bathrooms, and guest rooms. One of the main attractions is the large staircase made of Italian marble with 31 steps.
Around the palace, there are two ponds on each side, a big open field in front, and many trees such as mahogany, kamini, mango, and jackfruit, along with flower gardens. There was also a secret staircase at the back of the palace, but it is now closed.

If you take a bus from Dhaka to Kurigram, you can get off in front of the Rangpur Museum(tajhate jamider bari) Besides this, from Rangpur Shapla Chattar you can reach the museum gate by rickshaw for around 20 taka.

review_text: Tajhat Palace, located about 3 km southeast of Rangpur city center, is one of the most significant archaeological and historical landmarks in northern Bangladesh. The palace was built in the early 20th century (completed around 1917) by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, a wealthy jewelery tradesman of Punjabi descent. The name "Tajhat" refers to the local "hat" (market) where jewel-encrusted "Taj" (crowns) were sold by his ancestors. Reflecting Indo-Saracenic architecture, the palace structure blends Mughal and European styles. Its most striking feature is a grand central staircase made of imported white marble and a large central ribbed dome. After the abolition of the zamindari system, it served various administrative roles. It was used as a branch of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (Rangpur High Court) from 1984 to 1991. Afterwards, the palace and its premise has been enlisted by the Archeological Department as a historical site. There is a museum in the 1st floor enriched with various collections that include 10th–11th century terracotta artifacts, ancient Sanskrit and Arabic manuscripts (including copies of the Mahabharata and a Quran attributed to Emperor Aurangzeb), black stone carvings of Hindu deities as well as few handwritten manuscripts and letters by ancient Sultans and even by the great pioneer of women empowerment in Bengal Begum Rokeya Shakhawat Hossain. This palace has some marks of structural damage here and there which requires serious and immediate plans and actions by the concerned authority.

Constructed in the early 1900s by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, a wealthy Hindu zamindar of Tajhat, the palace reflects a blend of Indo-Saracenic and European architectural styles. The environment surrounding Tajhat Rajbari further elevates its charm. This tranquil environment not only complements the historical significance of the place but also provides a refreshing escape from the urban chaos of Rangpur city. Tajhat Palace,তাজহাট রাজবাড়ী,Tajhat Rajbari is a historic palace in Rangpur, Bangladesh.This palace now holds the Rangpur museum.Tajhat Palace is situated six km , south-east of the city of Rangpur, on the outskirts of town.

The palace, with about 76 metres frontage, rises two storeys and is faced east. An imposing broad staircase in the centre, paved with imported white marble, leads directly above the portico to the upper storey.

The palace is crowned by a ribbed conical days dome in the centre of the roof with a tall octagonal neck, partly supported on a series of slender semi-Corinthian columns. The balustrade on either side of the imposing staircase was originally embellished with various sculptures of classical Roman figures in Italian marble, but now these are missing. There are two semi-octagonal projections at each end of the front face and a central projecting porch. The balcony roof above the porch is carried on four graceful Corinthian columns with round shafts, while two similar columns on each of the projecting ends of the building support a triangular gable.

The palace is laid out in the form on a "U", with its open end to the west. Beyond the entrance at ground-floor level there is a very large hall, measuring more than 18 x 13 meters. A 3-meter wide corridor runs the entire length of the inner block. Two broad wooden staircases provide access to the upper floor. There are about 22 apartments on two floors.

The palace was built by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy in the beginning of the 20th century.It is believed that from the conspicuous appearance of his Taj or jeweled crown, his estate derived the name of Tajhat.

From 1984 to 1991 the palace was used as a Rangpur High Court Branch of the Supreme Court Of Bangladesh. In 1995 the palace was declared as a protected monument by the Department of Archaeology. Recognizing its outstanding architectural value the Government Of Bangladesh  shifted the Rangpur Museum to the second floor of the palace in 2005. The main room at the top of the marble stairs have a number of display cases which show 10th–11th century terracotta artifacts. There are a number of fine examples of Sanskrit and Arabic manuscripts, including copies of the Mahabharat, Ramayan, and a Quran whose provenance is attributed to none other than the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb. The back rooms have several examples of black stone Hindu carvings in its back rooms, mainly of the deity Vishnu. Photography is not permitted in the museum itself.

Tajhat Palace, an architectural gem located in Rangpur, Bangladesh, is a stunning example of the grandeur and opulence of the early 20th century. Built around 1908 by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, a wealthy Hindu zamindar (landlord) of the region, Tajhat Palace reflects the blend of Mughal and European architectural styles, making it one of the most significant historical landmarks in northern Bangladesh.

The palace is an impressive two-story structure with a grand central staircase made of white marble, leading up to the main entrance. The façade is adorned with intricate stucco work, featuring floral motifs and geometric patterns that add to the building’s majestic appearance. The central dome, flanked by four smaller domes at the corners, adds to the regal feel of the structure. The sprawling gardens that surround the palace further enhance its beauty, offering a tranquil setting for visitors to explore.

Inside, the palace originally housed the luxurious living quarters of the Maharaja and his family. The rooms are spacious and feature high ceilings, with large windows that allow ample natural light to filter through. The interior is decorated with ornate chandeliers, mirrors, and other elements that reflect the grandeur of the time.

Today, Tajhat Palace serves as a museum, showcasing a collection of artifacts from the region’s rich cultural history, including ancient manuscripts, coins, sculptures, and paintings. These exhibits provide a glimpse into the historical significance of the area and the lifestyle of the aristocracy during the British colonial period.

Tajhat Palace stands not only as a testament to the architectural brilliance of its time but also as a reminder of the cultural and historical heritage of Rangpur. Its beauty, combined with its historical significance, makes it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in the history and culture of Bangladesh.

Tajhat Zamindar Bari, located in Rangpur, Bangladesh, is one of the finest examples of zamindar-era architecture in the country. Built in the early 20th century by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, the palace reflects a blend of Mughal and European design. The massive two-storey structure is made of white marble and red bricks, giving it a majestic appearance. The grand staircase, beautifully carved pillars, and spacious halls showcase the artistic excellence of that time.

The palace has a symmetrical façade with a central dome, arched windows, and decorative motifs that immediately capture attention. It once served as the residence of the zamindar, reflecting his wealth and influence in the region. Later, in 1984, it was converted into a museum. Today, the Tajhat Palace Museum preserves important archaeological artifacts, manuscripts, and historical objects that narrate the cultural heritage of Bengal.

Surrounded by open fields and gardens, the palace offers a serene and historical atmosphere. Visitors can experience both history and beauty while walking through its corridors. Despite facing some damages in the past, the government’s restoration has kept it alive as a landmark of pride for Rangpur. Overall, Tajhat Zamindar Bari is a must-visit heritage site for history lovers and tourists alike.

Mahasthangarh Museum, Bogura

Mahasthangarh Museum is a wonderful place to explore the rich history and heritage of the Barendra region of Bangladesh. Located near the ancient archaeological site of Mahasthangarh, the museum offers a fascinating glimpse into thousands of years of civilization, culture, and historical development of this region.

The museum houses a valuable collection of ancient artifacts, including sculptures, terracotta plaques, coins, pottery, and other archaeological remains that reflect the glorious past of one of the oldest urban settlements in Bangladesh. Visiting this museum provides a deeper understanding of the lifestyle, art, religion, and traditions of the people who lived in this region centuries ago.

The overall experience is impressive, especially for history enthusiasts, students, and visitors interested in archaeology. The location, combined with the nearby ruins of Mahasthangarh, makes it a meaningful destination for anyone wanting to explore Bangladesh’s ancient heritage.

However, there is still room for improvement. The descriptions and historical explanations of the displayed artifacts could be expanded to provide visitors with more detailed context. A more engaging narration system or better-written information panels would make the experience even more informative. Additionally, the indoor lighting arrangement could be improved to highlight the beauty and importance of the exhibits more effectively.

Overall, Mahasthangarh Museum is a remarkable historical destination that preserves the memory of Bengal’s ancient civilization. With some improvements in presentation and visitor facilities, it has the potential to become an even more attractive heritage site.

review_text:
Mahasthangarh, located near Mahasthan village in Shibganj Upazila of Bogura District, is the earliest and one of the largest urban archaeological sites yet discovered in Bangladesh. Excavation finds — including a Prakrit inscription in Brahmi script — date human activity at the citadel to at least the 3rd century BCE, and the site served as the major city of Pundranagara (Paundravardhanapura) through several historic periods including Mauryan, Gupta and Pala rule. The citadel’s ramparts, gateways, towers and the wide ring of suburbs demonstrate a long-lived, well-planned urban centre with religious, administrative and commercial roles.

Archaeological work at Mahasthangarh began in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and continued more systematically from the 1920s onward; excavations revealed temples, residential mounds, pottery, coins and other artefacts that illuminate the city’s material culture and regional importance. A small site museum near Govinda Bhita displays many representative finds for visitors.

Today Mahasthangarh is both a cultural landmark and a site facing conservation challenges. It is promoted as a tourist destination and features in heritage initiatives (including a UNESCO tentative listing for the Mahasthan–Karatoya cultural landscape), but the site has suffered from erosion, occasional looting and unregulated building pressures in the past. Recent scholarly and conservation discussions emphasize adaptive reuse, improved site management and community engagement as priorities to preserve the ruins while supporting sustainable tourism. Continued investment in conservation, regular archaeological study, and responsible visitor facilities will be essential to protect Mahasthangarh’s long history for future generations.

Artifacts unearthed at the site—such as Ashokan Brahmi inscriptions, silver punch-marked coins, and intricate terracotta plaques—testify to its once-glorious status. review_text:
Mahasthangarh museum (“Mahastangor jadughar”) is located at the Mahasthangarh of Shibganj of Bogra. It’s just 15 kilometer apart from the main town. You can reach there using any publicly available vehicles. The museum is profound with numerous objects (status, coins, weapon, etc.) those are found after the excavation from the archaeological spots around the Mahasthangarh.
Dating back to at least the 4th century BCE, Mahasthangarh is the earliest urban archaeological site that has been discovered in Bangladesh.

Several historical sites are located within the rampart wall, including a mausoleum (Mausoleum of Shah Sultan Mahisawar Balkhi), a temple site (Bairgir Bhita), remnants of an ancient palace (Parshuram’s Palace) with an ancient well (Jiyat Kunda) as well as residential blocks in the eastern rampart area.
One of the highlights of Mahasthangarh is Govinda Bhita, where remnants of two Buddhist temples can be visited. The main temple was erected in the 6th century and next to it is a slightly smaller temple, which was built in the 11th century.
Opposite Govinda Bhita, near the north side of the citadel is the Mahasthan Archaeological Museum. The museum is quite small but has a well-maintained collection of pieces recovered from the archaeological site. These include the statues of Hindu and Buddhist gods and goddesses, terracotta plaques depicting daily life, as well as some well-preserved bronze images found in nearby monastery ruins that date back to the pre-Pala period. There are even some fragments of ring-stones which were used for rituals in the Mauryan period.

Mahasthan means a place that has excellent sanctity and garh means fort. Mahasthan was first mentioned in a Sanskrit text of the 13th century entitled Vallalcharita. It is also mentioned in an anonymous text Karatoya mahatmya, circumstantially placed in 12th–13th century. The same text also mentions two more names to mean the same place – Pundrakshetra, land of the Pundras, and Pundranagara, city of the Pundras. In 1685, an administrative decree mentioned the place as Mastangarh, a mixture of Sanskrit and Persian meaning fortified place of an auspicious personage. Subsequent discoveries have confirmed that the earlier name was Pundranagara or Paundravardhanapura, and that the present name of Mahasthangarh is of later origin.
Several personalities contributed to the discovery and identification of the ruins at Mahasthangarh. Francis Buchanan Hamilton was the first to locate and visit Mahasthangarh in 1808, C.J.O'Donnell, E.V.Westmacott, and Beveridge followed. Alexander Cunningham was the first to identify the place as the capital of Pundravardhana. He visited the site in 1879.

review_text:
Mahasthangarh – A Window to the Past
the entrance to the oldest archaeological site of the 3rd century B.C.

The ancient archeological site of Mahasthangarh is believed to date back as far as 700 BC and appears to have been occupied right up to the 1700s. Mahasthangarh is located in the Shibganj Upzila (subdistrict) of the Bogra District of Bangladesh, near the village of Mahasthan. It is the oldest urban-style fortified settlement discovered in Bangladesh to date, and includes a temple with the tomb of Shah Sultan Balkhi Mahisawar, a dervish (Muslim saint) of royal lineage who traveled to the area in the 14th century with the aim of converting the locals to the Islamic religion.

The name of the site is taken from the words Mahasthan meaning a place of exceptional sacredness, and garh, meaning fort. Later discoveries have led researchers to the conclusion that the name of the area was initially Paundravardhanapura or Pundranagara, referring to the Pundra Kingdom in Indian epic literature, which was said to rule over an area stretching from West Bengal, to Bangladesh and into the area of India now known as Bihar.

The archeological site of Mahasthangarh is located on one of the highest pieces of land in Bangladesh, along the Bogra-Rangpur highway, allowing easy access for visitors. The site was discovered in the early 1800s and a number of world-renowned archeologists were instrumental in uncovering its cultural and historical significance. Visitors to the site will note that the Karatoya River flows to the east of the rectangular citadel. Although this river is currently not much more than a stream, it was once a mighty river, considered to be sacred. It has been suggested that the proximity of the Karatoya River may have been one of the deciding factors when the founders of the settlement chose the site.

Within the fortifications of the city are a number of interesting features, including a well said to possess life and impart power known as Jiat Kunda; a palace called Parasuramer Basgriha dedicated to a king by the name of Parasuram; a place of stone said to be bestowed by God known as Khodar Pathar Bhita; and a bastion named Munir Ghon. There are gateways on all four sides and a flight of steps in the north-eastern corner.

Outside the fortifications are up to a hundred mounds spread over a radius of around nine kilometers, many of which still need to be excavated. On the banks of the Karatoya River is a temple dedicated to Govinda, as well as a museum displaying some of the fascinating artifacts discovered in and around the settlement. These include a limestone slab inscribed with words in Brahmi script dating back to the 3rd century BC; silver punch market coins from between the 4th century BC and the 1st to 2nd century AD; coins of the British East India Company which was founded in 1600; shards of ceramics; a 5th century stone sculpture of Buddha; and terracotta plaques. Mahasthangarh is a fascinating place to visit from a historical and cultural perspective, and from its elevated position it offers spectacular views of the surrounding areas.

Who would have thought that just outside Dhaka, in Rangpur, there would be such a mesmerizing resort? I was truly amazed to discover this hidden gem right here in Bangladesh! The moment I arrived, I couldn’t believe my eyes—this place is stunning!

Spanning over 100 acres, the resort is expansive and beautifully maintained. It's so vast that exploring the entire area in just two or three days would be quite a challenge. The cleanliness and organization of the resort are commendable, creating a pleasant atmosphere for relaxation and fun.

The staff are incredibly friendly, making you feel as though you’re at home. Their hospitality truly enhances the experience, contributing to the welcoming environment. The resort feels like a completely different world, providing a perfect escape from the hustle and bustle of everyday life. After a month of heavy workloads, this place was just what I needed to recharge my nerves.

The accommodations are excellent as well. The rooms are comfortable and well-appointed, offering a cozy retreat after a day of exploration. One standout feature is the pricing—it's very budget-friendly! My friends and I, all university students, found it easy to manage our trip costs without breaking the bank.

The resort also boasts a fantastic game zone with billiards, where time passes in a flash! It’s a great way to unwind and have some fun with friends. Additionally, there are two large pools—one of which is exceptionally clean, equipped with an integrated water filtration system that operates continuously. This pool is also very child-friendly, making it perfect for families.

Overall, this resort and amusement park is a fantastic destination for anyone looking to unwind and enjoy a little adventure. I highly recommend it for anyone seeking a perfect getaway!

Vinno Jogot (literally meaning "A Different World") is the largest and most popular amusement park and tourism center in Northern Bangladesh. Located in Ganjipur, under the Gangachara Upazila of Rangpur, this privately developed park spans approximately 100 acres of lush greenery and scenic landscapes. Established in 2001, it has become a cornerstone of local tourism, blending natural beauty with modern entertainment facilities.
Key Attractions and Features
The park is designed to transport visitors into a "different world" through a variety of unique installations:
Bangladesh’s First Planetarium: One of its standout features, allowing visitors to explore the cosmos and learn about the universe's origins, including the "Big Bang".
Seven Wonders of the World: The park features detailed replicas of global landmarks such as the Taj Mahal, the Egyptian Pyramids, the Great Wall of China, and the Eiffel Tower.
Thrilling Rides & Fun: Visitors can enjoy a wide array of activities including a 3D movie theater, a space journey simulator, robot zones, boat trips on the lake, and classic amusement rides like the spinning head and merry-go-round.
Natural Beauty: The park is home to thousands of native and exotic trees, creating a haven for various bird species and a serene environment for nature walks.
Facilities and Accommodations
Vinno Jogot is not just a day-trip destination; it is equipped to handle large groups and overnight stays:
Luxury Resorts: The park features the three-star Dream Palace and Royal Palace rest houses, offering various room types from VIP suites to rustic wooden houses.
Picnic and Events: It is the region's largest picnic spot, capable of hosting up to 500 individual groups simultaneously. It also includes modern conference halls, such as the 1,000-capacity Ashirbad hall.
Recreation: Amenities include a large swimming pool (with a separate kids' zone), a shopping mall, and a folk art museum.
Visiting Information
Located about 11 to 15 kilometers from Rangpur city along the Rangpur-Dinajpur Highway, the park is easily accessible via taxi or local transport.
Entry Fee: Approximately 100 BDT per person.
Timing: Open daily from 8:00 AM to 7:00 PM.
For more details on booking and facilities, you can visit the Official Vinno Jogot Website.

Vinnya Jagat is a wonderful amusement spot located in a serene environment, offering a perfect escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life. It is an ideal place to relax your mind and have fun with your family members. The area is beautifully designed with various sculptures of animals, fruits, and other creative installations, which make it a unique and visually appealing destination.

One of the highlights of Vinnya Jagat is the small artificial waterfall, which adds to the charm of the place. The base of the waterfall is home to a variety of colorful fish that attract the attention of visitors, especially children. Watching the fish swim in harmony is a peaceful experience that brings joy to everyone. The management has also provided a seating area near the waterfall where visitors can sit and enjoy the soothing sound of flowing water.

In addition to the scenic beauty, the place offers several food stalls that serve snacks and beverages to refresh you during your visit. The ticket price for entry is affordable, costing only 100 BDT per person, making it accessible for everyone. I had the pleasure of visiting this spot in November 2024 and was truly impressed by its charm and ambiance.

For families looking for a budget-friendly yet delightful outing, Vinnya Jagat is undoubtedly a must-visit destination.

It is the largest picnic spot and tourism center in this area. It is located in Gonjipur under Kholeya union of Gangachara Upazila . After entering the park and cross the iron bridge the world becomes different from it.
Cottage for birds, wildlife sanctuaries, shopping mall, 500-seat modern conference center, community center, skill test robot zone and swimming pool will be seen in a privately developed world in combination with the tradition of rural Bengal and modern technology.
There are also parks for children, round trip, helicopter fly zone, Nagarodola, Kangaroo moving, Spider Zone, Bumper car, Racing Horse, C-Paradise, Maki Train, Ajab Guha (strange cave), 3D Movie, Ice world, Space Journey, Shapla Chattar, different sculptures and boat journey on a big lake.
At the same time, there are at least five hundred separate picnic arrangements for the various groups. Eight to nine hundred car parking facilities available on the inside. There are seven cottages. One three star Dream Palace.
Various cultural events are organized here, during different festivals. Considering the advantages of tourists, there is an information center in a different world, which helps visitors find various types of information and find lost things.
How to go from Dhaka: Dipjol, Hanif, and Agomony are the best transport routes from Dhaka to Rangpur. Apart from this, the other buses are S.R. Paribahan, Shyamoli, ENA, etc. on this route. The buses from Kalyanpur and Gabtoli are available at different times from morning till night. In addition to the road, it is possible to go to Rangpur via rail.
There are good transport and communication system to go to Rangpur from other cities. From Rangpur Medical College, buses or autos are available to go there. After reaching Paglapir stand, you can hire an easy bike or a Rickshaw.
It will take 15-20 minutes from Paglapir stand to the main gate. There are also parking. Car parking can be made for different types of vehicles by paying different prices.
The park is open from 8 am to 7:30 pm. The entry fee in the park is 50Taka. Tickets for each ride are available at 30-50 Taka.
Where to stay: If you want to remain in the park, you can get to the resort. Rangpur city is also good for the stay. There are many good quality hotels here. The best hotels include
Hotel North View , NGO forum Rangpur, RDRS (Jail Road). Hotel Shah Amanat, Golden Tower Hotel Park, Hotel Tilottama (Thana Road), Hotel Bijay (Jail Road).

Architectural Review: The Sixty Dome Mosque (Shat Gombuj Masjid)
Located in the historic "Mosque City" of Bagerhat, Bangladesh, the Sixty Dome Mosque stands as the most formidable and aesthetically significant monument of the Bengal Sultanate. Commissioned by the Sufi saint-general Ulugh Khan Jahan in the mid-15th century (c. 1442–1459), this UNESCO World Heritage site is a masterclass in the Khan-e-Jahan style—a localized fusion of imperial Tughlaq austerity and indigenous Bengali craftsmanship.
1. Structural Composition and the "Sixty" Paradox
The mosque’s name is an etymological curiosity. While "Shat Gombuj" translates to "Sixty Domes," the structure actually features 77 domes over the main hall and 4 additional domes atop the corner towers, totaling 81.
* The Pillars: The name likely refers to the 60 slender stone pillars that divide the interior into seven longitudinal aisles and eleven deep bays.
* The Domes: The roof comprises 70 circular, low-slung domes and 7 unique Chauchala (four-segmented) domes in the central row. These Chauchala domes are particularly notable as they mimic the curved roofs of traditional Bengali bamboo huts, marking one of the earliest integrations of folk architecture into grand Islamic stone-and-brick masonry.
2. Architectural Features: The Khan-e-Jahan Style
Unlike the ornate, floral-heavy Mughal architecture that followed, the Sixty Dome Mosque is characterized by a "fortress-like" gravity.
* The Walls: Built from tapered red brick, the walls are exceptionally thick (1.8 meters or 6 feet), designed to provide natural insulation against the tropical heat and stability against the shifting deltaic soil.
* Corner Towers: Four massive circular towers anchor the corners. Reminiscent of Tughlaq bastions, they feature arched chambers at the top, which were likely used for the call to prayer (Adhan) rather than just aesthetic flair.
* The Facade: The eastern facade is pierced by 11 pointed arched doorways, while the north and south walls each have seven. This "forest of arches" creates a rhythmic play of light and shadow within the prayer hall, which can accommodate roughly 2,000 worshippers.
3. Decorative Nuance: Terracotta and Stone
While the exterior presents a stark, minimalist silhouette, the interior reveals the delicate artistry of the Sultanate period.
* The Mihrabs: There are ten arched mihrabs (prayer niches) on the western wall. The central mihrab is crafted from dark stone, while the others are made of brick and adorned with intricate terracotta floral scrolls, rosettes, and foliage.
* The Curvature: The cornice and battlements of the mosque are gently curved—a deliberate nod to the Bengali landscape, designed to shed the heavy monsoon rains efficiently.
4. Professional Assessment: Legacy and Preservation
The Sixty Dome Mosque is not merely a relic; it is an engineering triumph of the 15th century. It successfully adapted the rigid architectural language of the Delhi Sultanate to the humid, riverine climate of Southern Bengal.
Conservation Challenges:
* Salinity: Being near the Sundarbans, the greatest threat to the mosque is salt efflorescence from the soil, which degrades the ancient brickwork.
* Restoration: Ongoing efforts by the Department of Archaeology and UNESCO have focused on damp-proofing the foundations and carefully replacing damaged terracotta plaques with authentic reproductions.
Final Verdict
The Sixty Dome Mosque is a rare architectural bridge between the imperial and the local. It lacks the flamboyant marble of the Taj Mahal, but it possesses a "quiet power"—a massive, grounding presence that reflects the asceticism of its founder and the resilience of Bengali brick-making traditions. For any student of Islamic architecture or South Asian history, it remains an indispensable study in structural honesty.

A historic site, the central attraction of which is the Shatgumbuj Mosque and a huge water-body located behind it. The premises are pretty well-maintained. With a mosque of such a historic significance, it would have helped if there was a guide within, to relate the history of the mosque and its architectural significance to the multitude of visitors within.

Researching various sources, and talking to the "Imam" (the person who leads the prayers), I know that "Shatgumbuj" is a misnomer. That word, translated, means "sixty domes" (In Bengali, shat = sixty,  and gumbuj = dome). In fact, the mosque actually has 81 domes, and which literally covers the entire roof of the mosque. There are 7 domes, in 11 rows, totalling 77 domes. And with the 4 domes at each corner, it adds up to 81 domes. And that is the reason why this mosque was originally named "Chaat-gumbuj Mosque" -- where "chaat" in Bengali means "roof", indicating that the entire roof is comprised of domes.

On a later visit to this mosque about 3 - 4 years later, I took it upon myself to count the domes. I counted 77 (besides the 4 at each corner).

However, I was disappointed that the accessibility to the restrooms was rather restricted, for reasons best known to the authorities. Also the access roads to this historic site ought to have been less congested.

The Sixty Dome Mosque is one of the most important historical landmarks in Bagerhat district of Khulna division, Bangladesh. The mosque was built in the 15th century by the famous Sufi saint and Muslim ruler Khan Jahan Ali. It is believed that the mosque was constructed around 1459 AD. The structure is mainly made of burnt clay bricks and is considered a remarkable example of medieval Bengali architecture. The mosque is approximately 160 feet long and 108 feet wide. Inside the mosque there are 60 stone pillars, which support the roof containing 77 small domes. Because of these domes, the mosque became widely known as the “Sixty Dome Mosque.”

On the eastern side of the mosque there is a large pond known as Ghora Dighi, which covers an area of about 16 acres. According to historians, the total land area where the mosque complex was established was around 40–50 acres. At the four corners of the mosque there are four large towers (minarets) that resemble fortresses and add strength to the structure. Due to its historical, architectural, and cultural significance, the historic mosque and the entire historic city of Bagerhat were recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. Today, it is one of the most popular historical and tourist attractions in Bangladesh.

🕌 Sixty Dome Mosque (Shat Gombuj Masjid)

The Sixty Dome Mosque is one of the most magnificent and historic mosques in Bangladesh, located in Bagerhat district, built by the great Sufi saint and ruler Khan Jahan Ali (R.A.) during the 15th century. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a remarkable example of early Islamic architecture in Bengal.

---

🌍 Basic Information

Name: Sixty Dome Mosque

Bengali Name: ষাট গম্বুজ মসজিদ (Shat Gombuj Masjid)

Location: Khan Jahan Nagar, Bagerhat, Khulna Division, Bangladesh

Builder: Ulugh Khan Jahan Ali (R.A.)

Built in: Mid-15th Century (around 1442–1572 AD)

Architectural Style: Tughlaq-influenced Islamic architecture

---

🧱 Architectural Features

1. Number of Domes:
Despite its name “Sixty Dome,” the mosque actually has 81 domes —

77 small domes on the roof

4 large domes at the corners
The name “Sixty” (Shat) was used in a symbolic sense to mean “many” in Bengali.

2. Pillars (Columns):
There are 60 stone pillars supporting the roof — which is why it’s called “Sixty Dome Mosque.”

3. Doors and Windows:

11 doors on the front side

7 doors on each side

3 doors on the back
These were designed for maximum light and ventilation.

4. Design:
The walls are thick and made of burnt brick.
The domes are low and semi-circular.
The inside of the mosque produces beautiful echoes due to its perfect acoustics.

---

📜 Historical Background

Khan Jahan Ali (R.A.) was a Muslim saint, ruler, and social reformer who developed the Bagerhat region.

He established roads, mosques, ponds (dighis), and settlements for the local people.

The mosque served both as a place of worship and as a center for administration and education.

---

🏛️ UNESCO World Heritage Site

In 1985, UNESCO declared the mosque as part of the “Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat”, a World Heritage Site.

It is one of the most well-preserved medieval monuments in South Asia.

---

🕋 Religious and Cultural Significance

The mosque is still used for daily prayers.

Thousands of local and foreign visitors visit the site every year.

The shrine (mausoleum) of Khan Jahan Ali (R.A.) is located nearby.

---

📏 Dimensions

Length: About 160 feet

Width: About 104 feet

Wall Thickness: About 8.5 feet

---

🏗️ Current Condition

The mosque has been carefully preserved and renovated under the supervision of the Bangladesh Department of Archaeology and UNESCO.
The entire area is now a protected archaeological zone known as “Khan Jahan Nagar.”

The Sixty Dome Mosque is located about one and a half kilometers from the shrine of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali (R.) in Bagerhat district. Its architecture is adorned with vine and leaf decorations on red burnt clay. The mosque’s artistic beauty has given it a special place.

The magnificent mosque, adorned with exquisite craftsmanship by Hazrat Khan Jahan (R.A.), is located about one and a half kilometers west of his shrine. This mosque, over five centuries old, holds a special place in medieval architecture due to its construction techniques and the ornamentation of vine-like designs on red burnt clay. Although it is popularly known as the Sixty Dome Mosque (Shat Gombuj Masjid), it actually has 74 domes, including four domes over the four corners of the structure. Along with seven pitched Bengali-style domes in the central row, the total number of domes stands at 81.

It is especially noteworthy that the prayer hall's pitched roof and domes are supported by sixty stone and brick pillars through an intricate system of arches.

According to local legend, Hazrat Khan Jahan (R.A.) used his miraculous powers to transport all the stones for the construction of the mosque by waterway from faraway Chattogram and possibly even from Rajmahal in Odisha, India. The architectural design of this building reflects a strong influence of Tughlaq architecture. The mosque is surrounded by 8-foot-wide walls, with four minarets at each corner. The southern minaret has a chamber at the top known as the "Roshnai Kutir" (illuminated chamber), and it contains a staircase leading upward.

The mosque is built with small bricks. It is 160 feet long, 108 feet wide, and 22 feet high. In the center of the front facade, there is one large arch, flanked on either side by five smaller arches. On the western side, near the main mihrab, there is a total of 26 doors including one beside the main mihrab.

The Department of Archaeology and Museums has taken responsibility for preserving this historic mosque and the shrine of Khan Jahan (R.A.) as a protected heritage site. UNESCO has included the mosque in its list of World Heritage Sites.

At that time, Khan Jahan Ali excavated 360 ponds along with building 360 mosques in this area. It is believed that among all these ponds, Ghora Dighi was the first one excavated by Khan Jahan Ali, making it the earliest pond in this region. Located in the village of Sundarghona in the Sixty Dome Mosque Union of Bagerhat district headquarters, Ghora Dighi lies near the administrative center or Haweli established by Khan Jahan Ali, just to the west of the Sixty Dome Mosque.

This freshwater pond was listed as a protected archaeological site (protected waterbody) in 1986. In Bagerhat, Khan Jahan Ali's Ghora Dighi is the only protected waterbody in Bangladesh.

You are cordially invited to witness these beautiful landmarks of my Golden Bengal.
