The World Cultural Heritage:

"Historic Shait Gumbad Mosque"

A Great saint-warrior, Khan-l-Jahan, established a town in the 15th century AD. at the western peripheral land of present-day Bagerhat town. Based on numismatic evidence some scholars are of the opinion that the town was called Khalifatabad during the 16th century AD. At the time of its prosperity, the town was studded with many buildings, mosques, reservoirs, tombs, roads etc. Many have gone but of the surviving monuments, the Shait-Gumbad Mosque, Singair Mosque, Bibibegni Mosque, Chunakhola Mosque, Ranovijoypur Mosque, Khanjahan's Mausoleum and single-domed mosque adjacent to the Mausoleum, Tomb and Mosque of Zindapir & Rezakhoda Mosque are particularly notable. They spread over at least a 2.5KM. area from north to south and 6 KM. from east to west. Bagerhat was inscribed on the UNESCO world Heritage list in 1985 in recognition of its outstanding universal value for all mankind.

Source: World Heritage ID 321 Info board

Shopnopuri Artificial Amusement Park is a premier 400-acre entertainment and picnic destination located in Aftabgonj, Nawabganj Upazila, about 52 kilometers from Dinajpur city. Known as one of the largest and most popular artificial parks in Bangladesh, it features a blend of natural beauty, artistic sculptures, and diverse recreational activities.
Key Features of Shopnopuri (Dinajpur):
Major Attractions: Includes artificial lakes, hills, and a variety of gardens such as "Salbagan" and flower gardens. It also features unique zones like "Fish World," the "Animal Kingdom" with dinosaur and pegasus sculptures, and the "Rongdhonu" Art Gallery.
Rides & Activities: Offers numerous rides including a roller coaster, bumper cars, a merry-go-round, and boat rides on the lake. There is a dedicated children's park, horse-drawn carriages, and a mini zoo.
Picnic & Event Facilities: A major hub for picnics with rental facilities for ovens, utensils, and furniture. The park also includes a prayer room and a large-scale map of Bangladesh built into the grounds.
Accommodation: For overnight stays, the park provides five distinct cottages: Sandhyatara, Nilpori, Nishipodmo, Rojonigondha, and VIP Kunjo.
Entry & Timing: The standard entry fee is ৳100 per person. The park typically operates from 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM or 7:00 PM daily.
The park is a popular filming location for Bangladeshi movies and is best visited during the cooler months from November to February to avoid summer heat.

Karamjal, located within the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world, is a significant tourist destination in Bangladesh. Positioned on the eastern side of the Sundarbans in the Bagerhat district, Karamjal serves as both an entry point to the Sundarbans and a prime spot for experiencing the rich biodiversity of this UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Karamjal is particularly known for its wildlife breeding center, where efforts are made to conserve and rehabilitate various species native to the Sundarbans. The center focuses on breeding estuarine crocodiles and deer, and visitors can observe these animals in their natural habitat. This conservation effort plays a crucial role in preserving the unique ecosystem of the Sundarbans, where the delicate balance of life is maintained by the mangrove forests.

The area around Karamjal is also a haven for birdwatchers, as the dense mangroves are home to a wide variety of bird species, including the famous Kingfishers and Brahminy Kites. The waterways of Karamjal are teeming with life, from fish and crabs to the elusive Bengal tiger, although sightings of the latter are rare.

Visitors to Karamjal can explore the region via guided boat tours, which provide an up-close view of the intricate network of rivers and canals that crisscross the Sundarbans. These tours offer a unique opportunity to experience the tranquil beauty of the mangroves, with their dense foliage, winding waterways, and the occasional glimpse of wildlife.

Karamjal is not just a place of natural beauty, but also a reminder of the importance of conservation efforts in maintaining the ecological balance of one of the most unique environments on Earth. It offers a serene and educational experience, drawing attention to the critical role of the Sundarbans in protecting Bangladesh's coastline and supporting its diverse wildlife.

The Sundarbans, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is a mesmerizing mangrove forest located in the delta region of the Padma, Meghna, and Brahmaputra river basins. As I explored this natural wonder, I was captivated by its rich biodiversity and unique ecosystem.

Navigating through the intricate network of waterways, I witnessed the enchanting beauty of the mangrove trees, their roots creating a labyrinthine pattern. The Sundarbans is renowned for its diverse wildlife, and I was fortunate to spot elusive Bengal tigers, playful dolphins, and various species of deer and birds. The air was filled with the symphony of chirping birds and rustling leaves, creating a serene ambiance.

The local communities living in the periphery of the Sundarbans added a cultural dimension to my experience. Their unique lifestyle, traditional fishing methods, and friendly demeanor provided insights into the symbiotic relationship between humans and nature.

While the Sundarbans showcased nature's grandeur, it also underscored the need for conservation. The delicate balance of this ecosystem faces threats from climate change, habitat loss, and human activities. My visit to the Sundarbans left me in awe of its natural beauty and inspired a deeper appreciation for the importance of preserving such precious ecosystems for future generations.

Karamjal is one of the most beautiful gateways to explore the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The place is full of natural beauty—dense mangrove trees, winding canals, and a calm atmosphere that makes you feel truly connected to nature. It’s also home to deer, monkeys, crocodiles, and even the majestic Royal Bengal Tiger (though spotting one is rare). Karamjal has a crocodile breeding center and a deer park, which makes it quite interesting for visitors to learn about the wildlife and conservation efforts here.

Historically, the Sundarbans have always been a land of mystery and legends, protecting Bengal from natural disasters and serving as the natural habitat of many endangered species. Karamjal serves as the perfect entry point to experience this heritage.

📍 How to get there from Dhaka:
You can first travel to Khulna by bus (8–9 hours),From Khulna, you need to reach Mongla Port (about 40 km away). From Mongla, boats are available that will take you directly to Karamjal within 20–30 minutes. The boat ride itself is scenic and feels like part of the adventure.

This center is dedicated to the conservation and breeding of endangered and rare species, such as crocodiles, spotted deer, monkeys, and pythons. Visitors can observe these animals up close and learn about the conservation efforts taking place in the Sundarbans.

It's important to note that visiting the Karamjol Trail and the Sundarbans requires proper planning and adherence to safety guidelines. It is recommended to engage the services of authorized tour operators or forest authorities to ensure a safe and informative experience.

Overall, the Karamjol Trail offers nature enthusiasts and wildlife lovers an opportunity to immerse themselves in the breathtaking beauty and unique ecosystem of the Sundarbans. It allows visitors to appreciate the rich biodiversity and cultural heritage of the region while promoting conservation awareness.

Ramsagar National Park: A Historic Man-Made Wonder
​Ramsagar Dighi is a magnificent historic lake in Dinajpur, the largest man-made excavation in Bangladesh. It was built between 1750 and 1755 AD by Raja Ramnath to help the people during a terrible drought and lack of rain. Legend says that even after digging the massive lake, no water came out. To save the people, Prince Ram sacrificed his life by entering the dry lake, and miraculously, it filled with water.
​The lake is huge, with a length of 3,399 feet and an area of nearly 78 acres. Around 1.5 million laborers worked on this project, costing 30,000 Taka at that time. The entire area is now a National Park with a lush green forest, beautiful walkways, and a mini zoo with deer. It is a very well-maintained and peaceful spot for family trips.
​The best part of our visit was watching the sunset over the lake. The water was covered in a golden-orange glow from the sun, creating a special and peaceful feeling. It was the perfect ending to our day, looking at the calm water and remembering the story of the Prince.
​If you visit Dinajpur, Ramsagar is a must-see. The combination of its royal history, the legend of Prince Ram, and the beautiful nature makes it a unique experience. We highly recommend staying until the afternoon to see the stunning sunset.

Ramsagar National Park is a charming and historically significant national park located in the Dinajpur district of Bangladesh. Officially declared a national park in 2001, it covers an area of approximately 27.76 hectares and is centered around the impressive Ramsagar Dighi, one of the largest man-made reservoirs in Bangladesh. The park uniquely combines natural beauty with historical and cultural importance, making it a popular destination for tourists, nature lovers, and local visitors.

The centerpiece of the park, Ramsagar Dighi, was excavated in the mid-18th century by Raja Ram Nath to provide water for the local community. Measuring about 1,079 meters in length and 192.6 meters in width, the reservoir remains a striking visual landmark. Its calm waters reflect the sky and surrounding greenery, creating a serene environment that is ideal for relaxation, photography, and peaceful walks. The historical significance of the lake adds an extra layer of interest for visitors who enjoy combining nature with cultural exploration.

The park’s environment is relatively flat, featuring planted trees, grassy areas, and open spaces, which support both flora and fauna. Ramsagar National Park is home to a variety of wetland-associated plant species and attracts numerous waterbirds and migratory birds, making it a rewarding spot for birdwatching. Visitors may also encounter small mammals, reptiles, and aquatic life within the lake, providing opportunities for wildlife observation in a natural yet accessible setting.

Visitor facilities in Ramsagar National Park are simple but functional. Walking paths, shaded areas, and picnic spots allow families and groups to enjoy a day in nature. While the park does not have extensive commercial facilities, its open spaces, scenic views, and tranquil atmosphere make it a perfect location for a peaceful escape from urban life. Seasonal variations, particularly in winter, enhance the experience as migratory birds visit the area, adding color and life to the surroundings.

Ramsagar National Park is not only a natural attraction but also an important community space. Local residents often visit the park for recreation, cultural gatherings, and educational purposes. Its accessibility from Dinajpur town makes it an ideal destination for day trips, school outings, or casual visits for anyone interested in enjoying the outdoors while learning about the region’s history.

Overall, Ramsagar National Park offers a unique combination of historical significance, natural beauty, and recreational value. Although small compared to larger national parks in Bangladesh, its calm lake, diverse birdlife, and open green spaces provide a rewarding experience for visitors of all ages. It stands as a testament to the region’s rich cultural heritage while promoting the importance of preserving natural habitats. For anyone visiting Dinajpur, Ramsagar National Park is a serene and memorable spot that highlights the beauty and history of northern Bangladesh.

Ramsagar National Park (রামসাগর জাতীয় উদ্যান) is a national park in Bangladesh located at. 25°33'00"N 88°37'30"E Tejpur, near Dinajpur District in the north-west of the country. The Park is 27.76 hectare, in size, and is built around a large water reservoir known as "Ramsagar tank". The lake is 1079m in length and 192.6m in width. The soil is red-yellow clay.

The tank was built in the 18th century by Raja Ram Nath. It is believed that the lake was excavated by King Ramnath, Maharaja of Dinajpur before the Battle of Plassey. The tank was dug by 15 million workers at a cost of 30,000 Taka.

There are no big trees; the park consists of a big lake surrounded by embankments. Most of the flora and fauna are associated with wetland ecosystem.

The park is managed by staff members which include forest officers, gardeners, forest guards and  watchman. It was first established in year 1960 and was earlier recommended that the park be developed as class-B national park for recreation and education by the Government of east Pakistan in 1971. It was declared as national park on 30-4-2001 under the Bangladesh wildlife (Preservation) Amendment Act of 1947.

Flora:

272 plant species belonging to 132 families were recorded in this sanctuary. Mangifera indica, Syzygium cumini, Tamarindus indica, and Semecarpus anacardium are some of the trees found in the sanctuary.

Fauna:

The lake is full of different types of fishes. There are turtles and fresh water crocodiles in the lake. The animals found here are spotted deer, wild boar, blue bull, sloth bear and Asian black bear. The water birds mainly white breasted water hen, jacanas, river tern, kingfishers, ringed plover, grey heron and purple heron are found here.

The plants inside the park are removed by the local villagers for food, fodder, making furniture, medicine and fuel. There is a decrease in the indigenous fish species due to overexploitation. The other factors affecting the biodiversity of the park are agricultural pollution, siltation, diseases and floods.

This place holds the historical and natural beauty of Bangladesh.

The Park is 27.76 hectare, in size, and is built around a large water reservoir known as "Ramsagar tank". The lake is 1079m in length and 192.6m in width. The soil is red-yellow clay.

The tank was built in the 18th century by Raja Ram Nath. It is believed that the lake was excavated by King Ramnath, Maharaja of Dinajpur before the Battle of Plassey. The tank was dug by 15 million workers at a cost of 30,000 Taka.

There are no big trees; the park consists of a big lake surrounded by embankments. Most of the flora and fauna are associated with wetland ecosystem.

The park is managed by staff members which include forest officers, gardeners, forest guards and  watchman. It was first established in year 1960 and was earlier recommended that the park be developed as class-B national park for recreation and education by the Government of east Pakistan in 1971. It was declared as national park on 30-4-2001 under the Bangladesh wildlife (Preservation) Amendment Act of 1947.

Flora:

272 plant species belonging to 132 families were recorded in this sanctuary. Mangifera indica, Syzygium cumini, Tamarindus indica, and Semecarpus anacardium are some of the trees found in the sanctuary.

Fauna:

The lake is full of different types of fishes. There are turtles and fresh water crocodiles in the lake. The animals found here are spotted deer, wild boar, blue bull, sloth bear and Asian black bear. The water birds mainly white breasted water hen, jacanas, river tern, kingfishers, ringed plover, grey heron and purple heron are found here.

The plants inside the park are removed by the local villagers for food, fodder, making furniture, medicine and fuel. There is a decrease in the indigenous fish species due to overexploitation. The other factors affecting the biodiversity of the park are agricultural pollution, siltation, diseases and floods.

This place holds the historical and natural beauty of Bangladesh.

Ramsagar is a largest man made lake of Bangladesh situated in the village Tejpur 8 kilometer south of the Dinajpur town. The lake wide is about 1079 m north-south and length 192.6 m in East-West. The Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation has improve some tourist facilities around the Ramsagar Lake, such as rest-rooms, picnic spots and kiosks to sell refreshments, as well as playgrounds for children to enjoy.

The management of this park is totally worst, the authorities do not care about the biodiversity of this park. There is no infrastructure development. 50 TK ticket price is which is too much.

You can explore the entire park on foot or rent a local van for 80-100 TK.

review_text:
Located in the Dinajpur District in the north-west of Bangladesh, the Ramsagar National Park spreads out over an area of about sixty square kilometers, with a vast man-made water reservoir as its focal point. The area around the Ramsagar Lake is a popular picnic spot for both locals and tourists, and the abundant flora and fauna in the area enhances the peaceful sensation of being close to nature.

The water reservoir was built between 1750 and 1755 to provide local inhabitants with safe drinking water. Its construction was initiated by Raja Ram Nath and some 1.5 million laborers worked on the project. The reservoir was named in his honor. The Parjatan Corporation, which manages many tourism projects in Bangladesh, has developed some visitor facilities around the lake, such as rest-rooms, picnic spots and kiosks to sell refreshments, as well as playgrounds for children to enjoy. Popular activities in the area include fishing, boating and hiking. There is not much in the line of indigenous forest in the Ramsagar National Park, but the Forest Department of Bangladesh have planted a variety of ornamental and fruit trees that have flourished and become lush forested areas.

The lake is populated by a variety of fish, as well as fresh water crocodiles, while animals that visitors are likely to see on land include Sambar Deer, Chital Deer, Wild Boar, Blue Bull, Sloth Bear and Hyena. Birding enthusiasts can look out for resident White-Breasted Water Hen, Jacanas, Moorhen, River Tern, Sand Piper, Ringed Plover and Grey and Purple Herons. Moreover, the lake is a stop-over for innumerable migratory water-fowl, making for a spectacular sight during migration season.

With the concept of eco-tourism gaining in popularity all over the world, the Forest Department of Bangladesh is considering a number of the country’s national parks for developing this concept, and the Ramsagar National Park is on that list. Eco-tourism allows visitors, both local and international, to enjoy the natural beauty of the country, provides local communities with a sustainable income, raises awareness of the challenges of development versus conservation, and looks for ways to ensure that future generations will also have the opportunity of enjoying the beauty of Bangladesh.

✨ Unique Aspects of Ramshagor Dighi ✨

1️⃣ Largest man-made dighi in Bangladesh – not just big, but colossal, earning its name “Ramsagar” (literally, Ram’s Ocean).

2️⃣ Human labour on a mega-scale – about 1.5 million workers were employed, making it one of the largest public works projects of 18th-century Bengal.

3️⃣ Not for luxury, but survival – unlike palaces or forts, this was built to fight drought and famine, ensuring water security for locals.

4️⃣ Ecological oasis – today it’s home to migratory birds, fish, and lush greenery, showing how a 250-year-old project still sustains life.

5️⃣ Heritage + Tourism blend – where else can you find a Mughal-era water reservoir that doubles as a modern picnic and leisure spot?

6️⃣ Symbol of Bengal’s water wisdom – Ramshagor reflects the region’s tradition of investing wealth in water, valuing people’s needs over pomp.

Kotka beach is one of the beautiful tourist spots among the entire Sundarbans where you can do a jungle trail along with night stay. It is actually a sanctuary area for the wild animals and UNESCO declared world heritage site. In Kotka, deer and monkeys can be seen many in numbers and the predators as the Royal Bengal Tiger can be seen sometimes. It has been said locally that the tigers often being available where the deer are available. If it is managed to get a safari early in the morning with a small boat to the inlet part of the river through forest a lots of wild animal could watched.

Like the other part of Sundarbans, Kotka is also full of flora and fauna. It took a survey and said that there is about 245 genera and 334 types of plants are at The Sundarbans. Moreover, some extinct type of birds likes Grey Eagle, the vultures and hornbills. More than fifty species of birds found at kotka.

The forest authority made a reservoir to get the sweet water for the wild animals during dry season. There is a watch tower also and from the tower tourists get a wonderful view of the forest. Form the watch tower it takes half an hour in walking distance you will reach to a wonderful sea beach out there named as Jamtola Beach. In winter season tigers Paws & Footprint can be seen often in the Kotka Beach.

review_text:
Katka Beach – A Different Experience at the Wild Nature and the Sea Estuary

Beach Introduction and History:

Katka Beach is one of the most beautiful and wildlife-rich places in the Sundarbans. It is located in the eastern part of the Sundarbans, south of Khulna, and is home to various wildlife including tigers, deer, crocodiles. This beach is mainly famous for seeing the Royal Bengal Tiger, but it also attracts tourists for its white sand and secluded environment.

My Experience:

I got the opportunity to visit this beach while visiting the Katka Wildlife Sanctuary in the Sundarbans. The entire journey was exciting! First, I had to take a boat to cross the winding canals of the Sundarbans and reach Katka. When I got off there and reached the beach after crossing some jungle paths, my eyes were immediately captivated—the endless blue water in front of me, the white sand and the forest all around!

The beach was completely deserted, not as crowded as Cox's Bazar or Kuakata. Just nature and me! The sound of the waves and the calls of the forest birds created a different atmosphere. I saw several deer from a distance, which were roaming near the beach. However, you have to be careful, because there is a possibility of tigers here, although they are not seen much during the day.

An interesting fact is that no one usually goes to bathe on this beach, because it is part of the Sundarbans and the currents can be dangerous at times due to the tides. So I spent my time just walking, taking pictures and enjoying the beauty of nature.

In short:

⭐ Entry fee: A permit is required to enter the Sundarbans (may cost 200-300 taka per person)
⭐ How to get there: You have to reach the Katka Sanctuary of the Sundarbans by boat from Khulna or Mongla.
⭐ Best time: Winter (November-February), because then wildlife viewing and the weather are the best.
⭐ Things to do: Enjoy the beauty of the beach, see wildlife, boat trips, photography.

Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (4/5)

Katka Beach is a paradise for nature lovers! The solitude, purity of nature and the presence of wildlife give it a unique dimension. However, the access is difficult and some caution is required due to the fear of tigers, so I have given it 4 stars. Still, if you love nature and adventure, then Katka is the perfect destination for you!

কটকা সমুদ্রসৈকত – বুনো প্রকৃতি আর সাগরের মোহনায় এক অন্যরকম অভিজ্ঞতা

সৈকতের পরিচিতি ও ইতিহাস:

কটকা সমুদ্রসৈকত সুন্দরবনের অন্যতম মনোরম ও বন্যপ্রাণীসমৃদ্ধ স্থান। এটি সুন্দরবনের পূর্ব অংশে, খুলনার দক্ষিণে অবস্থিত এবং বাঘ, হরিণ, কুমিরসহ নানা বন্যপ্রাণীর বিচরণস্থল। এই সৈকতটি মূলত রয়েল বেঙ্গল টাইগার দেখার জন্য বিখ্যাত, পাশাপাশি এটি সাদা বালুকাবেলা ও নির্জন পরিবেশের জন্যও পর্যটকদের আকর্ষণ করে।

আমার অভিজ্ঞতা:

সুন্দরবনের কটকা ওয়াইল্ডলাইফ স্যাংচুয়ারি ঘুরতে গিয়ে এই সমুদ্রসৈকতে যাওয়ার সুযোগ পেয়েছিলাম। ভ্রমণের পুরো যাত্রাটাই রোমাঞ্চকর ছিল! প্রথমে নৌকায় চেপে সুন্দরবনের আঁকাবাঁকা খাল পার হয়ে কটকায় পৌঁছাতে হয়। সেখানে নেমে কিছুটা জঙ্গল পথ পেরিয়ে যখন সৈকতে পৌঁছালাম, তখনই চোখ ধাঁধিয়ে গেল—সামনে অবিরাম নীল জলরাশি, ধবধবে সাদা বালু আর চারপাশে বনভূমি!

সৈকতটা একেবারেই ফাঁকা, কক্সবাজার বা কুয়াকাটার মতো ভিড় নেই। শুধু প্রকৃতি আর আমি! ঢেউয়ের শব্দ আর বনের পাখিদের ডাক এক অন্যরকম পরিবেশ তৈরি করেছিল। বেশ কিছু হরিণ দূর থেকে দেখতে পেলাম, যারা সৈকতের কাছেই ঘোরাফেরা করছিল। তবে সতর্ক থাকতে হয়, কারণ এখানে বাঘের উপস্থিতির সম্ভাবনা থাকে, যদিও দিনে খুব একটা দেখা যায় না।

একটা মজার ব্যাপার হলো, এই সৈকতে সাধারণত কেউ স্নান করতে নামে না, কারণ এটি সুন্দরবনের অংশ এবং জোয়ার-ভাটার কারণে স্রোত অনেক সময় বিপজ্জনক হতে পারে। তাই শুধু হাঁটাহাঁটি করে, ছবি তুলে আর প্রকৃতির শোভা উপভোগ করেই সময় কাটালাম।

সংক্ষেপে:

⭐ প্রবেশ মূল্য: সুন্দরবনে প্রবেশের জন্য পারমিট লাগে (প্রতি ব্যক্তি ২০০-৩০০ টাকা হতে পারে)
⭐ কীভাবে যাবেন: খুলনা বা মংলা থেকে নৌকায় সুন্দরবনের কটকা অভয়ারণ্যে পৌঁছাতে হয়।
⭐ সেরা সময়: শীতকাল (নভেম্বর-ফেব্রুয়ারি), কারণ তখন বন্যপ্রাণী দেখা ও আবহাওয়া সবচেয়ে ভালো থাকে।
⭐ কি করবেন: সৈকতের সৌন্দর্য উপভোগ, ওয়াইল্ডলাইফ দেখা, নৌকা ভ্রমণ, ফটোগ্রাফি।

রেটিং: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (৪/৫)

কটকা সমুদ্রসৈকত প্রকৃতিপ্রেমীদের জন্য এক স্বর্গীয় জায়গা! নির্জনতা, প্রকৃতির বিশুদ্ধতা আর বন্যপ্রাণীর উপস্থিতি এটাকে এক অনন্য মাত্রা দিয়েছে। তবে, যাতায়াত কঠিন এবং বাঘের আতঙ্কের কারণে কিছুটা সাবধানতা দরকার, তাই একে ৪ তারকা দিলাম। তবুও, যদি তুমি প্রকৃতি ও অ্যাডভেঞ্চার ভালোবাসো, তাহলে কটকা তোমার জন্য পারফেক্ট গন্তব্য!

Katka is one of the most diverse places in the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans. The distance from Mongla Port to Katka is about 90 kilometers. There is a 40-foot high watch tower in Katka to enjoy the natural beauty of the Sundarbans. Katka beach is directly north of the Katka watch tower. Katka beach is known as Jamtala beach to the locals. The artwork of crabs can be seen all over the shoreline of the quite deserted and clean beach. Katka beach merges directly into Kachikhali to the east. The wave shape on this beach is very variable and it is quite risky to go into the water due to unknown sand drifts.

Launch is the main means of reaching Katka. Launches with tourists are anchored in Katka canal. On the west bank of the canal is the office of the Katka Forest Department, from there if you move a little west, you will see a brick-paved path. If you go ahead on this path, you will see the wonderful wild Katka sea beach. Katka beach is an ideal place to watch the sunset.

If you go to a quiet place in the Keora forest, north of the wooden tail behind the forest department office, you can see the beautiful Chitra deer. Apart from this, you can see monkeys, wild boars, wild cats and various species of birds, along with crocodiles in winter. Tiger footprints are often seen on the three tiger hills to the south of the forest. To the east, there is a dense forest and a freshwater pond. This pond is the only source of water for the coast guard, forest officers and local fishermen working here.

Kuakata Sea Beach: A Wonderful Land of Nature
Introduction:
Kuakata is a beautiful sea beach located in Kalapara Upazila of Patuakhali District in the southern part of Bangladesh. This 18-kilometer-long beach is also known as 'Sagar Kanya'. Its main attraction is that you can see both sunrise and sunset from here, which is rare in Bangladesh. On one side, the waters of the Bay of Bengal stretch out in the distance, and on the other, the greenery - all this gives Kuakata an extraordinary beauty.
Location and Transportation:
The distance from Dhaka to Kuakata is about 320 kilometers. It can be reached by road and waterway. There is a direct bus service from Dhaka. In addition, you can take a launch from Dhaka Sadarghat to Patuakhali or Kalapara, and from there you can reach Kuakata by bus or other local transport.
Features:
* Sunrise and Sunset: The main feature of Kuakata Sea Beach is its exceptional geographical location. From here, you can enjoy both the sunrise over the Bay of Bengal and the sunset over the sea in the evening.
* Long Beach: Walking along the sandy beach, which is about 18 kilometers long, is a wonderful experience. The beach here is relatively deserted and clean.
* Coconut Garden: There are numerous rows of coconut trees along the beach, which further enhances the beauty of this area.
* Historical Well: There is an ancient well near the beach, which gave its name to this area. It is said that the local Rakhine community dug it.
* Buddhist Temple: There are several ancient Buddhist temples and monasteries near Kuakata, which are a center of interest for history and culture lovers.
* Fishing Village (Jele Palli): If you go here, you get the opportunity to see the lifestyle of local fishermen up close. Buying fresh fish and learning about their culture can be a different experience.
* Red Crab Island: There is a red crab island near Kuakata, where numerous red crabs can be seen. This island can be reached by speedboat.
Tourism Potential:
Kuakata is a potential tourist center. The natural beauty and historical significance of this place attract domestic and foreign tourists. However, due to unplanned urbanization and environmental pollution, there is a risk of its beauty fading somewhat.
Some notable places:
* Zero Point: It is considered the center of Kuakata beach.
* Gangamati Char: This is a beautiful char located east of Kuakata, where various species of birds can be seen.
* Lemon Forest: This forest, which grows on the edge of the sea, has various types of mangrove plants.
* Fatra Forest: This is a part of the Sundarbans, which is located near Kuakata and can be visited by boat.
Current Status and Challenges:
Although Kuakata is currently a popular tourist destination, some challenges exist. It is important to protect the beach environment, control unplanned construction work, strengthen security measures and enhance tourism facilities.
Conclusion:
Kuakata beach is undoubtedly one of the most beautiful and attractive places in Bangladesh. Its natural beauty, historical significance and exceptional sunrise and sunset views make it unique. With proper planning and management, it is possible to turn this beach into a more attractive and environmentally friendly tourist destination.

ঢাকা থেকে কুয়াকাটার দূরত্ব প্রায় ৩২০ কিলোমিটার। সড়ক ও নৌপথে এখানে আসা যায়। ঢাকা থেকে সরাসরি বাস সার্ভিস রয়েছে। এছাড়া, ঢাকা সদরঘাট থেকে লঞ্চে করে পটুয়াখালী বা কলাপাড়া নেমে, সেখান থেকে বাস বা অন্যান্য স্থানীয় পরিবহনে কুয়াকাটা পৌঁছানো যায়।
বৈশিষ্ট্য:
* সূর্যোদয় ও সূর্যাস্ত: কুয়াকাটা সমুদ্র সৈকতের প্রধান বৈশিষ্ট্য হলো এর ব্যতিক্রমী ভৌগোলিক অবস্থান। এখান থেকে বঙ্গোপসাগরের বুকে সূর্যোদয় এবং বেলাশেষে সমুদ্রের জলে সূর্যের অস্ত যাওয়া – এই দুটি মনোরম দৃশ্যই উপভোগ করা যায়।
* দীর্ঘ বেলাভূমি: প্রায় ১৮ কিলোমিটার দীর্ঘ বালুকাময় বেলাভূমি জুড়ে হেঁটে বেড়ানো এক অসাধারণ অভিজ্ঞতা। এখানকার সৈকত তুলনামূলকভাবে নির্জন ও পরিচ্ছন্ন।
* নারিকেল বাগান: সৈকতের কোল ঘেঁষে রয়েছে অসংখ্য নারিকেল গাছের সারি, যা এই অঞ্চলের সৌন্দর্য্য আরও বৃদ্ধি করেছে।
* ঐতিহাসিক কুয়া: সৈকতের কাছেই রয়েছে একটি প্রাচীন কুয়া, যা এই অঞ্চলের নামকরণ করেছে। স্থানীয় রাখাইন সম্প্রদায়ের লোকেরা এটি খনন করেছিলেন বলে জানা যায়।
* বৌদ্ধ মন্দির: কুয়াকাটার কাছাকাছি রয়েছে বেশ কয়েকটি প্রাচীন বৌদ্ধ মন্দির ও বিহার, যা ইতিহাস ও সংস্কৃতি প্রেমীদের জন্য আগ্রহের কেন্দ্রবিন্দু।

* লাল কাঁকড়ার দ্বীপ: কুয়াকাটার কাছেই রয়েছে লাল কাঁকড়ার একটি দ্বীপ, যেখানে অসংখ্য লাল কাঁকড়া দেখতে পাওয়া যায়। স্পীডবোটের মাধ্যমে এই দ্বীপে যাওয়া যায়।

কুয়াকাটা একটি সম্ভাবনাময় পর্যটন কেন্দ্র। এখানকার প্রাকৃতিক সৌন্দর্য্য ও ঐতিহাসিক তাৎপর্য দেশি-বিদেশি পর্যটকদের আকৃষ্ট করে। তবে, অপরিকল্পিত নগরায়ন ও পরিবেশ দূষণের কারণে এর সৌন্দর্য্য কিছুটা ম্লান হওয়ার আশঙ্কা রয়েছে।

* লেবুর বন: সমুদ্রের কোল ঘেঁষে জেগে ওঠা এই বনটিতে বিভিন্ন প্রকার ম্যানগ্রোভ উদ্ভিদ রয়েছে।
* ফাতরার বন: এটি সুন্দরবনের একটি অংশ, যা কুয়াকাটার কাছে অবস্থিত এবং নৌকায় করে ঘুরে আসা যায়।
বর্তমান অবস্থা ও চ্যালেঞ্জ:

Hiron Point, also known as Nilkamal, is one of the most scenic and biodiverse spots within the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world. Located in Bangladesh, this UNESCO World Heritage Site is not just a paradise for nature lovers but also a critical ecological area. Hiron Point, in particular, is a must-visit destination for those seeking to explore the unique beauty of the Sundarbans.

A Haven for Wildlife

Hiron Point is renowned for its rich biodiversity, which includes the famous Royal Bengal Tiger, the world's largest population of this majestic species. Apart from tigers, visitors can also spot spotted deer, rhesus macaques, saltwater crocodiles, and various species of reptiles and amphibians. The area is a birdwatcher's dream, especially from October to March when migratory birds from different parts of the world make their stopover here. Species like kingfishers, white-bellied sea eagles, and different types of herons can be spotted, making it a prime location for bird enthusiasts.

Mangrove Forest and Riverine Beauty

The landscape of Hiron Point is defined by its dense mangrove forests, which are crisscrossed by a labyrinth of rivers and creeks. These waterways create an enchanting natural ambiance, with the changing tides continuously transforming the scenery. Taking a boat ride through these waters offers visitors the chance to truly immerse themselves in the quiet, almost surreal environment. The mangroves are not only beautiful but also play a vital role in protecting the coastal areas from erosion and storms, showcasing nature's delicate balance.

Tranquility and Serenity

Unlike the more developed tourist areas, Hiron Point retains a sense of wildness and tranquility, making it an ideal spot for those looking to escape the hustle and bustle of city life. The sounds of nature—chirping birds, rustling leaves, and the gentle flow of water—create a peaceful atmosphere that is rare in today's fast-paced world. This isolation and serenity make Hiron Point a perfect place for eco-tourism and responsible travel.

Accessibility and Conservation Efforts

Access to Hiron Point is generally via boat from Khulna or Mongla, and while the journey can be long, it is absolutely worth it for the serene experience that awaits. The area is also part of conservation efforts to protect the endangered species that call the Sundarbans home, with the Bangladesh Forest Department actively working to ensure sustainable tourism and wildlife protection.

In conclusion, Hiron Point in the Sundarbans offers an unparalleled natural experience. With its rich wildlife, unique mangrove ecosystem, and tranquil environment, it is an ideal destination for eco-tourists, photographers, and anyone seeking to reconnect with nature.

Sundarbans: The Sundarbans is one of the largest mangrove forest in the world (133,010 ha).  It lies on the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers on the Bay of Bengal. It spans the area from the Hooghly River in India's state of West Bengal to the Baleswar River in Bangladesh's Khulna Division.

Covering 133,010 ha, the area is estimated to comprise about 55% forest land and 45% wetlands in the form of tidal rivers, creeks, canals and vast estuarine mouths of the river. About 66% of the entire mangrove forest area is estimated to occur in Bangladesh, with the remaining 34% in India.

The most abundant tree species are Sundari (Heritiera fomes) and Gewa (Excoecaria agallocha). The forests provide habitat to 453 fauna wildlife, including 290 bird, 120 fish, 42 mammal, 35 reptile and eight amphibian species. It is total ban on all killing or capture of wildlife other than fish and some invertebrates.

The Sundarbans are an important habitat for the Bengal tiger (Panthera tigris). The forest also provides habitat for small wild cats such as the jungle cat (Felis chaus), fishing cat (Prionailurus viverrinus), and leopard cat (P. bengalensis).

Places to visit:

•	Kotka Beach and Jamtala Beach: Famous for its beauty, where you can often spot spotted deer and sometimes Royal Bengal Tigers.

•	Karamjal: A forest station and popular tourist spot, it is home to a crocodile breeding centre where baby crocodiles are kept before being released into the forest.

•	Hiran Point: A protected wildlife sanctuary with a long wooden walkway to view various animals including deer and monkeys.

•	Kochikhali: A beautiful tourist spot and an important area for wildlife watching, especially deer.

•	Dublar Char Island: A unique island destination within the Sundarbans, known for its fishing activities and picturesque views.

•	Harbaria: Considered an attractive ecotourism park with trekking trails and watchtowers for observing the forest and its wildlife.

•	Tin Kona Island: Another popular place in the forest for wildlife and bird watching.

•	Katka Beach Watch Tower: Another popular place in the forest for wildlife and bird watching.

By Vromon Vhela
Sundarbans: The Largest Mangrove Forest of The Earth
Forest is the lung of the Mother Earth. Without forest it’s impossible to live in the world. That’s mean no forest no life. The word “forest” comes from old French word forest (also fores). And the Bans word derives from the English Word Forest. The first known forests on Earth arose in the Late Devonian (approximately 380 million years ago), with the evolution of Archaeopteryx.

A mangrove is a shrub or small tree that grows in coastal saline or brackish water. The term is also used for tropical coastal vegetation consisting of such species. Mangroves occur worldwide in the tropics and subtropics, mainly between latitudes 25° N and 25° S. The total mangrove forest area of the world in 2000 was 137,800 square kilometers (53,200 sq mi), spanning 118 countries and territories.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees, also called halophytes, and are adapted to life in harsh coastal conditions. They contain a complex salt filtration system and complex root system to cope with salt water immersion and wave action. They are adapted to the low oxygen conditions of waterlogged mud. Although mangroves inhabit only 0.7% of global coastal zone, but they have a significant contribution to the global carbon. Primary production by mangroves provides a substantial source of energy for aquatic food webs.

In the coastal area of Bangladesh there are huge natural mangrove forests. Sundarbans is the biggest natural mangrove forest in the world, located between Bangladesh and India. The most beautiful part of the Sundarbans consists of Bangladesh and it is 60%. It is the deepest with the different types of geological periods and fauna. If you want to get a true experience of the mangrove forest, you must visit the Bangladesh side of the Sundarbans.

The Sundarbans mangrove forest covers an area of about 10,000 km2 (3,900 sq mi). Of which, forests in Bangladesh's Khulna Division extend over 6,017 km2 (2,323 sq mi) and in West Bengal, they extend over 4,260 km2 (1,640 sq mi) across the South 24 Parganas and North 24 Parganas districts.[6] The most abundant tree species are Sundri (Heritiera fomes) and Gewa (Excoecaria agallocha). The forests provide habitat to 453 faunal wildlife, including 290 bird, 120 fish, 42 mammal, 35 reptile and eight amphibian species.

In 2007, the landfall of Cyclone Sidr damaged around 40% of the Sundarbans. The forest is also suffering from increased salinity due to rising sea levels and reduced freshwater supply. Again in May 2009 Cyclone Aila devastated Sundarban with massive casualties. According to news paper source at least 1 lakh people were affected by this cyclone.[10][11] The proposed coal-fired Rampal power station situated 14 km (8.7 mi) north of the Sundarbans at Rampal Upazila of Bagerhat District in Khulna, Bangladesh, is anticipated to further damage this unique mangrove forest according to a 2016 report by UNESCO.

review_text:
Pride of Bangladesh.....

Sundarban is the biggest mangrove forest in the world. Sundarban is in South West part of Bangladesh, in the district of greater Khulna. India shares a bit of the forest with Bangladesh. The total area is about 38,000 square kilo meters.

Sundarban is the natural habitat of the world’s famous Royal Bengal Tiger, spotted deer, crocodiles, jungle fowl, wild boar, lizards and many more. Migratory flock of Siberian ducks flying over thousands of sail boats loaded with timber, Golpata, fuel wood, honey, shell and fish further add to the serene natural beauty of the Sundarban.

Famous spots
The main tourist point is Hiron Point (Nilkamal) for watching tiger, deer, monkey, crocodiles, birds and natural beauty. Katka is for watching deer, tiger, crocodiles, varieties of birds and monkey. Morning and evening symphony of wild fowls. Vast expanse of grassy meadows running from Katka to Kachikhali (Tiger Point) provide opportunities for wild tracking. Tin Kona Island for tiger and deer. Dublar Char (Island) for fishermen.  It is a beautiful island where herds of spotted deer are often seen to graze.

This visit to the Sundarbans National Forest was one of the most life-changing experiences. The mangrove forest is inhabited by the legendary Royal Bengal Tiger, so one can only imagine the beauty. I hired a guide, and his knowledge and passion for the subject did add to the pleasure. We saw a crocodile, deer, different colored birds, dolphins, and many more, and enjoyed the serene boat ride through serene rivers surrounded by lush greenery.

The forest is so well-preserved, and I loved how everything was so eco-friendly to make sure this natural wonder remains unspoiled for generations. The communities are so warm, and it's such a please to witness how tourism helps in the preservation process here.

The Sundarbans is an experience par excellence for any nature enthusiast, adventurer, or seeker of a perfect, peaceful fleeing into the undisturbed wilderness. This area is one of those places where every turn could seem like a picture postcard view, so don't forget your cameras. I left refreshed and inspired by the amazing biodiversity of this UNESCO World Heritage site.

This place is highly recommended if you're visiting Bangladesh; truly an unforgettable journey right into the heart of nature.

Visiting Shilaidaha Kuthibari was a deeply wonderful and nostalgic journey for me. Seeing Rabindranath Tagore's house and his personal belongings in person instantly brought back so many cherished childhood memories of reading his poems and stories.
​The centerpiece of the complex is the iconic 3-story mansion, which holds a rich historical value. Inside, you get to explore the rooms preserved with vintage almirahs, showcases, chairs, tables, beds, and beautiful paintings that give a clear glimpse into the poet's life and era.
​Beyond the main building, the entire property features a huge open space with vast green grounds, tall trees, and a very serene atmosphere that is perfect for walking around. There is also a quiet mosque in the corner of the complex, which is very convenient for visitors wanting to offer prayers in a peaceful setting.
​I visited during the rainy season, and it made the entire experience even better! The rain brought out a refreshing greenery, and the weather felt noticeably cooler, calmer, and much more enchanting.
​Perfect for anyone who loves history, peace, and timeless memories. This place should definitely be at the top of your Kushtia travel list!

review_text:
Shilaidaha Rabindra Kuthibari is a historically significant and culturally rich landmark located in Shilaidaha. This heritage site was the residence of the legendary poet and Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore during his time in Bengal, and it remains a place of immense literary and historical importance. For anyone interested in Bengali culture, literature, and history, visiting the Kuthibari is a deeply enriching experience.

The Kuthibari itself is an elegant, traditional estate surrounded by lush gardens and greenery. The architecture reflects the 19th-century Bengali style, with large verandas, high ceilings, and wooden detailing. Walking through the premises, one can feel the serene atmosphere that inspired many of Tagore’s works. review_text: Shilaidaha Rabindra Kuthibari, in short Shilaidah Kuthibari, is one of the major tourist places in Bangladesh. It is located seven kilometers north of Kushtia on the banks of Padma in Kumarkhali Upazila of Kushtia District.This Kuthi bari was built by an indigo-planter named Shelly which was later owned by Ramlochan Tagore. In 1807, Dwarkanath Tagore got the ownership of this kuthibari with the inheritance of estate. In 1892, due to the erosion of the river caused by the flood, the Kuthibari was likely to disappear, so it was demolished and a new building was constructed elsewhere in the next year. Dwarkanath Tagore's grandson Rabindranath Tagore came to Shilaidaha several times to look after the estate. He had the opportunity to stay in this cottage. He wrote many literatures during his stay at Shilaidah Kuthibari. During his stay here in 1912, he began the work of translating the Gitanjali into English.During his stay in this building in 1905, he wrote a song which is now the national anthem of Bangladesh.

This magnificent mansion was built by the Tagore family in the 19th century as a country retreat, and it became a significant residence for Rabindranath during his visits to manage family estates and compose many of his works.

The architectural design of Kuthibari is a beautiful blend of classical colonial and traditional Bengali styles. Constructed as a two-story structure with a large veranda, the house has wide, open spaces and high ceilings, which were ideal for the tropical climate. The lush gardens, ponds, and scenic surroundings add to the serene ambiance, providing an inspiring environment that greatly influenced Tagore’s creativity. review_text:
A historical place near the town of Kushtia. Young Rabindranath Tagore stayed at this place for a few years to supervise their estates (zamindari). He spent his prime years in this house, and wrote some most beautiful poems and lyrics while living here. If you’re a HUGE FAN of Tagore, you should visit here for the historical perspective this place offers.

However, as a tourist there’s nothing much to see here if I need to be honest. The builiding is small, houses only a few (maybe 7-8 pieces) things used by Tagore. It has some photographs of Tagore, his works and his family (probably downloaded from internet). Furthermore, almost all descriptions are in Bangla so you’ll be puzzled as a foreigner without a guide.

Although the building has nothing much to offer, the surrounding area is really nice. There’s a tennis court (used by Tagore), a large pond and a pretty park. You can spend an hour or two relaxing on the park benches.

The place usually closes at 5 PM. On Monday, it opens at 2 PM.

review_text:
The Kutibari of Rabindranath Tagore in Shilaidaha, Kushtia is truly a historical and spectacular place.  Can raise;
World poet Rabindranath Tagore's house in Shilaidaha village of Kumarkhali upazila of Kushtia.  This house is one of the places of pilgrimage of the zamindari of Jorasako Tagore family in the subcontinent and one of the places of literature and history of the poet.  In 1890, Rabindranath Tagore came to Kuthibari with the responsibility of zamindar.

In the green forest along the banks of the river Padma and in the twilight of the blue and white clouds, the beautiful scenery of nature at the same time, the image of ferry crossing in the golden sun and the various arrangements of fishermen fishing will attract anyone.  Here is the natural love of nature with the traditional rural way of life.  Where the poet has written all the famous books like Sonar Tari, Chitra, Chaitali, Gitanjali.

￼￼You will see

The three-storied pyramid house surrounded by a wave-shaped wall of the Padma River will greet you from afar before entering.  Seen from a distance, it looks like a wonderful portrait made of paper.  The house is surrounded by a carpet of green grass, adorned with colorful flowers.  And there is no doubt that the beauty of the Zhou tree, as well as the chirping of birds, the beauty of the surrounding nature will fascinate any tourist.

This is like a house of peace.  When you enter through the gate, you will be greeted by the soft melody of Rabindra Sangeet.  From the top of the house to the sixteen rooms on the ground floor, there are various paintings of the life of the poet's house, copies of letters, hand-painted pictures of the poet himself.  Which are still being written from page to page of the poet's memory, various images of Rabindranath's life have come up since childhood.

There are also sofas, cupboards, iron chests, armchairs, couches and couches used by Rabindranath.  Just looking at them will take you back to the old 18th century zamindari tradition.  And eight Bihar palanquins have been taken care of there.  It is said that traveling by palanquin by land was his favorite.  There are two speedboats named Chapla and Chanchal and Padmaboat anchor.  It is noteworthy that although the exhibits are many years old, they are preserved under close supervision and their brilliance still captivates the minds of the visitors.

On the west side of the house are the poet's favorite dighi and bakultala.  The place has been witnessed with innumerable songs and poems of the poet.  On the east side of the house there is a picture of Rabindranath engraved in marble and some sayings written by Rabindranath, which will give you greetings.  There is an open stage in front of the house, where a cultural program is organized every year on the occasion of Rabindra Janmajayanti by the joint initiative of Bangladesh and India.  In front of it there is an empty field, where the fair is organized.  There are many shops next to it.  Where there are statues of Rabindranath inlaid with artwork, Ektara, various wooden showpieces.  Rabindranath is everywhere in the house.

কুষ্টিয়ার কুমারখালী উপজেলার শিলাইদহ গ্রামে বিশ্ব কবি রবীন্দ্রনাথ ঠাকুরের কুঠিবাড়ি। উপমহাদেশে জোড়াসাকোর ঠাকুর পরিবারের জমিদারির তীর্থস্থান ও কবিগুরুর সাহিত্য আর ইতিহাসের অন্যতম স্থান এই কুঠিবাড়ি। ১৮৯০ সালে রবীন্দ্রনাথ ঠাকুর জমিদারের দায়িত্ব নিয়ে কুঠিবাড়িতে আসেন।

পদ্মা নদীর তীর ঘেষা সবুজ অরণ্যে আর নীল সাদা মেঘের গোধূলি  লগ্নে প্রকৃতির নয়নাভিরাম দৃশ্য এবই সেই সাথে পড়ন্ত বেলায় সোনালি রোদে খেয়া পারাপারের চিত্র আর জেলেদের মাছ ধরার নানা আয়োজন যেকাউকে আকৃষ্ট করবে। এখানে ফুটে উঠেছে চিরায়ত গ্রামীণ জীবন-যাপনের সাথে প্রকৃতির নৈসর্গিক প্রেম। যেখানে কবিগুরু রচনা করে গেছেন সোনার তরী, চিত্রা, চৈতালি, গীতাঞ্জলীর মতো বিখ্যাত সব গ্রন্থ।

review_text:
A chronicled landmark to safeguard the memory of Rabindranath Tagore. Green nature with wonderful climate.

Rabindranath Tagore every now and again visited and used to remain in Shilaidaha Kuthibari regarding the organization of his Zamindari and enhanced Bengali writing through his quality composition during that time.

He composed numerous critical sonnets during his visit here. He assembled it as his home/office for gathering income as a zamindar, from nearby workers.

It is presently an exhibition hall under the Archeology branch of the Ministry of Cultural Affairs.

Entry Fee- 20/- tk

review_text:
In January 2019, I had gone to Bangladesh along with my parents, mainly to recollect their childhood days when it used to be their home. While my mother hailed from Rajshahi proper, my father hailed from a small village called Boalmari near Pabna town. It was only when we reached Pabna we realised that all that stood between us and Kushtia district was a narrow strip of the Padma River! And right on the banks of Padma river beckoned the famed Shilaidaha Kuthibari - where the great Rabindranath Tagore spent a lot of his formative years, writing innumerable stories and poems, where his elder brother Jyotirindra Nath Tagore had painted the famous Lalan Fakir on their famous houseboat. The anecdotes are endless!

While the pictures I am uploading here are sufficient to tell you the wealth of historical artefacts that await you at this place, I must mention, the Govt of Bangladesh has done a great job in preserving the tiniest facets of Kobiguru's life in this palace which now doubles up as the Museum. I am intentionally not attaching the photos taken of artefacts inside the Museum as I strongly feel you should visit and see them for yourself to get the real feel. The campus, with the various sections, which you can view here, are enough to take you back in time.

Reaching there is a bit of an effort though. You need to reach Pabna Boat Ghat. If you are visiting in the Monsoons, then a ferry will take you straight to the Silaidaha Ghat. In other months the water levels are low, and almost half of the way is covered by rickshaw or auto, and the narrow water strip in between is navigated via boats. In total, it should not take you more than 100 Bangladesh Takas to go to and fro from Silaidaha. But given that Tagore and Lalan Shah are waiting on the other side, I would suggest you go for it!

review_text:
The Kuthibari is a picturesque three-storied, pyramid-shaped, terraced bungalow, constructed with bricks, timber, corrugated tin sheets and Raniganj tiles. The bungalow nestles amidst 11 acres of orchards of mango, jackfruit and other trees, a flower garden and two ponds

The peace and tranquility the Kuthibari inspired Tagore to pen some of his most unforgettable verses thus contributing to the enrichment of Bengali Literature. Many prominent personalities -- scientist Sir Jagadish Chandra Bose, dramatist and music composer DL Roy and litterateur Promoth Chowdhury, visited Tagore at this location.

Tagore stayed intermittently between 1891 and 1901 at Shilaidaha Kuthibari. Sitting at Kuthibari or on a boat on Padma, Tagore wrote a number of masterpieces such as “Sonar Tori”, “Chitra”, “Chaitali”, “Katha O Kahini”, “Kshanika”, most of the poems from “Naibedya” and “Kheya”, and songs from “Gitanjali” and “Gitimalya”. It was here, in 1912, that the poet started translating his “Gitanjali” into English, which earned him the Nobel Prize in 1913.

Shilaidaha is a relatively modern name; its old name was Khorshedpur. Before the Thakurs of Jorasanko acquired the village in the middle of the 19th century, there stood an indigo-Kuthi reportedly built by a planter named Shelly. A deep whirlpool used to form there at the confluence of the Gadai and the Padma, and hence the village was known as “Shelly-daha”, which ultimately came to be known as ‘Shilaidaha’.

Prince Dwarkanath Tagore, grandfather of Rabindranath Tagore, became the owner of this Zamindari in 1807 by means of a will executed in his favour by Ramlochan Tagore. Rabindranath assumed the responsibility of looking after the Zamindari and came to Shilaidaha for the first time in November 1889.

Shilaidaha Kuthibari is now a protected national monument. The renovation of Kuthibari has been completed by the Department of Archaeology, Ministry of Cultural Affairs. It is known as Tagore Memorial Museum where Tagore memorabilia like his bed, wardrobe, iron chest, lawn mower, framed pictures and a replica of a houseboat are displayed here. Tagore aficionados and art lovers will certainly be pleased to see some rare photos of Tagore and family, courtesy by Pranab Mukherjee, President of the Republic of India, and some exquisite paintings including a few self-portraits by Tagore.

In Tagore’s lifetime, the river Padma used to flow beside the Kuthibari. But over a course of time, it has changed its direction and now is far away from Tagore’s haven. However, the surrounding landscapes, large pond with bojra (boat), are still wonderful to see.

If you visit Meherpur, visiting Mujibnagar is a must. Mujibnagar has a very important place in the history of Bangladesh. On April 17, 1971, the Provisional Government of Bangladesh took oath here during the Liberation War. At that time, Mujibnagar was known as the provisional capital of Bangladesh. Because of its connection with the Liberation War and the history of Bangladesh, this place has a very special historical value.

Mujibnagar is around 18 km from Meherpur town and can be reached quite easily by Auto/CNG or other local transport. During my visit, I explored the whole historical complex, including the monuments, memorials and other important structures. I also visited the nearby Bangladesh-India border area, which made the trip even more interesting. The place was too quiet when I visited, and there were not many visitors. Some local people also told me that the number of visitors has become much lower than before.

After the political change on August 5, 2024, some statues, sculptures, lighting structures and other artworks in the complex were damaged. Because of this, the place now needs proper care and renovation. The Bangladesh map and some other parts of the complex also need to be cleaned and repainted.

I hope the authorities will soon take proper steps to renovate and maintain this important historical place. If the damaged parts are repaired, the Bangladesh map is properly painted, and the whole area is taken care of, I believe Mujibnagar can become as beautiful and attractive as it was before.

If you are visiting Meherpur, you must visit Mujibnagar. Especially if you are a history lover or interested in the history of Bangladesh, this is a place you should definitely visit. For me, a trip to Meherpur would not feel complete without visiting Mujibnagar.

Mujibnagar Monument signifies the memory of the formation of he first ever government of Bangladesh during the Liberation War of Bangladesh. It has been named after the Father of the Nation Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

The main complex has a huge map of Bangladesh displaying significant events around the country during the nine months of Liberation War in 1971. Tourists can take pictures there and can visit there to know about our country. The surroundind environment is beautiful too.

If you go a little ahead from the comolex, you’ll get to see the Mujibnagar Monument. Its very beautiful  and since we went there during the sunset, the environment was just perfect. There was a guide there who casted in several historical films. He provided us the significances of the historic monument.

Let me explain a bit  for the sake of foreign tourists. The monument is in the shape of a rising sun having 23 rays getting bigger in size from right to left. The rays signifies 23 years of atrocities the Banhladeshi people has faced from 1947 till 1971. The size of the rays indicates the importance of each movements occured in each year. The red rectangular surface is the place where the Mujibnagar Government, the first ever government of Bangladesh was formed. The pebbles signifies the number of people who accepted sacrifices during the war. As a whole, the Mujibnagar Memorial is built totally on the history of our country.

There is a 200 years old tree on a side of the monument too. I really liked the monument and recommend others to viait there too.

Sculptures depicting significant events can be found there, such as Bangabandhu's famous March 7th speech, the oath of the Mujibnagar administration, etc. The memorial is made up of 23 triangular walls. All the sculptures are so beautiful and made this place a photogenic spot.

This is an important historical place of Bangladesh. The first Independent temporary government was built there on 17th April 1971 during the liberation war of Bangladesh. Acting president Syed Nazrul Islam, prime minister Tajuddin ahmad, Khondakar Mostaq Ahmad as Minister of Foreign Affairs, Law and Parliamentary Affairs, M Mansur Ali as Minister of Finance, Industry and Commerce and AHM Qamaruzzaman as Minister of Home, Civil Supplies,Relief and Rehabilitation, Agriculture. They took oath on that day at Mujibnagar.

Mujibnagar government was divided into fifteen ministries and divisions. Besides, some divisions were placed under the Cabinet. The functions of the ministries and divisions were:
Ministry of defence staff MAG Osmany, Commander-in-Chief; SA Samad, Defence Secretary; Colonel Abdur Rab, Chief of Staff. The Ministry of Defence divided the war zone into eleven sectors and appointed a sector commander for each of the sectors. But there was no sector commander for sector No 10 or naval sector. Commandos used to fight under the command of the concerned sector commander whenever and wherever they carried out the operation in a particular sector. Besides, there were three brigades called Z force, K force and S force. Major Ziaur Rahman, Major Khaled Mosharraf and Major Km Shafiullah were the commanders of the brigades respectively.

As my favorite place, the Mujibnagar Monument Complex serves as a source of inspiration and a reminder of the resilience and determination that shaped our nation. It's a place where history lives on, waiting to be discovered by those who seek to honor and remember the sacrifices that paved the way for our freedom.

review_text:
Kuakata Sea Beach

Kuakata Sea Beach, known as the “Daughter of the Sea,” is a one‑of‑a‑kind natural gem in Bangladesh. Located in Kalapara Upazila of Patuakhali District, this beach stretches approximately 18 km in length and 3 km in width—making it one of the country’s most expansive sandy coasts. Far from the hustle and bustle of urban life, it offers a peaceful retreat that resonates deeply with the soul.

What sets Kuakata apart is its unique vantage point, allowing visitors to witness both sunrise and sunset from the same shore—a phenomenon quite rare within both Bangladesh and beyond. The billowing sand, the blue horizon, and the glimmering sun together create a breathtaking panorama that truly touches the heart. One TripAdvisor reviewer aptly described it as a “panoramic sea beach”—an experience that words barely capture.

The serene ambience is accentuated by surrounding natural forests like the jat and Gangamati Reserve Forests, which not only please the eyes but enrich the area with biodiversity. Just off the coast lies Fatrar Char (Red Crab Island), where thousands of red crabs gather—a truly enchanting sight.

However, this beauty faces natural threats. Erosion, pollution, and unregulated tourism are upsetting Kuakata’s ecological balance. In some seasons, up to 30–100 feet of shoreline have been claimed by the sea in a single year. Local tourism operators warn that if the beach’s natural charm diminishes, tourist numbers will drop, dealing a blow to the local economy.

Winter (November–March) is the best time to visit—during these months the weather is pleasant and peaceful. Kuakata is located about 320 km from Dhaka and is accessible by bus, boat, or car. Accommodation options range from hotels and resorts to guesthouses and homestays, offering varied experiences for different preferences.

Overall, Kuakata is a well‑rounded travel destination—peaceful, culturally rich, and naturally stunning. With its rare dual sunrise and sunset views, jat forests, red crab island, ancient Buddhist temple, and Rakhine cultural heritage, it offers an unforgettable journey. However, without responsible tourism and environmental conservation, this beauty could vanish. Sustainable, mindful travel is essential to preserve Kuakata’s charm and safeguard its future.

A long beach at the south-most part of Bangladesh. The beach is beautiful, safe and very peaceful, but not very well-maintained, so sometimes it gets crowded and dirty.

The tide is low here, usually you won't find big waves, specially in the winter. This beach is probably the safest in Bangladesh. You can go deep into the sea with a very low risk of any accident.

Tip: the zero point (where there is the road to enter the beach) is the busiest place. After entering the beach from there, go to the left of right for about 10 minutes on foot. Those places are calm and quite with less people. You can enjoy the beauty and the peace of the beach from there.

Kuakata Beach: The Daughter of the Sea

Kuakata Beach, located in the Patuakhali district of southern Bangladesh, is renowned for its unique 180-degree view of both sunrise and sunset over the Bay of Bengal. Spanning 18 kilometers of golden sands, the beach offers a serene atmosphere and a variety of recreational activities. Visitors can relax on deck chairs under colorful parasols, enjoying the ocean breeze and sound of waves.

For adventure seekers, Kuakata offers horse rides along the shoreline, speed boat excursions across the bay, and four-wheeler rides on the beach. These activities provide thrilling experiences and opportunities to explore nearby islands and fishing spots like Fatrar Char.

Kuakata’s sunrises and sunsets are breathtaking, with scenes of fishermen silhouetted against golden skies in the morning and vibrant hues at dusk. The local cuisine, featuring freshly caught seafood such as prawn curry and fried hilsa, enhances the experience with its authentic Bengali flavours.

Beyond the beach, visitors can explore Rakhine villages, Buddhist temples, and the Fatrar Char mangrove forest. Kuakata’s blend of natural beauty, adventure, and cultural richness makes it a must-visit destination for those seeking tranquility and excitement by the sea.

Fuad, my six-year-old son, had the time of his life at this breathtaking beach. From the moment we stepped onto the golden sands, he was filled with excitement. His eyes lit up as he spotted the rides and activities waiting for him.

The pirate ship ride was his first adventure. Fuad giggled with joy as the ship swung back and forth, pretending he was a brave sailor navigating the high seas. Afterward, the merry-go-round was his next stop. He hopped on his favorite horse, holding tightly as the ride spun him around, his laughter blending with the sound of the waves.

We took a break under the colorful parasols to enjoy fresh green coconuts. Fuad loved drinking the cool, sweet water through a straw, proudly holding his coconut like a trophy. The beach breeze and rhythmic sounds of the sea added to the moment’s charm.

The highlight of the day was the jet ski ride. Fuad sat in front as we sped across the Bay of Bengal. The spray of seawater and the rush of speed made him squeal with delight, shouting, “Faster, faster!” as we zoomed over the waves. The thrill on his face was unforgettable.

As the sun began to set, Fuad ran along the shore, collecting seashells and watching the vibrant hues of orange and pink light up the sky. Kuakata Beach was not just a day of fun but a memory we would treasure forever—a day where adventure and happiness met the sea.

By Sarkar Jahangir Alam

Location: Kuakata, Patuakhali District, Bangladesh

Multiple hotels, resorts, and guesthouses available (from budget to luxury).

Examples: Hotel Graver Inn, Kuakata Grand Hotel & Sea Resort.

review_text:
Boithakata floating market is a weekly farmers' market that sits on the Belua river and surrounding canals, by the side of Baithakata bazar. The market is entirely consists of farmers' small boats carrying goods to be sold and the wholesale buyers' larger boat to carry away the goods purchased from the farmers. The farmers' boats are rafted alongside the purchasers' boats.

The floating market spans about 1 kilometer from Talukdar Hula launch ghat on the east, to the south of Boithakata Bazar on the west. The market sits twice a week: on Saturdays and Tuesdays. The market begins after sunrise and ends in around 9-10 am.

Fresh vegetable, fruits, paddy, rice, seeds, saplings, flower seedlings and many more goods are sold in the market.

The market is only accessible with boats and trawlers. Although this market is not so photogenic and tourist friendly like the floating markets of Atghar-Kuriana and Bhimruli, the goods sold in the market are diverse and hold higher economic values.

For tourists I would advice to come to this market soon after sunrise with boat or trawler to have a good view of the floating market.

♿ Wheelchair accessibility: the dingy boats are not safe for wheelchairs to get on. Also I didn't see suitable facilities which are required for wheelchairs to embark on boats and trawlers such as ramps.

[Image of Bhimruli floating guava market in Bangladesh]

The market is open from July to September, which is the peak guava season. During this time, the river is filled with boats of all shapes and sizes, all selling guavas. The vendors are very friendly and they are happy to haggle over prices.

The Bhimruli floating guava market is a great place to experience the unique culture and traditions of Bangladesh. It is also a great place to buy fresh, delicious guavas.

* Visit during the peak guava season, from July to September.
* Be prepared to bargain with the vendors.
* Bring cash, as most vendors do not accept credit cards.
* Wear comfortable shoes, as you will be doing a lot of walking.
* Take a boat ride on the Padma River to get a better view of the market.

I would definitely recommend visiting the Bhimruli floating guava market if you are ever in Bangladesh. It is a truly unique and unforgettable experience.

Taking a boat ride is one basic option to enjoy not only the market but also the enchanting look of houses, schools, and wooden bridges along the canal. Many small boats loaded with guavas, some with bananas, and hog plums (‘Aamra’ in Bengali) move slowly, allowing me to experience the bustle of the market in the serene setting. Things truly came to life once I reached the crisscrossed canals in Bhimruli, where visitors flocked in and all boatmen waded professionally through narrow water channels like labyrinths. Monsoon is the time when floating guava markets on canals crisscrossing thousands of guava orchards, in Jhalakathi’s Bhimruli and Pirojpur’s Atghar Kuriana under Nesarabad upazila, become alive with visitors from all over the country.

A network of canals connects the guava orchards spread out across 30 villages where one will also find several hundred orchards of ambarella or hog plum, commonly known as aamra.
The 200-year-old guava markets of Bhimruli and Atghar Kuriana have gradually become hubs for all sorts of produce and agricultural products.

The best time to visit the markets is the months between July and October during the monsoon when the canals are full to the brim while the trees, full of ripe guavas, in the orchards wear eye-soothing green.

As a traveler passionate about literature and cultural heritage, visiting the Michael Madhusudan Dutt Memorial in Sagar Dari was a deeply moving experience. Nestled in the tranquil surroundings of Gangasagar, this modest yet powerful memorial honors one of Bengal’s greatest literary figures—Michael Madhusudan Dutt, the pioneer of modern Bengali poetry.
The moment I arrived, I felt a quiet reverence in the air. The memorial stands near the place where Dutt spent his final days, and being there, I could almost sense the lingering echoes of his thoughts and verses. A bust of the poet, encircled by gentle gardens and a peaceful path, stands as a tribute to his legacy. It's not grand in size, but it's rich in emotion and cultural depth.
What makes the visit especially worthwhile is the serene setting. The nearby river, the open skies, and the calmness of Sagar Island create a reflective mood—perfect for remembering a poet who gave Bengal some of its most revolutionary works, blending Western form with Indian soul.
Reading his lines etched in plaques, I was reminded of how he challenged norms and gave voice to new ideas. It felt like a poetic pilgrimage. Locals I spoke with were proud of their connection to Madhusudan, and their stories added depth to the visit.
For lovers of history, literature, or those simply seeking a quiet place of inspiration, the Michael Madhusudan Dutt Memorial offers a heartfelt journey through time, words, and Bengal’s cultural soul.

A nice museum made with a noble intention, but which is not being maintained very well. It includes the buildings and structures that once comprised the birthplace of Poet Michael Madhusudan Dutta.

There is a big lake as one enters the complex. Inside, there are exhibits that were once the possessions of Madhusudan's family. Also, the exact location where Madhusudan was born is clearly marked, for the benefit of the visitors. One can also walk into the adjacent property with an imposing building that happened to be the residence of Madhusudan's uncle.  The gardens in the premises also seem to be well taken care of.

However, it is quite noticeable that the exhibits within are not very well-maintained as evidenced by the dust and dirt on the glass enclosures. There are guides inside who do not seem in any way interested in volunteering to provide any relevant information. In fact, the guide sitting within the library seemed more interested in his cellphone that the visitors. Some of the buildings there also seemed to require some serious cleaning and painting of their walls.

The approach road to the museum is also narrow, with makeshift shops lining either side. Driving in, one also has to snake through the human traffic on that road.

Overall, a nice place to spend some time with family and friends.

Michel Modhusudan Datta, poet, dramatist and the creator of first epic written in Bangla was born in 24th January, 1828 at Sagordari of Keshobpur Upazilla situated in Jessore. His great grandfather Ramkishore Dutta was a resident of Gopalpur village of Tala Upazilla of Satkhira District. Modhusudan’s father Rajnarayan Dutta was made landlord of Sagordari and he built this famous house of Sagordari. In the village of Sagardari of Keshabpur upazila, the house of poet Madhukasudan Dutta is situated on the bank of the river Kopotakkho. An old two storey and multiple single storey buildings combine together in this house. In 26th October of 1965, government has declared this as an archeological site. At present a museum and library has been established at this house. The museum has a collection of furniture, utensils and other belongings used by the poet's family. In 1968, Department of Archeology renovated this house and built boundary wall, a gate, a cultural arena and reception building for the visitors. Surrounding this ancestral house of Madhusudan, Zilla Parishad Dakbanglow and Sagardari Tourism Centre is established.

Madhumela has become a part of Jessore's tradition. The fair is organized every year on the occasion of Michel Madhusudan Dutta's birth anniversary in the end of January under the direct supervision of the district administration. It is said that after the death of poet, his niece poet Manokumari Bose had first organized a memorial of this poet in Sagardari. Since that time Madhumelara was being venerated there. Madhumela is one of the biggest fairs in Bangladesh with attractions like varieties of stalls of local products, cultural performance, folk songs and drama shows where a spectacle of Bengali tradition and culture can be found.

Durgasagar is the largest historical pond (dighi) or water reservoir in the southern region of Bangladesh and one of the most popular tourist attractions in Barishal. It is located at Madhabpasha in Babuganj Upazila, about 12 kilometers north of Barishal city.

From Nathullabad Bus Terminal or the central bus station in Barishal, visitors can reach Durgasagar by local bus, Mahindra (three-wheeler), or auto-rickshaw on the Madhabpasha/Chakhar route. The journey takes only 20–25 minutes.

In 1780, Raja Shib Narayan, the then ruler of Chandradwip Pargana, excavated this large pond at Madhabpasha to address the local community's water shortage. The pond was named Durgasagar after his mother, Durga Devi. Unlike many historical sites that are maintained by the Department of Archaeology, Durgasagar is managed by the District Administration.

Every year, a variety of migratory birds visit Durgasagar, making it an attractive destination for bird watchers. The site also has a mini zoo where visitors can see emus, monkeys, deer, and peacocks.

Durga Sagar isn’t just a spot on the map — it’s a part of my childhood. I still remember when this place used to be flocked with “otithi pakhi” (migratory birds) during the winter months. The sight of those birds over the calm water was truly magical.

I’ve come here countless times to fish, and many of my best memories are of friends and family hangouts by the lake — laughing, running around as a kid, and watching the sun raise & sunset. Even today, the peaceful atmosphere and open water make it a wonderful escape from city life. But now there is a little zoo where you will find monkeys jumping around and deers as well.

I just hope it continues to be preserved and cared for so future generations can enjoy the same natural charm that we grew up with.

Durga Sagar is the largest lake in southern Bangladesh, named after Rani Durgabati, the mother of Raja Joy Narayan. It is situated in Madhabpasha village of Babuganj Upazila, about 11 kilometres away from Barishal town. Tourists can reach it by road through bus, auto van, or Alpha (local vehicle) from Barisal City.

review_text:
A Relaxing Day Trip to Durga Sagar

I recently visited Durga Sagar from Dhaka. The journey was enjoyable and easy to plan. Starting at 7:00 AM from the Technical Bus Stand, I took a Hanif Paribahan bus, which took about 4 hours to reach Barisal.

If you're planning to visit, inform the conductor to drop you at Goriarpar Bus Stand. From there, you can hire local transport for just 20 BDT per person to reach Madhobpasha. Ask the driver to stop at the Durga Sagar gate. Entry tickets cost 20 BDT per person.

Durga Sagar is a serene and picturesque spot. The main attraction is a beautiful man-made lake with historical significance. Legend has it that the lake was dug by King Shib Narayan, the ruler of Chandradip. In the middle of the lake, there is a small island that adds to its charm.

The area offers a long walking trail, plenty of seating for rest, and well-maintained picnic spots. A mini zoo and water boat services are also available for visitors. Public restrooms are conveniently located as well.

Interestingly, a few years ago, the lake used to attract many migratory birds, but their presence has diminished, possibly due to climate changes.

Durga Sagar is a perfect place to relax and connect with nature. If you're seeking tranquility and a glimpse of history, this destination is worth the trip.

I came back at 4:00 PM,  and take a return ticket for 6:00 pm towords dhaka from nathullabad bus counter. It was 17 hours of day trip.
