The tranquil hills of Bandarban, Buddha Dhatu Jadi, popularly known as the Golden Temple, stands as one of the most peaceful and spiritually uplifting destinations in Bangladesh. Visiting this temple feels like stepping into a serene world far removed from the noise and rush of everyday life. As a traveler, I found the journey itself enchanting—the winding roads, lush greenery, and fresh mountain breeze beautifully set the tone for the experience ahead.
The moment the golden structure came into view, shimmering under the sunlight, it felt almost surreal. The temple’s Burmese-style architecture is truly captivating, with its ornate designs, graceful curves, and the stunning golden hue that radiates calm and purity. The entire complex is incredibly well-maintained, reflecting the devotion and care poured into preserving this sacred place. Walking through its grounds, I felt a deep sense of tranquility, enhanced by the soft sound of prayer bells and the peaceful atmosphere that surrounds every corner.
One of the highlights of my visit was the panoramic view from the hilltop. The sweeping landscapes of Bandarban—rolling hills, distant valleys, and endless greenery—stretch out like a painting. It’s the perfect spot for reflection, photography, or simply soaking in the beauty of nature. The temple also houses a sacred relic of Buddha, making it spiritually significant for Buddhist devotees and culturally enriching for visitors of all backgrounds.
What touched me most was the quiet dignity of the place. Despite being a popular tourist destination, Buddha Dhatu Jadi retains its calm charm, encouraging visitors to slow down and appreciate the harmony between faith, architecture, and nature.
Whether you're a spiritual seeker, a nature lover, or a curious traveler exploring Bangladesh’s hill tracts, a visit to the Bandarban Golden Temple is an unforgettable experience—one that refreshes the mind, inspires the heart, and leaves you with lasting peace.

The Bandarban Golden Temple, also known as Buddha Dhatu Jadi, stands majestically atop a hill in Bandarban, Bangladesh, offering a serene sanctuary for spiritual seekers and travelers alike. This iconic temple, adorned with golden spires and intricate architectural details, is a testament to the rich cultural heritage and religious diversity of the region.

The journey to the Bandarban Golden Temple is as enchanting as the destination itself, with winding roads leading visitors through picturesque landscapes of rolling hills and verdant forests. Upon arrival, visitors are greeted by the sight of the gleaming golden pagoda rising gracefully against the backdrop of the azure sky.

Stepping into the temple grounds, one is enveloped by an aura of tranquility and reverence. The temple complex encompasses lush gardens, meditation halls, and prayer rooms, providing ample space for reflection and contemplation. Visitors can explore the intricate Buddhist sculptures and artwork that adorn the temple walls, each telling a story of wisdom and enlightenment.

One of the highlights of a visit to the Bandarban Golden Temple is the panoramic view it offers of the surrounding countryside. From the temple's vantage point, visitors can gaze out over the rolling hills and lush valleys, taking in the natural beauty that surrounds them.

Whether you're a devout Buddhist seeking spiritual enlightenment or simply a traveler looking to immerse yourself in the rich culture of Bangladesh, a visit to the Bandarban Golden Temple is a truly transformative experience that will leave a lasting impression on your heart and soul.

Saint Martin's Island is one of the popular places in Bangladesh. If you want to go there, you have to journey by ship, and this experience will stay in your memory for a long time. However, be cautious before booking a resort room because the resort owner may present a positive image, but in reality, it may not be the same, and they may ask for a high price. Another important thing is the food; there are many food hotels, but their food quality, taste, and hygiene may not be good, sometimes leading to food poisoning.

From my experience, I suggest "Euro Bangla Restaurant" as their food quality is better than any other restaurant, even though the prices are similar. The environment is also good. When you reach there, take care of your health and drink as much water as you can. The intense sunlight makes it advisable to bring sunglasses and sunblock cream to protect yourself. For a more enjoyable travel experience, explore the west part of the island; the sea views and sunset are excellent.

Don't miss the fish BBQ, and when doing so, choose fresh fish from the local fish market open after 5:00 pm. Enjoy your travels and keep your surroundings clean. Lastly, when going to Saint Martin's Island by ship, you will see lots of seagulls. They may approach you for food, but don't give them chips or biscuits as it can be harmful to their digestion. Seagulls prefer fish, so if you want to feed them, offer fish. Otherwise, refrain from giving any food. Have a nice trip!

review_text:
St. Martin is a small island in the south eastern part of Bangladesh. This is the southern most point of Bangladesh. It is in the north east part of Bay of Bengal. This island is almost flat and is 3.6 meter above sea level and about 8 kilometer long. St. Martin is the only coral island in Bangladesh. Exotic view of the sea, simple life style of the natives, quiet, peaceful and full of enthusiasm made this island best tourist island of Bangladesh.

St.Martin is a popular tourist destination in Bangladesh for both local and foreign travelers in Bangladesh. It is like a pearl dot in the Bay of Bengal. It is situated at the entrance of Bangladesh-Myanmar border river Naaf. The old name of this island is "Narikel Jinjira" means coconut garden. In 1717 christian priest father Martin came in this island and since then it has been named as Saint Martin's island.

Don't see only...feel the island

this island is much for feeling inside than seeing. You see the bay, the beach, coconut trees, birds, hear the sound of the waves like a melody , all of these you don't just see or hear, you feel them inside as well. Such a strong appeal is there in St.Martin's island.

If you enjoy staying in cottages in an island, don't miss to stay here also in St.Marins coz there are some wonderful resorts here. Real rural cottages are nicely decorated in the resorts. So, you will also be able to feel the ancient surroundings where there is no electricity at late night, get water only from coconut, moon lit bright night..its all thrill.

Every resort is along the beach. So, beach is where you actually stay. Most famous resorts among those are Shimana Periey, Nil Digonte etc. There are some hotels also here to stay such as Prashad Paradise, Blue Marine, Abakash parjatan motel etc.

Things to do

You can go around this island by motor boats. It is only about 8 km long and about 1000 meter to 1500 meter wide. Sun bathing is so enjoyable here as this island is so quiet. There are few facilities here for scuba diving and snorkeling.

Most attractive sight in St.Martin is Cherra dwip (detached island). This is a tiny part of this island which becomes detached from the main island during high tide. Her the water is so blue and quiet. Life under water is so nice to watch here.

Nilgiri, Bandarban is truly one of the most mesmerizing destinations in Bangladesh—especially if you’re lucky enough to catch the clouds rolling in. When the weather is right, it feels like you’re standing above the clouds, with soft mist swirling around the hills and panoramic views that will leave you speechless. The early mornings are particularly magical, with golden sunlight filtering through the mist. Photographers and nature lovers will find this place unforgettable.
However, while the natural beauty is world-class, the amenities fall short. There’s a noticeable lack of restrooms, which can be inconvenient—especially for families or those planning to stay a bit longer. Proper restaurants are also missing; you’ll find a few small stalls or local eateries, but don’t expect much in terms of variety, hygiene, or comfort.
If you plan to visit, bring your own snacks and water, and be prepared for minimal facilities. Still, the views alone make Nilgiri worth the trip. Try to go early in the morning or after a rainy night for the best chance to see the clouds. With a bit more infrastructure, this could easily become one of the top tourist destinations in the country.

review_text:
Nilgiri is truly the "Darjeeling of Bengal," and it's a destination that lives up to every bit of its reputation. As a passionate traveler and Local Guide, I can confidently say this is one of the most spectacular viewpoints in all of Bangladesh.

The Experience:
The main attraction here is the breathtaking panoramic view from 2200 feet above sea level. On a good day, you are literally among the clouds. The feeling of watching a sea of clouds drift below you is surreal and incredibly serene. The entire area is managed by the Bangladesh Army, so it's exceptionally clean, well-organized, and secure.

Planning Your Visit (Key Info for Travelers):

Getting There: It's about 50 km from Bandarban town. The journey itself is an adventure through winding hill roads. You'll need to hire a local vehicle like a "Chander Gari" (the open-top jeeps are the best for views), a regular Jeep, or a CNG. A round trip will cost between 3,000 to 5,000 BDT depending on the vehicle and season.

Costs: The entry fee is 50 BDT per person, and there's a separate parking fee for vehicles (around 300 BDT).

Best Time to Go: For the iconic sea of clouds, visit during the rainy season or autumn (July to October). For crisp, clear skies and stunning long-distance views, the winter months (November to February) are ideal.

Food: There's a restaurant on-site which is quite convenient. The food is decent, and you can expect to pay around 350-450 BDT per person for a meal.

Accommodation Tip:
If you want to wake up to the clouds, you can stay at the beautiful Nilgiri Resort. However, booking is extremely competitive. You need to book at least 1-2 months in advance, and it typically requires a reference from a high-ranking army official. The cottages range from 4,000 to 10,000 BDT per night. If you can't stay here, a day trip from Bandarban town is still absolutely worth it.

Nilgiri, located in the Bandarban District of Bangladesh, is an enchanting destination that offers visitors breathtaking scenic beauty. Situated approximately 40 kilometers from the Bandarban main town, reaching Nilgiri is an adventure in itself. The roads to Nilgiri are challenging, with numerous turns and hilly terrains making the journey far from easy or comfortable. However, the stunning landscape that greets you upon arrival makes the arduous trip worthwhile.

Traveling to Nilgiri from Dhaka involves a long journey of around 500 kilometers. The road conditions from Bandarban to Nilgiri are less than ideal, characterized by numerous turns and steep ascents and descents. Despite these difficulties, the trip is memorable for the breathtaking views of the lush green hills that surround you.

Nilgiri's natural beauty is unparalleled. The area is sparsely populated, allowing visitors to enjoy an uninterrupted expanse of green, tree-covered mountains. The panoramic views and the serene environment provide a perfect escape from the hustle and bustle of city life. Visitors often find themselves wanting to return to this tranquil haven, despite the challenging journey.

The Nilgiri resort, constructed and maintained by the Bangladesh Army, is well-organized and clean, ensuring a comfortable stay for visitors. The disciplined maintenance means you won't encounter any litter or unkempt areas, adding to the overall pleasant experience.

Given its location and the challenging terrain, security is a priority. The road to Nilgiri is monitored by the Bangladesh Army, and travelers must pass through several checkposts. Visitors are required to return to Bandarban before dusk, ensuring safety and security for all.

While the beauty of Nilgiri is undeniable, the long and challenging journey makes it more suitable for young travelers. It is not recommended for elderly individuals or families with young children due to the rough roads and the extended travel time.

For those without their own vehicle, local transportation options include CNGs and a type of vehicle known as "Chander Gari." However, these can be quite expensive due to a strong local syndicate. Traveling in groups can help minimize costs, as CNGs can accommodate five passengers and Chander Garis can seat up to eleven.

Nilgiri is a gem of natural beauty that promises an unforgettable experience for those willing to brave the journey. The pristine environment, managed meticulously by the Bangladesh Army, coupled with the stunning vistas, make it a destination worth visiting. Despite the long distance from Dhaka and the challenging travel conditions, the beauty of Nilgiri leaves a lasting impression, making every effort to reach it truly worthwhile.

Nestled amidst the lush greenery of nature's paradise, Nilgiri Mountain stands tall, beckoning adventurers seeking the thrill of a lifetime. This mountain is not for the faint-hearted; it's a wild ride filled with both breathtaking beauty and adrenaline-pumping challenges.

The journey to the summit of Nilgiri is an adventure for everyone, but be prepared for the unexpected. The streets leading to this majestic peak are not for the timid driver. They wind and twist, hugging the mountain's slopes, often narrowing to the point where passing another vehicle feels like threading a needle. The roads are risky and dangerous, demanding your full attention and skill behind the wheel. For those who dare, it's a true test of their driving abilities.

The sense of accomplishment that washes over you at Nilgiri's peak is unparalleled. You've conquered not only the treacherous roads but also your own fears. Whether you're a seasoned thrill-seeker or someone looking to challenge themselves, Nilgiri Mountain offers an adventure that will leave an indelible mark on your memory.

In conclusion, Nilgiri Mountain is a thrilling adventure that is not for the faint of heart. Its risky and dangerous roads will test your mettle, but the reward at the summit is worth every hairpin turn and nerve-wracking moment. The view from the top is a mesmerizing spectacle that makes this journey one you'll remember for a lifetime. So, gear up, embrace the challenge, and prepare for an adventure like no other on Nilgiri Mountain.

review_text:
If you want to touch the clouds, you will have to go to Nilgiri, Bandarban. At Nilgiri, the cloud will come to you, even you can catch it with your hands. On the above, the blue sky, and the white cloud are playing in the mountain of Nilgiri. It is a place of spectacular beauty. Due to Nilgiri, Bandarban is called Darjeeling of Bangladesh. For those who love adventure, the best night in your life may be the Nilgiri. On the way to Nilgiri, you can see the beauty of Bandarban.

Nilgiri is a place with the combination of the tallest peak, the tribal village with a vibrant culture and colorful lifestyle of the villagers, and the spectacular natural beauty. This place gives the visitors a feel like floating in the kingdom of clouds. The Nilgiri resort is a popular resort where you can stay Overnight. Travel to Nilgiri through zigzag hilly roads amidst green and blue landscape is a lifetime experience.

How To Go
If you want to go to Nilgiri from any part of the country, you have to come to Bandarban first. From Bandarban to Nilgiri, you can go by Jeep, Chander Gari, Mahendra, CNG, or by local bus. The best way is to get a reserve car. It will help you to explore some of the surrounding areas of Nilgiri and Bandarban. If you want to come back within the day, you have to pick up the car from Bandarban Jeep Station. According to different cars, it may cost you BDT 3000 to 5000. In a Chander Gari, you may go 12 – 14 people, with the Landcruizer type jeep, you may go 7 to 8 people, with the Small jeep you may go to 4 to 5 people and with CNG you may go 2 to 3 persons.

On the way to Nilgiri, due to security concerns, the name and addresses of the tourists need to be recorded on the army checkpoint. For this reason, there is no other way or not allowed to go to Nilgiri after 5 PM. So keep the eye on the time before travel. For traveling to the Nilgiri, as a tourist, you will need tickets with BDT 50 per person and BDT 300 for parking the car.

"Mayung Kopal, often referred to as 'স্বর্গের সিঁড়ি' (Stairway to Heaven), is a breathtaking natural marvel nestled in the serene landscapes of Bangladesh. This enchanting location is not just a destination; it's an experience that will leave you in awe of the beauty of nature.

As you embark on the journey to Mayung Kopal, the lush greenery and tranquil ambiance set the stage for what lies ahead. The pathway leading to the site is adorned with vibrant flora and fauna, offering glimpses of the rich biodiversity of the region. **Debtakhum (Debota Khum), Bandarban**
Debtakhum, also spelled *Debota Khum* or *Debtachhara*, is a stunning natural waterfall and stream located in the remote hills of Bandarban District, Bangladesh. Nestled near the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, it is part of the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT), renowned for its rugged terrain, dense forests, and indigenous cultural heritage.

### Key Features:
1. **Waterfall & Stream**:
- The site is famed for its cascading waterfall, which flows over layered rocks into a serene, crystal-clear pool. The stream meanders through rocky formations and lush greenery, creating a picturesque landscape.
- The name "Debtakhum" (or "Debota Khum") likely derives from local indigenous languages, with *"khum"* meaning "waterfall" in Marma or other CHT dialects.

2. **Location & Accessibility**:
- Situated near **Ruma Upazila**, Debtakhum is approximately 45 km from Bandarban town. Access requires a 4-5 hour trek from Ruma Bazar, often through challenging hilly trails.
- The journey involves crossing rivers, bamboo bridges, and indigenous villages, offering an adventurous experience for trekkers.

3. **Indigenous Cultural Context**:
- The area is inhabited by the **Marma** and **Bawm** indigenous communities, who rely on traditional jhum (shifting) cultivation. Visitors can experience their unique customs and hospitality.
- Local guides are essential for navigation, as trails are unmarked and remote.

4. **Ecotourism & Challenges**:
- Debtakhum remains relatively untouched by mass tourism, attracting adventurers and nature enthusiasts. Its isolation preserves its pristine beauty but also poses risks, such as limited infrastructure and communication.
- Conservation efforts are critical to protect the ecosystem from littering and unregulated tourism.

### Significance:
Debtakhum is part of Bandarban’s growing ecotourism circuit, alongside landmarks like **Nilgiri**, **Boga Lake**, and **Keokradong**. It highlights the CHT’s natural splendor and cultural diversity, though travelers must prioritize responsible tourism practices to sustain its fragile environment.

**Note**: Due to its proximity to the Myanmar border, visitors may require special permits from local authorities. Always coordinate with registered tour operators and respect local customs during visits.

Tucked away in the remote forested hills of Bandarban, Debotakhum is a place where myth and nature blend seamlessly. The name Debotakhum comes from two words: “Debota” meaning deity and “Khum” meaning deep water hole or gorge in the Marma language. According to local folklore, this mystical water body was once believed to be a dwelling place of guardian spirits or forest deities. The sacred silence of this place still carries a sense of divine presence—like nature itself is watching over.

The adventure begins far before you reach the khum. You trek through narrow forest paths, cross bamboo bridges, and follow the sound of gentle jhiri streams. In some places, waterfalls pour so gracefully down mossy stones that you might think you’ve accidentally walked into Kashmir. The air feels cooler, the light softer, and every turn reveals a new piece of hidden paradise.

Finally, you arrive at Debotakhum. Here, a small dinga boat glides over calm, emerald water between two towering cliffs, like something out of a fantasy film. The silence is surreal—no cell network, no GPS—just you, the water, and the soul of the hills.

What makes Debotakhum truly special is how untouched it feels. Most tourists don’t know about it. Even many local guides aren’t aware of the exact way in. That’s what makes it a true hidden gem—a secret carved into the forest, waiting for the right adventurer to find it.

Rating: 5/5 – If you’re seeking nature, myth, silence, and breathtaking beauty—Debotakhum is a place that will speak to your soul.

🌳 Debotakhum is like a magical forest where nature is at its best. We started our journey from Bandarban at 10 AM, riding in a special kind of taxi called CNG. By noon, we reached a place called Rowangchhari and got someone to help us, called a guide. We also had to stop at Kachapatali Bazar for a quick check by the Army.

Then, we began walking through the forest towards Debotakhum. It took about an hour of walking on the hilly paths, but when we finally got there, we were amazed by its beauty! We spent two fun hours there, riding on boats, taking lots of pictures, and just enjoying the view.

After that, we went back to Kachapatali Bazar and had lunch. It was a tiring but super exciting adventure, and Debotakhum is a place that everyone should see at least once! 🌿🚣‍♂️

review_text:
Debotakhum - the wonderland of adventure
Adventurous, divergent, and eye-catching – three words to describe Bandarban, one of the country's most beautiful places of enormous natural magnificence and scenery. The beauty of its rainforests, various waterfalls, highest peaks, and traditions of its 15 distinct ethnic groups draw visitors from home and abroad.
Bandarban is regarded as the Dynasty of Khumah, and the Debotakhum must adorn the crown of perfection in this kingdom. The scenery around Debotakhum, which is in the Rowangchhari Upazila of the Bandarban region, is beautiful and adds to the area's charm.

The Story of Debotakhum
The term 'khum' in Marma means a waterfall. Debotakhum is almost 50 to 70 feet deep and 600 feet long, making it considerably wider and larger than Belakhum, another adjacent khum.
Despite the name Debotakhum, there is no Hindu idol to be seen here. The naming of the place has an intriguing history.
As per the ethnic locals, this Khum contained an unidentified animal weighing more than 80 kg. Many people noticed this monster earlier in the khum's water, but now it can't be seen according to them. They regard this creature as a god. Since the Bengali word 'debota' means 'god,' the location became popular as Debotakhum.
If you wish to visit the Debotakhum, you must first get permission from the Kachaptali military camp and travel to Shilbandha para.
Visitors must make the bamboo whale from Shilabadha para. Then they need to pass Pong Su Ang Khum. The Debotakhum will begin after passing Pong Su Ang Khum. Sonakhum is the name given by the locals. In the Marma language, it is known as Thongchikhum.

Special Features of The Khum
Debotakhum's route is both lovely and dreadful. Although the trail is beautiful in the rainy seasons, sliding on the slick, rocky terrain is also dangerous. As a result, it is also quite risky.
Debotakhum is particularly dark on the interior due to its location in the middle of two large hills. It can drive your mind dreadfully. Sunshine is also scarce here.
The Khum is a hiking, adventure, risk, and whale kayaking package. You can hear the sounds of nature, water, and your own echo. The surroundings are so strange and quiet that you'll feel like you're on a true adventure.
There is no sound but the running river and no mobile network. There is complete silence all around, giving the impression of a haunted environment. The sound of water splattering will intensify the creepy ambience.
Visitors must navigate the passage by raft across the middle of two hills. From here, one can experience and appreciate the splendour of nature up close. This route may also serve as a reminder of how lovely the way to paradise might be.

How to Reach
To begin with, you can travel to Bandarban from anywhere in Bangladesh. You may take any CNG/bus/motorcycle to Rowangchhari. Then you may again need to take a bus or a CNG to Kacchaptali. Finally, it is just half an hour or an hour's walk to the destination.
Generally, the Non-AC Bus fare from Dhaka to Bandarban may be BDT 620. (it may vary). CNG rent from Rowangchhari to Kacchaptali would cost at least BDT 150-200.

Things to Keep in Mind
You need to go to Kacchaptali and verify the military camp with your guides. Keeping a copy of the NID card/passport is necessary. It is advisable to inform the guide about your intention to turn around ahead of time. There will be difficulties with the network.
On Kacchaptali, you can only use the Robi/Airtel network. However, you will be entirely disconnected from the network on your trip to Khum. If trekking is inconvenient, purchase. It will cost about TK 120-150. Don't forget to wear a life jacket while riding the boat.

review_text:
Devtakhum is a stunning natural reservoir, or "khum," nestled in the heart of Bandarban's Ruma Upazila, Bangladesh. It's an extension of the Tarasa Canal, characterized by towering hills and dense jungle on either side. Locals estimate its depth to be around 50-70 feet and its length approximately 600-700 feet, making it one of the largest and most captivating khums in the region. Unlike some other more accessible spots, Devtakhum offers a wilder, more mysterious experience.
Why Visit Devtakhum?
The primary draw of Devtakhum lies in its tranquil, secluded environment and the thrilling experience of exploring it on a bamboo raft. The sheer cliffs block direct sunlight, making the interior of the khum progressively cooler and more serene as you venture deeper. The crystal-clear water and the surrounding quiet create an exceptional sense of adventure and connection with nature.
Nearby, you'll also find Pong Su Ang Khum, a smaller khum that you typically pass through on the way to Devtakhum, and Shilbandha Waterfall, adding to the natural beauty of the area.
How to Get to Devtakhum
Your journey to Devtakhum begins in Bandarban city.
* Dhaka to Bandarban:
* Bus: Direct bus services from Dhaka to Bandarban are available. Non-AC buses usually cost around BDT 850-900, while AC buses range from BDT 1500-1800.
* Train: If you prefer train travel, take any Dhaka-to-Chittagong train. From Chittagong, you can then catch a bus or hire a private car to Bandarban.
* Bandarban to Roangchhari:
* Roangchhari Upazila is about 20 kilometers from Bandarban town. Buses depart every hour from the Bandarban bus stand for Roangchhari, costing approximately BDT 60.
* You can also hire a local jeep (known as a 'chander gari') for BDT 2000-2500 (fits 12-13 people) or a CNG auto-rickshaw for around BDT 150-200.
* Roangchhari to Kacchoptoli:
* Kacchoptoli Bazaar is about 5-7 kilometers from Roangchhari. A CNG will take you there for about BDT 150.
* Alternatively, you can book a direct jeep from Bandarban to Kacchoptoli.
* Permissions and Trekking:
* Permission is mandatory. You'll need to obtain permission from both the Roangchhari Police Station and the Kacchoptoli Army Camp. Remember to carry photocopies of your National ID card; the permission form usually costs around BDT 50.
* From Kacchoptoli, it's about an hour-long trek to Shilbandha Para. Devtakhum is close to Shilbandha Para, but you'll first cross Pong Su Ang Khum, which may require swimming or swinging across using tree roots.
* At Shilbandha Para, you'll need to arrange a sturdy bamboo raft. The cost for entering the khum, including raft rental and a life jacket, is around BDT 200 per person.
* It's compulsory to hire a local guide. One guide is required for every 10 people, and their fee is typically around BDT 1000 for the day.
Important Travel Tips
* Best Time to Visit: While Devtakhum can be visited year-round, November to April is ideal. During the monsoon (June to October), water levels are higher, which can make trekking challenging and the water less clear, though the surrounding greenery is vibrant. The local administration has announced Devtakhum reopened for tourists starting June 26, 2025, due to improving weather conditions, but caution is still advised during the monsoon.
* Safety First: Be very careful during trekking, as paths can be slippery, especially during or after rain. Always wear a life jacket inside the khum. Avoid any risky maneuvers.
* Preparation is Key:
* Carry at least two photocopies of your National ID card.
* Stock up on water and dry snacks at Kacchoptoli Bazaar, as it's the last place to buy supplies.
* Wear appropriate trekking sandals or shoes.
* Mobile network coverage might be limited to Robi/Airtel in some areas, so plan accordingly.
* Always travel in a group and with a local guide.
* Environmental Responsibility: Help preserve this beautiful natural wonder. Do not litter or harm the environment in any way.

Devatakhum as beautiful as the picture! 💙

But to enjoy this kind of beauty you have to go from the end of December or the beginning of January to the middle.

It is possible to come back from Bandarban city day by day and enjoy this unearthly beauty.

From Bandarban you have to travel 1.30 hours to Roangchhari, from there you have to take police clearance to Kachhapathali Bazar. From there you have to enter the army camp with the guide and start the journey to Devtakhum.

The entire road from Kachhapathali to Devatakhum has to be walked. The distance of the road is approximately 6 kilometers. It takes about 1 / 1.30 hours to walk.

There are two ways to go, one is hilly road (a little difficult) the other is jhiri path. If you want, one can go to one road and come back to another road.
Before going to Devtakhum, you will wear Shilbandha Para. Some of the way you have to go by boat and the rest of the way you have to go by raft. If you want, you can go all the way by boat, but the real fun is in the raft.

Eating and drinking, if the car is fixed in advance, you can stay worry-free. The guide will help you in this matter.

Happy traveling. 🖤

Debotakhum is a trail located at Kacchaptali Rowangchhari upazila under Bandarban. It might take 20/30 mins by bus from the main city of Bandarban.

A few things must be remembered since it’s crucial needed highly.

1. For tourists (not mandatory for local) must have to get permission from Rowangchhari Police Station and then head forward to Kacchaptoli Army Camp for another permission.

2. Tourists (not mandatory for local) cannot visit without "GUIDE".

3. If you want to lunch at Kacchaptali, make it sure with preorder at the local restaurants. Otherwise, you'll starve whole day.

4. Take off your soppy clothes, full pants, and shoes if you have, since the street you have to walk for about 1 hour or more from Kacchaptali is so slippery, muddy, rocky. Therefore, to avoid any kind of awkward or hindrance, you have to get yourself fit all the way.

5. Don’t get on the raft if you don’t know how to swim.

6. Please always follow the instructions by the GUIDE and the people who are assigned to the discipline.

NOTE: Please don’t throw anything made of plastic anywhere.

review_text:
Debotakhum is truly one of the most mesmerizing natural wonders in Bangladesh. Located deep in the Rowangchhari upazila of Bandarban, this khum (gorge) offers a surreal and almost mystical experience that feels like stepping into another world. Surrounded by towering limestone cliffs and dense green forest, the crystal-clear waterway stretches for nearly half a kilometer, and in some parts is so narrow you can touch both sides of the rock walls while floating on a boat.

The only way to explore the khum is by a locally crafted narrow wooden boat (dingi), which silently glides through the still water. The silence, broken only by bird calls and the dip of the paddle, is unbelievably peaceful. It’s best to visit early in the morning when the sun peeks through the cliffs and creates golden reflections in the water.

Reaching Debotakhum requires a bit of adventure—you’ll need to hike or take a bamboo raft from Remakri or Tindu, depending on your chosen route. It’s not very commercialized yet, which is part of its charm.

If you're looking for a mix of serenity, adventure, and raw natural beauty, Debotakhum should be at the top of your list. Just remember to travel responsibly and respect the pristine environment.

New Zealand Para is a stunning and popular village located in Khagrachhari district. It is about 1.5 kilometers south of Khagrachhari town, near Pankhai Para. The uniqueness of this village lies in its flat lands, which are rare in the hilly regions of Khagrachhari. Surrounded by lush green fields and hills, the serene environment makes it a charming destination.

Locals compare the natural beauty and green fields of this area to those of New Zealand. Hence, the village has been named "New Zealand Para."

A blend of flat, green farmland and surrounding hills. Tranquil environment and refreshing weather. Easy accessibility for tourists. New residential areas are being developed along the hillsides.

New Zealand Para is easily accessible from Khagrachhari town. You can take a CNG or auto-rickshaw for just 10 BDT to reach the village. It’s also a great stopover on the way to Sajek Valley.

If you love nature and wish to enjoy a peaceful setting, New Zealand Para is an ideal destination for you.

According to geologists in Bangladesh, Lake Bagakain is the result of a volcanic eruption of a dead volcano or the fall of a meteorite from space.  Many have also suggested that it could be caused by landslides.  It is made up of soft rocks of the Bhuban Foundation.  According to Banglapedia, its water is very acidic and therefore there are no algae or other aquatic plants in it, and no aquatic animals can live here. According to 2009 data, the waters of Boga Lake are very fertile, and the lake has a lot of algae, water lilies, water lilies and other aquatic plants, and lots of fish and even giant fish.

There are myths or legends of Bam, Marma, Mro, Khumi and Tripura about the creation of Lake Bagakain.  One such legend is that there is a Bom Para (Bagamukhpara) and a Murang Para next to Bagahra.  The indigenous tribes are other tribes including Bam, Murang or Mro, Thanchangya and Tripura.  According to local tribal legend, a long time ago a dragon lived in a cave in the mountains.  In Bam language, the dragon is called "Boga".  The locals used to offer cattle to please the dragon god.  But once a few people kill this dragon god, the peak turns into a submerged lake and destroys the villages.  Although there is no real evidence for this legend, the legendary fire-like dragon or white and volcanic structure of the lake coincides with the idea of ​​a dead volcano.

Another legend states that Boga Lake was a prosperous Mro village.  There was a big snake in a tunnel next to the village.  One day the snake was caught and eaten by the villagers.  Due to the revenge of Nagaraja for eating that snake, Boga Lake was created by giving the village along with the villagers.  There are still many bombs, Mro believes, that the water of the lake becomes cloudy when the Nagraj tail, which is deep in the lake, is moved.

review_text:
Nestled in the remote, rugged hills of Bandarban, Bangladesh, Boga Lake is a breathtaking natural wonder that captivates with its mystique and serene beauty. Also known as Bagakain Lake, this stunning body of water sits approximately 1,200 to 1,800 feet above sea level, making it the highest natural lake in the country. The journey to Boga Lake is an adventure in itself, a testament to the raw, untamed beauty of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
​The lake itself is a spectacle of nature, with its deep blue water reflecting the ever-changing sky. Geologists believe the lake was formed by a volcanic crater or a meteorite fall nearly 2,000 years ago, and its water level is sustained primarily by rainfall. The color of the water is a mesmerizing shade of blue, though it can turn muddy at certain times of the year, a phenomenon that adds to its enigmatic allure.
​Surrounded by a dense, tranquil landscape of bamboo forests and towering peaks, the lake is a sanctuary for both nature lovers and adventurers. The local communities, primarily the Bawm and Khumi tribes, live in small villages around the lake and offer a glimpse into their rich, indigenous culture. Their simple cottages provide the only accommodation for trekkers, offering a rustic and authentic experience.

review_text:
Sajek Valley, often hailed as the "Queen of Hills" or the "Roof of Rangamati," is a breathtaking destination nestled in the Kasalong range of the Chittagong Hill Tracts in Bangladesh. Situated at an altitude of approximately 1,800 feet above sea level, this valley is renowned for its otherworldly scenery where visitors can literally walk through floating clouds. It is located in the Baghaichhari Upazila of Rangamati District, very close to the Mizoram border of India.
The valley is a tapestry of lush green ridges and dense forests, home to indigenous communities like the Chakma, Marma, Tripura, and Lushai. Visitors often stay in traditional-style wooden or bamboo cottages that offer panoramic views of the shifting landscape. Key attractions include the trek to Konglak Hill, the highest point in the valley, and the serene sunsets at the local helipad. While the journey involves an adventurous ride in a "Chander Gari" (open jeep) through winding mountain roads, the unique experience of the "Kingdom of Clouds" makes it one of the most sought-after retreats for nature lovers and backpackers alike.

I recently visited Sajek Valley, one of the most beautiful tourist destinations in Bangladesh, and I must say it was a truly memorable experience. We stayed there for two days and one night, and during this short time, Sajek managed to leave a deep impression on my mind and heart.
The natural beauty of Sajek is beyond description. Surrounded by endless hills, green landscapes, floating clouds, and a calm sky, the place feels like a piece of heaven on earth. The fresh air, peaceful environment, and scenic views make Sajek an ideal destination for anyone who wants to escape the noise and stress of city life. Watching the sunrise and sunset from the hilltops is an unforgettable experience—the way the sun slowly disappears behind the hills while the sky changes colors is simply magical.
Sajek is also a paradise for photography lovers. Almost every corner of this place looks picture-perfect. The roads, hills, clouds, and small local shops together create a unique charm. Spending time here gives a sense of mental peace and refreshment that is hard to find elsewhere.
However, along with all these wonderful aspects, there are a few issues that slightly affected my overall experience. One of the major concerns is the high hotel rent. Compared to the facilities provided, hotel prices are quite expensive, which may not be affordable for many regular tourists. Another noticeable problem is the shortage of water. Access to sufficient water for daily use can be difficult, which creates inconvenience for visitors, especially during peak tourist seasons.
I sincerely hope that the concerned authorities and local management will take necessary steps to resolve these issues soon. If hotel pricing becomes more reasonable and the water problem is properly addressed, Sajek Valley will become an even more attractive and tourist-friendly destination. These improvements will surely encourage more local and international tourists to visit this beautiful place.
Despite these limitations, my overall experience at Sajek Valley was very positive. The breathtaking natural beauty, peaceful atmosphere, and unique hill environment make it a destination worth visiting at least once in a lifetime. I would definitely recommend Sajek Valley to nature lovers and travelers who are looking for calmness, beauty, and a refreshing travel experience.

Nestled in the Kasalong range of the Chittagong Hill Tracts, Sajek Valley is often celebrated as the "Roof of Rangamati" for its elevated position and panoramic vistas. The valley is home to indigenous communities, including the Chakma, Marma, Tripura, and Lushai tribes, each contributing to its rich cultural tapestry.

Anticipation vs. Reality
With high expectations, our group of 27 embarked on a journey to Sajek Valley, eager to experience its famed beauty. We chose to stay at Shoilo Kuthir Resort, drawn by its promise of eco-friendly accommodations crafted from wood and bamboo. However, upon arrival, the resort's capacity seemed stretched for our large group, leading to cramped spaces and inadequate lighting, which diminished the comfort of our stay.

The Overwhelming Evening
Exploring the valley that evening, we were met with unexpected crowds. The proliferation of resorts and ongoing constructions disrupted the natural landscape, making it challenging to find a tranquil spot. The bustling atmosphere, reminiscent of a crowded marketplace, detracted from the serene experience we had envisioned.

A Morning's Respite
The following morning, at 6:30 AM, a friend and I ventured out, hoping to capture the valley's essence. The early hours bestowed a different charm: the roads were enveloped in light fog, a gentle breeze accompanied our steps, and the absence of crowds offered a sense of safety and peace. Our walk led us to the helipad, where, unlike the previous evening's throngs, we encountered only a few individuals. This serene morning walk allowed us to appreciate the valley's true beauty.

Insights into Sajek Valley
Sajek Valley's allure lies in its natural beauty and cultural richness. The valley serves as a cultural mosaic, with indigenous communities like the Chakma and Marma tribes contributing to its diversity. Visitors can immerse themselves in unique traditions, colorful festivals, and local handicrafts.

For those planning a visit, it's advisable to explore the valley during early morning hours to truly appreciate its tranquility. Being prepared for crowds during peak times and choosing accommodations that align with group sizes can enhance the experience.

In conclusion, while Sajek Valley offers moments of unparalleled beauty, it's essential to approach the journey with realistic expectations and thoughtful planning to fully embrace its offerings.

Stay in a hilltop resort for the best morning cloud views.

Sajek Valley, located in the Rangamati district of Bangladesh, is a breathtaking hill station and a popular tourist destination known for its scenic beauty and tranquil atmosphere. Nestled in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, it is often referred to as the "Roof of Rangamati" due to its elevation of approximately 1,800 feet above sea level. The valley is surrounded by lush green hills, dense forests, and a serene river, making it a haven for nature enthusiasts.

One of the highlights of Sajek is its vibrant sunsets and sunrises, offering mesmerizing views that captivate visitors. The valley is also known for its clouds that often hang low, giving the sensation of being above the sky. The indigenous Chakma, Marma, and Tripura communities reside in the area, enriching the cultural experience for travelers.

Key attractions include the Kanglak Hill, the highest peak in Sajek, and the Sajek River, which forms a natural border between Bangladesh and India. Tourists also enjoy exploring the local tribal markets, trying traditional cuisine, and trekking through the hills.

The journey to Sajek Valley itself is an adventure, with winding roads and picturesque landscapes. Accessible primarily via Khagrachari, the area has become increasingly popular for its eco-friendly lodges and campsites. Sajek is an ideal retreat for those seeking a blend of natural beauty, cultural richness, and serene relaxation​

Risang offers a peaceful escape into nature, with lush greenery and a quiet atmosphere that’s perfect for a weekday visit. The viewpoint itself is serene, and the surrounding forest feels untouched. But while the visuals are lovely, the experience comes with a few caveats.

Important Note: The path is steep and risky, especially after rain. There are no proper railings or safety measures, so visitors should tread carefully, this isn’t ideal for children or elderly travelers.

I captured some nice shots of the greenery and a local signboard, but compared to other waterfalls I’ve visited, especially the one in Moulvibazar, Risang falls short. Moulvibazar’s waterfall offers a more dramatic cascade, better accessibility, and a richer overall experience.

I visited on a weekend, so there was a big crowd, but I’d still recommend going with proper footwear and a buddy for safety.

Final Thought: Worth a visit if you’re nearby, but if you’re chasing the best waterfall experience in Bangladesh, Moulvibazar still reigns supreme.

Alutila Cave: Alutila Cave is a natural cave located in Matiranga Upazila of Khagrachhari District, Bangladesh. It is located 8 km west of Khagrachhari city on the top of Alutila (Alur Pahar) or Arbari Hill, which is 3,000 feet above sea level.

This cave is also called Alutila Mysterious Cave. The locals call it Matai Haq or God's Cave.

This cave is 150 meters long inside a 1000-meter-high mountain, which takes about 10 to 15 minutes to enter the cave from one side and exit from the other. The height of the cave is very low in some places, so you have to walk leaning.

It is surrounded by deep green forests at the foot of Alutila Hill. Since sunlight does not enter, the cave is very dark and cold. The cave is so dark that torches or locally sold burning lights are used to walk around the cave. The bottom of the tunnel is slippery and rocky and a spring flow below.

This is a great adventure tourist attraction in Khagrachari.

review_text:
Alutila Tourist Center

Alutila Tourist Center, located in the Matiranga Upazila of Khagrachhari district, is well-known for its tourist attractions, natural beauty, mysterious cave, and serene hilly environment.

Situated about 600 feet above sea level, the Alutila Tourist Center offers breathtaking views of the surrounding hills. One of its main attractions is the hanging bridge, a 184-foot-long iron or cable bridge built to connect two hills. For adventure-loving visitors, the bridge features a glass balcony, allowing them to look down and experience the thrilling sight of the hills from above — as if they are floating in the air.

The area also includes Nandonkanon, a stage modeled after the Roman Colosseum, and a watchtower that offers a panoramic view of the hilly landscape. After an exciting adventure inside the mysterious cave, standing atop the watchtower and breathing in the calm mountain air will surely wash away all your fatigue and fill you with peace.

I visited Alutila Cave a few days ago, and I can confidently say that it is one of the most fascinating and memorable natural attractions I have ever explored in Bangladesh. From the moment I reached the Alutila hill area, I was surrounded by breathtaking natural beauty, fresh mountain air, and a peaceful environment that instantly made the journey worthwhile.
The Alutila Cave itself is absolutely amazing. Walking through the cave felt like stepping into a mysterious underground world. The inside of the cave is naturally dark, cool, and slightly adventurous, with a small stream of water flowing beneath your feet. Using a torch or light makes the experience even more exciting, as every step reveals the raw beauty of nature carved over thousands of years. The rocky paths, narrow passages, and natural formations make the cave exploration thrilling yet safe if you are careful.
What impressed me the most, apart from the cave, were the beautiful bridges located near the cave area. The hanging bridge is truly stunning and offers a wonderful view of the surrounding hills, forests, and valleys. Standing on the bridge and looking around gives you a feeling of calmness and freedom that is hard to describe in words. There is also another bridge nearby (the name slips my mind), which is equally beautiful and adds to the charm of the entire place. These bridges are perfect spots for photography and for simply enjoying the scenic landscape.
The area around Alutila Cave is clean, well-maintained, and full of greenery. Local people and guides are helpful and friendly, which makes the visit more comfortable, especially for first-time travelers. The overall atmosphere feels natural, peaceful, and refreshing—far away from city noise and stress.
Alutila Cave is not just a tourist spot; it is an experience of nature, adventure, and tranquility combined. Whether you love adventure, nature photography, or simply want to enjoy a calm and beautiful environment, this place has something special for everyone.
I highly recommend Alutila Cave to anyone visiting Khagrachhari. It is a must-visit destination in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. I would love to visit again in the future.
A perfect place for nature lovers, adventure seekers, and peace lovers. Truly deserving of five stars!

When travelers finally see the light at the end of the cave, it feels both exciting and rewarding.
Besides adventure, Alutila Hill is also a peaceful place for relaxation. Families and friends often visit to spend quality time together, take photographs, and enjoy the calm environment. Small shops near the entrance sell local snacks and handmade items, allowing tourists to experience a touch of local culture.
In conclusion, Alutila Hill is a perfect blend of natural beauty, adventure, and tranquility. Anyone visiting Khagrachari should not miss the chance to explore this wonderful destination. It truly reflects the charm and serenity of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and leaves visitors with lasting memories.

In conclusion, Alutila Hill is a perfect blend of natural beauty, adventure, and tranquility. Anyone visiting Khagrachari should not miss the chance to explore this wonderful destination. It truly reflects the charm and serenity of the Chittagong Hill Tracts and leaves visitors with lasting memories.

review_text:
Alutila Cave is a natural cave located in Khagrachari district of Bangladesh. Alutila cave is located in the Alutila or Arbari hill at an altitude of 3000 feet above sea level, 7 km west of the main town in Matiranga upazila of Khagrachari district. Locals call it Matai Hakar or God's Cave. This cave is very dark and cold. The small torch in your hand is the only source of light in the cave. The bottom of the tunnel is slippery and rocky and a spring flows beneath it. The cave looks like an underground tunnel with a length of about 350 feet. It takes approximately 10 to 15 minutes to enter from one side of the cave and exit from the other side. As the height of the cave is very low at times, one has to crawl through it at one stage.
The main attraction of Alutila tourist center is its mysterious tunnels. At the foot of the Alutila hill below 266 steps from the top of the hill is the location of this mysterious tunnel built in the folds of rock and soil. The mouth of the cave is about 18 feet in diameter. Before people used bamboo flare to walk across the dark cave. review_text:
Horticulture Heritage Park

Located just 3 kilometers away from the Zero Point of Khagrachhari town — the city of hilly beauty — the Horticulture Heritage Park is managed by the Khagrachhari Hill District Council. Surrounded by lush greenery and built in a beautifully landscaped environment, this park is one of the most popular recreation centers in Khagrachhari. Spread over approximately 22 acres of land, the park’s cottages, entrance gate, and colorful architectural designs captivate visitors with their charm.

Inside the Horticulture Heritage Park, there are stunning attractions such as a hanging bridge, swimming pool, artificial lake, swings, toy train, kids’ zone, boat rides, horse rides, and beautifully arranged flower gardens surrounded by diverse species of trees and plants. The park also includes picnic spots, a guest house, a birds’ park, an observation tower, and an open stage for cultural events. Along the lakeside, there are shops selling various handicrafts made by local hill tribes.

On weekends and holidays, countless nature and fun-loving visitors come here with family and friends to spend quality time amidst the serene and scenic beauty of the hills.

Who does not want to visit or travel the shrine of Hazrat Shajalal (RAH) in Sylhet? The Graveyard or Mazar (Majar) is an attractive place for the Muslims. As they think he is one of the saint who made Sylhet area significant for Islamic believers.

Hazrat Shahjalal (RA) was a famous saint of the Indian subcontinent. Islam spread in the Sylhet region through him. Raja Gour Govinda’s persecution of the first Muslim Sheikh Burhan Uddin of Sylhet and in this context the arrival of Hazrat Shahjalal (RA) and his traveling companion 360 Auliyas in Sylhet is a significant event in the history. For this reason Sylhet is called the land of 360 Auliyas. Some even call Sylhet a holy land. Dargah Sharif is a very sacred place for everyone, so it is not used to attract tourists. For this reason, the custodians of the Dargah decide who can enter the Dargah. Many times visitors are turned away for not wearing decent clothes. So when entering the Dargah, you must pay attention to your clothes.

Thousands of people from different parts of the country, irrespective of religion and caste, come to Sylhet every day to visit the shrine of Hazrat Shahjalal (RA). Many call Sylhet a holy land because of Shahjalal’s touch. Hazrat Shahjalal (Rah) is a famous saint. Islam spread in the Sylhet region through him. Raja Gourgobind’s persecution of the first Muslim Sheikh Burhan Uddin of Sylhet and the consequent arrival of Hazrat Shahjalal (Ra) and his traveling companion 360 Auliya in Sylhet is a significant event in history. There is a pond to the north of Shahjalal’s shrine. There are innumerable Carrot (Gojar) fish in this pond. These fish are considered sacred and are given to the small fish farms by the visitors. Carrot fish floating in the pond gives joy to the visitors.

Recognizing the spiritual power of Hazrat Shahjalal (RA), Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya (RA) welcomed him. As a token of love, he gave her a pair of surma-colored pigeons or jalali pigeons. The Surma-colored pigeons that are now seen in Sylhet and its environs are the descendants of the pair and are known as Jalali pigeons. Pigeons are seen flying in flocks in the area of ​​Shahjalal’s shrine every day. There are many rumors about this pigeon in the minds of the people of Sylhet.

There is a well next to Shahjalal’s shrine. The location of these well silver colored fish can be seen. Water is flowing day and night in this well. If you go to the west side of the shrine, you can see the fountain. Fountain water is sold by filling bottles.

There is a pond to the north of the shrine of Hazrat Shahjalal (RA). And the beauty of this pond is enhanced by innumerable carrot fish. It is said that Hazrat Shahjalal (RA) came to Sylhet with 360 Aulia and brought this fish. These fish are fed by the visitors, giving a lot of pleasure to the tourists floating in the fish pond. There is a well next to the shrine of Shahjalal (RA). Gold and silver colored fish can be seen in this well.It is rumored that Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya, on learning of the spiritual power of Hazrat Shahjalal (ra), welcomed him and gave him a pair of surma-colored pigeons as a sign. This pigeon is now widely known as Jalali pigeon. Pigeons entertain the visitors by flocking to the shrine.

To the south of the shrine is a room just two feet wide with a star-studded grill. It was used as a shrine by Hazrat Shahjalal (RA). It is said that Hazrat Shahjalal (RA) spent about 23 years in worship here. On the left side of the Dargah Madrasa building, in the house of Mufti Nazimuddin Ahmed, there are various things used by the visitors such as swords, clogs, plates, bowls etc. used by Hazrat Shahjalal (RA).

review_text:
Hazrat Shahjalal (R.) Mazar Sharif is one of the most important spiritual and historical landmarks in Sylhet, Bangladesh. Located in the heart of Sylhet city, the shrine attracts devotees and visitors from across Bangladesh and beyond.

A Brief History
Hazrat Shah Jalal (R.), also known as Shah Jalal Mujarrad, was a renowned Sufi saint whose life is closely connected with the spread of Islam in the Sylhet region.
Historical sources connect Shah Jalal (R.) with the Muslim conquest of Sylhet in 1303 AD. According to historical accounts, Sultan Shamsuddin Firuz Shah's forces fought against Raja Gaur Govinda, and Shah Jalal (R.) and his companions became associated with the campaign. After the conquest, Shah Jalal (R.) remained in Sylhet and devoted himself to spiritual practice and preaching.
One of the most notable historical visitors to Shah Jalal's khanqah was the famous Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta, who visited Bengal in the 14th century and met Shah Jalal (R.) in 1346. Historical sources indicate that Shah Jalal (R.) died around 1347 AD and was buried in Sylhet.

The shrine has continued to hold immense religious and cultural importance for centuries. Today, thousands of devotees and visitors come to pay their respects, make dua, and experience the spiritual atmosphere surrounding the historic mazar. The tomb itself is recognized among the important heritage sites of Sylhet.

My Review
Visiting Hazrat Shahjalal (R.) Mazar Sharif is a unique experience. The first thing that stands out is the peaceful and spiritual atmosphere despite the shrine being located in a busy part of Sylhet city.

The site has a strong sense of history. Standing there and thinking about Shah Jalal (R.), his companions, and the centuries of people who have visited this place gives the location a special feeling.

The surrounding area can become very crowded, particularly during busy periods and religious occasions. However, the large number of visitors also reflects how deeply Hazrat Shahjalal (R.) is respected by people.
For anyone visiting Sylhet, I would recommend including this place in their itinerary—not simply as a tourist attraction, but as a significant part of the religious, historical, and cultural heritage of Sylhet.

To the south of the shrine is a room just two feet wide with a star-studded grill. It was used as a shrine by Hazrat Shahjalal (RA). It is said that Hazrat Shahjalal (RA) spent about 23 years in worship here. review_text:
A Profound Spiritual Experience at Hazrat Shahjalal Mazar Sharif
📍 Ambarkhana, Sylhet, Bangladesh
Visiting the holy Mazar Sharif of Hazrat Shahjalal (R.A) in Sylhet is an unforgettable spiritual journey filled with reverence, reflection, and cultural richness. As one of the most sacred and historic Islamic sites in Bangladesh, this shrine attracts pilgrims and tourists from all over the country and beyond.
🕌 Historical & Spiritual Significance:
Hazrat Shahjalal (R.A), a revered Sufi saint and Islamic scholar from the 14th century, played a vital role in spreading Islam in this region. His legacy continues to influence the spiritual and cultural identity of Sylhet. The moment you step into the compound, there is a distinct sense of peace and devotion in the air. The white marble grave, beautifully kept under a green canopy, is surrounded by verses of the Qur'an and supplications from the devotees.
🌿 Ambiance & Architecture:
The Mazar compound blends traditional Islamic architecture with a serene natural environment. The pond with large catfish (often fed by visitors) adds to the uniqueness of the place. There are old trees that give the area a calm, shaded feel—ideal for meditation and silent prayer.
The central shrine structure is modest yet spiritually powerful. The green and white hues of the mosque and tomb, combined with the smell of rosewater and incense, create a deeply immersive environment. The azaan from the nearby mosque further intensifies the spiritual atmosphere.
🧕 Devotional Environment:
Every day, people of all walks of life come to offer Fatiha (prayers) and pay respect. Many visitors bring flowers, chadors (cloth covers), and food to distribute among the poor. Fridays and special Islamic days such as Eid Milad-un-Nabi or Urs of Hazrat Shahjalal are especially crowded and spiritually charged.
Men and women have separate areas, and the staff and caretakers (Mujavirs) are generally respectful and helpful in guiding newcomers through the proper etiquettes of visiting a Mazar.
🧭 Accessibility & Amenities:
The shrine is located in Ambarkhana, a central and easily accessible area in Sylhet City. It is about 20 minutes from the airport and just a few minutes from major bus terminals or train stations. Local rickshaws, CNGs, and rideshare services are available right outside the main gate.
Nearby, you’ll find:
•	Shops selling prayer items, food, and Islamic books
•	Public washrooms (though cleanliness can be improved)
•	Small restaurants and tea stalls for refreshment
•	Security presence is visible, especially during busy hours
🔁 Room for Improvement:
While the spiritual experience is unmatched, some logistical issues persist:
•	Cleanliness of public areas (especially the toilets and outer premises) could be better managed.
•	Better crowd control is needed during peak times and special events.
•	Some aggressive donation collectors can be intrusive—official regulation would help improve the atmosphere.
✅ Final Verdict:
Hazrat Shahjalal Mazar Sharif is not just a religious site—it’s a spiritual heritage that embodies centuries of faith, Sufi tradition, and communal harmony. Whether you're a devout Muslim or a curious traveler interested in history and culture, a visit to this sacred site will leave you introspective and inspired.
Highly recommended for anyone visiting Sylhet.
📅 I have last visited on 10-June-2025.

Jalāl Mujarrad Kunyāī (شيخ جلال مجرد كنيائي),[1] popularly known as Shah Jalal, was a celebrated Sufi figure of Bengal. His name is often associated with the Conquest of Sylhet and the spread of Islam into the region, part of a long history of interactions between the Middle East, Turkestan, and South Asia.[2] Various complexes and religious places have been named after him, including the largest airport in Bangladesh, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.

In 1303, Sultan Shamsuddin Firoz Shah of Lakhnauti was engaged in a war with the neighbouring Gour Kingdom in the Sylhet region, then under the rule of the Hindu king Gour Govinda. This began when Shaykh Burhanuddin, a Muslim living in Sylhet, sacrificed a cow for his newborn son's aqiqah (birth celebration).[14] Govinda, in a fury for what he saw as sacrilege, had the newborn killed as well as having Burhanuddin's right hand cut off.[15]

When word of this reached Sultan Firoz Shah, an army commanded by his nephew, Sikandar Khan and later his Sipah Salar (Commander-in-chief) Syed Nasiruddin, was sent against Gour. Three successive strikes were attempted, all ending in failure due to the Bengali armies inexperience in the foreign terrain as well as Govinda's superior military strategy.[16][15]

A fourth attack, now with the aid of Shah Jalal and his companions (at this point numbering 360) was undertaken.[17] Jalal may have been summoned by Firoz Shah for aid after the initial failed attacks against Gour Govinda. Alternatively, he may already have been present in Sylhet, fighting against the Hindu king independently prior to being approached by the Sultan.[17][18] The combined Muslim forces ultimately claimed victory against Gour. Govinda was forced to retreat and Sylhet was brought under Muslim control. According to tradition, Shah Chashni Pir at this point compared the soil in Sylhet with that which was previously given to Jalal by his uncle, finding them to be identical. In any case, following the battle, Jalal and his followers settled in Sylhet.[14][17]

A Persian inscription from 1303 has since been discovered in Jalal's dargah. It mentioned Sikandar's victory in Arsah Srihat with the aid of the saint during the reign of Firoz Shah. This inscription can now be found in Bangladesh National Museum.[1]

Recently I visited sylhet and go to Shajalal Mazar.  Thousands of people from different parts of the country, irrespective of religion and caste, come to Sylhet every day to visit the shrine of Hazrat Shahjalal (RA). Many call Sylhet a holy land because of Shahjalal's touch. Hazrat Shahjalal (Rah :) is a famous saint and saint. He is called Olikul Shiromani. It was through him that Islam spread in the Sylhet region.

Raja Gourgobind's persecution of the first Muslim Sheikh Burhan Uddin of Sylhet and the consequent arrival of Hazrat Shahjalal (ra) and his traveling companion 360 Auliya in Sylhet is a significant event in history. There is a pond to the north of Shahjalal's shrine. There are innumerable carrot fish in this pond. These fish are considered sacred by the visitors and given to small fish farms. Carrot fish floating in the pond gives joy to the visitors.

Recognizing the spiritual power of Hazrat Shahjalal (ra), Hazrat Nizamuddin Aulia (ra) welcomed him. As a token of affection, he gave her a pair of surma-colored pigeons or jalali pigeons. The Surma-colored pigeons that are now seen in Sylhet and its environs are the descendants of that pair of pigeons and are known as Jalali pigeons. Pigeons are seen flying in flocks in Shahjalal's shrine area every day. There are many rumors about this pigeon in the minds of the people of Sylhet. There is a well next to Shahjalal's shrine. The location of these coupesona and silver colored fish can be seen. Water is flowing day and night in this well. If you go to the west side of the shrine, you can see the fountain. Shower water is sold by filling bottles.

Inside the one-storey house on the east side of the shrine, there are three large stoves. These were donated by Mir Murad of Dhaka. The dishes are not cooked. Every day visitors donate a lot of money to the dekchis for the purpose of charity. The place is only two feet wide. It is said that Hazrat Shahjalal spent 23 years of his life in worship in this shrine.

The city of Sylhet is renowned as a 'holy land' due to the 360 saints. Among the Pirs (spiritual guides) and Dervishes (ascetics) resting in the soil of Sylhet, Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) is one of the foremost. For this reason, he is called the 'Crown Jewel among Saints' (Olikul Siromoni). Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) was revered by people of all religions. Every year, during visitation (Ziyarat) to the shrine (Mazar) of Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA), a huge influx of people can be seen, irrespective of religion or caste.

To the north of Hazrat Shah Jalal's (RA) shrine, there is a pond. Numerous Gar fish enhance the beauty of this pond. It is said that when Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) came to Sylhet with the 360 saints, he brought the Gar fish. Visitors find joy watching these fish swimming in the pond and feed them. Beside Shah Jalal's (RA) shrine, there is a well. Golden and silver-colored fish can be seen in this well.

Folklore holds that upon learning of Hazrat Shah Jalal's (RA) spiritual power, Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya (RA) warmly received him and gifted him a pair of Surma-colored pigeons as a token. Those pigeons are now widely known as Jalali pigeons. Flocks upon flocks of pigeons at the shrine entertain the visitors.

To the south of the shrine, enclosed by a grill, is a star-studded room only two feet wide. Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) used this as his *Chillakhana* (place of seclusion and meditation). It is said through oral tradition that Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) spent nearly 23 years here in devotion and worship.

Inside the Dargah Madrasa building, on the left towards the house of Mufti Nazimuddin Ahmed, arrangements are made for visitors to see various items used by Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA), such as his sword, wooden sandals (Kharam), plate, bowl, etc.

The main sacred shrine (Dargah Sharif) of Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) is a holy place. While walking around the area, please be mindful of the sanctity of the Dargah.

Among the Pirs (spiritual guides) and Dervishes (ascetics) resting in the soil of Sylhet, Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) is one of the foremost. For this reason, he is called the 'Crown Jewel among Saints' (Olikul Siromoni). Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) was revered by people of all religions. Every year, during visitation (Ziyarat) to the shrine (Mazar) of Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA), a huge influx of people can be seen, irrespective of religion or caste.

To the north of Hazrat Shah Jalal's (RA) shrine, there is a pond. Numerous Gar fish enhance the beauty of this pond. It is said that when Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) came to Sylhet with the 360 saints, he brought the Gar fish. Visitors find joy watching these fish swimming in the pond and feed them. Beside Shah Jalal's (RA) shrine, there is a well. Golden and silver-colored fish can be seen in this well.

Folklore holds that upon learning of Hazrat Shah Jalal's (RA) spiritual power, Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya (RA) warmly received him and gifted him a pair of Surma-colored pigeons as a token. Those pigeons are now widely known as Jalali pigeons. Flocks upon flocks of pigeons at the shrine entertain the visitors.

To the south of the shrine, enclosed by a grill, is a star-studded room only two feet wide. Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) used this as his *Chillakhana* (place of seclusion and meditation). It is said through oral tradition that Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) spent nearly 23 years here in devotion and worship.

Inside the Dargah Madrasa building, on the left towards the house of Mufti Nazimuddin Ahmed, arrangements are made for visitors to see various items used by Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA), such as his sword, wooden sandals (Kharam), plate, bowl, etc.

The main sacred shrine (Dargah Sharif) of Hazrat Shah Jalal (RA) is a holy place. While walking around the area, please be mindful of the sanctity of the Dargah.

Role in Sylhet: Shah Jalal is renowned for his role in the battle against Raja Gaur Govinda, a Hindu king of Sylhet, alongside the local ruler, Burhanuddin. His support helped Burhanuddin defeat the king, leading to the establishment of a significant Muslim presence in Sylhet. Shah Jalal is celebrated for his compassion, wisdom, and humility, drawing many locals to Islam.

2. The Mazar Sharif (Shrine)

Location and Surroundings: The shrine is in the heart of Sylhet and is surrounded by lush greenery. The holy site includes his tomb, a mosque, a pond, and other facilities for visitors.

The Tomb: Shah Jalal’s tomb is the centerpiece of the Mazar Sharif. Devotees visit to pay their respects, offer prayers, and seek blessings. The tomb is adorned with Islamic calligraphy and intricate decorations.

Architecture: The architecture is a mix of Mughal and local styles, featuring domes, arches, and intricate stone and woodwork. The mosque within the shrine complex reflects traditional Islamic architecture with a simple but elegant design.

Hazrat Shah Jalal University of Science and Technology (SUST): Named in honor of the saint, this major public university in Sylhet underscores his lasting influence on education and culture in the region.

Place in Folklore: Shah Jalal’s life and deeds are a vital part of Bangladeshi folklore, with many stories celebrating his miracles and piety. His legacy has also inspired poems, songs, and local lore, keeping his memory alive in cultural narratives.

Tourism and Pilgrimage Site: The Mazar Sharif is one of Bangladesh's most popular pilgrimage destinations, attracting both religious and cultural tourists. The area around the shrine has many shops, food stalls, and hotels catering to visitors.

Shāh Jalāl ad-Dīn al-Mujarrad al Naqshbandi, popularly known as Hazrat Shah Jalal (Arabic: شاه جلال الدين‎‎, Bengali: শাহ জালাল), (1271 CE – 15 March 1346 CE) is a celebrated Sufi Muslim figure in Bengal. Jalal's name is associated with the spread of Islam into north-eastern Bengal (Sylhet) through Sufism, part of a long history of travel between the Middle East, Persia, Central Asia and South Asia. According to a tablet inscription found in Amber Khana, he arrived at Sylhet in 1303.  The largest airport in Bangladesh, Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, is named after him.

His biography was first recorded in the mid 16th century by a certain Shaikh 'Ali (d. 1562), a descendant of one of Shah Jalal's companions. Thus there is a gap of several centuries between the life of the saint and that of his earliest biographer. According to this account, Shah Jalal had been born in Turkestan, where he became a spiritual disciple of Saiyid Ahmad Yasawi, one of the founders of the Central Asian Sufi tradition.[2] Therefore, although his existence is not debated, much of his life story is debated.

Right in the middle of a busy and noisy city like Dhaka, Ramna Park feels like a breath of fresh air. It is one of the best places for those who want to escape the city's mechanical life and spend some quiet time close to nature.
Natural Beauty & Environment:
The environment inside the park is wonderful. Century-old massive trees, colorful flowers, and the beautiful lake in the middle enhance the park's beauty immensely. Sitting by the lake provides a unique sense of peace. The calm and serene atmosphere is absolutely ideal for spending some quiet time or simply enjoying the beauty of nature.
Photography & Exploring:
For those who enjoy landscape, nature, or portrait photography, this is an excellent spot. The soft morning sunlight or the fading afternoon light creates amazing frames featuring the trees and the lake.
Walking & Exercise:
Ramna Park is one of the best places in Dhaka for morning walks or jogging. The walkways are quite wide and well-paved. A lot of people come here every morning and afternoon to exercise or take a stroll. There are also plenty of benches inside for visitors to rest.
Security & Cleanliness:
The overall cleanliness of the park has improved significantly compared to before. There is now strictness regarding littering. Additionally, the presence of security personnel makes the environment quite safe. You can easily and safely spend quality time here with family and friends.
A Few Tips:
It gets quite crowded on weekends (especially Friday afternoons). If you want to spend some peaceful time, it is better to visit on weekdays or very early in the morning.
Mosquitoes can be a bit of a nuisance after dusk, so it is good to be prepared for that.
It is a good idea to carry a water bottle with you, though light snacks and water are available inside and just outside the gates.
Overall Assessment:
Ramna Park is a fantastic place to get a touch of nature and refresh your mind. Having such a green and well-maintained park inside Dhaka is truly a blessing. Highly recommended for nature lovers!

Ramna Park:

Ramna Park, located in the Ramna area of Dhaka city, is an important example of modern urban park planning. Although the park was formally inaugurated in 1949, its development in the modern sense began mainly after 1952. It covers approximately 68.5 acres of land, including a water body of about 8.76 acres. At present, the park contains a rich collection of tree and plant species, which enhances its ecological significance. The greenery and natural environment attract numerous visitors. Today, Ramna is also well known both at home and abroad as a major venue for Pahela Baishakh celebrations.

The name “Ramna” originated during the Mughal period and has been in use since the mid-17th century. In the early 17th century, the area was known as “Bagh-i-Badshahi,” suggesting that a well-planned garden existed there at that time. Later, in the 19th century, the area turned into dense jungle. In 1825, Charles Dawes, the British Magistrate of Dhaka, had the area cleared by prisoners. He is often regarded as one of the key figures in the early development of modern Dhaka.

Following the Partition of Bengal in 1905, Dhaka became the capital of the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam. As part of urban development, the British administration undertook plans to build a new city centered around Ramna. The “Ramna Green” project was a component of this initiative; its implementation began in 1908 and continued for nearly two decades. The aim of the project was to develop Dhaka as a garden city. The responsibility for executing the plan was entrusted to Robert Lewis Proudlock, a horticulturist associated with the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London. However, it is not certain whether any of the trees planted by him still survive in the area today. Initially, there was a zoo here; after independence, it was relocated to Mirpur.

With a history spanning nearly 400 years, Ramna Park stands as a symbol of national heritage and pride. In line with ongoing urban development, it is important to continue efforts for the park’s improvement, as well as the classification and identification (taxonomy) of its plant species.

Ramna Park is an urban green space renowned for its historical significance and recreational amenities, situated at the centre of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Described as the "lungs of Dhaka City", the park was built during the British colonial era with a lake at its core, undergoing several transformations over the years and evolving into a popular public space. Ramna Park hosts cultural events and festivals, notably, the yearly Bengali New Year celebrations.

Ramna Park is situated at the centre of Dhaka and presently covers an area of 68.50 acres (277,200 m2), of which the lake covers 8.76 acres (35,500 m2). Walkways inside park have been widened and five new gates built for entry from different sides.

Ramna Park contains a total of 71 species of flowering plants, 36 species of fruit trees, 33 species of medicinal plants, and 41 species of forestry plants, along with an additional 11 species.

Now the 70-acre Ramna Park is one of the signature places to run in Dhaka. There are long pathways passing by numerous species of flowers, trees, and other greenery.
