review_text:
Nestled in the heart of Dhaka, Ramna Park (রমনা পার্ক)—often hailed as the "green lungs" of the city—offers a refreshing escape from the urban rush, blending history, nature, and culture into one serene setting.

Spanning approximately 68.5 acres, the park features a central lake covering around 8.76 acres, framed by shaded walking paths, garden benches, and lush lawns . Its botanical richness is remarkable, boasting over 200 species including 71 flowering plants, 36 fruit trees, 33 medicinal plants, and assorted forestry specimens . Towering banyan trees, vibrant Krishnachura blossoms in spring, and distinctive species like Nagalingam and Arjuna add to the park’s ecological allure .

A Historical and Cultural Hub: The park's roots trace back to the Mughal era when it served as a royal garden. It was redesigned under British colonial rule in the early 1900s and officially inaugurated in 1949, with its current design laid out in 1952 . Today, it stands as a focal point for cultural celebrations—most notably Pohela Boishakh (Bengali New Year)—where thousands gather early in the morning under the historic Ramna Batamul banyan tree to celebrate with traditional music, dance, and the colorful Mangal Shobhajatra, organized by Chhayanaut .

Recreation and Atmosphere: Whether you're a jogger, family, or nature enthusiast, Ramna Park caters to all. Spacious walkways, scenic views, lakeside benches, and even children’s play facilities make it ideal for morning strolls, fitness routines, or quiet relaxation . Recent renovations have enhanced its charm with LED lighting, wooden decks over the lake, red-brick walkways, modern seating areas, toilets, and a dedicated children’s corner . Especially at dawn or dusk, the park becomes alive with joggers, birdwatchers, and families .

Community & Experience: As one visitor noted, “It turns from dense city to literal jungle trees” . Another echoed its therapeutic value: “Now that was a peaceful lone stroll… It was monitored… and there are people there almost all the time” .

In essence, Ramna Park is more than urban greenery—it’s a cultural cornerstone and a peaceful haven in the bustling capital. Its botanical diversity, historic legacy, recreational possibilities, and cultural vibrancy make it a must-visit landmark that beautifully embodies Dhaka’s soul.

Ramna Park is one of the most beautiful and peaceful public parks in Dhaka, Bangladesh, offering a refreshing green space in the heart of the busy city. Located near Shahbagh and surrounded by important institutions such as the Supreme Court, Bangla Academy, and Dhaka University, the park plays a significant role in the cultural and social life of the capital. Spread over a large area with lush green lawns, tall trees, flowering plants, and a serene lake, Ramna Park provides a natural environment where people can relax and escape from the noise and pollution of urban life. Every morning and evening, the park becomes lively with walkers, joggers, families, and elderly people who come to enjoy fresh air and exercise.
Ramna Park has a long historical background and has witnessed many important events in the history of Bangladesh. During the Pakistani period, the Ramna Race Course area nearby was used for public gatherings, and the historic speech of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 7 March 1971 was delivered close to this area. The park also suffered damage during the Liberation War but was later restored and developed as a public park. One of the most notable features of Ramna Park is the Ramna Batamul, where the traditional Bengali New Year (Pohela Boishakh) celebrations are held every year by Chhayanaut, attracting thousands of people from all walks of life.
In addition to its historical and cultural importance, Ramna Park plays a crucial role in environmental balance by helping to reduce air pollution and providing a habitat for birds and small wildlife. It is not only a place for recreation but also a symbol of cultural heritage, unity, and resilience. Ramna Park remains a cherished landmark of Dhaka, representing harmony between nature, history, and modern city life.

Location: Shahbagh, Dhaka, Bangladesh
Type: Public Park & Recreational Space
Entry Fee: Free

🔹 Overview

Ramna Park is one of Dhaka’s most iconic and historic green spaces. Nestled near Dhaka University, Shahbagh, and Suhrawardy Udyan, it offers a refreshing escape from the city's hustle and bustle. With sprawling lawns, tall trees, and a large lake at its center, the park is a favorite spot for morning walkers, joggers, families, students, and tourists.

🔹 Scenic Beauty & Environment

The park is lush with greenery, dotted with flowering plants, ancient banyan trees, and seasonal blooms. Birds chirp from the treetops while gentle breezes flow across the lake. It’s a great place to reconnect with nature, read a book, do yoga, or simply take a peaceful stroll.

At sunrise, the park comes alive with fitness enthusiasts, and in the evening, it turns into a calm social space for people of all ages.

🔹 Cultural & Historical Significance

Ramna Park holds deep cultural importance in Bangladesh. It is adjacent to the Ramna Kali Mandir (destroyed in 1971) and near the site of many national movements. Most notably, it is the epicenter of Pahela Baishakh (Bengali New Year) celebrations every year, where thousands gather to welcome the new year with traditional songs, processions, and joy.

🔹 Facilities

Walking and jogging paths

Benches and shaded seating areas

A large lake with beautiful views

Restrooms (though maintenance varies)

Security presence (daytime)

✅ Pros

Calm and scenic environment in central Dhaka

Perfect for walking, relaxing, or exercising

Rich cultural and historical background

Suitable for families and solo visitors alike

❌ Cons

Can get crowded during peak hours or festivals

Limited parking space nearby

Cleanliness can be an issue during public holidays

Street vendors and noise from surrounding traffic may affect the peaceful vibe

📝 Summary

Ramna Park is a timeless gem in the heart of Dhaka. Whether you're a local looking for a daily walk or a tourist seeking natural beauty mixed with culture and history, this park offers something for everyone. A must-visit for those who want to see Dhaka breathe in green.

The Star Mosque, or Tara Masjid, is one of the most beautiful and unique mosques in Dhaka. Located in Armanitola, Old Dhaka, it was first built in the early 19th century by Mirza Golam Pir as a simple Mughal-style mosque. Later, in 1926, a local merchant named Ali Jan Bepari transformed it into the stunning structure seen today by decorating it with colorful mosaics. In 1987, the mosque was further expanded from three domes to five to hold more worshippers.

What makes the mosque special is its Chinitikri mosaic work — a decoration made from pieces of broken Chinese porcelain, glass, and tiles. The walls and domes are covered with blue stars, floral patterns, and other designs, giving the mosque its name “Star Mosque.” This creative artwork even includes small scenes like Mount Fuji, showing the blend of local and foreign influences. The mosque is so well loved that it appears on Bangladesh’s five-taka banknote.

Visitors are welcome, and entry is free. However, since it’s an active place of worship, modest clothing is required — long pants for men and a headscarf for women. It’s best to visit between prayer times when it’s less crowded. The mosque sits within the busy lanes of Old Dhaka, so a rickshaw ride is the easiest way to get there.

A visit takes about 30 minutes, and it’s easy to combine with nearby attractions such as Ahsan Manzil or the Armenian Church for a fuller experience of Old Dhaka’s history.

WHEN THE STAR MOSQUE (OR Tara Masjid in Bengali) in Dhaka was first built in the first half of the 19th century, the original Mughal design included a large dome in the center and two smaller ones on each side. Through the years, additions were built and the interior was decorated—changes that were met with criticism, as they subverted the architectural sensibilities of the Mughal style.

Today, with the old design all but gone, the main appeal of the mosque is the striking mosaics decorating it. The artisans who created these patterns used a technique called Chinitikri, which uses broken shards of China porcelain as mosaic pieces. (Pieces of broken bottles were also used at times because colored ceramics were costly.) The size of the pieces varied from half an inch to 2.5 inches, and the preferred shapes were rhomboid and triangular.

The mosque is now one of the few extant examples of an architectural work decorated with Chinitikri-style mosaics. Most notable is the Chinitikri blue star motif that gives the structure its popular name, Star Mosque. Hundreds of blue-colored stars adorn the white marble domes, and this star theme is echoed by the mosaics of flowers and rosettes found on the façade and the interior of the mosque.

Tara Masjid, renowned for its iconic design, is a testament to the architectural marvels of the first half of the 19th century. This historical mosque, crafted by the skilled hands of Mirza Golam Pir, stands as a captivating representation of artistic brilliance. The ornate designs adorning Tara Masjid draw the eye with intricate detailing, and the unique touch of blue star motifs adds an enchanting charm to the overall aesthetic.

Constructed in the early 1800s, this mosque not only serves as a place of worship but also stands as a living piece of history. Mirza Golam Pir's dedication to craftsmanship is evident in every facet of Tara Masjid, from its structural elegance to the symbolic blue stars that grace its exterior.

Beyond being a religious site, Tara Masjid has become a cultural landmark, inviting visitors to appreciate the fusion of art and history. Its intricate detailing and historical significance make it a must-visit destination, offering a glimpse into the rich architectural heritage of the 19th century.

This place is truly a hidden gem for nature lovers and those seeking peace amidst the city's hustle. Located in Mirpur, it offers a refreshing escape with its vast greenery, fresh air, and scenic walking paths. It’s perfect for anyone looking to clear their mind, take a quiet walk, or simply enjoy some alone time.

The large open spaces, shady trails, and calm lakes make it a great spot to relax, take photos, or read a book under a tree. The air feels noticeably fresher here, which is a big relief from the usual city pollution.

Extending the time would allow more people to enjoy its beauty. Also, the management should be more careful about preventing illegal or harmful activities inside to protect the environment and ensure safety for everyone.

Overall, this place is a wonderful spot that refreshes both body and mind. With a little more care and attention, it has the potential to be one of the top natural attractions in the city.

The National Botanical Garden in Mirpur, Dhaka, is a sprawling haven of greenery and biodiversity, offering a serene escape from the city's chaos. Spread over 84 hectares, it houses over 56,000 plants, including rare and exotic species, medicinal herbs, and vibrant seasonal flowers. The garden's highlights include the cactus house, orchid collection, and a picturesque man-made lake that adds a calming charm to the environment. Walking trails, shaded seating areas, and open lawns make it a perfect spot for leisure, picnics, or quiet contemplation. Birdwatchers and photographers will also appreciate the variety of birds, butterflies that thrive in this lush ecosystem. While the garden offers immense beauty, some areas lack adequate maintenance, with overgrown pathways and insufficient signage being notable issues. Despite these challenges, the garden remains a popular destination for nature lovers, families, and students interested in botany.

The best time to visit is during the winter months when seasonal flowers are in full bloom, adding vibrant colors to the landscape. Early mornings or late afternoons are ideal for avoiding the heat and enjoying the tranquil atmosphere.

With its rich flora, diverse fauna, and tranquil environment, the National Botanical Garden serves as both an educational and recreational space, offering visitors a refreshing retreat and a deeper appreciation for nature.

That's all for today!
Cheers!!

Location and Overview
The National Botanical Garden of Bangladesh, located in Mirpur, Dhaka, is the largest botanical garden in the country, covering an area of approximately 84 hectares. Established in 1961, it offers a serene and green oasis in the midst of the bustling city. The garden is adjacent to the Bangladesh National Zoo, making it an attractive destination for nature lovers, students, researchers, and families seeking a peaceful retreat.

Plant Collection
The garden boasts a rich and diverse collection of over 50,000 species of trees, plants, and shrubs, both indigenous and exotic. Visitors can explore a wide variety of plants, including medicinal herbs, cacti, orchids, palms, and aquatic plants. Notable highlights include the iconic banyan tree, towering palm trees, and an exquisite array of rare flowers and plants from different regions of the world. The garden is divided into several sections, such as a cactus house, orchid house, and medicinal plant garden, offering something for every plant enthusiast.

Visitor Experience
The garden is an ideal place for those seeking tranquility and a close connection to nature. It provides wide, shaded walking paths, perfect for a relaxing stroll amidst the lush greenery. The natural beauty of the garden, with its well-maintained lawns, artificial lakes, and peaceful ponds, creates a soothing environment for visitors.

Families often visit the garden for picnics, while photographers enjoy capturing the scenic landscapes. Birdwatching is another popular activity, as the garden attracts a variety of bird species. However, some areas of the garden, particularly the restrooms and seating arrangements, could benefit from better maintenance. Visitors have noted that certain sections feel neglected, with overgrown vegetation and a lack of clear signage.

Educational Value
The National Botanical Garden plays a significant role in the research and conservation of plant species in Bangladesh. Students and researchers regularly visit to study the wide variety of plants. However, the garden could enhance its educational potential by offering more guided tours, interpretive signs, and interactive programs to raise public awareness about the importance of plant conservation and biodiversity.

Conclusion
In summary, the National Botanical Garden is a haven for nature lovers and a valuable resource for plant conservation and education in Bangladesh. Despite needing better upkeep in certain areas, its vast collection of flora and peaceful environment make it a worthwhile visit for anyone looking to escape the city's chaos and reconnect with nature.

The National Botanical Garden of Bangladesh, situated in Mirpur, Dhaka, stands as the country's largest plant conservation centre.  Established in 1961, it spans approximately 84 hectares and is managed by the Department of Forestry under the Ministry of Environment and Forests  . Adjacent to the Bangladesh National Zoo, the garden serves both as a sanctuary for diverse plant species and a recreational space for visitors.

Home to over 56,000 individual trees, shrubs, and herbs, the garden boasts a vast collection of native and exotic flora.  Notable species include the Anthurium crystallinum, Cinnamomum camphora (camphor tree), and the Victoria amazonica (giant water lily)  . The garden is systematically divided into 57 sections, featuring specialized areas such as a cactus house, orchid house, and aquatic plant ponds.  Facilities like a tissue culture laboratory and vegetative propagation arrangements support the cultivation of rare species.

Beyond its botanical significance, the garden offers amenities like walking trails, watchtowers, and artificial lakes, making it a favored spot for morning walks, meditation, and birdwatching.  Seasonal migratory birds add to its ecological diversity, attracting nature enthusiasts and photographers alike.

Administratively, the historic Baldha Garden, located in Wari, Dhaka, operates as a satellite unit of the National Botanical Garden  . Together, they play a pivotal role in plant conservation, research, and education in Bangladesh.

review_text:
The National Botanical Garden in Dhaka is a beautiful place to take a morning walk. The garden is home to a wide variety of flora and fauna, and the morning light casts a warm glow over the entire area. As you walk through the garden, you’ll be greeted by the sweet fragrance of blooming flowers and the chirping of birds. The garden is well-maintained and has a peaceful atmosphere that is perfect for a relaxing morning stroll. You can also enjoy the view of the Chiriakhana Road from the garden. It’s a great way to start your day and get some fresh air.

The Garden is open every day from 9:00 AM to 5:00pm. It is a beautiful place to visit throughout the year, but the best time to visit is during the winter months (November to February) when the weather is cool and dry. During this time, the garden is in full bloom, and you can enjoy the beautiful flowers and lush greenery in a comfortable temperature. However, if you prefer to visit during the summer months, it’s best to go early in the morning or late in the afternoon to avoid the heat and humidity.

From 2011 since I stepped into the city till today, I have witnessed many improvements over the years. But few things which ultimately known as the core value of this place or excites me everyway is actually the main attraction for this place.
1. One of the best Botanical garden for the diversity of plants.
2. Its a completely different ecosystem or an escape from the pollution of Dhaka city.
3. Yes, if planned and done well, a walk in the sunrise can fulfil the desire of a sightseeing at outside Dhaka.
4. You can experience a different experience in each different weather condition in each different month.
5. Has 25000 different species of plants and they dont look same all the time, so each visit has possibility to experience something new.

Apart from the core value, there are many major improvements over the years.
1. Better road and many part of the garden is being connected by placing walkways.
2. Signs and posts in every corner.
3. A huge improvement on security.
4. A huge improvement on the attire of overall location where many disrespectful practices were minimized.
5. People are now more comfortable to bring their families.
6. A increased number of morning joggers.
7. Last but not least, an overall structural improvement without disturbing the serenity of the nature which compliments its core values every way.

review_text:
Botanical_Garden.
When I was in class five (probably) I went to the botanical garden with my family, for the first time,anyway.
I was more interested in going to the zoo than seeing the plants, for which I did not like the botanical garden.
But recently the environment there has improved.
Besides, there has been a new renovation, so we,four School-friends went to visit there.
There are several buses to the zoo-road, including the Dishari bus.
💵Bus fare 10tk per person.
💵Botanic Garden entrance fee is 20 tk.
(💵Next to the zoo, entrance fee 50tk).
🕰️We went to the botanical garden around 10:30 or a little later.
[The Botanical Garden is generally open from 09:00 AM to 05:00 PM during winter.]
In the morning, the crowd is very less. We found many beautiful spots to take pictures. It is also a great place for a small picnic.
You can easily spend time sitting by the lake, there is a beautiful bridge, although the maingate was locked.
We looked around, took many pictures.
The situation in the botanical garden is much better than before, to say that there is security. Especially when young visitors  are seen wearing uniform during school/college hours, the authorities are calling their parents for questioning and informing them, which is a very necessary step.
I saw the area reserved for the naval forces, the general public is not allowed to enter, still the place was quite amazing.
There were different types of trees, I liked some of them.

When we school friends get together we laugh like villains, which is indescribable.

There is a small park. There were swings, sleepers, Seesaw etc,two people could easily sit on the swings.Children and adults were enjoying the rides.
A place of 215 acres, from 10:30 am to 2:30 pm, we could not explore even half of the place (as we had to return home quickly).
But I spent the day very happily, Alhamdulillah.
A great place for a picnic with friends or just spending quality time.

Open 7 days a week.
Note: You can take a picture of the map given there at the beginning, as a result, you will not miss any place to visit.

The National Botanical Garden, located in Dhaka, Bangladesh, is a prominent botanical garden that plays a crucial role in conservation, research, and education regarding plant diversity. Here’s an overview of its key features:

General Information

Location: Situated in the Mirpur area of Dhaka, it covers approximately 205 acres of land.

Established: The garden was established in 1961 and has since become a major center for botanical research and education in the country.

Features

Plant Collections: The garden houses a diverse collection of over 50,000 plants, including native and exotic species, medicinal plants, and ornamental plants.

Thematic Sections: The garden is divided into various sections, such as:

Medicinal Plant Section: Featuring plants used in traditional medicine.

Orchard: Showcasing fruit-bearing trees.

Flower Gardens: Displaying seasonal flowers and landscaped areas.

Aquatic Plants: Highlighting plants that thrive in water bodies.

Facilities

Visitor Amenities: The garden offers facilities for visitors, including walking paths, benches, and shaded areas for relaxation.

Educational Center: An information center provides resources for visitors interested in learning about the flora and conservation efforts.

Research and Conservation

Research Activities: The National Botanical Garden conducts research on plant species, their conservation, and propagation techniques.

Conservation Programs: It participates in various conservation initiatives aimed at protecting endangered species and promoting sustainable practices.

Activities and Events

Educational Programs: The garden hosts workshops, seminars, and guided tours for students, researchers, and the general public to raise awareness about biodiversity and conservation.

Public Engagement: It often organizes events to engage the community in gardening, plant care, and environmental awareness.

Accessibility

Entrance Fees: The garden has a nominal entrance fee, making it accessible to a broad audience.

Transport: It is well-connected by public transport, including buses and rickshaws, making it easy for visitors to reach.

Importance

Ecological Role: The garden plays a vital role in preserving plant biodiversity and provides a green space for the urban population of Dhaka.

Cultural Significance: It serves as a recreational space for families and individuals, promoting appreciation for nature and environmental conservation.

Overall, the National Botanical Garden in Dhaka is an essential institution for education, conservation, and the enjoyment of nature, contributing significantly to the environmental and cultural landscape of Bangladesh.

I recently visited Hatirjheel Lake to spend an evening away from the usual city rush, and the experience was truly memorable. As soon as I arrived, I was impressed by how open and well-planned the area felt. The wide roads, bridges, and the large water body created a calm atmosphere that’s rare in Dhaka. It immediately felt like a place designed for people to relax and enjoy the city from a different perspective.
I started by walking along the lakeside, and the view was beautiful, especially as the sun began to set. The reflection of the lights on the water, the cool breeze, and the skyline around made the whole environment feel refreshing. Many people were jogging, cycling, or simply sitting by the railings, enjoying the moment. It felt lively but not chaotic — more like a shared space where everyone comes to unwind.
Later, I sat near one of the bridges and just watched the traffic flow smoothly while boats moved quietly on the water. The contrast between the busy city and the calm lake was striking. There were small vendors selling snacks and tea, which made it easy to enjoy a light refreshment while relaxing. I also noticed families taking photos and friends hanging out, which added to the friendly vibe of the place.
What stood out to me most was how clean and organized Hatirjheel felt compared to many other public spots. The walking paths were comfortable, and the lighting in the evening made the area feel safe and welcoming. Of course, during peak hours it gets crowded, and sometimes finding a quiet corner becomes difficult, but that also shows how popular and loved the place is.
Overall, my experience at Hatirjheel Lake was excellent. It’s a place where you can go for a peaceful walk, enjoy the city lights, spend quality time with friends or family, or simply sit and clear your mind. I would highly recommend Hatirjheel Lake to anyone looking for a refreshing outdoor experience in Dhaka — it’s one of those places that leaves you feeling relaxed and wanting to come back again.

review_text: There were many land properties in the Tejgaon area, including Hatirjheel in Bhawal state. Over time, the estate's elephant herd used to bathe or drink water in the lake here, so it was named Hatirjheel. Hatirjheel is an area in Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, which was created for public transportation. The project area was inaugurated and opened to the public on January 2, 2013. As a result of the launch of this project, the residents of Tejgaon, Gulshan, Badda, Rampura, Mouchak, Farmgate, Karwan Bazar and Moghbazar areas of Dhaka, including passengers traveling on this route, are getting special benefits. The Hatirjheel project is being implemented and supervised by the 'Special Works Organization' of the Bangladesh Army. One of the main goals of this project is to conserve rainwater, prevent waterlogging and floods, develop the sewage drainage system, reduce traffic congestion in the capital and increase prosperity. The architect of this project was Ehsan Khan.

Lalbagh Fort is an incomplete 17th-century Mughal fort complex in Old Dhaka, Bangladesh, situated by the Buriganga River. Construction began in 1678 by Prince Muhammad Azam Shah but was halted when he was recalled to Delhi. The fort remained unfinished after his successor, Shaista Khan, abandoned the project following the death of his daughter, Pari Bibi. Today, it is a popular tourist site featuring the unfinished gate, the Mausoleum of Pari Bibi, the Hall of Audience (now a museum), and a three-domed mosque.
History
Construction began: In 1678 by Prince Muhammad Azam Shah, the son of Emperor Aurangzeb.
Project halted: Construction stopped when Azam Shah was recalled to Delhi.
Re-started: Shaista Khan resumed work on the fort in 1680.
Project abandoned: The fort was never completed due to the death of Shaista Khan's daughter, Pari Bibi, which was considered a bad omen.
Key structures
Southern Gate: The most impressive of the surviving gateways, it is a three-story structure.
Mausoleum of Pari Bibi: The final resting place of Shaista Khan's daughter, it is known for its exquisite use of white marble, black basalt, and colorful tiles.
Hall of Audience (Diwan-i-Aam): A two-story structure that now houses a museum with Mughal artifacts.
Three-domed Mosque: A beautifully constructed mosque with white stone and three domes.
Other features: A roof garden with a water reservoir, underground rooms, and a network of terracotta pipes connecting various establishments.

Lalbagh Fort, also known as Qila Aurangabad, is a historic Mughal fort located in the old city of Dhaka, Bangladesh. It's a fascinating and popular tourist destination, known for its impressive architecture and rich history. Here's a glimpse into what makes Lalbagh Fort so special:
A Story of Unfinished Grandeur:
* Construction of the fort began in 1678 by Prince Muhammad Azam Shah, son of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, who was the governor of Bengal at the time.
* Unfortunately, the fort remained incomplete due to various factors, including the prince's recall by his father and later, the death of Shaista Khan's daughter, Pari Bibi, which led him to abandon the project.
* Despite being unfinished, Lalbagh Fort still showcases the grandeur of Mughal architecture and gives us a glimpse into the vision its creators had.
Architectural Marvels:
* The fort complex houses several notable structures:
* The Tomb of Pari Bibi: A stunning marble mausoleum with intricate designs, dedicated to the beloved daughter of Shaista Khan.

* Diwan-i-Aam: The hall of public audience, showcasing Mughal architectural elements.

* The Three-Domed Mosque: A beautiful mosque with three domes, reflecting Mughal architectural style.

* The fort also features lush gardens, fountains, and water channels, adding to its beauty and charm.
Historical Significance:
* Lalbagh Fort stands as a symbol of the Mughal era in Bengal and serves as a reminder of the region's rich history.
* It offers insights into the architectural prowess and cultural influences of the Mughal period.
Visiting Lalbagh Fort:
* Lalbagh Fort is a must-visit for history enthusiasts, architecture lovers, and anyone interested in exploring Dhaka's cultural heritage.
* It's a great place to wander through the courtyards, admire the intricate designs, and imagine the lives of those who once lived within its walls.
Additional Information:
* Lalbagh Fort is open to the public from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM on all days except Sundays.
* The entry fee is Tk. 20 for Bangladeshi citizens and Tk. 100 for foreign nationals.

Construction began in 1678 under the direction of Prince Muhammad Azam, the son of Emperor Aurangzeb. However, the fort was never completed, adding to its air of mystery and intrigue.

The complex houses three main architectural structures: the Tomb of Pari Bibi, the Diwan-i-Aam (Audience Hall and Hammam), and the mosque—all of which reflect the elegance of Mughal design. Surrounded by lush gardens, historical relics, and a tranquil ambiance, the fort offers a peaceful escape from the hustle of Dhaka city.

A visit to Lalbagh Kella is like stepping back in time. Tourists can explore the intricate carvings, the Mughal water systems, and the museum filled with centuries-old artifacts. It’s a perfect spot for history lovers, photographers, and those seeking to connect with the heritage of Bengal.

Whether you’re wandering through the gardens at sunset or standing in awe of the fort’s majestic architecture, Lalbagh Kella is a must-visit destination for anyone exploring the cultural and historical depths of Dhaka.

Lalbagh Fort (Lalbagh Kella) is an incomplete 17th century Mughal fort complex built by Muhammad Azam Shah (S/O Emperor Aurangzeb) in 1678 during his vice-royalty in Bengal. Later Shaista Khan continued construction but abandoned it after the death of his daughter Pari Bibi who was buried inside the fort.

There is several structures Inside the Fort:
# Qila Mosque – A small but elegant mosque still in use.
# Pari Bibi’s Mausoleum – The tomb of Shaista Khan’s beloved daughter.
# Diwan-i-Aam (Audience Hall) – A palace like structure believed to be the governor’s residence.
# Fort Walls & Gates – The southern gate is the most prominent.

Some believe the fort is cursed due to Pari Bibi’s untimely death, leading Shaista Khan to abandon it. Many hidden tunnels are rumored to exist beneath the fort.

Lalbagh Fort is located in Old Dhaka. It is opened for visitors from Monday to Saturday 10 AM – 5 PM.

Every year, many tourists, historians, and students visit Lalbagh Fort to learn about the past and admire its historical significance.

Lalbagh Fort: A Timeless Symbol of Mughal Architecture
Lalbagh Fort, located in the heart of Old Dhaka, is one of the most iconic historical sites in Bangladesh. Built during the Mughal era, this unfinished yet breathtaking fort stands as a testament to the grandeur and architectural brilliance of the Mughal Empire. Whether you are a history enthusiast, an architecture lover, or a casual visitor, this fort offers a journey back in time.

Historical Significance
Construction of the fort began in 1678 under Mughal Subahdar Shaista Khan, but it was never completed due to political shifts in the empire. Despite being unfinished, Lalbagh Fort holds great historical value, as it witnessed significant events during the Mughal period and later played a role during the 1857 Sepoy Mutiny against British rule.

Architectural Beauty
The fort complex features several remarkable structures, including:
✔ The Mausoleum of Pari Bibi – The most beautiful part of the fort, where Pari Bibi, the daughter of Mughal governor Shaista Khan, rests. The combination of white marble and black basalt gives it a striking look.
✔ The Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) – A magnificent two-story structure that was once used for state affairs.
✔ The Lalbagh Mosque – A classic example of Mughal architecture, adorned with elegant domes and minarets.
✔ The Fortification Walls & Secret Passages – These add to the mystery of the fort, making it a fascinating place to explore.

A Peaceful Escape in the Heart of Dhaka
Despite being in the middle of a bustling city, the lush green gardens and serene environment inside the fort provide a refreshing escape from Dhaka’s chaos. It’s an ideal place for a leisurely stroll, photography, or simply soaking in the history.

Entry Fee & Facilities
The entrance fee is very affordable, making it accessible to everyone. The fort is well-maintained, with clear walking paths, informative plaques, and seating areas. There are also guides available for those who want a more in-depth understanding of the fort’s history.

Final Thoughts
Visiting Lalbagh Fort is like stepping into the pages of history. The architectural elegance, historical depth, and peaceful atmosphere make it a must-visit landmark in Bangladesh. Whether you're a local or a tourist, this place is bound to leave you mesmerized.

Lalbagh Kella (Lalbagh Fort) is a historical Mughal-era fort situated in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It is one of the most significant and iconic landmarks in the country. Here's a detailed history of the fort:

---

Construction and Origin

The construction of Lalbagh Fort began in 1678 under the orders of Subahdar Muhammad Azam Shah, the third son of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb. He was serving as the governor of Bengal at the time.

The fort was initially planned to be a grand structure, symbolizing Mughal dominance in Bengal.

---

Incomplete Construction

Muhammad Azam Shah had to leave Bengal in 1679 to ascend the Mughal throne, leaving the fort unfinished.

The next governor, Shaista Khan, continued the construction but halted it after the tragic death of his daughter, Bibi Pari, within the fort premises. This led him to believe that the site was inauspicious.

Consequently, the fort was never completed.

---

Main Structures in the Fort

1. The Mosque

A three-domed mosque within the fort premises is a prime example of Mughal architectural style. It remains a functioning mosque.

2. The Tomb of Bibi Pari

The mausoleum of Bibi Pari is located inside the fort. It is made of white marble and is considered the most significant structure in the complex.

The tomb has intricate floral designs, and the walls are decorated with precious stones and carvings.

3. The Diwan-i-Aam (Audience Hall)

This was used as the governor’s residence and administrative center.

It features a unique blend of Mughal and Bengali architectural styles.

---

Architectural Features

The fort combines traditional Mughal architectural elements like domes, arches, and ornate carvings.

Red sandstone and marble were predominantly used in the construction.

---

Later Developments

After being abandoned, the fort fell into disrepair over centuries.

During British rule, the site was used as a police barracks and administrative office.

---

Modern Restoration and Preservation

Today, Lalbagh Fort is a protected heritage site managed by the Bangladesh Department of Archaeology.

The site has been partially restored and serves as a museum, attracting thousands of tourists and history enthusiasts every year.

---

Significance

Lalbagh Fort is a symbol of Dhaka's rich history and Mughal heritage.

Despite being incomplete, it showcases the grandeur of Mughal architecture.

Habib Rahman

সাদা মাটির পাহাড়, বা "শাদা মাটির পাহাড়," বাংলাদেশের নেত্রকোনা জেলার বিরিশিরি অঞ্চলে অবস্থিত একটি অত্যন্ত সুন্দর প্রাকৃতিক স্থান। এই পাহাড়গুলি মূলত সাদা চুনাপাথরের গঠিত এবং তাদের অনন্য রঙ ও আকৃতি জন্য বিখ্যাত। জায়গাটি ভ্রমণকারীদের কাছে আকর্ষণীয় কারণ এর প্রাকৃতিক সৌন্দর্য এবং নিরিবিলি পরিবেশ।

বিরিশিরির এই পাহাড়গুলি সোমেশ্বরী নদীর পাড়ে অবস্থিত, যা জায়গাটির প্রাকৃতিক সৌন্দর্য আরও বাড়িয়ে তোলে। নদীর পানির স্বচ্ছতা ও পাহাড়ের সাদা রঙের সমন্বয় এক অসাধারণ দৃশ্য তৈরি করে।

এই অঞ্চলটি মূলত গারো পাহাড়ের অংশ, যা বাংলাদেশ ও ভারতের সীমান্ত এলাকায় বিস্তৃত। গারো পাহাড়ের এই অংশটি ভিন্ন ধরণের ভূতাত্ত্বিক বৈশিষ্ট্যের জন্য পরিচিত, বিশেষ করে সাদা চুনাপাথরের জন্য। এই চুনাপাথর বাংলাদেশের অন্যান্য অঞ্চলে খুব কম পাওয়া যায়।

সাদা মাটির পাহাড় ও এর আশপাশের অঞ্চলটি ভ্রমণকারীদের জন্য নানা আকর্ষণীয় স্থান সরবরাহ করে। এখানে এছাড়াও রয়েছে গারো আদিবাসী সম্প্রদায়ের গ্রাম, যেখানে ভ্রমণকারীরা তাদের সংস্কৃতি ও জীবনধারা সম্পর্কে জানতে পারেন।

পর্যটকদের জন্য এখানে বেশ কিছু দর্শনীয় স্থান রয়েছে যেমন সোমেশ্বরী নদী, বিজয়পুর চুনাপাথরের খনি এবং রূপসী গারো পাহাড়ের সৌন্দর্য।

সব মিলিয়ে, সাদা মাটির পাহাড় বাংলাদেশের অন্যতম সুন্দর ও আকর্ষণীয় প্রাকৃতিক স্থান, যা প্রকৃতিপ্রেমীদের জন্য একটি অবশ্যই ভ্রমণযোগ্য স্থান।

Nature has spread its genuine beauty on the rivers and plain hills. The clear water of the Someshwari River flowing down from the mountains has brought aesthetics. Such is the view of a territory in Bangladesh bordering the Indian state of Meghalaya.

I am talking about the plain hills and Someshwari River in Durgapur Upazila of Netrakona district.

The 'plain soil of Bijoypur' in Durgapur Upazila has been recognized as a Geographical Indication Product (GI). This recognition has given a different dimension to this region. In 2017, the Deputy Commissioner of Netrakona applied for GI recognition for the plain soil of Bijoypur, which is known as a valuable and rare mineral resource. For this, he submitted a proposal to the Department of Patents and Designs Trademarks (DPDT). After much scrutiny, the product was recognized this year.

In the plain soil project area of ​​Bijoypur, this soil was extracted from a very deep depth by cutting down hill hills. In addition, there are layers of soil of several colors including black, brown, purple and blue. Although excavation work is currently suspended, layers of various colored soil can still be seen when visiting previously excavated areas, which attracts tourists.

I visited Gulshan Society Lake Park one early morning to escape the bustle of Dhaka for a bit — and it was really refreshing. The greenery is lush: there are many trees (you even spot mango trees), and the design feels thoughtfully laid out.

Walking along the paved paths that curve around the lake is peaceful. The lake itself adds calm — it’s not huge, but big enough to feel like a real urban oasis.  There are benches all around, so you can stop, sit, and just watch the water or read a book.

For fitness lovers, it’s a great spot for jogging. Several visitors mention the walkways are well-planned and safe.  A few workout stations (like for calisthenics) exist, though some feel there could be more.

The park also has a children’s play area, which makes it nice for families.  And there’s a horticulture shop inside — I saw flowers and saplings for sale, which added to the “green retreat” feeling.

Security feels solid: the Gulshan Society maintains the park, and there are guards.  The smell of the park is mostly clean, though in some analysis, traffic noise from nearby roads still reaches parts of the park.

On the downside, some reviews mention pollution / water quality issues in the lake.  Also, while the park feels safe and well-kept, the space isn’t super large — in peak times, walking paths may feel more crowded.

Overall, my visit felt like a much-needed breath of fresh air in the city. For early morning jogs, relaxing walks, or just a quiet spot to think or chat with friends, it’s a great pick. For nature lovers in Dhaka who want a peaceful, maintained green space — Gulshan Lake Park really delivers.

It's a well-maintained and beautifully decorated park. You can visit with family, friends, or kids and have a great time. While it's not particularly encouraged as a hangout spot for unmarried couples due to the large number of children playing around, no one is actively stopping anyone from visiting.

About 2–3 years ago, this place felt much more peaceful and cozy. There were fewer visitors, gentle breezes, plenty of greenery, a few cats roaming around, and even some foreigners jogging. It was one of those rare quiet corners in busy Dhaka where you could truly relax. Unfortunately, that's no longer the case. The park is now packed with people most of the time, so if you previously visited for its calm atmosphere, you may not find the same experience today.

That said, it's still a better option than Justice Shahabuddin Park, which has become heavily overcrowded due to social media hype. It's a common pattern—once a genuine hidden gem gets too much attention online, the crowds soon follow.

review_text:
The story of the Sonargaon Folk Art and Craft Museum begins with a vision — the dream of the legendary artist Zainul Abedin, who wanted to preserve the fading beauty of rural Bengal’s traditions. In 1975, he brought that dream to life by founding this museum in Sonargaon, the ancient capital of Bengal. Set within the Bangladesh Folk Arts and Crafts Foundation complex, the museum stands as a vibrant tribute to the artistry, craftsmanship, and soul of the Bengali people.

At the heart of the complex lies Boro Sardar Bari, a grand mansion built in 1901 by a wealthy Hindu merchant. Its elegant architecture and intricate details reflect a time when Sonargaon was alive with trade and culture. After careful restoration, the mansion itself has become one of the highlights of the visit—a glimpse into a bygone era of prosperity and grace. Nearby stands the Folk Art Museum building, where the spirit of Bengal lives on through its displays of Muslin textiles, Nakshi Kantha quilts, wooden crafts, and traditional boats. Every corner tells a story—of weavers, potters, and artisans whose hands shaped the region’s heritage.

Wandering through the museum galleries, visitors encounter a world of creativity: wood carvings, terracotta works, brass and copper crafts, folk paintings, masks, musical instruments, and ornaments once cherished in village homes. Outside, the atmosphere is just as enchanting. A large lake, lush gardens, and a peacock-shaped stage for folk performances invite travelers to linger, relax, and experience the living pulse of Bangladeshi culture.

Reaching the museum is easy from Dhaka, with buses heading toward Moghrapara and short rickshaw rides leading to the gates of the foundation. And just a short walk away lies Panam Nagar, an abandoned colonial-era street frozen in time, lined with hauntingly beautiful townhouses. Together, these two sites—Sonargaon Museum and Panam Nagar—offer visitors not just a sightseeing experience, but a journey through history, art, and the enduring heart of Bengal.

Visiting the সোনারগাঁও লোকশিল্প জাদুঘর/ Bangladesh Folk Art & Carft Foundation, was a truly immersive cultural experience. Established by Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin in 1975 and relocated in 1981 to the historic Sardar’s house (a ~100-year-old mansion), the museum beautifully preserves and presents the rich folk heritage of rural Bengal .

Nestled just about 24–25 km southeast of Dhaka in the historic Panam Nagar of Sonargaon , the open-air museum sprawls across a 150-bigha landscape, blending traditional elements with natural surroundings .
So to go Their from Dhaka,
1️⃣ You can choose Doyel Paribahan / Sodesh Paribahan / Borak AC bus service, the will leave you in Mograpara , Sonargaon.
2️⃣ Then take a TukTuk or CNG autorickshaws, it will cost 10/20 tk per head.
3️⃣ Then You have to buy entrance ticket, that'll cost 50 Tk for locals and 300 Tk for foreigners. You can add Sordar Bari, that will cost extra 100 Tk.

Inside, there are thematic galleries housed within the Sardar Bari, showcasing everything from wood carvings and tribal crafts to brassware, terracotta artifacts, rural ornaments, masks, folk musical instruments, and daily-use folk items,  Archeological stuffs from 14s to 19s. Thats a great destination for visiting, study tour and family vacations.
‼️Warning : Don’t' go to these hotels in fronts of the site for lunch. These are the worst and overpriced food i've ever consumed. Just go to Mograpara by a tuktuk, you'll find a lot of good option.

As a local guide, I highly recommend a visit to the Bangladesh Folk Art & Crafts Museum in Sonargaon, a fascinating day trip from Dhaka. The museum is more than just a building; it's an entire complex set on a beautiful, sprawling landscape that includes artificial lakes, manicured gardens, and picnic spots.
The main attraction is the museum itself, housed in the grand Boro Sardar Bari, a beautifully restored zamindar mansion. Inside, you'll find an impressive collection of traditional artifacts that tell the story of rural Bengali life and heritage. The exhibits showcase everything from exquisite woodwork, intricate pottery, and vibrant textiles like Nakshi Katha, to folk musical instruments and beautifully crafted metalwork. There's also a separate gallery dedicated to the works of Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, the renowned painter who founded the museum.
The serene environment offers a perfect escape from the city's chaos. After exploring the museum, take a leisurely stroll around the grounds or enjoy a relaxing boat ride on the lake. The combination of historical artifacts and a tranquil setting makes this a truly enriching experience. Don't forget to visit nearby Panam Nagar, an abandoned city that adds to the historical charm of the area. It's a must-see for anyone interested in Bangladesh's rich cultural roots.

A month-long folk festival begins on the premises of the Bangladesh Folk and Craft Foundation in Sonargaon Upazila of Naryanganj. The program has been arranged to present the country's crafts and folk culture and to introduce the uniqueness of folk culture with the new generation.

A large number of visitors thronged the fair on opening day. People visited different stalls selling decorative items, crafts, fabrics, and other items like shital pati from Sylhet region, shokher hari, and masks from Rajshahi, clay, and brass crafts from Dhaka, jamdani, and nakshikantha from Sonargaon.

Around 60 artisans from across the country are demonstrating various crafts making techniques at the event.

Besides, visitors can enjoy traditional performances like baul gaan, pala gaan, kobigaan, jatra pala, puppet show, bioscope, and others every day in the evening at the fair.

Folk artistes including Abdus Kuddus Boyati, Samir Baul, Aynal Haque Baul, and others entertained the visitors presenting traditional songs on the opening day of the fair.

The Bangladesh Folk and Crafts Foundation, also known as the Sonargaon Folk Art Museum, is a government-run institution dedicated to preserving and showcasing the rich cultural heritage of Bangladesh's folk art and traditional crafts. Here's a brief overview:

Basic Information

Location: Sonargaon, Narayanganj, near Dhaka

Established: 1975

Founder: Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, a prominent artist of Bangladesh

Administered by: Ministry of Cultural Affairs, Government of Bangladesh

Purpose and Activities

Preservation of Folk Culture: The foundation collects, preserves, and exhibits traditional art, crafts, and everyday objects used by rural people.

Exhibitions: It features permanent and temporary exhibitions showcasing items like nakshi kantha, pottery, masks, musical instruments, and more.

Crafts Fair: It organizes folk festivals and handicraft fairs, especially the annual Folk Art and Crafts Fair held in January–February.

Sonargaon Folk-Arts & Crafts Museum

Sonargaon Folk-Arts and Crafts Museum is the most popular tourist spot in Sonargaon. It is the most popular tourist spot for the locals near Dhaka. There are two museums inside the premises of Sonargaon Folk-Arts and Crafts Museum. The original museum was established by famous painter Joynul Abedin in 1975 on an old house called Bara Sardar Bari built in 1901.

Artifacts related to the heritage of Bengal from 17th century onward are being displayed on this museum. You can see here things people used to use in their everyday life which the city-based new generation are unaware of. Daily-life tools, ornaments, furniture, treasure box, arms, musical instruments, boats, decoration pieces, and many other things related to the heritage of Bengal are the main attraction of this museum. This building is now being beautifully renovated to its original state and closed for display.

Visiting this place on a rainy morning around 11 AM made the whole atmosphere truly magical and serene. At just 30 BDT per ticket, it offers tremendous value, especially given how well-maintained and clean the entire ground is. The moment you step inside, the three historic buildings immediately grab your attention with their striking architecture. While the indoor museum has limited exhibits, the outdoor heritage structures and greenery more than make up for it.
The facilities on-site are quite commendable. Dustbins are placed at convenient intervals to help maintain cleanliness, and there are dedicated, decently clean washrooms available for both men and women. It is a shared responsibility, so every visitor should do their part to keep the restrooms and surroundings clean without littering or plucking flowers from the gardens.
However, a couple of issues require immediate attention from the management. A few local individuals enter without tickets and hang around certain corners, playing loud music and staring at female visitors, which creates an uncomfortable environment. Authorities need to monitor unauthorized entry more strictly. Additionally, visitors should keep in mind that this is a family-friendly heritage site rather than a private dating spot, and everyone should maintain basic decorum. Despite these minor hiccups, it remains a wonderful, peaceful place that is totally worth a visit.

one of the largest and most beautiful historical palaces near Dhaka. It is located in Saturia Upazila and is a perfect destination for a short historical trip.
To reach the palace, I first traveled toward National Martyrs' Memorial and then went to Nabinagar Bus Stand. From Nabinagar I took a local bus and got down at Golora Bus Stop. From Golora bus stop I took a CNG auto-rickshaw to Saturia bazar which cost around 30 BDT per person. After the partition of India in 1947 the zamindar family left the area and the palace remained abandoned for many years before being preserved by the government.
The architecture of the palace is very impressive. The complex contains several large buildings with nearly two hundred rooms, long corridors, tall pillars, and beautiful European-style design. Behind the palace there is a large pond with ghats that were once used by the zamindar family. Some rooms now display historical items related to the zamindari period.
The beauty of Baliati Zamindar Bari is truly remarkable. The grand buildings, wide courtyards, and peaceful surroundings make visitors feel the royal atmosphere of the past. Walking through the palace feels like stepping back into history. It is a wonderful place for history lovers, travelers, and photographers, and definitely one of the most fascinating heritage sites to visit near Dhaka.

Baliati Zamindar Palace – A Hidden Gem of Bengal’s Aristocratic Past

Baliati Palace is located in Baliati village of Saturia Upazila, approximately eight kilometers west of the Manikganj district headquarters and thirty-five kilometers from the Dhaka district headquarters. This Zamindar Bari is located with a total of seven structures. Not all the buildings of this Baliati Zamindar Bari or Palace were built together. Various buildings under this palace were built at different times by different generations of the Zamindar family. Currently, the central block is a museum. This palace is preserved and managed by the Bangladesh Archaeological Department.

The Baliati Zamindar Palace is a stunning testament to 19th-century Renaissance-style architecture in Bangladesh. Spread over more than 20 acres, this historic complex comprises seven grand buildings, once the seat of a powerful zamindar family led by Govinda Ram Saha, a salt merchant turned landlord.

The palace is surrounded by high boundary walls and features majestic arched gateways carved with lion motifs. While the central block has now been turned into a museum, the western part still holds lesser-known, mysterious structures that offer deeper glimpses into aristocratic life—such as private quarters, guesthouses, and storehouses.

Whether you're a history enthusiast, an architecture lover, or just seeking a peaceful escape into the past, Baliati Palace promises an unforgettable experience.

A visit to Baliati Palace is not just a journey into the past, but also a chance to experience the elegance and resilience of Bengali heritage. It remains a symbol of pride, reminding us of the country’s rich historical tapestry and architectural legacy.

The Baliati Zamindar House is one of the most important examples of 19th century architecture. The almost two hundred year old Zamindar House stands as a witness to history and tradition. This house gives an insight into the life, livelihood, lifestyle, entertainment and hobbies of the people of that time.

Manikganj Sadar Upazila is bordered by Saturia to the north, Harirampur to the south, Ghior Upazila to the west and Dhaka district to the east. Baliati Palace is one of the few historical structures in Manikganj. The palace stands as a witness to history about fifty kilometers northwest of Dhaka and about eight kilometers east of Manikganj district town.

This house was built in the 19th century. The Baliati zamidar dynasty originated from a lower-class Saha family.

Govinda Roy Saha, the ancestor of the landlords of Baliati, was a wealthy salt merchant. There was a large salt storehouse in the north-western part of this house. For this reason, this house was named Golabari. At that time, the Baruni fair was held in the premises of the golabari and the chariot festival was organized on the banks of the palm pond to its west. The chariot fair used to be held. However, due to lack of sufficient space, the chariot fair is not held at this place now, but next to the Kali temple in the old market of Baliati village.

The Renaissance Gem of Manikganj
Located in Saturia, the Baliati Jamidar Bari (also known as Baliati Palace) is an absolute must-visit for history enthusiasts and photography lovers. Sprawling over nearly 6 acres, this massive complex is one of the largest and most magnificent zamindar palaces in the country, featuring seven distinct palatial blocks and approximately 200 rooms.

​A Rich Historical Legacy
The history of this estate dates back to the late 18th century. It was founded by Gobinda Ram Shaha, a wealthy salt merchant who transitioned from trade to land ownership. His descendants the influential Roy Chowdhury family expanded the estate throughout the 19th century. The family is not just known for their wealth but also for their contributions to education, having founded prestigious institutions like Jagannath College in Dhaka. The palace is often referred to as the "Dosh-ani-Zamindar Bari" due to the complex way the estate was partitioned among the heirs.

​Architectural Grandeur
The architecture is a stunning fusion of Renaissance and Colonial styles. As you enter through the towering gateways adorned with stone lions you are greeted by a 400-foot-long facade that feels like stepping into a European estate. Baliati Zamindar House is one of the masterpieces of 19th century architecture. The almost two hundred year old zamindar house stands as a witness of history. From this house, the life-livelihood, movement, pleasure and entertainment of the people of that time can be found.

Baliati Zamindarbari is built on about five acres of land. The entire area of the zamindarbari is surrounded by a high wall. It consists of seven palatial buildings, with a total of 200 rooms. In 1987, the Directorate of Archeology declared the Baliati Palace as a protected antiquities and is preserved and managed by the Bangladesh Archaeological Department.

According to local history, Gobind Ram Saha founded the Baliati Zamindar family, he was a salt merchant. The zamindars of Baliati ruled the area for more than 200 years from the first part of the 18th century. During this time they built various important structures. Baliati Zamindarbari is one of them. Zamindar Gobindram Shah built Baliati Zamindarbari in the middle of eighteenth century. And gradually his successors built several more structures here.

I don't want to say that Jaflong was small or has grown now. In fact, the beauty of a place cannot be judged by small or big. The ability to appreciate beauty and the mindset to accept it are the real thing.

Once upon a time, only Cox's Bazar or the Sundarbans were our familiar travel spots. Later, numerous places in Sylhet became popular. Places like white stones are now the center of people's interest. Similarly, yesterday we visited the only white mountain in Bangladesh, Bijoypur Zero Point, Someshwari River, and the immense beauty of Birishiri.

The things that impressed me the most during my trip to Birishiri:

• Ancient trees on both sides of the road and vast bodies of water
• White/chinese clay hills visible after crossing the winding road
• Cold clear water of the Someshwari River coming down from neighboring Meghalaya, strong current and reddish coarse sand underfoot
• Good food restaurants within a small budget
• Small shops of small ethnic groups and a touch of their culture
• Numerous wild flowers and trees growing on the hills and along the road
• The historical and cultural atmosphere of Sagar Dighi, Rajbari and Sadhu Joseph's Dharmapalli

All in all, Birishiri/Bijoypur lake is not only the pride of Mymensingh division, but can also develop into one of the most promising tourist destinations in Bangladesh in the future. Birishiri is truly a wonderful place for those who know how to experience nature.

Shusong Durgapur of Birishiri is located at Netrokona district about 200 km north from Dhaka. It’s not only blessed by charismatic natural beauty, is also reach in ethnic culture as there are many ethnic groups like – Hajong, Garo, Achik and Mandi etc lives here. Many people around the world come here to learn the ethnic culture and livings.

The main attraction of Birishiri is the ceramic hill of Durgapur and the picturesque landscape along the Shomeshwari River. Except the rainy season it’s hard to find any water in the river and that’s why the river changes its landscape color with the seasons. There is also an ethnic museum at Birishiri. It’s a must place to visit while you are in Birishiri.

Main Attractions:

-Shomashwari River
-Bangladesh/India Border
-Ceramic Lake
-Garo Village
-Cultural Academy
-Ranikong Church

Where to Stay:

There is two way to get yourself accommodate. One is you can camp on the hills if you come here in a group. And the other way is to book rooms of YMCA rest house. Chittagong's historic 'Elephant Bungalow'

Everyone wants to see such a natural scene with high mountains all around, lush greenery and the sound of birds chirping. If you move forward a little, you might think that a huge elephant is standing with its trunk raised.

Although it looks alive from a distance, when you get a little closer, you will see a 131-year-old duplex house built in the shape of an elephant. Although it looks exactly like an elephant, it is actually an ancient building built of bricks and stones. It is also known as the 'Elephant Bungalow' to the locals.

This beautiful house, located on the hills of CRB, the lungs of Chittagong, has an ancient history. This century-old history may not be known to many. Looking into history, it is known that in 1893, the construction of the railway from Chittagong to Feni began under the British engineer Brownzer.

Engineer Brownzer himself built the bungalow for the residence of railway officials in the mid-19th century. However, due to the passage of time, the bungalow has become uninhabitable today. If you walk forward through the Ladies Club in the Lalkhan Bazar area of ​​Chittagong and go a little to the right, you will see this elephant bungalow.

Currently, this elephant bungalow, which is part of the history and heritage of Chittagong, is in a dilapidated state. There is no maintenance, as a result, the beauty of the bungalow is being lost. It has been seen on site that the bungalow has a total of 12 round windows in the front and back.

In addition, there are two round holes on both sides of the balcony built in the shape of an elephant's trunk, which look a lot like the eyes of an elephant. This duplex building has 4 bedrooms on the ground floor and one on the second floor. Currently, all the doors and windows of the establishment are broken and rusty.

All the windows made of wood are in a dilapidated state. In addition, moss has grown all over the walls of the building, and the plaster has started to fall off. Various types of dirt and dry leaves are piled up all around the house. A railway employee now lives in a bedroom inside this aesthetic bungalow.

Many visitors come to see the elephant bungalow in the afternoon. In addition to taking pictures, various short films are often shot here. Built with 'ferro' cement in the mid-19th century, this bungalow is still in a very strong condition even though it is 132 years old.

However, the beauty of this tradition is being lost day by day due to lack of maintenance. This structure is also painted gray to match the color of the elephant's body, but due to lack of maintenance, the color of the building has now faded.

This elephant bungalow has been lying around for years, without any steps or proper maintenance. If initiatives are taken to preserve this aesthetic architecture, it will become more attractive to visitors.

Author: Student, Department of Journalism and Media Studies, Port City International University, Chittagong.

চট্টগ্রামের ঐতিহাসিক ‘হাতির বাংলো’

চারপাশে উঁচু পাহাড়, সবুজের সমারোহ ও পাখির কিচিরমিচির শব্দ, এমন প্রাকৃতিক দৃশ্য দেখার ইচ্ছে সবার মধ্যেই আছে। এর মধ্যে দিয়ে একটু সামনে এগিয়ে গেলেই দূর থেকে দেখে যে কারো মনে হতে পারে বিশাল একটি হাতি শুঁড় তুলে দাঁড়িয়ে আছে।

দূর থেকে জীবিত মনে হলেও, সামান্য কাছে যেতেই দেখা মিলবে হাতির আদলে নির্মিত ১৩১ বছরের পুরোনো একটি ডুপ্লেক্স বাড়ি। দেখতে অবিকল হাতির মতো মনে হলেও এটি মূলত ইট-পাথরে নির্মিত একটি প্রাচীন ভবন। স্থানীয়দের কাছে এটি ‘হাতির বাংলো’ নামেও পরিচিত।

চট্টগ্রামের ফুসফুসখ্যাত সিআরবির পাহাড়ে দৃষ্টিনন্দন আদি এই বাড়ির সঙ্গে জড়িয়ে আছে প্রাচীন ইতিহাস। শতবর্ষ পুরোনো এই ইতিহাস হয়তো অনেকেরই অজানা। ইতিহাস ঘেটে জানা গেছে, ১৮৯৩ সালে চট্টগ্রাম থেকে ফেনী পর্যন্ত রেলপথ নির্মাণ কাজ শুরু হয় বৃটিশ প্রকৌশলী ব্রাউনজারের অধীনে।

ঊনিশ শতকের মাঝামাঝিতে রেলওয়ে কর্মকর্তাদের বসবাসের জন্যই বাংলোটি নিজেই নির্মাণ করেন প্রকৌশলী ব্রাউনজার। তবে কালের আবহমানে বাংলোটি আজ বসবাসের অযোগ্য হয়ে পড়েছে। চট্টগ্রামের লালখান বাজার এলাকার লেডিস ক্লাবের ভেতর দিয়ে সামনে এগিয়ে হাতের ডানে সামান্য গেলেই চোখে পড়বে এই হাতির বাংলো।

বর্তমানে চট্টগ্রামের ইতিহাস ও ঐতিহ্যের অংশ এই হাতির বাংলো পড়ে আছে অনেকটা জীর্ণশীর্ণ অবস্থায়। নেই কোনো রক্ষণাবেক্ষণ, ফলে হারাতে বসেছে বাংলোটির সৌন্দর্য। সরেজমিনে দেখা গেছে,বাংলোটির সামনে ও পেছনের অংশ মিলিয়ে মোট ১২টি গোলআকৃতির জানালা আছে।

এছাড়া হাতির শুঁড়ের আদলে নির্মিত বারান্দার দু’পাশেও আছে গোলাকার দুটো ছিদ্র, যা দেখতে অনেকটাই হাতির চোখের মতো। ডুপ্লেক্স এই ভবনের নীচতলায় ৪টি ও দোতলায় একটি শয়নকক্ষ আছে। বর্তমানে স্থাপনাটির সবক’টি দরজা-জানালাই ভেঙে পড়ার পাশাপাশি মরিচা ধরেছে।

কাঠ দিয়ে নির্মিত সব জানালাগুলোই পড়ে আছে জরাজীর্ণ অবস্থায়। এছাড়া ভবনের দেয়ালজুড়ে পড়েছে শ্যাওলা, খসে পড়তে শুরু করেছে পলেস্তারা। বাড়ির চারপাশজুড়ে জমে আছে বিভিন্ন ময়লা আর শুকনো পাতা। নান্দনিক এই বাংলোতে এখন একজন রেলওয়ে কর্মচারী ভেতরের একটি শয়নকক্ষে কোনো রকমে থাকেন।

বিকেল হলেই অনেক দর্শনার্থী হাতির বাংলো দেখতে ছুটে আসেন। দর্শনার্থীরা ছবি তোলার পাশাপাশি এখানে অনেক সময় বিভিন্ন শর্টফিল্মের শুটিংও হয়ে থাকে। ঊনিশ শতকের মাঝামাঝিতে ‘ফেরো’ সিমেন্ট দিয়ে নির্মিত এই বাংলোর ১৩২ বছর পেরিয়ে গেলেও এখনো বেশ মজবুত অবস্থায় আছে।

তবে রক্ষণাবেক্ষণের অভাবে দিনদিন হারাতে বসেছে এই ঐতিহ্যের সৌন্দর্য। হাতির গায়ের রঙের সঙ্গে মিলিয়ে এই স্থাপনাতেও ধূসর রং করা হয়, তবে রক্ষণাবেক্ষণের অভাবে ভবনের রং পুরোটাই এখন বিবর্ণ ধারণ করেছে।

বছরের পর বছর ধরে পড়ে আছে এই হাতির বাংলো, নেই কোনো পদক্ষেপ কিংবা যথাযথ রক্ষণাবেক্ষণ। নান্দনিক এই স্থাপত্য সংরক্ষণের উদ্যোগ নিলে এটি দর্শনার্থীদের কাছে আরো আকর্ষণীয় হয়ে উঠবে।

Last month some of my friends and I visited Murshidabad, the capital of Bengal during the Nawab rule. We were six in all on the tour. On December 2, at about 12 a.m., we started for Murshidabad from Howrah Railway Station. The very next morning we reached Murshidabad. After taking some rest, we started visiting the places of historical interest – First, we visited the Khosbag where Alibardi and Sirajudaullah lie in eternal sleep. From the Khosbag we went to Motijhil and saw the remains of the buildings of Ghoseti Begum. Next, we saw the Hajarduari, a majestic palace containing one thousand doors. It is at the same time an art gallery, museum, library, and an armory. We saw there many famous pictures, the courtroom of the Nawabs, mummies of many birds, and many precious manuscripts in Persian. At last, we visited the mosque of Katra. It is in ruins. Only the lower halves of the two sky-kissing towers have survived the onslaught of time. The visit to Murshidabad left a sad impression on my mind. It opened my eyes to the mutability of earthly things. This visit to Murshidabad will forever remain imprinted on my mind.

The works of legendary painter Shilpaacharya Zainul Abidin are kept in the house of Saheb Quarter Nalini Ranjan Sarkar on the banks of the Brahmaputra river.

Next to the Mymensingh Circuit House, near the Shilpaacharya Zainul Abedin Museum, a park has been built by the dam. Shilpaacharya Zainul Abedin Park, on the other hand, is the name of this park.

Among the many attractions in Zainul Abidin Park are stunning fountains, swings, trains, and magic boats, as well as miniature zoos, the Boishakh Manch and horse-drawn carriage rides.

Entry Fee and Time:

Entry fee is BDT 20 per person.

From Saturday through Wednesday, the museum is open from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and from 3 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Fridays. The museum closes on Thursdays every week.

How to go:

Shilpaacharya Zainul Abedin Park can be reached by rickshaw from Mymensingh Railway Station or Bus Station.

Chinamati Hills, located in the Bijoypur area of ​​​​Susang Durgapur in Netrakona district, are famous for their unique natural beauty. It is mainly a mineral area, where white clay hills and mountains can be seen. Since 1957, commercial extraction of chinamati has started here, which is used as the main raw material in the ceramic industry.
Due to soil excavation, many small and large lakes have been created in different places on the hill. Due to the white soil, the water of the lakes is sometimes clear blue, and sometimes greenish blue or pink, which presents an extraordinary scene. Its length is about 15.5 kilometers and width is 600 meters. The Someshwari River is next to this hill, which enhances its beauty many times over.
Currently, it is known as a popular tourist destination, where numerous tourists come every day to enjoy the charming view of white clay hills and colorful water lakes.

মাটি খননের ফলে এই পাহাড়ের বুকে বিভিন্ন স্থানে ছোট-বড় অনেক হ্রদের সৃষ্টি হয়েছে। সাদা মাটির কারণে হ্রদগুলোর পানি কোথাও স্বচ্ছ নীল, আবার কোথাও সবুজাভ নীল বা গোলাপি রঙের দেখায়, যা এক অসাধারণ দৃশ্যের অবতারণা করে। এর দৈর্ঘ্য প্রায় ১৫.৫ কিলোমিটার এবং প্রস্থ ৬০০ মিটার। এই পাহাড়ের পাশেই রয়েছে সোমেশ্বরী নদী, যা এর সৌন্দর্যকে আরও বহুগুণ বাড়িয়ে তোলে।

The Chinamat Hills of Vijaypur, Netrakona, are a place where you will feel like you have entered a dream world. The colors of these hills are so beautiful that even taking a camera cannot capture their beauty. And the shape and size of these hills are also extraordinary. It will seem that an artist has made them very beautifully.
When you go here, you will see a huge plain on top of the hill. And a river of blue water is flowing through the middle of that plain. You may have never seen such a scene before. Honestly, the Chinamat Hills of Vijaypur are a wonderful place.
However, keep in mind that these hills look most beautiful at sunset. So, if possible, reach there before evening. And yes, leave a little earlier on your way back, because the way out from there is a little difficult.

review_text:
The China Clay Hills or Sadamati Hills, located in Bijoypur, Durgapur Upazila, Netrokona District, are a historical and natural tourist attraction [1, 10]. After the discovery of mineral resources in the region in 1957, Kohinoor Aluminium Works first started extracting the clay in 1960 [1]. It is mainly of the Tertiary period [10] and is used as the main raw material in the ceramic industry [10, 14].
Detailed history of Bijapur China Clay Hills:
Location and geographical features: These hills are located in the villages of Ara Para, Maijpara, Shasarpar and Baheratoli in Bijoypur Union, Durgapur Upazila, Netrokona District [10]. It is about 15.5 km long and 600 m wide [1, 14].
Recognition as a mineral: In 1957, a survey by the Mineral Resources Development Bureau estimated that there were about 2.47 million metric tons of clay reserves here, which is capable of meeting the needs of Bangladesh for 300 years [1].
Mining and use: Kohinoor Aluminium Works was the first to commercially mine this soil in 1960 [1]. Later, BCIC took over mining in 1973 [1].
Naming and variety: Although it is called plain soil, reddish, grey, light blue, pink, yellow and teal colored soils are also found here [14].
Current condition: Due to years of mining, deep lakes have been formed here between the high and low hills [7]. These blue-green lakes are now one of the main attractions for tourists [5, 7].
It is located at the foot of the Garo Hills and the Someswari River flows through it

নেত্রকোণা জেলার দুর্গাপুর উপজেলার বিজয়পুরে অবস্থিত চীনের মাটির পাহাড় বা সাদামাটির পাহাড় একটি ঐতিহাসিক ও প্রাকৃতিক দর্শনীয় স্থান [১, ১০]। ১৯৫৭ সালে এই অঞ্চলের খনিজ সম্পদের খোঁজ পাওয়ার পর ১৯৬০ সালে কোহিনুর এলুমিনিয়াম ওয়ার্কস প্রথম মাটি উত্তোলনের কাজ শুরু করে [১]। এটি মূলত টারশিয়ারি যুগের [১০] এবং সিরামিক শিল্পের প্রধান কাঁচামাল হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হয় [১০, ১৪]।
বিজাপুর চীনামাটির পাহাড়ের বিস্তারিত ইতিহাস:
অবস্থান ও ভৌগোলিক বৈশিষ্ট্য: নেত্রকোণা জেলার দুর্গাপুর উপজেলার বিজয়পুর ইউনিয়নের আড়া পারা, মাইজপাড়া, শসারপাড় ও বহেড়াতলী গ্রামে এই পাহাড়গুলোর অবস্থান [১০]। এটি প্রায় ১৫.৫ কিলোমিটার দীর্ঘ এবং ৬০০ মিটার প্রস্থ [১, ১৪]।
খনিজ হিসেবে স্বীকৃতি: ১৯৫৭ সালে খনিজ সম্পদ উন্নয়ন ব্যুরোর জরিপে এখানে প্রায় ২৪ লক্ষ ৭০ হাজার মেট্রিক টন সাদামাটির মজুত ধরা হয়, যা বাংলাদেশের ৩০০ বছরের চাহিদা পূরণে সক্ষম [১]।
উত্তোলন ও ব্যবহার: ১৯৬০ সালে কোহিনুর এলুমিনিয়াম ওয়ার্কস প্রথম বাণিজ্যিকভাবে এই মাটি উত্তোলন শুরু করে [১]। পরবর্তীতে ১৯৭৩ সালে বিসিআইসি (BCIC) মাটি উত্তোলনের দায়িত্ব নেয় [১]।
নামকরণ ও বৈচিত্র্য: একে সাদামাটি বলা হলেও, এখানে লালচে, ধূসর, হালকা নীলাভ, গোলাপি, হলুদ ও টিয়া রঙের মাটিও দেখা যায় [১৪]।
বর্তমান অবস্থা: বছরের পর বছর ধরে মাটি কাটার ফলে এখানে উঁচু-নিচু পাহাড়ের মাঝে গভীর হ্রদ বা লেকের সৃষ্টি হয়েছে [৭]। এই নীল-সবুজ পানির হ্রদগুলো এখন পর্যটকদের জন্য একটি অন্যতম প্রধান আকর্ষণ [৫, ৭]।

Ahsan Manzil, also known as the "Pink Palace," is a historic landmark in Dhaka, Bangladesh, and a national museum. Located on the banks of the Buriganga River, it was the official residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka, with construction beginning in 1859 and completing in 1872. The building showcases Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture, featuring a prominent pink exterior and a central dome. Today, it houses 23 galleries displaying artifacts related to the Nawab era and the region's history.
History: The site was once a 17th-century garden house owned by Sheikh Enayet Ullah. It was later acquired by French traders and then became the property of the Nawab of Dhaka, Nawab Abdul Ghani, who named it after his son, Khwaja Ahsanullah. The palace suffered damage from a tornado in 1888 and an earthquake in 1897, leading to its reconstruction and expansion.
Architecture and layout: The two-story building is constructed on a raised platform and is divided into two main sections: the eastern "Rangmahal" and the western "Andarmahal". It features distinctive architectural elements like a large, octagonal dome and ornate wooden ceilings. The interior includes a drawing room, library, and assembly hall, among other rooms.
Museum exhibits: The museum showcases the lifestyle of the Nawabs through various exhibits, which include family portraits, furniture, and even the skull of Nawab Abdul Ghani's favorite elephant. Some exhibits are displayed based on photographs taken during the palace's heyday.
Significance: Ahsan Manzil is a significant cultural heritage site in Bangladesh, offering insight into the country's colonial history. Its restoration in the late 1980s, aided by old photographs, saved it from disrepair and allowed for its preservation as a museum for future generations.

Ahsan Manzil Is The One Most Beautiful and old architectural style of the landlord's residential palace which is located in the poran Dhaka ,Kumartoli area beside Buriganga River of Dhaka, Bangladesh.This is a Historical Place. Ahsan Manzil is associated with the centuries-old history of Dhaka. Ahsan Manzil is considered one of the best old structures in Dhaka. This palace, which is full of memories of the Nawab family, is currently being run as a museum. "Ahsan Manzil" is a rich repository of Bengal's glorious history and Nawabi heritage. In the middle of the 18th century, the landlord Sheikh Inayet Ullah built a palace called Rang Mahal on the present site of Ahsan Manzil. Later, his son Sheikh Matiullah sold Rang Mahal to French merchants. In 1830, Khwaja Alimullah, father of Nawab Abdul Ghani, bought it. In 1859, Nawab Abdul Ghani started building a palace there. It took 13 long years to build the palace. He named it ‘Ahsan Manzil’ after his beloved son Khwaja Ahsanullah.
Once upon a time, the highest dome in Dhaka was the beautiful dome on the roof of the Ahsan Manzil Palace. The veranda and floor of this two-storey building are made of marble. Inside the palace there is a dining room, library, water tank, court hall and billiard room. And on the second floor of the palace there are guest rooms, a drawing room, a dance hall, a library and some other living rooms. There are car verandas on the north and south sides of the palace, one story high. On the south side, an open staircase goes down from the veranda of the second floor to the front garden. Just in front of the palace is a beautiful flower garden and a green field.
Ahsan Manzil is considered to be the first brick and stone architectural monument in the city of Dhaka. And the first electric light was lit in this building by the Nawabs of that time. The architectural style of Ahsan Manzil attracted the West equally, there is evidence that Lord Curzon actually stayed in this building when he was in Dhaka. This palace was a major political center of Bengal from the mid-19th century for about 100 years. In 1906, a meeting held here decided to establish the Muslim League. Architectural style
There is a beautiful dome on the roof of this palace. At one time, the top of this dome was the highest in Dhaka city. The three-arched entrance outside the main building is also beautiful to look at. Similarly, the stairs leading up to it also attract everyone's attention. There are two beautiful arches on the east and west ends, which are the most beautiful. There are two parts inside Ahsan Manzil. There is a sitting room and a library in the east part. There is a dance hall and other residential rooms in the west part. There is a courtroom and a dining room on the ground floor.
The two-story palace building, built on a 1-meter-high altar, measures 125.4 meters and 28.75 meters. The height from floor to ceiling on the ground floor is 5 meters and 5.8 meters on the second floor. There are car balconies on the north and south sides of the palace, which are the same height as one floor. A large open staircase leads down from the second-story balcony through the front garden to the riverbank. In front of the staircase was a fountain in the garden, which does not exist today. There are wide balconies with semicircular arches on the north and south sides of both floors of the palace. The floors of the balconies and rooms are decorated with marble. To build the dome of Ahsan Manzil, first the four corners of the square room on the ground floor were filled with bricks and given a round shape. Above this, a similar round room built on the second floor was made octagonal near the roof by squinching the upper part. This octagonal room became the barrel of the dome on the roof. Finally, the pointed heads of the octagonal arms are gradually tilted towards the center and the dome in the shape of a lotus has been created. The height of the dome top from the ground is 27.13 meters. In 1992, the tourist attraction was renovated and converted into a museum (Ahsan Manzil Museum)।
