review_text:
Ahsan Manzil, known as the Pink Palace, is one of Dhaka’s most famous landmarks. It sits on the bank of the Buriganga River in Kumartoli and was once the official residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka. Built between 1859 and 1872 in a blend of Mughal and European styles, it now serves as a branch museum under the Bangladesh National Museum.

The palace’s history mirrors the rise and fall of Dhaka’s aristocracy. The site first belonged to a Mughal landlord named Sheikh Enayetullah, and later to French traders in the 18th century. In 1830, Khwaja Alimullah bought it, and his son Khwaja Abdul Ghani turned it into the grand palace we see today, naming it after his own son, Ahsanullah. The building was badly damaged by a tornado in 1888 but was rebuilt with its now-iconic dome. Over time, it became a political center where major decisions and meetings were held, including early gatherings of the All India Muslim League. After the Nawabs’ decline, the palace fell into neglect until it was restored and opened as a museum in 1992.

The palace has two main parts — Rangmahal, which contained formal rooms like the drawing and guest rooms, and Andarmahal, which housed private areas like the dining and music rooms. A wooden bridge once connected the two. The large central dome, shaped like a lotus bud, rises above the structure and is one of Dhaka’s most recognizable sights.

Visitors can tour the museum for a small fee (ranging from 40৳ for locals to 500৳ for foreign tourists). It’s open Saturday to Wednesday and on Fridays in the afternoon, but closed on Thursdays. A one-hour visit is enough to explore its galleries and enjoy the palace’s beauty. Its location in Old Dhaka also makes it easy to visit along with nearby attractions like Lalbagh Fort and the Star Mosque.

Ahsan Manzil Museum located in Dhaka, is a testament to the architectural grandeur of the past and offers a glimpse into the opulent lifestyle of the Nawabs during the British colonial period. This iconic pink palace—standing proudly on the banks of the Buriganga River—has been meticulously restored and transformed into a museum.
The museum is open for visitors six days a week, from Tuesday to Saturday (10:30 AM - 5:30 PM) and Sunday (2:30 PM - 7:30 PM). It remains closed on Thursday and public holidays, so planning your visit in advance is essential. Tickets cost 40 tk for locals, 300 tk for SAARAC, and 500 tk for all other foreigners.
Visiting Ahsan Manzil has numerous positives. The beautifully preserved structure and its exhibits, including artifacts, furniture, and photographs from the Nawabi era, transport you back in time. The museum also has a vibrant and photogenic courtyard, making it a favorite spot for photographers and history enthusiasts. The panoramic view of the Buriganga River adds to the charm, especially during sunset.
However, visitors may encounter some challenges. The area surrounding the museum is often congested, and reaching it can be time-consuming due to Dhaka’s notorious traffic. Limited parking space adds to the inconvenience. Inside, while the exhibits are fascinating, the lack of modern interpretive tools (such as audio guides) can leave international visitors wanting more context. Additionally, the museum can get crowded on weekends and holidays, making it harder to explore at your own pace.
Despite these struggles, Ahsan Manzil Museum offers a unique cultural and historical experience. It’s an excellent destination for anyone looking to dive into the rich heritage of Bangladesh.

Situated on the banks of the Buriganga River, this former residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka stands as a powerful reminder of the city’s cultural, political, and architectural heritage.

Each room tells a story—about the Nawabi lifestyle, colonial-era politics, social customs, and the evolution of Dhaka itself. The surrounding area is lively and chaotic, which makes the calm and dignity of Ahsan Manzil even more striking. Despite being located in the heart of Old Dhaka, the palace manages to preserve a sense of order and nostalgia. It’s a perfect place for photography, history enthusiasts, students, and anyone interested in understanding Dhaka beyond its modern skyline.
Overall, Ahsan Manzil is more than just a museum—it’s a symbol of Dhaka’s identity and resilience. A visit here offers valuable insight into the city’s past and leaves you with a deeper appreciation of its rich and layered history. Highly recommended for locals and tourists alike.

review_text: Ahsan Manjil is located at Kumartuli, Dhaka South city Corporation, Dhaka. I have a chance to visit it along with my wife on 03 February 2024 at about 1415 hours. Before today I had visited it so many times. It is the former residence and seat of the Nawab of Dhaka. In the Mughal Empire, Sheikh Enayet ullah, Zamindar of the Jamalpur, Porgona district had a garden house on this property and added a palace which he called Rangmahal. After his death his son Sheikh Moti ullah was sold to French Traders. They erected a trading house beside the property. In the year of 1835 Nawba Abdul Ghani's father Khwaja Alimullah purchased the property from the French traders. He had renovated it and started living there as a “Nawab” house. In the year of 1872 Nawab Khwaja Abdul Ghani also renovated it and named the property as “Ahsan Manzil” for his son Khwaja Ahsan Ullah. He also continued renovations; the old building was renamed Ondor Mohol and the new building was called Rangmahal. The Government of Bangladesh acquired the palace and property in 1985 and also renovated it. Renovations were completed in the year of 1992 and ownership was transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum. Now it is an old Dhaka heritage site of Bangladesh. It is always busy with national visitors and foreign tourists. It is open at 10:30 am and closed at 0530pm regularly. Thursday is a weekly holiday. Entrance fee adult Tk40/, Child Tk20/ for hoste, SARAC Tk300/ and foreign Tk 500/ each only. There is♿wheelchair accessible entrance,♿ wheelchair accessible car park  and ♿ wheelchair accessible toilets facilities. Ref:wikipedia.

Ahsan Manzil - A Must-Visit Historical Gem in Dhaka!

Rating: ★★★★★

I recently had the pleasure of visiting Ahsan Manzil, and it was an unforgettable experience! Here's why you should add this historical gem to your must-visit list when in Dhaka:

Historical Significance:
Ahsan Manzil, also known as the Pink Palace, is a magnificent reminder of Dhaka's rich history. Built in the 19th century, it served as the official residence of the Nawab of Dhaka and now stands as a museum showcasing the grandeur of that era.

Ticket Prices:
The entrance fee is very reasonable. For locals, it's around 40 BDT, and for foreigners, it's approximately 100 BDT. It's worth every penny considering the wealth of history and beauty you'll experience inside.

Architecture & Exhibits:
The architecture of Ahsan Manzil is stunning, with its vibrant pink exterior and intricate designs. Inside, you'll find a plethora of artifacts, furniture, and photographs that offer a glimpse into the Nawab's lifestyle. The well-preserved rooms and detailed exhibits are a history lover's dream.

Environment & Atmosphere:
The palace is surrounded by lush gardens and overlooks the Buriganga River, providing a serene and picturesque setting. It's a perfect spot for photography enthusiasts. The environment is well-maintained, and the staff are friendly and informative.

Nearby Attractions:
While in the area, make sure to explore other nearby attractions. The Sadarghat River Port is just a short walk away, where you can witness the bustling river traffic. Lalbagh Fort, another historical site, is also close by and offers further insights into Dhaka's history. For a more modern experience, the bustling streets of Old Dhaka with their vibrant markets and street food are just around the corner.

Tips for Visitors:
- Visit early in the morning to avoid the crowds and enjoy a more peaceful experience.
- Don't forget your camera; the palace and its surroundings are incredibly photogenic.
- Allocate at least 1-2 hours to fully appreciate the exhibits and the beauty of the palace grounds.

Ahsan Manzil is not just a visit; it's a journey through time. Highly recommended for anyone interested in history, architecture, or simply looking to enjoy a beautiful day out in Dhaka!

Ahsan Manzil is indeed a historical landmark and museum located in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It holds great cultural and historical significance for the country. Let me provide you with some information about Ahsan Manzil and its history:

Ahsan Manzil, also known as the Pink Palace, is a magnificent mansion situated on the banks of the Buriganga River in Old Dhaka. It was originally built in the 19th century during the era of the Nawabs of Bengal. The construction of the palace began in 1859 and was completed in 1872.

The Ahsan Manzil served as the official residential palace of the Nawab family and was particularly associated with Khwaja Alimullah, who was a wealthy landlord and a prominent member of the Dhaka Nawab family. It later became the residence of Nawab Abdul Gani, his son. The palace was named after Nawab Khwaja Ahsanullah, the son of Nawab Abdul Gani.

The architectural style of Ahsan Manzil is a fusion of Mughal and European influences, predominantly reflecting the Indo-Saracenic architectural style. The palace complex covers an area of around 5 acres and features a magnificent pink-colored building with a distinct dome and grand portico.

Unfortunately, Ahsan Manzil suffered extensive damage during a tornado in 1888 and a devastating earthquake in 1897. However, the palace was reconstructed and restored under the supervision of Lord Curzon, the then Viceroy of India. The reconstruction was completed in 1901, and the palace regained its former glory.

In 1985, the Bangladesh government converted Ahsan Manzil into a museum to showcase the rich heritage and history of Dhaka and its Nawabi era. The museum exhibits a wide range of artifacts, photographs, paintings, furniture, and other items that provide insights into the lifestyle, culture, and traditions of the Nawab family and the bygone era.

Ahsan Manzil is a popular tourist attraction, drawing visitors who are interested in exploring the architectural beauty, historical significance, and cultural heritage of Bangladesh. The museum offers a glimpse into the opulent lifestyle of the Nawabs and provides a fascinating journey back in time.

Shoshi Lodge
Shoshi Lodge is a royal mansion located in the district town of Mymensingh. In the 19th century, Maharaja Suryakanta Acharya Chowdhury, the Zamindar of Muktagacha, constructed this magnificent palace. He named the palace 'Shoshi Lodge' after his adopted son, Shashikanta Acharya Chowdhury. Locally, it is also known as the Mymensingh Rajbari (Royal Palace). After the building was damaged in the earthquake of 1897, Shashikanta Acharya Chowdhury rebuilt it. Built on a nine-acre estate, the main gate of the Shoshi Lodge complex features sixteen domes.

There is a beautiful garden in front of the main building of Shoshi Lodge. At the center of the garden stands a white marble fountain accompanied by a marble statue of the Greek goddess Venus. Behind the main building—which comprises eighteen spacious rooms—lie a two-story bathhouse, a pond, and a marble-paved ghat (steps leading to the water). When the Women's Teachers' Training College was established at Shoshi Lodge in 1952, the main building served as the principal's office and administrative headquarters. On April 4, 2015, the Department of Archaeology of the Government of Bangladesh acquired Shoshi Lodge to establish a museum.

Shashi Lodge is one of the most important historical structures in Mymensingh. Based on verified information, we have prepared a 200+ word Google Maps review.

Shashi Lodge is a famous historical palace and architectural monument in Mymensingh city, also known locally as Mymensingh Rajbari. Maharaja Suryakanta Acharya Chowdhury, a descendant of the Muktagachha zamindar family, built this palace in the name of his adopted son Shashikanta Acharya. The original two-story building, built in the late 19th century, was severely damaged in the terrible earthquake of 1897. Later, Shashikanta Acharya built a new building on the same site, the construction of which was completed around 1905 and its beautification and renovation were carried out in 1911.

Spread over an area of ​​about 9 acres, the architecture of Shashi Lodge shows the traces of European influence as well as the opulence of the zamindari period. The magnificent arches of the entrance, spacious green courtyard, ornate fountains, old ponds, marble construction, large halls, elaborate doors and windows, and historical interior architecture attract visitors. Various works of art and historical monuments associated with the palace have also increased its importance.

Shashi Lodge was declared a protected monument of the Department of Archaeology in 1989. Later, the activities of the Mymensingh Museum were also added to it. As a result, it is not just an old landlord's house, but an important monument of the history, zamindari culture, architecture, and archaeological heritage of Mymensingh.

As a historical monument, the preservation, cleanliness, and security of the Shashi Lodge are very important. For history and architecture lovers, Shashi Lodge is a must-see place on a trip to Mymensingh. Combining the palace's historical atmosphere, architectural style, and long past, one can experience an important chapter in the history of the zamindari of Mymensingh by coming here. 🏛️🌿📜

প্রায় ৯ একর জায়গাজুড়ে বিস্তৃত শশী লজের স্থাপত্যে ইউরোপীয় প্রভাবের পাশাপাশি জমিদারি আমলের ঐশ্বর্যের ছাপ দেখা যায়। প্রবেশপথের দৃষ্টিনন্দন খিলান, প্রশস্ত সবুজ প্রাঙ্গণ, অলংকৃত ফোয়ারা, পুরোনো পুকুর, মার্বেলের নির্মাণকাজ, বড় হলঘর, কারুকার্যময় দরজা-জানালা এবং ঐতিহাসিক অভ্যন্তরীণ স্থাপত্য দর্শনার্থীদের আকর্ষণ করে। প্রাসাদের সঙ্গে যুক্ত বিভিন্ন শিল্পকর্ম ও ঐতিহাসিক নিদর্শনও এর গুরুত্ব বাড়িয়েছে।

শশী লজ ১৯৮৯ সালে প্রত্নতত্ত্ব অধিদপ্তরের সংরক্ষিত প্রত্নস্থাপনা হিসেবে ঘোষিত হয়। পরবর্তীতে এর সঙ্গে ময়মনসিংহ জাদুঘরের কার্যক্রমও যুক্ত হয়েছে। ফলে এটি শুধু একটি পুরোনো জমিদারবাড়ি নয়, বরং ময়মনসিংহের ইতিহাস, জমিদারি সংস্কৃতি, স্থাপত্য ও প্রত্নঐতিহ্যের একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ স্মারক।

ঐতিহাসিক স্থাপনা হিসেবে শশী লজের সংরক্ষণ, পরিচ্ছন্নতা ও প্রত্নসম্পদের নিরাপত্তা অত্যন্ত গুরুত্বপূর্ণ। ইতিহাস ও স্থাপত্যপ্রেমীদের জন্য ময়মনসিংহ ভ্রমণে শশী লজ অবশ্যই দেখার মতো একটি জায়গা। প্রাসাদের ঐতিহাসিক পরিবেশ, স্থাপত্যশৈলী ও দীর্ঘ অতীত মিলিয়ে এখানে এসে ময়মনসিংহের জমিদারি ইতিহাসের একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ অধ্যায় অনুভব করা যায়। 🏛️🌿📜

review_text:
When visiting Mymensingh city, you can visit Shashi Lodge once. The place is mainly interesting for its history and old architecture. As beautiful as it looks from the outside, you can feel the atmosphere of the old landlord's house quite well when you enter.

The whole place has a different historical atmosphere. Looking at the design of the old building, large rooms, balconies, doors and windows, arches and various architectural works, it is understood that this is not just an ordinary old house. The beauty of the establishment lies in its simplicity and old features. Those who like to see history, antiquities or old architecture should like the place.

There are also some beautiful places to take pictures. Especially in the front part of the building and the open areas around it, good pictures can be obtained. However, since it is a historical establishment, you should be a little careful when visiting. You should not damage any part of the walls or establishment with your hands, throw dirt or spoil the environment.

I liked the old atmosphere of the place the most. There isn't much to do here like a modern entertainment center, but it's a good place to take a leisurely stroll, enjoy the architecture, and spend some time with history.

If you're planning a day trip to Mymensingh, Sashi Lodge can be included in your list, along with Muktagachha or other places to visit. It doesn't take much time, so it's easy to explore from within the city. Overall, Sashi Lodge is a beautiful and enjoyable place to get a closer look at the history and heritage of Mymensingh.

ময়মনসিংহ শহরে ঘুরতে গেলে শশী লজে একবার যাওয়া যায়। জায়গাটি মূলত ইতিহাস ও পুরোনো স্থাপত্যের জন্য আকর্ষণীয়। বাইরে থেকে দেখলে যেমন সুন্দর লাগে, ভেতরে ঢুকেও পুরোনো দিনের জমিদারবাড়ির পরিবেশটা বেশ ভালোভাবে অনুভব করা যায়।

পুরো জায়গাটিতে একটা আলাদা ঐতিহাসিক আবহ আছে। পুরোনো ভবনের নকশা, বড় বড় কক্ষ, বারান্দা, দরজা-জানালা, খিলান ও বিভিন্ন স্থাপত্যের কাজ দেখলে বোঝা যায় যে এটি শুধু একটি সাধারণ পুরোনো বাড়ি নয়। স্থাপনাটির সৌন্দর্য অনেকটাই এর সরলতা ও পুরোনো বৈশিষ্ট্যের মধ্যে। যারা ইতিহাস, পুরাকীর্তি বা পুরোনো স্থাপত্য দেখতে পছন্দ করেন, তাদের কাছে জায়গাটি ভালো লাগার কথা।

ছবি তোলার জন্যও বেশ সুন্দর কিছু জায়গা আছে। বিশেষ করে ভবনের সামনের অংশ ও আশপাশের খোলা জায়গায় ভালো ছবি পাওয়া যায়। তবে এটি ঐতিহাসিক স্থাপনা হওয়ায় ঘুরতে গেলে একটু যত্নশীল থাকা উচিত। দেয়াল বা স্থাপনার কোনো অংশে হাত দিয়ে ক্ষতি করা, ময়লা ফেলা বা পরিবেশ নষ্ট করা একেবারেই উচিত নয়।

আমার কাছে সবচেয়ে ভালো লেগেছে জায়গাটির পুরোনো পরিবেশটা। আধুনিক কোনো বিনোদনকেন্দ্রের মতো এখানে অনেক কিছু করার নেই, কিন্তু শান্তভাবে ঘুরে দেখা, স্থাপত্য উপভোগ করা এবং কিছু সময় ইতিহাসের সঙ্গে কাটানোর জন্য জায়গাটি বেশ ভালো।

ময়মনসিংহে একদিনের জন্য ঘুরতে গেলে মুক্তাগাছা বা অন্যান্য দর্শনীয় স্থানের পাশাপাশি শশী লজকেও তালিকায় রাখা যেতে পারে। খুব বেশি সময়ও লাগে না, তাই শহরের মধ্যে থেকে সহজেই ঘুরে দেখা সম্ভব। সব মিলিয়ে, ময়মনসিংহের ইতিহাস ও ঐতিহ্যকে কাছ থেকে দেখার জন্য শশী লজ একটি সুন্দর ও উপভোগ্য জায়গা।

review_text:
Shoshi Lodge is a notable historical establishment in Mymensingh, which was built in the 19th century during the reign of Maharaja Suryakanta Acharya Chowdhury. This palace from the Zamindari period still attracts visitors for its traditional architecture, old-time nobility and history.

Its royal and traditional architectural style is evident from the outside. Although it is an old building, its walls, design and structure still reflect the aristocratic impression of that time.

The interior environment is also quite peaceful and pleasant. The view of the pond is especially beautiful - a wonderful atmosphere has been created by the combination of water, green plants and historical establishments. Spending some time here gives you a lot of peace.

If you want to enjoy history, architecture and the beauty of nature together, Shoshi Lodge is definitely a place to visit. It is also a good spot to spend time with your family. I would definitely recommend visiting the place if you go to Mymensingh.

শশী লজ (Shoshi Lodge) ময়মনসিংহের একটি উল্লেখযোগ্য ঐতিহাসিক স্থাপনা, যা ঊনবিংশ শতাব্দীতে মহারাজা সূর্যকান্ত আচার্য চৌধুরীর আমলে নির্মিত হয়েছিল। জমিদারি আমলের এই প্রাসাদটি তার ঐতিহ্যবাহী স্থাপত্য, পুরোনো দিনের আভিজাত্য ও ইতিহাসের জন্য এখনো দর্শনার্থীদের আকর্ষণ করে।

বাহির থেকে দেখলেই এর রাজকীয় ও ঐতিহ্যবাহী স্থাপত্যশৈলী চোখে পড়ে। পুরোনো ভবন হলেও এর দেয়াল, নকশা ও গঠনশৈলীতে সেই সময়ের অভিজাত ছাপ এখনো বেশ ভালোভাবেই বোঝা যায়।

ভেতরের পরিবেশও বেশ শান্ত ও মনোরম। বিশেষ করে পুকুরপাড়ের দৃশ্যটি খুবই সুন্দর—পানি, সবুজ গাছপালা ও ঐতিহাসিক স্থাপনার সমন্বয়ে চমৎকার একটি পরিবেশ তৈরি হয়েছে। কিছু সময় এখানে বসে কাটালে বেশ প্রশান্তি পাওয়া যায়।

ইতিহাস, স্থাপত্য ও প্রকৃতির সৌন্দর্য একসঙ্গে উপভোগ করতে চাইলে Shoshi Lodge অবশ্যই ঘুরে দেখার মতো একটি জায়গা। পরিবার নিয়ে সময় কাটানোর জন্যও এটি বেশ ভালো একটি স্পট। ময়মনসিংহে গেলে জায়গাটি ঘুরে দেখার জন্য অবশ্যই সুপারিশ করব।

review_text:
Bijoypur Border, Netrokona is located near at the India–Bangladesh border, at Kulagora Upazila of Durgapur Thana. This camp is beside the tranquil river Shomeswari. The ambient atmosphere of that area is really enthralling. Anyone can enjoy the outline hills from Indian portion from there. If you are lucky, you can see the floating clouds over the hills too. It is the season of winter, but I guess rainy season will be the best to visit that place.

Troops from BGB camp will not allow you to go beyond after that area. But if you have time, you can bypass the camp using far side route, and go further near to the border. We didn’t have enough time, otherwise I might have taken that chance.

It will be a nice experience for you to ride on the boat beside the camp. Basically there is no such boats are available. You’ll find few boats are crawling over the river for caring the collected coal from the river. You can hire few of those (if you can convince those reluctant boatmen). The exact GPS coordinate of Bijoypur BGB camp is (25°10’42.58″N, 90°39’23.78″E).

Referred to how to go to Netrokona from Dhaka, click here. You can hire rickshaw costing 300 taka. It’s actually somewhere between 200-300 for visiting that place. Alternately you can hire motorbike too. Those are faster and less time, but won’t allow you to enjoy the village atmosphere during the ride. So, will be using the rickshaw is preferable. That rickshaw puller will be your guide throughout the expedition.

By road approximately 16 km (Netrokona-Mymensingh -39 km, Mymensingh City -3 km and Mymensingh-Dhaka 120 km). Also to travel directly different locations from the main city.

review_text: Bijoypur White Clay Hill. This is a unique and beautiful place in Birishiri and is constantly playing a role in the national economy. The White Clay Hill is one of the most spectacular places in Birishiri. Here is the China Clay Hill, whose chest has been torn open by this blue-green water lake. The color in the middle of the white clay has made it even darker. However, you will not be able to see this beautiful scene just by coming to Birishiri. You will have to go a little further to Bijoypur China Clay Hill. There are China Clay mines in Bijoypur and its surrounding areas of Durgapur Upazila. China Clay is basically the raw material of the ceramic industry. According to the 1957 information of the Mineral Resources Bureau, the reserves of China Clay in this area are about 2.4 million 40 thousand metric tons. It was said at that time that it is possible to meet the three hundred years' demand of Bangladesh with this. A few private companies are extracting China Clay here with permission from the Mineral Resources Development Bureau. Thousands of workers are working on mining projects every day. Then it is transported to the ceramic industry factories. These hills or mountains of china clay are very attractive to see. The color of the clay in Bahari. Red, white, blue. It is like another natural environment. The white clay of Bijoypur is located in Aarapara and Maijpara mouzas of Kullagara Union, 7 kilometers northwest of Durgapur Upazila Parishad. This is one of the largest mineral areas of white clay as a natural resource in Bangladesh. This mineral area is about 15.5 kilometers long and 600 meters wide across small hills and plains. According to the information of the Mineral Resources Development Bureau, the amount of white clay in this area in 1957 was estimated at 24 lakh 70 thousand metric tons, which can meet the needs of Bangladesh for 300 years. You can reach the plain clay area of ​​Bijoypur by crossing the Someshwari River and taking a rickshaw or Honda through a semi-unpaved road.
review_text_original: বিজয়পুর সাদা মাটির পাহাড়। এটি  বিরিশিরির অনন্য সুন্দর একটি  স্থান সেই সাথে জাতীয় অর্থনীতিতে ভূমিকা রাখছে প্রতিনিয়ত। সাদামাটির পাহাড় বিরিশিরির অন্যতম দর্শনীয় স্থানগুলোর মধ্যে অন্যতম। এখানে চীনামাটির পাহাড়, যার বুক চিরে জেগে উঠেছে এই নীলচে-সবুজ পানির হ্রদ। সাদা মাটির মাঝে রঙটাকে যেন আরও বেশি গাঢ় করে দিয়েছে। তবে বিরিশিরি এসেই আপনি এ সুন্দর দৃশ্য আপনি দেখতে পারবেন না। আপনাকে যেতে হবে আরেকটু দূর বিজয়পুর চীনা মাটির পাহাড়ে। দুর্গাপুর উপজেলার বিজয়পুর ও এর আশপাশের এলাকায় রয়েছে চিনামাটির খনি। চিনামাটি মূলতঃ সিরামিক শিল্পের কাঁচামাল। খনিজ সম্পদ ব্যুরোর ১৯৫৭ সালের তথ্যানুযায়ী, এ এলাকায় চিনামাটির মজুদ প্রায় ২৪ লাখ ৪০ হাজার মেট্রিক টন। এটি দিয়ে বাংলাদেশের তিনশ বছরের চাহিদা পূরণ সম্ভব বলে তখন বলা হয়েছিল। খনিজ সম্পদ উন্নয়ন ব্যুরো থেকে অনুমতি নিয়ে কয়েকটি বেসরকারি কোম্পানী এখানকার চিনামাটি আহরণ করছে। প্রতিদিন হাজার হাজার শ্রমিক মাটি খননের কাজ করছে খনিজ প্রকল্পগুলোতে। এরপর তা পরিবহন করে নিয়ে যাওয়া হচ্ছে সিরামিক শিল্পের কারখানাগুলোতে। চিনামাটির এসব টিলা বা পাহাড় দেখতে খুবই মনোমুগ্ধকর। বাহারি এর মাটির রঙ। লাল, সাদা, নীলাভ। এ যেন প্রকৃতিক আরেক নিসর্গ। দূর্গাপুর উপজেলা পরিষদ থেকে ৭ কিলোমিটার উত্তর-পশ্চিমে কুল্লাগড়া ইউনিয়নের আড়াপাড়া ও মাইজপাড়া মৌজায় বিজয়পুরের সাদা মাটি অবস্থিত। বাংলাদেশের মধ্যে প্রকৃতির সম্পদ হিসেবে সাদা মাটির অন্যতম বৃহৎখনিজ অঞ্চল এটি। ছোট বড় টিলা-পাহাড় ও সমতল ভূমি জুড়ে প্রায় ১৫.৫ কিলোমিটার দীর্ঘ ও ৬০০ মিটার প্রস্থ এই খনিজ অঞ্চল। খনিজ সম্পদ উন্নয়ন ব্যুরোর তথ্য অনুযায়ী ১৯৫৭ সালে এই অঞ্চলে সাদামাটির পরিমাণ ধরা হয় ২৪ লক্ষ ৭০ হাজার মেট্রিক টন, যা বাংলাদেশের ৩ শত বৎসরের চাহিদা পুরণ করতে পারে। সোমেশ্বরী নদী পার হয়ে রিক্সা বা হোন্ডায় অর্ধ  কাচা-পাকা রাস্তা দিয়ে বিজয়পুরের সাদামাটি অঞ্চলে যাওয়া যায়।

review_text: Brief Description: Bijoypur white clay is located in Arapara and Maijpara mouzas of Kullagara Union, 7 kilometers northwest of Durgapur Upazila Parishad. This is one of the largest mineral areas of white clay as a natural resource in Bangladesh. This mineral area is about 15.5 kilometers long and 600 meters wide across small and large hills and plains. According to the Mineral Resources Development Bureau, the amount of white clay in this area in 1957 was estimated to be 24.7 million metric tons, which can meet the needs of Bangladesh for 300 years. Background and History: Although the ancient history of Chinese clay is not known, the work of extracting this soil started in 1957. In 1960, an organization named Kohinoor Aluminum Works was the first to start extracting this soil. Later, BCIC joined in extracting this soil in 1973. Currently, 9 companies are working to extract this soil. About 300 workers are involved in extracting this soil. The beautiful beauty of different colored soil, water and nature captivates the mind. White, pink, yellow, purple, brown, and blue colored hills of soil delight the eyes. Tribal settlements are spread throughout the plain area. review_text:
Naval Sea Beach (Chittagong) is a fantastic coastal spot, and the transition from evening to night here offers two completely different, amazing vibes.

The Evening Vibe: It starts off incredibly lively and scenic. It’s the perfect time to sit on the concrete blocks, enjoy the cool sea breeze, and watch a beautiful sunset over the water.

The Night Vibe: As darkness falls, the atmosphere shifts into a much more relaxed, peaceful, and cooler hangout spot. Sitting by the shore under the night sky with the sound of the waves is deeply therapeutic.

The Ultimate Food Highlights:
You absolutely cannot visit this beach without diving into its famous street food culture. The local stalls serve up some of the best seaside snacks:

Crab Fry & Fish Fry: Freshly caught, heavily spiced, and fried crisp right in front of you. It is a seafood lover's paradise.

Peyaju: Piping hot, extra crunchy, and perfectly spiced—making it the ultimate accompaniment to a warm cup of tea by the sea.

Verdict: Whether you want to enjoy a buzzing evening sunset or a quiet night-time sea breeze, Naval Beach is highly recommended for its great food and unmatched coastal energy!

One of the highlights is watching the sunset, with ships visible on the horizon, making the scenery even more memorable.

There are food stalls, a cafeteria, restrooms, and parking facilities, making the visit comfortable for tourists. Due to security restrictions, access may be limited in some areas, but the beach remains an excellent place to enjoy nature, take photos, and unwind.

Overall, Naval Sea Beach is a hidden gem in Chattogram and is highly recommended for anyone looking for a peaceful coastal escape.

review_text:
Neval Sea Beach – The Hidden Coastal Gem of Chattogram
Neval Sea Beach, located in the Banshkhali area of Chattogram, is a rising destination for travelers seeking a peaceful and less-crowded seaside experience. Unlike the commercial beaches of Cox’s Bazar, Neval offers untouched natural beauty, calm waves, and a serene coastal atmosphere that truly refreshes the soul.
The beach stretches along a quiet shoreline lined with greenery, fishing boats, and soft brown sand. It’s a perfect spot for those who enjoy long walks by the sea, photography, or simply sitting in silence while listening to the rhythmic sound of waves.
As the sun begins to set, Neval Sea Beach becomes even more magical—the sky turns shades of orange and purple, creating an unforgettable view that attracts nature lovers and young travelers. Local fishermen returning with their daily catch add a unique cultural charm to the scene.
The nearby villages, mangrove areas, and peaceful environment make it an ideal destination for family picnics, small tours, and weekend escapes from the busy city life. Though still developing as a tourist spot, its untouched beauty offers a different kind of coastal experience—simple, raw, and deeply calming.
Neval Sea Beach isn’t just a place to visit; it’s a place to breathe, relax, and reconnect with nature.

Naval Beach in Patenga, Chittagong, is a well-known tourist spot with its beautiful seaside environment and proximity to the Naval Academy. However, visitors have raised several concerns that impact their experience.
- Negative Aspects
1. High Food Prices:
The food offered at local stalls and shops is often overpriced, making it less affordable for many visitors.
2. Poor Hygiene in Food Shops:
Many food shops in the area do not maintain proper hygiene standards, raising concerns about food safety and cleanliness.
3. Construction Issues Affecting Road Access:
Ongoing construction projects in the area make roads less accessible and create a chaotic environment for visitors.
4. Obstructed Sea View:
Construction activities and the setup of numerous shops have blocked clear views of the sea, which is a key attraction for visitors.
5. Seating Restrictions:
Chairs and seating areas are often controlled by food vendors, who allow seating only if food is purchased from them. This restriction leaves visitors with limited or no place to rest if they choose not to buy food.

These issues significantly reduce the enjoyment of visiting Naval Beach. High food prices, poor hygiene, limited seating, and restricted sea views make the experience less welcoming and convenient, discouraging repeat visits.

While Naval Beach has the potential to be a popular tourist spot, addressing these concerns is essential to improve visitor satisfaction and ensure a better experience.

review_text:
Hillview Park and Cafe - A Serene Haven in Bhatiyari, Sitakundo, Chittagong, Bangladesh 🌳🍃

Nestled amidst the picturesque landscape of Sitakundo, the Hillview Park and Cafe offers a delightful escape into nature's embrace. This tranquil oasis is not just a park; it's an experience that beckons you to unwind, explore, and savor.

🌅 Nature's Abode:
As you step into Hillview Park, you're greeted by the symphony of chirping birds and the gentle rustling of leaves. The park boasts a pristine lake that mirrors the surrounding greenery, creating a mesmerizing backdrop for your visit. The lush gardens and well-maintained paths make it ideal for leisurely strolls and family picnics.

🏞️ Bangladesh Army's Care:
Operated and meticulously maintained by the Bangladesh Army, Hillview Park and Cafe stands as a testament to their commitment to preserving natural beauty. The park exudes a sense of security and cleanliness that ensures a pleasant outing for all visitors.

🎟️ Entry Fee:
- Children: 30 BDT
- Regular: 50 BDT
(And it's absolutely free for our dedicated Army personnel)

🍽️ Hillview Cafe:
Tucked within the park is the Hillview Cafe, offering a variety of refreshments and snacks. It's a perfect spot to grab a quick bite or sip on a hot cup of tea while taking in the breathtaking views. Prices are reasonable, ensuring a pocket-friendly experience.

🏡 Jungle House:
Adjacent to Hillview Park, you'll find Jungle House, another gem worth exploring. With a charming ambiance and wallet-friendly menu, this restaurant offers a delightful dining experience. It's an excellent alternative if you're in the mood for something different.

In summary, Hillview Park and Cafe in Bhatiyari, Sitakundo, is a slice of heaven for nature enthusiasts and families alike. The serenity, well-maintained surroundings, and affordable entry fees make it a must-visit destination in Chittagong, Bangladesh. So, pack a picnic, bring your loved ones, and immerse yourself in the beauty of Hillview Park and Cafe. 🌲🍂🌼

An incredible journey back in time through a preserved ghost city!
​Panam City in Sonargaon is one of the most fascinating historical and architectural landmarks in Bangladesh. Walking down its single main street flanked by dozens of late 19th- and early 20th-century merchant mansions feels like stepping into a forgotten era of Bengal's rich trading history.
​Highlights: Intricate colonial and Indo-Saracenic brick architecture, detailed arches, terracotta decorations, and vintage balconies along a single cobbled street.
​Photography & Vibe: Unbeatable location for historical photography, cinematic video footage, and detailed architectural shots. The moody, weathered red-brick facades make for incredible visuals.
​Traveler Tips: Located just a short distance from the Folk Art and Crafts Museum in Sonargaon. Entry tickets are required at the main gate. Visit early in the morning on a weekday to avoid crowd traffic and capture clean, quiet shots of the historic street!
​A must-visit heritage site for history enthusiasts, photographers, and travelers.

review_text:
Panam Nagar – The Lost City of Bengal / El Dorado of Bengal.

Panam Nagar, located in Sonargaon, Narayanganj, is one of the most fascinating heritage sites in Bangladesh. Often called the “Lost City,” it offers a rare glimpse into the golden days of Bengal’s trading history. This ancient township was built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by wealthy Hindu merchants who thrived during the colonial period. They constructed elegant residential mansions, showcasing a remarkable mix of Mughal, British colonial, and traditional Bengali architecture.

The main street of Panam Nagar stretches about 600 meters and is lined with 52 historic buildings, each carrying the scars of time yet still reflecting their former grandeur. Many houses feature ornamental facades, large wooden doors, arched windows, carved pillars, and intricate brickwork. Walking through the deserted street almost feels like traveling back in time, where one can imagine horse-drawn carriages and busy merchants once filling the area.

Historically, Sonargaon itself was the capital of Bengal during the medieval Sultanate era and a vital hub of the world-famous Muslin trade. Merchants from across Asia and Europe came here to trade textiles, spices, and other goods. Panam Nagar represents a later chapter of that heritage, where affluent traders settled and displayed their prosperity through architecture. However, following political changes, communal riots, and the Partition of 1947, Panam Nagar was abandoned and fell into decline. Today, it stands as a silent witness to centuries of history, prosperity, and eventual decline.

What makes Panam Nagar special is not only the architectural beauty but also the atmosphere. The abandoned mansions, overgrown with trees and plants, create an almost cinematic experience—haunting yet beautiful. For visitors, photographers, and history enthusiasts, it is one of the most photogenic and culturally rich places in Bangladesh.

📍 How to Get There from Dhaka:
Panam Nagar is only about 27 km southeast of Dhaka, making it a perfect half-day or day trip. From Gulistan bus terminal, you can take a local bus ( Doyel / Sodesh / Borak) heading to Mograpara, Sonargaon (1–1.5 hours depending on traffic). From Sonargaon, you can take a rickshaw directly to Panam Nagar’s entrance costing about 20/30 Tk per head.

🎟 Ticket Price:

Locals: 20 BDT

SAARC Nationals: 100 BDT

Foreigners: 300 BDT

⏰ Visiting Hours:
Open from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (closed on Wednesdays, and half-day on Thursdays).

🌿 Nearby Attractions:

Sonargaon Folk Art & Craft Museum: Showcasing Bangladesh’s traditional crafts and heritage.

Goaldi Mosque: A beautiful 15th-century mosque with unique terracotta work.

Meghna River boat rides: A relaxing way to end your Sonargaon trip.

✨ Overall Experience:
Panam Nagar is not just a tourist spot, but a journey through time. It tells the story of Bengal’s trade, culture, and the rise and fall of a community. While many buildings are in ruins, the government and archaeological department have started preservation efforts, making it a more organized and educational site for visitors.

If you are in Dhaka, Panam Nagar is one of the must-visit heritage destinations to truly understand the history and culture of Bengal.  Highly recommended for short tour.

Panam Nagar – The Lost Capital of Bengal

Located near Dhaka in Sonargaon, Panam Nagar is one of Bangladesh’s most fascinating historical cities. Once a thriving administrative and commercial hub, this ancient city played a key role in Bengal’s medieval history. It is said that during the 15th century, the region served as a capital, and the influential leader Esha Khan of the Baro Bhuiyan clan established his rule here.

Walking through the narrow streets of Panam Nagar feels like stepping back in time. The centuries-old buildings showcase a unique blend of Mughal, Sultanate, and British colonial architecture. Each structure tells a story of a once-prosperous city, famous for trade and the world-renowned muslin textiles.

Although many buildings have suffered damage over the centuries, the charm of Panam Nagar remains intact. The calm environment, historical architecture, and timeless ambiance make it a perfect spot for history enthusiasts, photographers, and cultural travelers.

Visiting Panam Nagar is not just sightseeing—it’s experiencing a piece of Bengal’s rich heritage, the legacy of the Baro Bhuiyans, and the historical rule of Esha Khan. With proper preservation, it has the potential to become one of South Asia’s top heritage destinations.

Panam City, or Panam Nagar, stands as a hauntingly beautiful testament to a bygone era. Located in Sonargaon, about 40 kilometers east of Dhaka, Bangladesh, this deserted city whispers tales of prosperous merchants, intricate architecture, and the ebb and flow of history.

A Historical Tapestry:
Panam City's history is deeply intertwined with that of Sonargaon, a once-thriving capital of Bengal. It served as a vital trading and commercial hub, attracting merchants and travelers from far and wide. The city's architecture reflects a blend of influences, showcasing elements from the Mughal and colonial periods. It was notably a place where wealthy hindu cotton merchants resided. The decline of Panam City can be attributed to various factors, including the partition of Bengal in 1947 and the subsequent migration of its residents.

Architectural Marvels:
Panam City is renowned for its row of well-preserved, albeit decaying, residential buildings. These structures, characterized by their intricate designs and decorative facades, offer a glimpse into the lifestyle of the city's former inhabitants. The architecture is a fascinating mix of styles, showcasing the wealth and sophistication of the merchants who once called Panam City home. The fact that so many buildings exist in such close proximity, gives the location a very unique feel.

A Site of Historical Significance:
Panam City is a crucial cultural heritage site in Bangladesh, offering valuable insights into the region's past. Its preservation is essential for understanding the historical and architectural legacy of Bengal. The World Monuments Fund recognized the site, highlighting the importance of its preservation. The city has been visited and documented by many historical travelers.

Challenges and Preservation:
Panam City faces numerous challenges, including the effects of time, weather, and human encroachment. Preservation efforts are crucial to safeguarding this historical treasure for future generations. Factors such as flooding, vandalism, and illegal occupation pose ongoing threats.

In essence, Panam City is more than just a collection of old buildings; it's a living museum that encapsulates the rich history and cultural heritage of Bangladesh. It is a location that deserves to be visited, and respected.

One of the twelve land lords(baro Bhuiyan) Issa khan ruled Bengal in 16th century .
He made Sonargaon as the capital of Bengal . Panam was one of the most beautiful city of Bengal in that period.

The city was built on twenty acres of land .Basically it was a city of traders . They import from Europe normal cloths and export Muslin .The ruin tells the tale that the city was well planned and well organized .

There are two canals and five ponds . Some of the houses had deep well as source of water .The houses were mostly two storied buildings made of bricks. Though some of the decoration were done with iron hardly any iron rods were used in beam and column . But used to make roof . Currently 52 ruined houses are there . Some of them are on the brink of collapse .Withered exposed houses bear sign of centuries ,the wealthy inhabitants, But time took away all . Only the skeleton remained in the abandoned houses .

Now it is under Archeological dept .
The city is 24 Km from city center connected by public transport . Sunday is closed. Civilian ticket Price 15/- tk per person. For the foreigners the ticket price 100/- tk per Person.

Since no standard hotel is available around ,visitors are advised to carry pack lunch in case of long day program..

Nestled in the heart of Sonargaon, Narayanganj, just 30 kilometers from Dhaka, lies a hauntingly beautiful ghost town that whispers stories of grandeur, culture, and decline — Panam City (also known as Panam Nagar). Once a vibrant center of trade and aristocratic life during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, this historic city now stands as a striking example of Bangladesh’s colonial architectural heritage.

A Glimpse into History

Panam City was developed in the late 1800s during the British colonial era. It was primarily inhabited by wealthy Hindu merchants, zamindars, and landowners who built elegant mansions and commercial buildings in European-inspired styles. This area formed part of the ancient city of Sonargaon, which served as the capital under the medieval Sultanate of Bengal and later as a prominent trading hub during the Mughal period.

While the greater Sonargaon region boasts relics from as early as the 13th century, Panam Nagar specifically rose to prominence during the British rule, reflecting a blend of Mughal, Indo-European, and neoclassical architectural influences.

Architectural Beauty

Panam City consists of a single narrow street flanked by around 52 buildings, most of which are now in ruins. The buildings are typically two or three stories high, with ornate balconies, tall arched windows, intricate stucco work, and spacious courtyards. The architectural details reflect a mixture of Bengali craftsmanship and colonial finesse, with some influences of Greek revival elements.

Each structure once served as a home, warehouse, or office space for its wealthy owners. Walking through the city today, one can still imagine the once-bustling street filled with traders, palanquins, and the sounds of life.

Decline and Abandonment

Panam City’s decline began in the early 20th century due to a combination of factors — political unrest, the partition of Bengal in 1947, communal tensions, and the gradual migration of Hindu families to India. By the 1960s, most of the city was abandoned. Over time, natural decay, lack of preservation, and occasional vandalism contributed to its ruined state.

Cultural and Touristic Significance

Today, Panam City is under the care of the Bangladesh Department of Archaeology and is recognized as a protected heritage site. It draws tourists, history enthusiasts, photographers, and researchers from across the country and abroad. The site is also close to the Folk Art and Craft Museum and the ancient Goaldi Mosque, enriching the visitor experience.

Despite its historical and cultural importance, Panam City faces threats from urban encroachment, lack of funds for conservation, and environmental damage. Preservation efforts have been initiated, but more sustainable and community-driven approaches are needed to restore and protect this unique site.

Final Thoughts

Panam City is more than a collection of ruined mansions; it is a silent witness to Bangladesh’s colonial past, trade legacy, and changing demographics. As the country modernizes rapidly, preserving such heritage sites becomes essential to maintain a tangible connection to its multifaceted history. A walk through Panam is a walk through time — echoing stories of elegance, power, and eventual decline.

Location and Geography
Bisnakandi is approximately 60 kilometers from Sylhet city, nestled in the northeastern part of Bangladesh. It lies near the foothills of the Meghalaya mountain range in India. The area is characterized by a convergence of several small streams that flow down from the Khasi hills, eventually forming a larger body of water. This unique confluence of streams creates a tranquil and picturesque setting, where clear water flows over rocks and stones, framed by lush greenery and rolling hills.

Natural Beauty and Attractions
Waterfalls and Streams: The primary attraction of Bisnakandi is the network of streams and waterfalls that flow from the Meghalaya hills. The water is crystal clear, and visitors often enjoy wading through the shallow parts of the streams, feeling the cool, refreshing water against their skin.

Green Hills and Clouds: The scenic beauty of Bisnakandi is enhanced by the surrounding green hills, which are often shrouded in mist or low-hanging clouds, especially during the monsoon season. This creates a magical, almost otherworldly atmosphere that captivates visitors.

Boating: Visitors can take boat rides along the streams, which offer a peaceful way to explore the area. The gentle flow of the water and the lush scenery make for a relaxing experience, perfect for photography or simply enjoying nature.

Best Time to Visit
The best time to visit Bisnakandi is during the monsoon season, typically from June to September. During this period, the streams and waterfalls are at their fullest, and the surrounding hills are covered in vibrant green foliage. The water levels are higher, making the landscape even more breathtaking. However, visitors should be cautious during heavy rains, as the area can become slippery and challenging to navigate.

The traditional practices and lifestyle of the people in Bisnakandi reflect a deep connection to the land.

How to Reach Bisnakandi

From Sylhet, local transportation such as CNG auto-rickshaws or hired cars can be used to reach Bisnakandi. The journey from Sylhet city to Bisnakandi takes around 2 to 3 hours, depending on road conditions.

How to get there and tips:

It is located 25 kilometers North of Sylhet City in Gowainghat Upazila. There are more than one way to go to Bisnakandi. Tourists can use the Sylhet-Guainghat Road via the airport and take a left turn to reach Hadarpar from where a local boat may be hired to arrive at Bisnakandi. Visitors can go to Hadarpar by CNG-run auto-rickshaws, which are available for hire at Amberkhana Point in Sylhet city. It took us two and a half hour to reach there and one hour ten minutes to return. So you can imagine how important is your route selection. Although we did not regret as it was a beautiful scenic road.

An alternative would be to go to Pangthumai first, and then hire a boat near Borhill Fall and ride along the branch of the Piyan which flows west towards Bisnakandi. The boat ride, which takes a little over an hour, on the sinuous river with lush green mountains on both sides is an unforgettable experience. To go to Bisanakandi only, the boat will charge 1,450 taka. For both Bisanakandi and Pantumai, they will charge 2,100 taka. The boat can accommodate up to 10 adults.

Bisanakandi is located 315 km away from Dhaka. Bisanakandi is 25 km away from Sylhet. Alternative routs are 59 km and 66 km from the city center.

As you will love to get yourself wet under the cold water for a long time and fight with the current and enjoy the view at Bisanakandi, I recommend to get started within 9:00 am in the morning from Sylhet. Bring a towel and extra clothing with you.

You can take a morning flight to Sylhet and visit there as it is very close to the airport.

I loved the place. Who ever loves travelling, must go there.

review_text:
Place: Bisnakandi, Sylhet
Date: 08 March, 2019

Bisnakandi is located in the Rustampur union of Goainghat Upazila of Sylhet. Sylhet’s Goainghat Upazila is filled with mountains, fountains, and greenery. The Upazila has the border with India. The beauty of the places fills the attractions of the tourist. The rocky river, forest, tea orchard in the hills overwhelm the mind! Tourists come to see the beauty of Sylhet’s diversity. At the festival like Eid, these tourist centers are crowded.

As like Jaflong, Bisnakandi is a place where the river is filled with the stone. It makes the surrounding enchanting. However, due to the uncontrolled stone lifting, the beauty of Jaflong is on the verge of destruction today, but the Bisnakandi retains its youth. Many of the steps of the Khasia Hills on the Bangladesh-India border have come from one side to the other, and the hills have the highest springs of Meghalaya in India. The main attraction of the Bisnakandi to the tourists is the transparent water stream that flows over the rocks and the whirlwind of white clouds over the mountains. At first, you will feel like a stone bed, and the calmness that you get in the clear water will bring you the peace of mind again and again. It is as though the mountains, rivers, fountains, and rocks have laid the natural bedding in Bisnakandi.

Visited the M. A. G. Osmani Museum in Sylhet today, a place that quietly holds layers of personal and national history. The building itself, known as *Nur Monjil*, originally belonged to Osmani’s father. Following the death of General M. A. G. Osmani in 1984, the house was later converted into a museum around 1987.

The structure consists of five rooms, two of which are used for administrative purposes, while the remaining three serve as exhibition spaces. The first room offers an intimate glimpse into his daily life, displaying personal items such as his bed, chairs, tables, clothing, a hanger, and a collection of photographs.

The second room focuses more on his public and military life. It showcases medals, badges, and honors he received throughout his career as a Major General. Alongside these are pieces of furniture he used to host guests, as well as paintings by various artists depicting him and moments from the Liberation War.

The final room brings together more of his personal and domestic life. Here, visitors can see another bed, a prayer mat, his personal work table, and a large room-sized map of Bangladesh that he reportedly used during the Liberation War. The room also includes his family dining space, an old refrigerator, dinnerware, and photographs from the later years of his life—some of which are in color, adding a different emotional texture to the experience.

Entry tickets are quite affordable, costing only 20 BDT for Bangladeshi visitors, while foreign visitors are charged a higher fee. The staff members are knowledgeable and engaging, often interacting with visitors and sharing insights about Osmani’s life and contributions.

The outdoor area is equally well maintained, with greenery that adds to the calm atmosphere. There is also a swing in the yard, along with a grave. According to the guard, the grave belongs to the original owner of the property. The Osmani family chose not to relocate it, preserving it as a mark of respect.

Overall, the museum offers a thoughtful and grounded experience, connecting personal memory with the broader history of Bangladesh.

review_text:
Osmani Museum, Sylhet
The Osmani Museum is named after Bangabir General Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani, the Commander-in-Chief of Bangladesh Forces (12 April 1971 – 7 April 1972) during the liberation war. It is situated at the heart of the Sylhet City Corporation area in the Sylhet Division of Bangladesh. It is about 12 km from the Sylhet Osmani International Airport and 3 km from the Sylhet Railway Station. Owned aoperated by the Bangladesh National Museum, this museum was established to pay rich tribute to the great hero of Bangladesh for his outstanding contributions in the liberation war of the country and founding the armed forces of Bangladesh. The foundation stone had been laid on 16 February 1985 and it was inaugurated on 4 March 1987 by the then president of Bangladesh H M Ershad.

Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani also known as Bangabir (the Hero of Bengal) was born on 1 September 1918 in Sunamganj of Sylhet. He was the commander-in-chief of the Mukti Bahini during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War and was the first Bengali four star general. Osmani’s career spanned over five decades, beginning with his service in the British Indian Army in 1939. He fought in Burma during World War II, and served in the Pakistan Army until 1967. Osmani was appointed head of the Bengali armed resistance in 1971 by the Provisional Government of Bangladesh, and he is regarded as the founder of the Bangladesh Armed Forces. General Osmani retired in 1972. He died on 16 February 1984 in London.

review_text:
Osmani Museum is a museum in Kotwali Thana of Sylhet, Bangladesh.
The ancestors' home of Bangabir General Muhammad Ataul Gani Osmani, the Commander-in-Chief of Bangladesh Forces (12 April 1971 – 7 April 1972) has been transformed into today's famous "Osmani Museum". It is situated at the heart (Dhopa Dighir Par) of the Sylhet City Corporation area in renowned Sylhet Division of Bangladesh. It is about 12 km from the Sylhet Osmani International Airport and 3 km from the Sylhet Railway Station. Maintained and organised by the Bangladesh National Museum, this museum has been established to pay rich tribute to the great hero of Bangladesh for his outstanding accomplishments. This will surely act as a stimulus to the future generations. The foundation stone was laid on 16 February 1985 and it was inaugurated on 4 March 1987 by the then president of Bangladesh H M Ershad.

1 Gallery 1
2 Gallery 2
3 Gallery 3
4 Relevant information

Gallery 1

The entire room has been decorated with showpieces similar to a bedroom. There are four chairs made of cane and two centre tables, one simple wardrobe and one wooden bed with two side tables. The favourite wrist watch, which General Osmani wore till the last hours of his life; military stick, two briefcases, a telephone set, number of books and used crockery, are kept on one side. The other side is decorated with an Alana, which contains two suits, two uniforms (khaki and deep green), two shirts (white and light blue), two panjabi, a brown sleeveless coat, four pairs of shoes including one military boot, a black umbrella, brown colour well decorated walking stick. A round table and a wooden book shelf with many books and magazines from home and abroad including "Who's Who in the World" (editions: 1978–1979 and 1980–1981) are placed in a corner.
Gallery 2

Decorated as a drawing room, there are few furniture made of cane, which includes chairs – four 1 sitter, one 3 sitter, one 2 sitter, a centre table, two side tables etc. First one contains the badges, medals, ranks of General and the passport of General Osmani. And the third one displays number of credentials, which includes the Certificate of Independence Award – 1985 along with the invitation card and brief biography of the award winners. One card contains the autograph of Mrs. Indira Gandhi of India along with envelop sent to General Osmani. Among them the important few are; General Osmani speaking to the audiences after the ceremonial guard of honour presented by the army on the occasion of the grand arrival of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 10 March 1971, landing at Sylhet airport in 1972, General Osmani with the sector commanders of the liberation war of Bangladesh, with acting president of Mujib Nagar government Syed Nazrul Islam, with president Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, with Shaheed president Ziaur Rahman, with ex president Ershad, with the martyrs family at the East Bengal Regimental Centre in 1981 etc.

Gallery 3

A black reading table and chair, bed, prayer stand, Jaynamaz (Prayer Cloth), prayer cap etc. are lay down meticulously as exhibits. The other items include one black almirah, one fridge, dining table with six chairs, antique crockery and others. The operational map of Bangladesh (scale 1: 2,50,00), used by the General during the liberation war of Bangladesh, is also displayed in this room along with numerous credentials presented by the civil society.

Relevant information
Osmani Museum remains open every day except Thursday. From Sunday to Wednesday the timings is from 10:30 AM to 5:30 PM. On Friday and Saturday it remains open from 3:30 PM to 5:30 PM. The museum authority celebrates the birth (1 September) and death (16 February) anniversaries of General M A G Osmani along with the independent (26 March) and victory day (16 December) at the museum premises. Total 11 hard working individuals are taking proper care of this precious establishment.

A Decent Spot for a Family Picnic - 3.5/5 ⭐
Visited Foys Lake recently and had a fairly enjoyable day out. The location is scenic and makes for a nice picnic destination, especially if you’re going with family and kids.
The Good:
•	The bumper cars were fun and well-maintained
•	Sea World with the wave pool was definitely a highlight - kids absolutely loved it!
•	Staff members were genuinely helpful and friendly throughout our visit
•	The natural surroundings and lake views create a pleasant atmosphere
The Average:
•	Food quality was moderate - nothing spectacular but decent enough
•	Facilities were average - functional but could use some upgrades
•	Price range is on the higher side considering what’s on offer
The Disappointing:
•	Very limited rides, and most are geared toward children
•	No thrilling attractions like rollercoasters for adults or teenagers
•	For the price point, I expected more variety in activities
Overall: Foys Lake is a good option for a family picnic, especially with younger children. However, if you’re looking for exciting rides or activities for adults, you might find it lacking. The helpful staff and wave pool save the day, but the limited options and high prices keep it from being a must-visit destination.
Recommended for: Family outings with kids under 12
Not ideal for: Thrill-seekers or groups looking for diverse activities

Foy’s Lake is a magnificent man-made reservoir located in the Khulshi area of Chattogram, Bangladesh, covering approximately 336 acres of picturesque hilly terrain. Originally excavated in 1924 under the supervision of British railway engineer Mr. Foy, the lake was initially designed to provide a steady water supply to the nearby Assam-Bengal Railway colony. Today, it has evolved into a premier tourist destination managed by the Concord Group, featuring a sprawling complex that includes the Foy’s Lake Concord Amusement World, Sea World Water Park, and luxury lakeside resorts.
Visitors are drawn to the lake’s serene emerald waters, which are framed by lush green ridges like Asmani, Gagandwip, and Jaltungi, and the towering Batali Hill. The area is a biodiversity hotspot, home to various species of deer, rabbits, and over 15 species of birds, making it a haven for nature photographers and families alike. Adventure seekers can enjoy modern rides such as roller coasters and bumper boats, while those looking for tranquility can take scenic boat cruises across the 80-foot-deep waters. With its observation towers offering a bird’s-eye view of the port city and its dedicated picnic spots, Foy's Lake stands as a perfect blend of historical utility and modern recreation. You can find more details and plan your visit on the official Foy’s Lake Concord website.

A perfect blend of nature and adventure, I visited Foy’s Lake with my family, and it remains one of the best spots in Chattogram for a full day out. Here’s a breakdown of the experience:
> ​Vibe & Scenery: The natural beauty is the highlight. Taking a boat ride deep into the lake reveals beautiful hill views that make you forget you're still in the city. It’s very peaceful and great for photography.
> ​Amusement & Water Park: We spent the afternoon at Sea World. The wave pool is a blast, though it can get quite crowded on weekends. The dry park rides (like the roller coaster) are fun for kids, though some of the older rides could use a bit of maintenance.
> ​Facilities: The area is generally clean and well-secured. There are several food corners, though the prices are a bit higher than outside. The "Lake View Restaurant" offers a decent meal with a great view.
> ​Pro Tip: Try to visit on a weekday to avoid the heavy crowds. Also, the combined ticket for the boat and water park is usually a better deal than buying them separately.
> ​Pros: Stunning landscapes, great for families, variety of activities.
> Cons: Entry fees and ride costs can add up quickly; gets very busy on public holidays.

review_text:
In 1925, according to the plan and design of Mr. Foy an engineer of Assam Bengal Railway, an artificial lake was created here in a beautiful and natural environment. In time, it became known as Foy’s Lake after the name of engineer Foy. In 2004, Bangladesh Railway and Tourism Corporation signed a tripartite agreement with Concord Group, one of the country’s leading companies, to create an environment conducive to travel and private time on Foy’s Lake.

Foy’s Lake is now a world-class tourist and family entertainment destination with its unique beauty and impressive recreational facilities that make it an ideal feature in the tourism of Bangladesh and the entertainment world, there is the greatest emphasis on safety and cleanliness, including entertainment. Foy’s Lake is a combination of mountains, lake and crystal clear water with an observation tower, photo corners, aquatic corner, artificial waterfall and international standard resort. There are also modern restaurants, merchandise shops, gift shops and Sea World Concord, the largest water park in the country. Founded in 1925, Foy’s Lake has a total land area of 336.69  acres, a watershed of 47.75 acres and a mountain range of 262.96 acres. The lake’s water depth is a maximum of 78 to 80 feet and a minimum of 38 to 40 feet.

For exclusive entertainment in Foy’s Lake, there are many international standard rides such as the Ferris Wheel, Family Roller Coaster, Bumper Car, Pirate Ship, Coffee Cup, Dry Slides, Circus Train, Pony Adventure, Baby Dragon, Baby Carousel, Circus Swing, Apollo Flight, Large Boats, Small Boats, Speed Boats, Paddle Boats, Racing Boats, Duck/Anchor Paddle Boats, Sampan and many more.

In Foy’s Lake, there are –

International standard accommodation facilities like Resorts, Bungalows, Honeymoon Chalets etc.

Exclusive boats (Large Boat, Speed Boat, Paddle Boat, Sampan etc.)

Air-conditioned Lake View Restaurants, Floating Restaurants along with Merchandise & Gift Shops.

Arrangements for hiking & trekking in the hilly forests and access to the tall observation tower for the best scenic views.

This lake is a vivid example of how modern civilization is destroying the natural environment.

review_text:
This place is dead.

The only thing alive here are the trees and the handful few people who go there.
This place is outright neglected and in total disrepair. The roadways are not maintained and some buildings have been abandoned for years, and are in total ruin. There are no attempts at the most basic aesthetics of the place. The clogged and suffocating water-bodies are full of stagnant water, with dead trees leaning or fallen into those. It's as if this place is deep in the Amazon jungle where no humans visit. Whatever growth is happening here is Nature itself. In other words, there is no human touch - not even enough directional/destination signs.

This park does not have a most basic washroom. There is one that is not maintained at all, and does not even have running water.

This place has no proper food area. The only thing that exists is a rudimentary rural-type hut that is a pathetic excuse of a convenience store.

We came across abandoned rest-houses, and there is a watchtower, that happens to be an outright safety concern. There was only a single rest house that was in any decent shape.

Bottom-line: Do not waste your time, energy and effort visiting this place.

​The park’s landscape is dominated by towering Sal trees (Shorea robusta), which create a dense, rhythmic canopy that stays green throughout the year. It feels like a "breathing lung" for the region. ​Wildlife: While large animals are rare now, you can still spot monkeys (rhesus macaques), various bird species (like the Brown Wood Owl), and occasionally deer in the mini-zoo area.
​Family & Picnics: With over 30 designated picnic spots and several rest houses, it is a top choice for family gatherings and corporate outings, especially during the winter months.

review_text:
Bhawal National Park was established in 1982. It is spread over Gazipur Sadar and Sreepur Upazilas of Gazipur district. Its total area is 5022 hectares. It is managed under the Dhaka Wildlife and Nature Conservation Department. Being very close to the capital city, the park receives a lot of tourist pressure. Especially during the dry season (November-February), a lot of people come here for picnics. According to official figures, about 375,000 visitors visit the forest every year. More than 5,000 people depend on this forest for their livelihood. It is a tropical, moist deciduous forest. The main species here is sal. They are also called regenerating forests because of their ability to regrow from the original cut trees. The current sal forest here is basically a second-stage sal forest. Which originates from Kapich. In this forest, 10 species of mammals, 6 species of amphibians, 9 species of reptiles and 39 species of birds are often seen. Among the wildlife, the most notable are the otter, gecko, tiger, rabbit, porcupine, bee etc. The main reptiles are the snake, python, turtle etc. About 220 species of trees are seen here.

There are several picnic spots and rest houses of the Forest Department here. These rest houses can be used during the day with prior permission from the Forest Department. If you want to have a picnic during the dry season, you have to book well in advance. There is a direct road connection from Dhaka to this national park. The park is located on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway. You can go to this park by any bus from Mohakhali in Dhaka towards Mymensingh. You can also go directly by renting a car.
The general entry fee is 20/-.

Bhawal National Park, located in Gazipur, Bangladesh, is a lush forest reserve just 40 kilometers north of Dhaka. Covering approximately 3000 acres, it serves as a vital green retreat for nature lovers, tourists, and researchers. The park is part of the remnants of the once-vast Madhupur Sal forest, featuring tall Sal trees and diverse plant species.

It is home to various wildlife, including monkeys, foxes, jungle cats, and numerous bird species. The park’s serene environment and shaded walking trails make it a popular destination for picnics, hiking, and educational tours. Several lakes and man-made canals enhance the park’s natural beauty and attract migratory birds in winter.

Bhawal National Park also holds historical significance, being associated with the mysterious story of the Bhawal Sannyasi. Eco-cottages and facilities developed by the Forest Department promote eco-tourism while preserving biodiversity. As a green sanctuary close to the bustling capital, the park plays a crucial role in environmental conservation and offers city dwellers a much-needed escape into nature.

review_text:
Bhawal National Park is 40 km away from the capital Dhaka and has been developed in the shadow of Joydevpur in Gazipur. It is also known as Bhawal's Gajari Madha by many due to its abundance of Gajari trees. Spread over an area of about 5022 hectares, Bhawal National Park was recognized as a National Park in 1982. Among the 221 species of plants in the park are 43 species of trees, 19 species of shrubs, 3 species of palms, 27 species of grasses, 24 species of vines and 104 species of medicinal plants. There are also 64 different species of animals including 13 species of mammals, 9 species of reptiles, 5 species of birds and amphibians. Many people organize picnics and various events in this park, full of natural beauty and biodiversity. Entering through gate number 3 of Bhawal Garh, the first thing you will notice are the two elephant sculptures at the terracotta entrance. Inside the park there are 31 picnic spots, 19 beautiful cottages, state-of-the-art rest houses, butterfly garden, turtle breeding center and children's park. If you are tired of walking among the rows of trees in the garden, there are benches or canopies for rest. Green paddy fields, ponds or small lakes can be seen in the midst of this extensive forest. Along with a boat ride on the lake, there is a towering watch tower to view the entire park.
The distance between Gazipur Sadar and Bhawal Ghazari, ie Bhawal National Park, is only 3 km. After crossing the Jaidebpur intersection and moving a little further, the main entrance of Bhawal Garh will be noticed on the right hand side. You can go to Bhawal Udyan by your own car from Dhaka or by any bus bound for Mymensingh from Mahakhali, Airport or Rajendrapur Chowrasta via Dhaka-Mymensingh Highway. Everyone is invited to see this beauty of nature.

review_text: So recently I have joined a new office and to my surprise I was invited to go relax and have fun in the first month of my office. It was selected from office that we would go to Bhawal National Park. At first I was a bit disappointed that what is there to see in some random park while facing the huge traffic jam of Gazipur. We started our journey from Baridhara DOHS and to avoid traffic of Tongi we changed our route from Abdullahpur and took the Kamarpara Bypass road to reach Tongi Mill Gate. Overall to reach Bhawal National Park it took about 1 hour and 40 minutes approximately. For each person the entry fee was Twenty Taka only and if you have a car then it would take 150 taka for your car. Inside the park it is huge. I think we only covered one fifth of the total park. There were nothing out of extraordinary but we went there at the time of Spring so every plant was brimming with beauty and when you visit a place that surrounded with trees as long as you can see it, the beauty of spring even increases. It is a nice place to hangout with your close ones and friends / colleagues.

However, it's advisable to bring your own food and water as there may not be many food options available within the park. It's also recommended to wear comfortable shoes and carry insect repellent for a more enjoyable experience.

Beyond its recreational offerings, Bhawal National Park plays a vital role in the conservation of biodiversity in Bangladesh. Efforts are made to protect the park's natural resources, preserve endangered species, and raise awareness about environmental conservation.

Whether you're seeking a tranquil escape or an adventurous exploration, Bhawal National Park promises a memorable experience amidst its diverse ecosystems and abundant wildlife.

Within its boundaries, visitors can encounter an array of wildlife including deer, monkeys, foxes, wild boars, and a variety of bird species. The park provides a natural habitat for these animals and offers a chance to observe them in their native environment.

For those looking to immerse themselves in nature, Bhawal National Park offers a range of activities. Visitors can enjoy wildlife viewing, where they can spot various species of animals and birds. The park also features nature walks, allowing visitors to explore the lush surroundings and discover the diverse plant life.

Bhawal National Park provides basic facilities for visitors, including picnic spots, rest areas, and toilets. However, it's advisable to bring your own food and water as there may not be many food options available within the park. It's also recommended to wear comfortable shoes and carry insect repellent for a more enjoyable experience.

Beyond its recreational offerings, Bhawal National Park plays a vital role in the conservation of biodiversity in Bangladesh. Efforts are made to protect the park's natural resources, preserve endangered species, and raise awareness about environmental conservation.

Whether you're seeking a tranquil escape or an adventurous exploration, Bhawal National Park promises a memorable experience amidst its diverse ecosystems and abundant wildlife.

review_text:
Ratargul Swamp Forest is one of the most magical natural spots I’ve visited in Bangladesh. Just about 26 km from Sylhet city, this freshwater swamp forest offers a rare and serene escape — especially during the monsoon season when much of the forest is submerged under water. Riding through the flooded channels with trees like koroch, hijal, and kadam rising out of the water feels like entering another world.

What I loved:

The boat ride through narrow waterways was peaceful and beautiful. You glide under green canopies, past reflective water, and listen to bird calls — it’s calming.

Lots of plant diversity. Trees like Pongamia pinnata (koroch), Murta (Schumannianthus dichotoma), Hijal (Barringtonia acutangula), Kadam etc. give the forest a rich green texture that changes with the season.

Birdlife & wildlife. I saw kingfishers, egrets, some monkeys, snakes, small water‐birds. If you go in winter or during migration, there are even more species.

The watchtower gives a nice overview of the forest canopy. A good spot for photos.

What could be better:

Littering is a problem. Plastic bottles, food wrappers, even floating trash sometimes, which spoils the beauty and might harm the wildlife.

Too many tourists sometimes — especially on weekends, holidays, and during peak season. This crowding creates noise, disturbs animals and birds, and puts stress on the forest environment.

Facilities are minimal. There are no places to stay inside the forest, limited shelter if it rains, few places to rest, etc. If you plan a long trip, good preparation is needed.

Tips:

Visit in the monsoon season (June-October) for the full submerged-forest experience. But be ready for water, rain, mosquitoes.

Hire a boat and a local guide — guides know good spots, the right paths, and can help avoid disturbances.

Bring snacks, water, rain gear, and insect repellent.

Try to avoid peak times (weekends, holidays) for a quieter, more immersive experience.

---

Overall, Ratargul is one of Bangladesh’s natural gems. It offers an unforgettable feeling of being in a “forest on water,” somewhere in the intersection of the wild and peaceful. If conservation and respectful tourism are maintained (and waste managed better), I think it can remain a wonder for many visitors to come.

On June 1st, 2025, we had the incredible opportunity to visit Ratargul Swamp Forest in Sylhet, Bangladesh—and the experience was beyond words. Known as the only freshwater swamp forest in the country, Ratargul is a place where nature breathes in its rawest form. But what made my visit even more magical was the weather that day. It was raining, and with the occasional lightning illuminating the sky, the entire forest transformed into something surreal—almost mythical.

As we approached the forest, clouds loomed low and heavy. The earthy scent of wet leaves and soil filled the air. We boarded a small wooden boat, and the moment we entered the swamp area, I felt like I had stepped into a dream. The rain gently pattered on the canopy above us, occasionally breaking through and splashing on our faces. It wasn’t heavy enough to be a nuisance—just the right kind to make the entire journey feel more cinematic. Each drop added to the melody of the forest.

The trees, mostly Koroch and Hijol, stood tall and majestic with their trunks submerged in calm water, giving off reflections that shimmered and rippled with every movement of the boat. Rainwater mingled with the swamp, enhancing the sense of immersion and purity. It was so quiet, yet so alive. The only sounds were the splash of oars, raindrops on leaves, and distant thunder rolling through the hills of Sylhet.

Then came the lightning.

Every few minutes, a flash of light would streak across the sky, briefly illuminating the entire forest in a cold, electric blue. For those few seconds, everything stood still—the trees, the water, the sky—and I could see the entire swamp lit up like a painting. It wasn’t scary; it was powerful, beautiful, and humbling. Nature was putting on a light show, and we were just lucky enough to witness it. The contrast between the soft rain and the sharp lightning created a rhythm that made the boat ride feel like something out of a fantasy novel.

Despite the rain, or perhaps because of it, the views were astonishing. Every turn in the narrow waterways revealed new corners of the forest, each more photogenic than the last. Some trees bent over the water, their branches dipping gently in. Others stood alone, noble and silent, their trunks covered in moss. Occasionally, we spotted birds darting through the rain, unfazed, adding even more life to the scenery.

The rain also brought out the colors of the forest in a way that sunlight couldn’t. The greens were richer, deeper, almost glowing. The water appeared darker, creating stunning reflections. It was hard to put the camera down, but even harder not to just sit and absorb the moment. The experience wasn’t just visual—it was emotional. It made me feel small in the best way, like I was just a quiet observer in a world that existed long before me.

Ratargul, in the rain, during lightning, is something you have to experience to truly understand. It’s peaceful, mysterious, and absolutely beautiful. Whether you're a nature lover, a photographer, or someone just looking to escape the noise of city life, this place will leave you spellbound. I went with high expectations—and Ratargul exceeded every one of them.
