Nijhum Dwip নিঝুম দ্বীপ - Noakhali District

Nijhum Dwip নিঝুম দ্বীপ which means Quiet Island, is a small island under Hatiya upazila. Total area of 14050 acres. It is situated in Noakhali District of Chittagong Division in Bangladesh. Once it was called Char Osman.

A cluster of islands (mainly, Ballar Char, Kamlar char,Char Osman and Char Muri) emerged in the early 1950s as an alluvium in the shallow estuary of the Bay of Bengal On the south of Noakhali. These new sandbanks first drew the notice of a group of fishermen, who named it Baular Char (literally, the alluvium of sand) later transformed into Ballar Char.

During winter, thousands of migratory birds flock in to island. The fishermen use the airy and sunny land as an ideal place for drying their catches from the sea. Sometimes many of them also construct straw huts on the island as seasonal residences.

There are different types of animal at Nijhum Dwip. Spotted deer, Monkeys, Estuary reported to harbor the Ganges River Dolphin include Clawless Otter, Cat, Snakes, Tortoises and Turtles. During winter, thousands of migratory birds visit the islands and around a dozen of which are considered to be globally critically endangered, enhancing its splendor even further.

In 1974 the Forest Department took a forestation program for a duration of twenty years in the north side of the island. Covering an area of nine thousand acres, it has now developed into a deep forest with a variety of plant species. Among the trees Keora is much seen. Besides this Gewa, Kankra, Bain, Babul, Karamja, Pashur and many other species are seen.

On 8 th April, 2001 the government declared the 40390 acres of forest of Jahajmara range including 9550 acres of forest land on Nijhum Dwip as a National Park for the protection and development of the biodiversity of the forest. But in practice, there a very lazy appearance of that declaration.

.How to Go: From Dhaka, Sadarghat toTamaruddin of Hatiya Dweep. Then Nijhum Dwip by local motor boat. Or Bus / Train to Chittagong. Then to Hatiya island by motor boat.

From Hatiya to Jahazmara Bazar by tempo or jeep. Then to Amtali Ghat or Katakhali Ghat by rickshaw. These boats run depending on the wave and tide of sea.I loved the place! It's beautiful and adventurous at the same time. If you are travelling by road then be ready for some pain staking thrill while crossing Hatiya Island. Major part of the road is made of brick and damaged and you will have travel on a 'chander gari'. The sea truck crossing is also beautiful and 'mud-filled' at the same time (if they are not using the main dock). Travelling by the river using 'MV TASHRIF' is the most amazing part but time consuming as well! In this case there will be an additional 2:30 hrs journey by 'troller' is required which includes the non-stop breathtaking view of Monpura Island on the way. The place is nice and I really like to visit again!

Nijhum Dwip Bangladesh: A Complete Travel Guide

￼

Nijhum Dwip is previously known as Char Osmani, Baluar Char, Golden Island, etc. which is located at Hatiya Upazila in Noakhali District Bangladesh. It is a little island occupying 164 Square kilometers, is a great tourist attraction in Bangladesh. It is surrounded by Bay of Bengal and Meghna River. Nijhum Dwip is a cluster of Islands. With the combination of Ballar Char, Kamlar Char, Char Osman and Char Muriform the Nijhum Island. Recently the government of Bangladesh declares this island as Nijhum Dwip National Park.

Nijhum Dwip Location & Geographical Description

It is mentioned earlier that Nijhum Dwip is encircled with the Bay of Bengal and Meghna Channel. It is two kilometers south-east from the Hatia upazilla and 120 kilometers south of Maijdee bazaar, Noakhali. Which According to the Google, Nijhum Dwip map Longitude and latitude are 21°35′0″N and 92°01′0″E respectively? This is 4-5 meter high from the sea level.

History of Nijhum Island

To find out the real history of this island we have talked with the local people living there. According to their information, More than 100 years ago, a fisherman of Bay of Bengal find this island but at that time, it was the primary stage which is under water. Time has been passed. Golden color sand forms this island. At that point, it was known as Golden Island. It was also known to all as Baluarchar.

A Cowboy named Osman first build his house on this island. From that time, it was known as Char Osman. A Member of Parliament of Bangladesh changed this island’s name from Char Osman to Nijhum Dweep later. After 1970 people started to set up their houses on this island.

How to go Nijhum Dwip from Dhaka

From Dhaka Sadarghat regular steamer services are available to Hatia. MV Farhan, MV Tipu, etc. provide quite good services. It will cost 130 for standard deck rent to 1500. After reaching Tamruddin Ghat, there are two ways to reach Nijhum Island. You may choose a boat which approximate cost is about 2000 taka, or you may go by Baby Taxi which cost 400 takas. By baby taxis, you will reach Mortara Ghat. After crossing the river by boat which takes only 3-4 minute, you will reach Nijhum Dwip, your final destination.

Weather of Nijhum Dwip

The Climate of Nijhum Dwip almost remains the same around the year. The average Highest temperature of this island is around 32 degree Celsius, and the lowest is about 14 degree Celsius. During the rainy season, half of this island goes under water.

People of Nijhum Dwip

About 10000 people live there. Most of them are fishermen and some of them make their living by cultivating different kinds of agricultural product. There are six Bazaars which full filled the necessity of daily things and only the source of electricity. Two primary schools, 2 Madrasha, ten canals, 5.5 kilometers road and numerous ponds are available here.

Nijhum Dwip Hotels

Only one hotel named Hotel Abakash is available there which cost 500-2500 taka. You may choose to board. But they are not good at all. Recently there are some resorts are made near Nijhum Dwip.

Nijhum Dwip travel guide

If you don’t want to face a big wave of seas, it is the best time to visit from October to February. By this period, you can thoroughly enjoy the beauty of nature. If you don’t know how to swim, it will be the best practice to take lifejacket. Different Travel Agency offer different Nijhum Dwip tour packages. One can contact them and visit Nijhum Dwip easily.

Nijhum Dwip (Bengali: নিঝুম দ্বীপ, lit. 'Silent Island')[1] is a small island under Hatiya upazila. It is situated in Noakhali District in Bangladesh. Once it was called Char Osmani,Baluar Char, Golden Island [2]

A cluster of islands (mainly, Ballar Char, Kamlar Char, Char Osman and Char Muri) emerged in the early 1950s as an alluvium in the shallow estuary of the Bay of Bengal on the south of Noakhali. These new sandbanks first drew the notice of a group of fishermen, who named it Baular Char (literally, the alluvium of sand) later transformed into Ballar Char. Occupying an area of 14,050 acres (5,686 hectares), the island is situated between 21 0 1 / to 22 0 6 /North latitude and 90 0 3 / to 91 0 4 / East longitude

Migratory Birds in Nijhum Dwip: During winter, thousands of migratory birds flock in to island. The fishermen use the airy and sunny land as an ideal place for drying their catches from the sea. Sometimes many of them also construct straw huts on the island as seasonal residences.

In 1974 the Forest Department took an afforestation program for a duration of twenty years in the north side of the island. Covering an area of nine thousand acres, it has now developed into a deep forest with a variety of plant species. Among the trees Keora is much seen. Besides this Gewa, Kankra, Bain, Babul, Karamja, Pashur and many other species are seen.

On 8 April 2001 the government declared the 40,390 acres (16,345 ha) of forest of Jahajmara range including 9,550 acres (3,865 ha) of forest land on Nijhum Dwip as a National Park for the protection and development of the biodiversity of the forest. But in practice, there a very lazy appearance of that declaration.

It was named 'Nijhum Dwip' by former Minister Amirul Islam Kalam in 1979 observing its isolation and mild nature.

review_text:
Sylhet is well known as a scenic place to visit. The choices to admire soothing nature retreat are aplenty. The availability of so many destinations, draws tourists both local and international. Although it is safe to presume that the number of local tourists far outnumber international ones. For local tourists and local residents alike, it doest not harm to add another destination to the varied options they have to visit within Sylhet. This is where the amusement park can add some value.

The park is well managed and a great place to spend quality time with family and friends! It is surprisingly well managed and pretty clean. The location is spectacular and offers great views once atop the giant wheel. The surrounding hills offers a picturesque setting that makes the the place almost idyllic. As far as the rides are concerned though, I cannot endorse them as great or amazing but they are certainly not bad. Most are reminiscent of Shishu park at Shahabag, Dhaka or Sishu mela at Mirpur, Dhaka. Some are certainly inspired by the likes of Fantasy Kingdom at Savar, but in terms of thrills and shrills it barely weighs up. Nevertheless, one shall not regret a casual visit.

Rangpani Zero Point, located near the Indo-Bangladesh border in the Mokampunji area of Jaintapur upazila, Sylhet, is a truly captivating and relatively unexplored natural spot. It offers a beautiful, peaceful alternative to the main Jaflong area.

The river's water originates from the Ranghangkong waterfall in the Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, India.

The place has a quiet, rural atmosphere.
Not too far from Jaflong, yet secluded enough for a relaxing stroll.
If you are traveling with family, it is not recommended, as the place is a bit remote for a family trip. And if you are traveling alone or with a group of friends, you can safely visit.
From Sylhet, take the bus to Jaflong and get off at Mokampunji Gate. After walking for 2-3 minutes, you will reach the front of the school, then you will find two gates on the right and left. জায়গা হিসেবে নিরিবিলি, গ্রাম্য পরিবেশ পাওয়া যায়।
জাফলং থেকে বেশি দূরে না তবুও যথেষ্ট নির্জন ঘুরার জন্য জায়গা হিসেবে।
সাথে পরিবার থাকলে পরামর্শ থাকবে না আসার জন্য, জায়গাটা কিছুটা দূর্গম পরিবার সাথে নিয়ে ঘুরার প্রেক্ষাপটে।  আর একা বা বন্ধুদের গ্রুপের সাথে থাকলে নিশ্চিন্তে ঘুরে আসতে পারেন।
সিলেট থেকে জাফলং এর বাসে উঠে মোকামপুঞ্জির গেটে বাস থেকে নেমে পড়বেন৷ সামনে ২-৩ মিনিট হাটার পর স্কুলের সামনে পৌছাবেন, এরপর হাতের ডানে আর বায়ে দুটো গেট পাবেন। ডানের গেট দিয়ে গেলে ১-২ মিনিট পর নতুন রাস্তা পাবেন, ঐরাস্তার ডানদিকে নিচ ধরে হাটলে কিছুসময় পর রাংপানির দেখা মিলবে।

review_text: Rangpani is one of the most attractive and peaceful tourist destinations in Sylhet. Tourists do not usually come here, which is why you can enjoy this incredibly beautiful place in a very peaceful environment. Among all the tourist destinations in Sylhet, Rangpani is a little different because there are incredibly large pieces of stone here. In addition, there is water here 12 months of the year. The water of Rangpani is absolutely crystal clear. You can enjoy your time in the clear and cold water very well. In addition, on the way to Rangpani, you have to pass through Khasia, this incredibly beautiful Khasia village is another tourist destination. Where you will see betel nut trees and various types of fruit trees that are not usually seen in Bangladesh, such as cashew nuts. Overall, I hope you will like this incredibly beautiful tourist destination.

review_text: Rangpani Zero Point is a very popular tourist spot in Sylhet, known for its natural beauty and peaceful environment. This place is located near the India-Bangladesh border and offers a wonderful view of the surrounding hills, rivers and tea gardens. Their dedication and hard work ensure that the tea produced here maintains its rich taste and aroma. The estate management also focuses on maintaining quality and sustainability.

Apart from its economic value, Nurjahan Tea Estate has become a popular spot for visitors. People come here to explore the beauty of the tea garden, take photos, and learn about tea cultivation. Overall, Nurjahan Tea Estate is a perfect blend of natural beauty, cultural importance, and economic contribution to Bangladesh.

Just about 8 kilometers from the main town of Srimangal, this privately-owned tea garden offers a refreshing escape into nature. While the core area is private, the roadside sections remain open to the public, allowing visitors to enjoy the lush, green scenery. With a bit of luck, you might even spot monkeys playing in the trees!

Since the garden is located in a remote area, it's best to travel by car. For safety and convenience, ask your hotel manager to arrange a reliable local driver—many of whom are also great tour guides with local knowledge. A perfect off-the-beaten-path experience in the tea capital of Bangladesh! 🌿🍃

Shapla beel" refers to wetlands in Bangladesh that become spectacularly adorned with blooming water lilies, known locally as "shapla." These natural wonders transform landscapes into vibrant displays, particularly during the monsoon season.
Here's a breakdown of what makes them so special:
The most iconic feature is the abundance of water lilies, often in shades of pink and white, that carpet the water's surface. This creates a visually stunning scene, drawing both local and international visitors.
The peak blooming season typically occurs during the rainy months, when the wetlands are fullest.
These wetlands are vital ecosystems, providing habitats for various aquatic life and contributing to the region's biodiversity.
They also play a role in water regulation and flood control.
For local communities, shapla beels offer opportunities for income generation. During the tourist season, residents may provide boat rides or sell local products.
The water lilies themselves have economic value, as they are sometimes harvested for food.
Regional Variations.
Also in the Sylhet region, there are beautiful shapla beel's.
These areas are becoming increasingly popular tourist destinations, and contribute to the natural beauty of Bangladesh.
In essence, shapla beels are more than just beautiful sights; they are integral parts of the natural and cultural landscape of Bangladesh.
Overall it is a very nice and beautiful place.

review_text:
Shapla Beel, DBir Haor — Silent Poetry of Nature

The Shapla Beel of DBir Haor in Sylhet is like a silent wonder of nature. During the monsoon season, this beel transforms into a vast water kingdom, and the combination of white and pink lotuses floating on its chest brings an unearthly beauty to the eyes. As far as the eye can see—only water, sky, and the fascination of lotuses.

Riding a boat through the beel, it seems as if time slows down a little here. The light scent of kachuri leaves and lotuses in the air, the distant village houses, and the occasional call of birds—all combine to create a unique sense of peace. Away from the hustle and bustle of the city, Shapla Beel is an ideal place to get lost in the lap of nature.

The beauty of Shapla Beel is especially evident in the soft light of the morning or afternoon. It is a paradise for photography lovers, and anyone who loves nature will not return without being moved.
Usually, a boat rent is 500 taka, and 6/7 people can travel in one boat.

শাপলা বিল, ডিবির হাওর — প্রকৃতির নীরব কবিতা

সিলেটের ডিবির হাওরের শাপলা বিল যেন প্রকৃতির এক নিঃশব্দ আশ্চর্য। বর্ষা মৌসুমে এই বিল রূপ নেয় বিশাল জলরাজ্যে, আর তার বুকে ভেসে থাকা সাদা ও গোলাপি শাপলার সমাহার চোখে এক অপার্থিব সৌন্দর্য এনে দেয়। চারদিকে যতদূর চোখ যায়—শুধু জল, আকাশ আর শাপলার মুগ্ধতা।

নৌকায় চড়ে বিলের ভেতর দিয়ে চলতে চলতে মনে হয়, সময় যেন এখানে একটু ধীরে চলে। বাতাসে হালকা কচুরিপানা আর শাপলার গন্ধ, দূরে গ্রামের ঘরবাড়ি, আর মাঝেমধ্যে পাখির ডাক—সব মিলিয়ে এক অনন্য শান্তির অনুভূতি তৈরি করে। শহরের কোলাহল থেকে দূরে, প্রকৃতির কোলে হারিয়ে যাওয়ার জন্য শাপলা বিল এক আদর্শ জায়গা।

বিশেষ করে সকাল কিংবা বিকেলের নরম আলোতে শাপলা বিলের সৌন্দর্য সবচেয়ে বেশি ফুটে ওঠে। ফটোগ্রাফি প্রেমীদের জন্য এটি স্বর্গসম, আবার প্রকৃতি ভালোবাসেন এমন যে কারো মন এখান থেকে নাড়া না দিয়ে ফেরে না।

review_text:
DB Haor, Jaintapur, Sylhet.

Last year, after seeing a picture of this place on a website, I had made a mental plan to try to come here this year. When I saw the picture, the Shapla season had just ended here. So there was no choice but to wait for a year. Of course, there is no shortage of Shapla in this country. However, for those who like to travel, there are two places in the country that are quite popular for seeing Shapla. One is in a village called Shatla in Ujirpur, Barisal, and the other is in Jaintapur, Sylhet. Shapla is available in Shatla during the monsoon and in Jaintapur during the winter.

As winter approached, I had been planning to go to Jaintapur for a few days. At that time, I received an invitation to a batchmate-colleague's wedding in Sylhet. I did not want to be foolish enough to miss such an opportunity. Finally, after attending the wedding on December 15, I left for Jaintapur, 42 km from Sylhet, in the morning of December 16. There were 4 more people with me. After passing Jaintapur Bazar on the Sylhet-Tamabil road, a signboard appeared on the right hand side, which said DB Haor Special BGB Camp. After one km along that road, you will see DB Haor covered in millions of lotus flowers. The place is right on the Bangladesh-India border. Therefore, the hills of Meghalaya have increased the beauty of the place many times. This is where DB Haor sets itself apart from Shatla.

The memory of Raja Ram Singh of Jainta state is intertwined with this DB Haor. He was drowned in this haor. In the middle of the haor stands a dilapidated temple, about 200 years old, with the memory of Raja Ram Singh.

Lotus flowers remain in DB Haor for about 3/4 months. You can see this wonderful beauty only if you go in November-January. However, you have to go very early in the morning for this. When the sunlight falls on the lotus flowers, the petals of the flowers slowly close.

It can be reached from Sylhet in an hour. We left Sylhet at 7 am and reached DB Haor around 8 am. If you go between 9.00-9.30 am, you will see the awake Shaplar. If they fall asleep, you will not be able to wake them up.

You can go around the Haor by boat. If you go, you will definitely get on the boat. The fare will be 300 taka per hour. This fare is fixed by the upazila administration. 7/8 people can easily get on a medium-sized boat.

How to go -
Sylhet from any place in Bangladesh.
From Sylhet, take a bus/laguna plying on the Sylhet-Tamabil route and get off at the board marked DB Haor a little after Jaintapur. The fare will be 40-50 taka per person. It takes about 1 hour. If you reserve CNG from Sylhet, the return fare will be around 1000 taka. We had reserved CNG. CNG is available for 1500 taka for the whole day.

Please do not leave any kind of plastic items or do anything that spoils the beauty of nature while you are out and about.
review_text_original:
ডিবির হাওর, জৈন্তাপুর, সিলেট।

গতবছর একটা ওয়েবসাইটে এখানকার একটা ছবি দেখেই মনে মনে প্ল্যান করে রেখেছিলাম এবছর এখানে আসার চেষ্টা করবোই। যখন ছবিটা দেখি তখন মাত্র এখানে শাপলার সিজন শেষ হয়েছে। তাই একবছর অপেক্ষা করা ছাড়া উপায় ছিলোনা। এদেশে অবশ্য শাপলার বিলের অভাব নেই৷ তবে যারা ঘুরতে পছন্দ করেন তাদের কাছে দেশের মধ্যে শাপলা দেখার জন্য দুইটা জায়গা বেশ পছন্দের। একটা বরিশালের উজিরপুরের শাতলা নামক গ্রামে, আরেকটা সিলেটের জৈন্তাপুরে। শাতলায় শাপলা থাকে বর্ষায় আর জৈন্তাপুরে শীতে।

শীত আসতেই জৈন্তাপুরে যাবো যাবো করছিলাম কিছুদিন ধরেই। ঠিক সেই সময়েই সিলেটে ব্যাচমেট-কলিগের বিয়ের দাওয়াত পেয়ে গেলাম। এমন সুযোগ হাতছাড়া করার বোকামি করতে চাইনি। শেষমেশ ডিসেম্বরের ১৫ তারিখ বিয়েতে এটেন্ড করে ১৬ই ডিসেম্বর একদম সকালেই রওনা দিলাম সিলেট থেকে ৪২ কি.মি. দূরের জৈন্তাপুরে। সাথে ছিলো আরো ৪ জন। সিলেট-তামাবিল সড়ক ধরে জৈন্তাপুর বাজার পেরিয়ে একটু এগোলেই হাতের ডানে একটা সাইনবোর্ড চোখে পড়ে যেখানে লেখা ডিবির হাওড় বিশেষ বিজিবি ক্যাম্প। সেই রাস্তা ধরে এক কি.মি. গেলেই চোখে পড়বে লাখ লাখ শাপলায় ছেয়ে থাকা ডিবির হাওর। জায়গাটা ঠিক বাংলাদেশ-ভারত সীমান্তে। তাই মেঘালয়ের পাহাড়গুলো যায়গাটার সৌন্দর্য্য বাড়িয়ে দিয়েছে বহুগুন। এখানেই ডিবির হাওর নিজেকে আলাদা করেছে শাতলার চেয়ে।

জৈন্তা রাজ্যের রাজা রাম সিংহের স্মৃতি জড়িয়ে আছে এই ডিবির হাওরে। উনাকে এই হাওরে ডুবিয়ে মারা হয়েছিলো। হাওরের মাঝে দাঁড়িয়ে আছে রাজা রাম সিংহের স্মৃতি বিজড়িত প্রায় ২০০ বছরের পুরোনো জীর্ন একটি মন্দির।

ডিবির হাওরে শাপলা থাকে মোটামুটি ৩/৪ মাস। নভেম্বর-জানুয়ারি গেলেই দেখা মিলবে এই অপরূপ সৌন্দর্য্যের। তবে এজন্য যেতে হবে একদম সকাল সকাল। সূর্যের আলো শাপলার গায়ে পড়লে আস্তে আস্তে ফুলগুলোর পাপড়ি বন্ধ হয়ে যায়।

সিলেট থেকে এখানে পৌছানো যায় ঘন্টাখানেকের মধ্যেই। আমরা সিলেট থেকে সকাল ৭ টায় রওনা দিয়ে ৮ টার দিকে ডিবির হাওরে পৌছাই। মোটামুটি ৯.০০-৯.৩০ এর মধ্যে গেলে জাগ্রত শাপলার দেখা মিলবে। ওরা ঘুময়ে গেলে কিন্তু তখন আর ডেকে তুলতে পারবেন না।

হাওরে নৌকায় ঘুরতে পারবেন। গেলে তো অবশ্যই নৌকায় উঠবেনই। ভাড়া নিবে ঘন্টায় ৩০০ টাকা। এই ভাড়া উপজেলা প্রশাসন থেকে নির্ধারন করে দেয়া। মাঝারি সাইজের এক নৌকায় ৭/৮ জন উঠা যায় অনায়াসেই।

যেভাবে যাবেন-
বাংলাদেশের যেকোন যায়গা থেকে সিলেট।
সিলেট থেকে সিলেট-তামাবিল রুটে চলাচলকারী বাস/লেগুনায় করে জৈন্তাপুর এর একটু পরেই ডিবির হাওর লেখা ফলকের ওখানে নামবেন। ভাড়া নিবে জনপ্রতি ৪০-৫০ টাকা। সময় লাগে ১ ঘন্টার মত। সিলেট থেকে সিএনজি রিজার্ভ করে নিলে আসা-যাওয়া ভাড়া নিবে ১০০০ টাকার মত। আমরা সিএনজি রিজার্ভ করে গিয়েছিলাম। সারাদিনের জন্য সিএনজি ১৫০০ টাকায় পাওয়া যায়।

দয়াকরে ঘুরতে গেলে সেখানে কোনপ্রকার প্লাস্টিক দ্রব্য ফেলে রাখা বা প্রকৃতির সৌন্দর্য্য নষ্ট হয় এমন কোন কাজ করবেন না।

review_text:
DB Haor (commonly known as 'Lal Shaplar Beel') is a very picturesque wetland located at the foot of the Meghalaya Hills, bordering India, in Jaintapur Upazila of Sylhet District in northeastern Bangladesh. Every year at the beginning of winter, thousands of red lotuses bloom, turning the entire haor into a red carpet.
​Geographical location and structure
​DB Haor is mainly composed of four distinct beels:
​DB Beel
​Yam Beel
​Horfkata Beel
​Kendrikendri Beel
​The four beels together cover an area of ​​about 900 acres. The vast Khasia-Jaintia Hills of the Indian state of Meghalaya stand just behind the haor.
​Main attractions and beauty
​Red Lotus Fair: During autumn and winter (especially from October to January), countless red lotuses bloom throughout the entire water body. From a distance, it looks like a red sheet has been spread on the water.
​Reflection of Meghalaya Mountains: The reflection of the huge Meghalaya Mountains and clouds on the calm water creates a wonderful scene.
​Bird calls: A large number of native and migratory birds arrive here during the winter season, which is attractive for bird lovers.
​Historical background: According to local folklore and history, this area was once part of the Jainta kingdom. There are various monuments and old tombs associated with the memory of Jainta King Ramsingh next to the beel.
​Best time and schedule to visit
​Season: October to December/January is the best time to see the beauty of red lotus.
​Time of day: It is best to go between 6 am and 8 or 9 am. As the sun rises, the lotus flowers start to fade.
​Transportation
​From Sylhet city: From Kadamtali or Subhanighat in Sylhet city, take a bus or CNG-powered auto-rickshaw to Jaintapur Bazar (distance is about 40-42 km).
​From Jaintapur to Beel: You can easily reach DB Haor by tomtom, rickshaw or walking along the unpaved road past Jaintapur Bazar or Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) camp.
​Boat trip: Small indigenous boats are available for rent from local fishermen to explore the beel.
​Environmental protection precautions
​It is inappropriate to tear lotus flowers and leaves unnecessarily while traveling in a boat.
​It is important to refrain from throwing plastic or non-biodegradable waste to protect the environment and biodiversity of the haor.
​Since this is a border area, it is necessary to follow the instructions of the BGB and local administration.

​রক্তিম শাপলার মেলা: শরৎ ও শীতকালে (বিশেষ করে অক্টোবর থেকে জানুয়ারি) পুরো জলাশয় জুড়ে অগণিত লাল শাপলা ফোটে। দূর থেকে দেখলে মনে হয় যেন পানির ওপর লাল চাদর বিছিয়ে রাখা হয়েছে।
​মেঘালয় পাহাড়ের প্রতিফলন: শান্ত জলের বুকে বিশাল মেঘালয় পাহাড় ও মেঘের প্রতিচ্ছবি চমৎকার এক দৃশ্যের অবতারণা করে।
​পাখির কলকাকলি: শীতের মৌসুমে এখানে প্রচুর দেশি ও পরিযায়ী পাখির আগমন ঘটে, যা পাখিপ্রেমীদের জন্য আকর্ষণীয়।
​ঐতিহাসিক পটভূমি: স্থানীয় লোকগাথা ও ইতিহাস অনুযায়ী, এই এলাকা একসময় জৈন্তা রাজ্যের অংশ ছিল। বিলের পাশেই রয়েছে জৈন্তা রাজা রামসিংহের স্মৃতিবিজড়িত বিভিন্ন নিদর্শন ও পুরনো সমাধি।
​ভ্রমণের সেরা সময় ও সময়সূচি

​দিনের সময়: ভোর ৬টা থেকে সকাল ৮টা বা ৯টার মধ্যে যাওয়া সবচেয়ে ভালো। রোদ বাড়ার সাথে সাথে শাপলা ফুল বুজে যেতে শুরু করে।
​যাতায়াত ব্যবস্থা
​সিলেট শহর থেকে: সিলেট শহরের কদমতলী বা সুবহানীঘাট থেকে জাফলংগামী বাস বা সিএনজিচালিত অটোরিকশায় করে জৈন্তাপুর বাজারে পৌঁছাতে হয় (দূরত্ব প্রায় ৪০-৪২ কিমি)।
​জৈন্তাপুর থেকে বিল: জৈন্তাপুর বাজার বা বর্ডার গার্ড বাংলাদেশ (বিজিবি) ক্যাম্পের পাশ দিয়ে কাঁচা-পাকা রাস্তা দিয়ে টমটম, রিকশা বা হেঁটে সহজেই ডিবির হাওরে যাওয়া যায়।
​নৌকা ভ্রমণ: বিলের ভেতর ঘুরে দেখতে স্থানীয় মাঝিদের ছোট দেশি নৌকা ভাড়া পাওয়া যায়।
​পরিবেশ সুরক্ষায় সতর্কতা
​নৌকায় ঘোরার সময় অপ্রয়োজনে শাপলা ফুল ও পাতা ছেঁড়া অনুচিত।
​হাওরের পরিবেশ ও জীববৈচিত্র্য রক্ষায় প্লাস্টিক বা অপচনশীল বর্জ্য ফেলা থেকে বিরত থাকা জরুরি।
​এটি সীমান্তবর্তী এলাকা হওয়ায় বিজিবি ও স্থানীয় প্রশাসনের নির্দেশনা মেনে চলা আবশ্যক।

Madhabkunda Waterfall is not just a tourist spot — it feels like nature suddenly decided to show off. The long walk through the green forest builds the excitement step by step, and then the sound of roaring water hits before the view does. When the waterfall finally appears, it’s powerful, misty, and honestly a little humbling.
What I loved most is how the place changes your mood. The cool spray in the air, the echo of water crashing on rocks, and the surrounding hills make you forget phone notifications and city noise. If you stand quietly for a moment, you’ll hear birds, flowing streams, and wind through the trees — a full natural orchestra.
The path is fairly easy but can be slippery near the waterfall, so good footwear helps. There are small shops outside for snacks and drinks, but the real refreshment is the cold natural air inside.
Best time to visit is during or just after the rainy season when the waterfall is at its strongest and most dramatic. Great place for photos, but even better for just standing still and feeling small in front of something so powerful.
A must-visit natural wonder of Bangladesh. I’d come again just to hear that sound of falling water.

Madhabkunda Falls: Madhabkunda Falls is one of the highest waterfalls in Bangladesh. Located in Baralekha Upazila of Moulvibazar District, this waterfall is a popular tourist destination in Bangladesh. The surrounding forests, springs and ecological parks attract numerous tourists for picnics and day trips.

Gangamara Falls flows 162 feet (49 m) down the rocky Patharia Hills to form the Madhabkunda Falls, which later merges with the Madhabchhara Falls below. The water of Madhabchhara flows westwards and finally meets the Hakaluki Haor.

The main stream usually maintains a steady flow throughout the year. During the monsoon, a small river forms alongside the main river, and as the monsoon intensifies, the two rivers merge to form a powerful stream. This intense flow flows downstream and forms a huge pond below. As it falls into the pond, the depth of the pond continues to increase.

The area is important to Hindus, with a temple nearby where Hindu rituals are held every year and a fair is held there. On the right side, next to the pond, there is a cave, which is revered as a pilgrimage site.

Local Hindus believe that the last Hindu king of Sylhet, King Govardhan of Gaur, met a meditating monk named Madhaveshwar during a hunting expedition in 1335 AD. The monk expressed his desire to unite with the goddess Ganga and requested to take a dip in the spring. At the monk's request, he united with the Ganges and a divine voice uttered "Madhav Madhav Madhav" three times, resulting in the name Madhavkund. According to another legend, the name is derived from "Madhav", which is a name for Shiva, as Shiva is believed to have appeared at this place.

review_text:
Madhabkunda Waterfall is one of the highest and most popular waterfalls in Bangladesh, located in the Barlekha Upazila of the Moulvibazar District, within the Sylhet Division. It is a significant natural attraction, surrounded by lush green hills, tea gardens, and the Madhabkunda Eco Park.
Key Details
Height: The waterfall cascades down approximately 200 feet (61 meters) from the rocky Patharia Hill.
Best Time to Visit: The monsoon season (June to September) offers the most spectacular view due to maximum water flow. The dry season (November to March) provides calmer weather for exploring, though with less water.
Entry Fee: The admission fee to the Eco Park is around BDT 20-30 per person.
Facilities: Basic facilities like restrooms and small food stalls are available, along with a government-run rest house and motel.
Activities: Visitors can enjoy sightseeing, photography, nature walks, and exploring nearby tribal villages and tea plantations.
Getting There from Sylhet
The waterfall is about 80 km and a two-hour journey from the main Sylhet town.
By Bus: Take a bus from Sylhet's Kadamtali bus station to Kulaura or Barlekha, and then hire a local CNG auto-rickshaw or microbus to reach Madhabkunda.
By Train: The nearest railway station is Kulaura Junction. From there, you can hire a CNG or car for the remaining distance.
Safety Tips
The rocks around the waterfall can be very slippery, especially during the rainy season, so wear appropriate footwear.
Avoid getting too close to the falling water or swimming in deep areas of the natural pool due to strong currents and safety concerns.
Carry insect repellent and be mindful of your belongings due to the presence of wildlife like monkeys.

By Train: The nearest railway station is Kulaura Junction. From there, you can hire a CNG or car for the remaining distance.
Safety Tips
The rocks around the waterfall can be very slippery, especially during the rainy season, so wear appropriate footwear.
Avoid getting too close to the falling water or swimming in deep areas of the natural pool due to strong currents and safety concerns.
Carry insect repellent and be mindful of your belongings due to the presence of wildlife like monkeys.

Madhabkunda Waterfall: A Natural Wonder of Bangladesh

Madhabkunda Waterfall, the largest and one of the most popular waterfalls in Bangladesh, is located in Moulvibazar district within the Sylhet division. Surrounded by lush green tea gardens, tropical forests, and rocky hills, this breathtaking waterfall is a major tourist attraction and a symbol of natural beauty in the country.

The waterfall drops from a height of about 200 feet, creating a thundering sound as the water crashes into the natural pool below. During the rainy season, the flow becomes even stronger, offering visitors a spectacular view of nature’s raw power. The area is also rich in biodiversity, home to various species of birds, butterflies, and rare plants, making it a paradise for nature lovers and photographers alike.

Madhabkunda is not only a site of natural beauty but also holds cultural and historical significance. Local legends suggest that the place is named after a Hindu saint named Madhabeshwar, who is believed to have meditated near the waterfall. Today, it attracts both domestic and foreign travelers who seek tranquility, adventure, and a glimpse of Bangladesh’s scenic landscapes.

Finlay Tea Estate stands as a majestic testament to the rich heritage of tea cultivation in Sreemangal, Moulvibazar. Established by the East India Company, this sprawling estate boasts of being one of the largest and most magnificent tea gardens in Bangladesh. As you wander through its verdant expanses, you'll be greeted by the sight of thousands of tea trees, their lush greenery extending as far as the eye can see. The beauty of the green environment is truly awe-inspiring, making it a captivating destination for tourists from all corners of the country.

Step foot into Finlay Tea Garden, and you'll find yourself immersed in a world of natural splendor and tranquility. The meticulously manicured landscape, adorned with vibrant tea bushes, serves as a testament to the tireless efforts of the thousands of workers, especially the female workers who tirelessly pick tea leaves throughout the day. Despite its grandeur, access to the inner sanctum of the garden is restricted, adding an air of mystery to its allure.

As you explore the vast expanse of Finlay Tea Estate, you'll feel as though time stands still, with no end in sight to its sprawling beauty. The days here are filled with serenity, allowing you to immerse yourself in the soothing embrace of nature and refresh your mind amidst the tranquil surroundings. However, as night falls, the silence of the tea garden can be both enchanting and eerily haunting, adding an intriguing dimension to your experience.

While general visitors may not be permitted to enter the heart of the estate, there are still treasures to be discovered on its periphery. Perched atop the hills are temples that welcome all, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. These sacred sites serve as vantage points, allowing visitors to marvel at the breathtaking beauty of the tea garden from a different perspective.
Finlay Tea Estate is not just a tea garden; it's a sanctuary of natural beauty and cultural heritage. With its lush greenery, serene ambiance, and captivating vistas, it offers a truly unforgettable experience for those fortunate enough to explore its hallowed grounds.

review_text:
The largest tea estate in Bangladesh is Finlay Tea Estate.

Finlay Tea Estate is an important and ancient name in the history of the tea industry in Bangladesh. It began during the British colonial rule, in the late 19th century. The Scottish-based British business company James Finlay & Company established large-scale tea gardens in the Sylhet and Srimangal regions as part of the expansion of the tea industry in the subcontinent, within which Finlay Tea Estate was established. At that time, this region was very suitable for tea cultivation, so the British started producing tea here in a modern way.
Finlay Tea Estate was mainly managed by the British and the tea here was exported to international markets including Europe. The development of worker settlements, railways and communication systems in the surrounding areas centered on this garden, which played a major role in shaping the economic structure of the entire Srimangal-Moulvibazar region. The colonial imprint is still visible in the plans of the manager bungalows, factory buildings and gardens built during the British period.
After Bangladesh gained independence, many tea estates, including Finlay Tea Estate, underwent changes in ownership and management. Later, it was operated under local management and continues to make a significant contribution to the tea industry of Bangladesh. Today, Finlay Tea Estate is not only a production center, but also a tourist attraction for the natural beauty, historical environment and scenic views surrounding the tea estate. Overall, Finlay Tea Estate is a historical site deeply intertwined with the development of the tea industry in Bangladesh, British colonial history and the identity of the Srimangal region.

বাংলাদেশের সবচেয়ে বড় চা বাগান হলো Finlay Tea Estate (ফিনলে টি এস্টেট)।

ফিনলে টি এস্টেট বাংলাদেশের চা–শিল্পের ইতিহাসে একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ ও প্রাচীন নাম। এর সূচনা ব্রিটিশ ঔপনিবেশিক শাসনামলে, উনিশ শতকের শেষভাগে। স্কটল্যান্ডভিত্তিক ব্রিটিশ ব্যবসায়িক প্রতিষ্ঠান James Finlay & Company উপমহাদেশে চা শিল্প বিস্তারের অংশ হিসেবে সিলেট ও শ্রীমঙ্গল অঞ্চলে বড় আকারে চা–বাগান স্থাপন করে, যার মধ্যেই ফিনলে টি এস্টেট গড়ে ওঠে। তৎকালীন সময়ে এই অঞ্চলটি চা চাষের জন্য অত্যন্ত উপযোগী হওয়ায় ব্রিটিশরা এখানে আধুনিক পদ্ধতিতে চা উৎপাদন শুরু করে।
ফিনলে টি এস্টেট মূলত ব্রিটিশ ব্যবস্থাপনায় পরিচালিত হতো এবং এখানকার চা ইউরোপসহ আন্তর্জাতিক বাজারে রপ্তানি করা হতো। এই বাগানকে কেন্দ্র করে আশপাশের এলাকায় শ্রমিক বসতি, রেলপথ ও যোগাযোগ ব্যবস্থার উন্নয়ন ঘটে, যা পুরো শ্রীমঙ্গল–মৌলভীবাজার অঞ্চলের অর্থনৈতিক কাঠামো গঠনে বড় ভূমিকা রাখে। ব্রিটিশ আমলে নির্মিত ম্যানেজার বাংলো, কারখানা ভবন ও বাগানের পরিকল্পনায় সেই ঔপনিবেশিক ছাপ আজও দেখা যায়।
বাংলাদেশ স্বাধীন হওয়ার পর ফিনলে টি এস্টেটসহ অনেক চা–বাগানের মালিকানা ও ব্যবস্থাপনায় পরিবর্তন আসে। পরবর্তীতে এটি দেশীয় ব্যবস্থাপনার অধীনে পরিচালিত হতে থাকে এবং বাংলাদেশের চা শিল্পে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ অবদান রেখে চলেছে। বর্তমানে ফিনলে টি এস্টেট শুধু একটি উৎপাদন কেন্দ্র নয়, বরং চা–বাগান ঘেরা প্রাকৃতিক সৌন্দর্য, ঐতিহাসিক পরিবেশ ও নৈসর্গিক দৃশ্যের জন্য পর্যটকদের কাছেও পরিচিত। সব মিলিয়ে, ফিনলে টি এস্টেট বাংলাদেশের চা শিল্পের বিকাশ, ব্রিটিশ ঔপনিবেশিক ইতিহাস এবং শ্রীমঙ্গল অঞ্চলের পরিচয়ের সঙ্গে গভীরভাবে জড়িয়ে থাকা একটি ঐতিহাসিক স্থান।

Finlay Tea Estate is a traditional and ancient tea estate in Bangladesh, whose historical importance, natural beauty and economic contribution are all significant. It is mainly widely known in the Sylhet division - Srimangal and Moulvibazar regions.
Finlay Tea's journey began during the British colonial period.
It was founded by a Scottish company named James Finlay & Co., who developed the tea industry in various parts of India and Bangladesh.
Even after Bangladesh became independent, the Finlay name remained and it is now operated as Finlay Tea Company (Bangladesh).
They also have many lands and tea factories in Srimangal and Moulvibazar.
Finlay Tea Estates produce high-quality orthodox and CTC tea.
The estates have their own processing units (tea factories) where full-bodied tea is prepared from green tea leaves.
Some estates also produce rubber and timber.
Finlay Tea is known in the export market in addition to the domestic market in Bangladesh.
The company is one of the oldest and largest tea companies in the country, with a well-organized tea garden, tea processing center, and marketing system.

Spacious green hilly area across the tea garden

Neatly lined rows of tea trees

Finlay Tea Estate produces high-quality tea

This is one of the tourist attractions in Srimangal

Travelers can visit the tea garden

---

**Tanguar Haor**

Tanguar Haor is one of the largest and most important wetlands in Bangladesh, located in the Tahirpur upazila of Sunamganj district. It is a unique natural treasure, formed by a combination of rivers, canals, and low-lying lands that create a vast water-based ecosystem.

In 2000, Tanguar Haor was declared a Ramsar Site, which means it is recognized internationally as a wetland of great ecological importance. It became the second Ramsar Site in Bangladesh after the Sundarbans. The haor covers a huge area and contains more than forty smaller wetlands, known locally as "beels."

During the rainy season, Tanguar Haor turns into a massive sheet of water, almost like a sea, connecting with the sky at the horizon. In winter, the water level decreases, revealing wide stretches of grassland and creating a completely different landscape. This seasonal change makes the haor look different throughout the year.

The haor is home to rich biodiversity. Every winter, thousands of migratory birds travel from Siberia and the Himalayan region to take shelter here. Various species of fish, aquatic plants, and freshwater turtles also live in this wetland, making it an important habitat for wildlife.

Tanguar Haor has also become a popular tourist destination, especially between November and February. Visitors enjoy boat rides across the vast water, bird watching, and the beautiful view of the Meghalaya hills in the background. Nearby places like Neeladri Lake and Tekerghat add extra charm to the journey.

However, the haor faces serious threats due to illegal fishing, encroachment, and excessive tourism. Local authorities and environmentalists are working to protect its natural balance so that future generations can also enjoy this treasure.

In conclusion, Tanguar Haor is not only a beautiful natural site but also an important part of Bangladesh's ecological wealth. Protecting it should be a shared responsibility of the government, local people, and visitors alike.

I recently went on a tour to Tanguar Haor with friends, organized by Travel Sylhet. It was a wonderful experience, especially the boat ride and swimming in the haor. I hadn’t gone on a trip for about 2–3 years (my last one was a study tour to Srimangal), so this felt refreshing.

The bus ride wasn’t great the bus was a bit strange and didn’t even have music, which is usually a must for trips. The conductor said they didn’t have any, but some of the seniors on the trip sang Bangla songs, which made it lively. I usually have vomiting issues when traveling by bus, but surprisingly, I didn’t face it this time maybe because I was too excited.
The trip cost only 1,200 BDT per person, which was quite cheap considering everything. The bus experience wasn’t good, but once we reached Sunamganj and got on the boat, it was amazing. I had never experienced a boat trip like this before.
Since it was only a one-day trip (morning to night), we could only cover 3 spots. Usually, renting a boat in Tanguar Haor for 3–4 days costs around 20–30k, but that’s a completely different experience because you can explore more and enjoy your time fully. So, I’d suggest anyone planning a trip here to go for 3–4 days and book a boat it’s absolutely worth it.

Overall, I’d rate my experience 8/10. I’m keeping 2 points off because of the bus ride.

• Livelihood: It sustains the livelihoods of over 40,000 local people, mainly through fishing and seasonal farming.
• Geography: It is famous for its seasonal transformation, swelling into a large water body during the monsoon and offering views of the Meghalaya Hills in India.

Tanguar Haor – A Hidden Paradise in Bangladesh
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Tanguar Haor, located in Sunamganj district, is one of Bangladesh's most breathtaking wetlands, covering around 100 square kilometers. This vast haor (floodplain) is surrounded by the Meghalaya hills of India and consists of over 50 small villages, making it a unique blend of water, land, and rural life.

Natural Beauty & Experience
During the monsoon season, Tanguar Haor turns into a vast, serene lake where boats become the only mode of transport. The endless blue waters, the reflection of the sky, and the distant green hills create a mesmerizing view. In winter, it becomes home to thousands of migratory birds, making it a paradise for bird watchers and photographers.

Best Time to Visit
Monsoon (June–September): For the best boating experience and breathtaking views.
Winter (November–February): Ideal for bird watching and enjoying the calm waters.
Things to Do
Boat rides – Experience the vastness of the haor on a traditional wooden boat.
Camping – Stay overnight on a boat or in nearby villages to enjoy the peaceful surroundings.
Birdwatching – Spot thousands of migratory birds in winter.
Swimming & Relaxation – The clear waters of the haor are perfect for a refreshing swim.
Exploring Barek Tila – A nearby hilltop offering a spectacular view of Tanguar Haor.
Why Visit?
Tanguar Haor is not just a tourist destination—it is a Ramsar wetland, recognized for its ecological significance. It offers a rare combination of natural beauty, biodiversity, and local culture, making it a must-visit for nature lovers, adventure seekers, and photographers.

review_text:
Tanguar haor is unique wetland ecosystem with enormous natural beauty. This haor having an area of 100sq km and consisting of 120 small and large (canals) is in its youth during the monsoon. During the winter the haor becomes home migratory birds. Nature lovers and tourists may make an arrangement for at least two days to make a trip to the fascinating Tanguarhaor.

Tanguarhaor is located in the Dharmapasha and Tahirpur upazilas of Sunamganj District Bangladesh covering 10 villages. This wetland is home to about 208 species of birds, 150 species of water plants, 34 species of reptiles and 11 species of amphibious.

There are more than 140 species of fresh water fish in the haor. You can have a taste of the haor fishes if you make a visit to the haor. The more predominant among them are: rui, katol, ayir, boal, gang magur, tara, baim, gulsha, gutum, tengra, titna, gaajar, garia, beti, kakia etc.

Leuchchhamara and Berberiabils are free abodes for birds of many species in Tanguarhaor. Besides, you will find birds in other bils, including RouarBil, GazariarBil, AlomerDoar, SangsarBil, KoikhaliBil, ChhunkholaBil, JittolarGop, FoillarBil, RupabhuiBil, Sattar Bil, MoisherGata, BaloarDoba, AmchharerBil, KauarBil, AnsarerBil, KhajuriBil, AinnarBil and NolkathirBil. Keeping a binocular while travelling will make watching the birds more enjoyable.

You can choose either of Shyamoly Paribahan, Hanif Enterprize, Ena Paribaha and Mamun Paribahan, if you want to go to Sunamganj from Dhaka by road. The bus tickets will be available within the range of 55o taka.

You have to get off at Surma Bridge before entering Sunamganj town. From there, you have to go to Tahirpur or Solemanpur by leguna or bike. However, it is better to go to solemanpur in February because water level in Boulai (Tahirpur to Solemanpur) falls during this period.

You will have to pay 800 to 1200 taka to hire a leguna to reach Solemanpur from Sunamganj. At least 8 people can get on board of a leguna. A motorbike will charge 300 to 400 taka for two persons. From Solemanpur you have to hire engine-driven boat to reach Tanguarhaor through Patlai River. You have to pay 1000 to 1500 taka each day to hire an engine-run boat. You can even stay on these boats at night. You have to buy cooking ingredients to take with you while visiting. You will need to take necessary medicines, camera and back-up charger for mobile phone.

You can stay at Tahirpur Dakbanglow if you wish to.

review_text: Tanguar Haor is one of the largest group of water mahals in Bangladesh. The biodiverse freshwater A Haor located in Dharmapasha and Tahirpur upazilas of Sunamganj district in the north-eastern corner of Bangladesh is the 2nd Ramsar site of Bangladesh. Khasia, Meghalaya, India At the foothills of the Jainta Hills, dotted with rows of hijals, Tangguar Haor is a vast sanctuary for fish, birds and other aquatic life. At present the total number of reservoirs is 51 and the total area is 6,912.20 acres. However, the area of the entire haor during the monsoon season including Nalkhagra forest, Hijal Karach forest is about 20,000 acres. Tanguare Haor is blessed with the bountiful bounty of nature. A haor is not only a water house or a place for fish rearing, conservation and harvesting. It is a mother fishery. Hijal Karach's visionary Nandan Sari has made Haor charming. Apart from this, there are more than two hundred species of plants including Nalkhagra, Dudhilata, Neel Shapla, Panifal, Shola, Helancha, Shatamuli, Shitalpati, Swarnlata, Bantulsi etc. in this surrounding area. As a result of the effective and sustainable measures taken by the district administration, there are currently 141 species of 208 species of birds, 1 species of amphibians, 34 species of reptiles, 6 species of turtles, 7 species of chameleons and 21 species of snakes. The reed forest has increased several times. During the winter season, Tanguare Haor is buzzing with massive bird arrivals and locations, breaking all previous records. The almost extinct palaces eagle, giant grey-kingstork, vulture and a large number of guest birds were the unforgettable sight of Tangua Haor. The collection of local species of birds such as pankauri, kalem, baidar, dahuk, various types of sand ducks, gangchils, bucks, cranes etc. is also amazing. In general, 20/25 lakh birds are estimated to have been in Tangua Haor each past winter season. In some places only birds can be seen floating over an area of more than a kilometer. Tanguar Haor is a unique ecosystem of interdependent fish, birds and plants. It is most important as a fish sanctuary.

It is one of the largest freshwater wetlands in Bangladesh and is recognized as a Ramsar site, indicating its international importance for biodiversity and conservation. Here's an overview of Tanguar Haor:

**Location and Geography**:
Tanguar Haor covers an area of approximately 10,000 hectares (24,710 acres) during the monsoon season and shrinks to around 5,000 hectares (12,355 acres) during the dry season. It is characterized by its extensive marshes, lakes, and water bodies. Tanguar Haor is part of the Surma Valley and is nestled amid the picturesque hills of northeastern Bangladesh.

**Biodiversity**:
One of the most remarkable aspects of Tanguar Haor is its rich biodiversity. It serves as a critical habitat for various plant and animal species, including numerous resident and migratory birds. The haor is a vital stopover point for many migratory waterfowl along the Central Asian Flyway. It's estimated that over 200 species of birds, including the rare Baer's Pochard, visit Tanguar Haor.

**Aquatic Life**:
The wetland is also home to a diverse range of aquatic life, including various fish species. The local communities depend on fishing in Tanguar Haor for their livelihoods, and the wetland supports a significant portion of the region's fish production.

**Flood Control and Agriculture**:
Tanguar Haor plays a crucial role in the region's ecosystem and agriculture. During the monsoon season, the haor acts as a natural flood storage basin, helping to control flooding in surrounding areas. In the dry season, the water recedes, exposing fertile land that is used for rice cultivation and other crops.

**Conservation and Ramsar Designation**:
Due to its ecological importance, Tanguar Haor was designated as a Ramsar site in 2000. This designation signifies the commitment to protect and conserve the wetland's biodiversity and ecosystem. Efforts have been made to implement sustainable resource management practices and raise awareness about the importance of preserving Tanguar Haor.

**Sustainable Tourism**:
Tanguar Haor is increasingly becoming a destination for eco-tourism. Visitors can explore the wetland's natural beauty, birdwatch, and enjoy boat rides. Sustainable tourism initiatives aim to promote responsible travel that supports the local economy while preserving the environment.

**Local Communities**:
The wetland is home to several indigenous communities, including the Khasi, Manipuri, and Tripura people. These communities have adapted their way of life to the seasonal changes of Tanguar Haor and play a role in its conservation efforts.

**Challenges**:
Tanguar Haor faces challenges related to overfishing, pollution, and habitat degradation. Conservation efforts focus on mitigating these threats while ensuring the sustainable use of the wetland's resources.

Tanguar Haor stands as a prime example of the delicate balance between human livelihoods and environmental preservation. Its significance as a Ramsar site highlights the global importance of protecting such unique and diverse wetland ecosystems.

I visited Hum Hum Waterfall in June, and it turned out to be one of the most challenging yet rewarding trips I’ve taken. The trail was muddy, slippery, and demanded a lot of effort — but the waterfall was at its fullest and most powerful, making every step worthwhile.
Hum Hum sits deep inside the Rajkandi Reserve Forest in Moulvibazar. From Sreemangal, we traveled to Kolabonpara village, where our local guide was waiting. I can’t stress this enough — a guide is essential. The trails are unmarked, and in the rainy season, the forest can change quickly, with new muddy sections, stream crossings, and hidden hazards.
The trek took about two and a half hours each way. From the very start, the path tested us. The recent rains had turned parts of the trail into slippery clay, and some sections were steep enough that we had to hold on to bamboo or tree roots for balance. Several stream crossings required careful footwork, with wet rocks ready to trip you if you rushed.
Despite the difficulty, the forest was alive and beautiful. Towering  bamboo groves and thick undergrowth surrounded us. Birds called from somewhere high above, and every now and then we’d hear the rustle of wildlife in the distance. The air smelled fresh and earthy, the kind of scent you only find deep in the forest after rain.
The sound of the waterfall reached us before the sight did — a deep, constant roar that grew louder with each turn. By the time we stepped into the clearing, all the exhaustion disappeared.

review_text:
Together me and my wife we went for a day long trekking to Hum Hum Waterfalls during the end of this July from Sreemangal..! Located in Moulvibazar district, this is very close to the Indian border, you have to go to Sreemangal from Dhaka by bus, train or private vehicle. And, there is no proper place for families at, or, around the Hum Hum Waterfalls for night stay. So, it must be a day trip to and from this place. Though, few of my traveler and Cyclist friends took tents with them and camped during the night just outside of the forest.

This was a great journey this time to the falls, some places the path was muddy, some slippery, some places you had to cross small strings, galleys and canals..! You will have to climb up and down walking both the ways.. through a jungle trail. During rainy season, there would be leeches found on your feet few times, not big deal at all, however check often. Its an excellent trail to trek, so this is not at all only about the Water Falls..! A must to go place..!!!

As said earlier, in most/ usual cases it has to be a day trip. So, start from Sreemangal by 7:00/ 7:30 am, DO NOT START LATE...!!!

How to go to and from Sreemangal from Dhaka:
i) By bus: Hanif Poribahan (bus service) and Shyamoli Poribahan have bus to Sreemangal every hour all day long..! Ena has AC buses on in the morning and another in the afternoon (google for latest update). However, if would like to save hotel bills you may travel both ways during the nights. Bus starts from Sayedabad, each of the bus companies have their ticket counters for purchasing the ticket and waiting.
For AC Bus: it might take something like 700 or 800 taka one way, for non AC 450 taka..! Caution: If you have a weak heart please do not dare to go by Hanif, they drive like Nascar drivers..!

ii) By Train: All the train from Dhaka starts from Komlapur Rail Station, there is a train that starts in the morning and another at 9:30 pm in the evening. Train fare starts from 240 to 1,000 taka. However, the night train reaches Sreemangal as early as 2:30 am/ 3:00 am/ 3:30 am that is inconvenient for many reasons, accordingly choose day time train if you are wiling and enthusiast about train.

iii) By Cycle or private/ hired car: Its only 180 Km road trip from Dhaka, so no matter what you take its great journey. You may follow Dhaka to Sylhet Highway through Kulshi 300 feet road, Kanchanpur bridge, Maona, Sylhet highway..! Quality of Road is fine all the ways only need to be a bit more careful during Kanchanpur to Maona and Voirob to Bramhanbaria junction due to more traffic in these sections.

Transport: From Sreemangal you may take CNG Auto Rickshaw for the whole day to go and come back with the same one. The Auto Rickshaw will wait for the whole day until you come back. You wont get anything from there on the way back, if you don't contract for the whole day. It will take 1,500 to 2,000 taka for the whole day. Nothing additional. You may take a Chander Gari (old 4 wheel jeep) it would go further than CNG upto Kolabon para.. and would be faster with 3,000 to 4,000 taka for the whole day. From Kolabon para.. it is around 4 Km trekking/ hiking..!

Food and Drinks: Take dry food and energy/ peanut/ chocolate bar, dry dates, water, Chanachur, chips/ fries.. with you..! As there wont be any shop both ways. You would get bottled water, packet snacks at the falls site. But be very care not litter but bring with foils and packs with you for the sake of environment.

Trekking Guide: At the entry gate of  you would get some tea garden laborer and locals sitting, you would get a guide within 400 taka.. for the entire day.. till the end of the trip. Guides are good and reliable..! We had Bidhan as guide, you may also search for him.

Caution: Start as early as possible in the morning, don’t litter, prefer a Chander Gari (old jeep), take some dry food and water with you.

Have a Great Trip...!!!

review_text:
For people used to walking, and dare I say non-bangladeshis (no offence guys!), I would say this is quite an easy, short trail. Locals will tell you that's it's extremely difficult and that you definitely should take a guide, but there is really no way you could get lost so it's really not necessary. There are even some guys selling snacks along the way, so of course you can just follow the trail of trash! it's quite a straightforward hike of about an hour and a half each way, with no difficult accents and a bit of hopping across the stream at the end. Probably tricky in monsoon season though. Having said all that, it's a beautiful day trip from srimongol and I would definitely recommend it!

You can take the bus from srimongol to kamalganj (20 taka) and then a shared CNG from there to kurmaghat at least (50 or 60 taka), so also quite a cheap day out!

review_text:
About
Uncover the hidden beauty of Humhum water Falls. Who dare to discover true wild life and see mighty Hamham by himself...?
Description
Hammam Waterfall, Bangladesh -

Humhum is the name of a waterfall. This is located at Kamalganja, Moulvibazar district of Bangladesh. People of that location pronounces this as Humhum, in some Print media it is also written as Humhum. But the real spelling would be Hammam. I got this confirmation from some local educated people, who includes govt officials and school teachers.

We were four in our team and i was the youngest. By the by, I am running now 42 years and rest all are 47-48 years old. Quite young and energetic a team, no doubt.

On 13 February,2011, we went to Kamalganja bazaar. This bazaar is about 20 minutes ride from Srimangal. After reaching there, we were in a dilemma about passing the night. However, lastly we got two rooms in a local boarding house and somehow passed the night by gossiping.

On 14 February, 2011; at 07 a m we started from this bazaar and reached Karma BOP after 30 minutes drive. From this location our foot march started. I will narrate the details of the journey in the following paragraphs.

The main beauty of this waterfall is in it's surrounding ground features. Anybody visiting this place will enjoy the whole route to the fall. But the final climax of the beauty is in the waterfall itself.

Location

This waterfall is located at Kamalganja Upazilla of MaulviBazar district of Bangladesh.

Karma BOP is the last vehicle pliable point. The tea garden of National Tea Company is located beside this BOP. From the BOP, we moved by 3 motorcycles to the last edge of tea garden, which is about 5 km. From this point, we started our route march to reach the waterfall. You want to go there? OK, I am describing you.

The Road to Hammam

The total walking time is about 2 hours 30 minutes to reach the destination. If you plan to move to see the waterfall, following precautionary arrangements should be made:
1.	Be mentally ready to walk on bare foot.
2.	Carry a small pack with you for carrying a camera, If possible a GPS, a water bottle and light first aid items.
3.	Don't forget to get a guide from the Karma Bazar to lead you.
4.	Have a bamboo stick while walking to avoid slips and fall.

The whole route is full of numerous types of landscapes. From the very start point you will be walking through a forest with some some small hillocks.

After walking through this for about 30 minutes, you will have to get down in a natural fountain (locally called chhara or nala), where you will have to walk trough water. The height of this water level will vary from ankle level to your thigh level time to time.

You may find some people cutting bamboo in and around that fountain. Even if you don't meet them end route, you will come across the signs of bamboo extraction in that fountain. Be very careful while walking through those as to avoid leg injury by those.

In many places, You will find the bottom surface of the fountain is with stones. At times those are very slippery. You need to be more careful while walking through those. That is why i mentioned for a stick to use as a support.

review_text:
The Heart of Rajshahi’s Riverfront!
​As a frequent traveler and Local Guide, I can confidently say that the T-Groin (locally known as T-Badh) is the soul of Rajshahi city. This T-shaped hydraulic structure, originally built to protect the city from the Padma’s erosion, has evolved into the most popular social hub for locals and tourists alike.

​The Experience & Popularity:
The atmosphere here is electric, especially during late afternoons. It’s the perfect spot to catch a breeze and watch the sunset over the horizon. During the monsoon, the water level rises right up to the concrete blocks, creating a sea-like vibe, while in the winter, the vast "Char" (river islands) emerge, offering a different kind of beauty. It is almost always crowded on weekends, reflecting its status as the city's top hangout spot.

​Boat Rides & The Sandbars (Char):
One of the highlights of visiting T-Badh is taking a traditional engine boat or a speed boat across the Padma. For a small fee (usually BDT 50-100 per person for group trips), you can reach the massive sandbars in the middle of the river. These "chars" feel like a mini-desert where you can walk for miles. It’s a must-do for photographers and nature lovers.

​Food & Street Delicacies:
The food scene here is vibrant and affordable. The area is famous for:
​Fuchka & Chotpoti: Numerous stalls offer some of the best spicy snacks in the city.
​Street Snacks: Kalai Ruti (a local Rajshahi specialty made of black gram flour) is often available nearby and is a must-try with duck meat or eggplant mash.
​Tea: Numerous tea stalls line the embankment, perfect for "adda" (socializing).

​Pro-Tips for Visitors:
​Timing: Visit between 4:00 PM and 6:30 PM to witness the breathtaking sunset.
​Safety: If you take a boat ride, ensure the boat isn't overloaded, especially during the monsoon when the current is strong.

​Cleanliness: As a Local Guide, I urge everyone to keep this beautiful embankment clean by using the designated bins for plastic waste.
​Whether you are a local student or a traveler visiting from afar, your trip to Rajshahi is incomplete without a walk along the T-Badh.

review_text: T-Badh: T-Badh (T-Dam) is an important protective structure and a popular tourist destination located on the banks of the Padma River in Rajshahi, Bangladesh. It is named after its 'T' shape. One long section of the dam extends along the river bank and the other extends directly into the water. Built to protect the city from river erosion and flooding, this 'T'-shaped dam is known for its scenic views, especially the mesmerizing view of the setting sun over the Padma River. It is a major attraction for those who want to enjoy the riverside environment. Visitors often enjoy boat trips, evening walks and picnics. The area is known for its local delicacies like fuchka, jhalmuri and various types of fruit juices, pickles available from the vendors nearby. There is a unique coconut grove and flower garden that further enhances its aesthetic appeal.

A Serene Escape by the Padma River
Rajshahi's T-Badh, aptly named for its distinctive "T" shape, is far more than just a protective embankment against the mighty Padma River's erosion. It has evolved into a beloved recreational hub and a symbol of the city's connection to its majestic river. This scenic spot offers a tranquil escape from the urban bustle, drawing both locals and tourists with its picturesque views and calming ambiance.
The primary draw of T-Badh is the breathtaking panorama of the Padma River, especially at sunset. As the sun dips below the horizon, it paints the sky in vibrant hues, which are beautifully reflected on the river's calm waters, creating a truly mesmerizing spectacle. The gentle breeze, the rhythmic lapping of the waves, and the vast open sky combine to create a deeply soothing experience. Visitors often take leisurely strolls along the embankment, enjoying the fresh air and the natural beauty.
Beyond its scenic appeal, T-Badh offers a lively atmosphere, particularly in the afternoons and evenings. You'll find numerous food stalls offering local snacks and refreshments, adding to the vibrant community feel. Boat rides on the Padma are a popular activity, providing a unique perspective of the river and its surroundings. While primarily a place for relaxation and enjoyment of nature, T-Badh also serves as a testament to the ongoing efforts to protect Rajshahi from the river's powerful currents, showcasing a blend of functionality and natural charm. It's an essential stop for anyone visiting Rajshahi, offering a true taste of its riverside charm.

Varendra Research Museum in Rajshahi is a treasure trove of Bangladesh's rich history and cultural heritage. As the country's first museum, it boasts an impressive collection of ancient artifacts, including sculptures, coins, pottery, and manuscripts from the Gupta, Pala, and Sultanate periods.

The museum's collection includes:

- Over 4,000 artifacts, including rare Buddhist and Hindu sculptures
- A vast collection of coins, including ancient punch-marked coins
- Terracotta artifacts and pottery from the Mahasthangarh and Paharpur regions
- Manuscripts and rare books, including a 16th-century Quran
- A stunning collection of traditional Bengali art, including paintings and sculptures

The museum's building itself is a stunning example of colonial architecture, with lush gardens and a serene atmosphere. Visitors can explore the galleries, attend exhibitions and lectures, and even participate in workshops and cultural events.

Some notable exhibits include:

- The famous Mahasthangarh inscription, a 3rd-century BC stone slab with Brahmi script
- The stunning bronze Buddha statue, a masterpiece of Pala-era art
- The intricate stone carvings from the Paharpur Vihara, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

The museum is located in the heart of Rajshahi city, near the Rajshahi University campus. It's easily accessible by public transport, including buses and rickshaws.

Opening hours:

- Summer: 10 AM to 6 PM
- Winter: 9 AM to 5 PM
- Closed on Fridays and national holidays

Admission fees:

- Adults: ₹20
- Students: ₹10
- Foreigners: ₹100

Guided tours are available in English and Bengali, and photography is allowed with permission.

Varendra Research Museum: Varendra Museum is a museum located in the heart of Rajshahi city, Bangladesh, which serves as a major research center and tourist attraction. It houses over 19,000 historical artifacts from the Indian subcontinent, especially the Varendra region of northern Bangladesh. It is run by the University of Rajshahi.

It is considered the oldest museum in Bangladesh, as it was the first museum established in East Bengal on 27 September 1910. The museum began its journey as the collection of the Varendra Research Association and received its present name in 1919.

The kings of Rajshahi and Natore, especially Prince Sarat Kumar Roy, donated their personal collections to the Varendra Museum. Varendra refers to an ancient city. Varendra (or Barinda) was a region of Bengal, which is now in Bangladesh. It included the Pundravardhan or Pundra kingdom. According to Cunningham, Varendra was bounded on the west by the Ganges and Mahananda, on the east by the Karatoya, on the south by the Padma, and on the north by the Cooch Behar and the Terai. The Varendra Brahmins originated from this region.

The Varendra settlement, known as Janakbhavu (fatherland), was one of the most prosperous regions of the ancient Indian subcontinent. Literary and epigraphic evidence shows that a distinct artistic community had attained wide fame here during the Pala dynasty, and this artistic tradition continued uninterruptedly until the Sena dynasty.

Main Collections and Galleries: The museum houses about 19,000 artifacts spanning several millennia, including artifacts from the Indus Valley, Pala, Sena, Maurya and Gupta periods. The museum's collection is spread across seven galleries, showcasing thousands of years of civilization:
•	Gallery 1: This houses the collection of the Indus Valley Civilization (2500 BCE) and some of the 265 artifacts recovered from the excavations at Sompur Paharpur (8th-12th centuries). It also houses ancient Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian inscriptions. There is also a significant collection of gold and silver coins from various economic and political periods.
•	Galleries 2-5: This houses rare stone, bronze and modern wooden sculptures of Buddhist, Hindu (Surya, Shiva, Vishnu, Durga and various Bodhisattvas from the Pala, Sena, Maurya and Gupta periods) and Jain gods and goddesses.
•	Gallery 6: This displays Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit and ancient Bengali inscriptions and carved stones from the Muslim period. Handwritten Holy Quran, Arabic and Persian inscriptions and Sher Shah's bronze cannon are displayed here. There are more than 10,000 books and 15,000 rare manuscripts in Sanskrit, Bengali and Arabic.
•	A new gallery has been added to showcase the indigenous and tribal culture of the Rajshahi region. The traditional culture, tools and jewellery of the indigenous people of the Rajshahi region are displayed here.

Opening hours:
Saturday – Wednesday: 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
Friday: 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM (with a prayer break from 1:00 PM to 2:30 PM).
Thursday: Closed for weekends.

Varendra Research Museum (RAJSHAHI)
Varendra Research Museum is the first museum in Bangladesh established in Rajshahi city. It is rich in archaeological collections. This archaeological museum was established in 1910 on a private initiative. It is currently managed by Rajshahi University. Varendra Research Museum is located in Hetem Khan, the center of Rajshahi city. It is the first museum in Bangladesh. It is one of the museums in South Asia in terms of archaeological collections. The significant contributions of Sarat Kumar Roy, a landlord of the Dighapatia royal family of Natore, lawyer Akshay Kumar Maitreya and Ramprasad Chandra, a teacher of Rajshahi Collegiate School, have contributed to the establishment of Varendra Museum.[5] In 1910, they formed the Varendra Research Society to collect and preserve the heritage and artifacts of Bengal. That year, they conducted research in various places in Rajshahi and collected 32 rare artifacts. To preserve these artifacts, the construction of the museum's own building began on the land donated by Sarat Kumar Roy. The construction was completed in 1913. On November 13 of the same year, the then Governor of Bengal, Carmichael, inaugurated the museum.

review_text: The Barind Research Museum is located at Hetem Khan, the heart of the Rajshahi metropolis. This is the first museum in Bangladesh. It is one of the archeological collections in South Asia. Sarat Kumar Roy, zamindar of the Dighapatiya royal family of Natore, lawyer Akshay Kumar Maitreya and teacher of Rajshahi Collegiate School Ramprasad Chandra have made significant contributions to the establishment of the Barind Museum. In 1910, they formed the Barindra Research Society to collect and preserve the heritage and artifacts of Bengal. In that year, they searched various places in Rajshahi and collected 32 rare specimens. Construction of the museum's own building began on land donated by Sarat Kumar Roy to preserve the artefacts. Construction was completed in 1913 AD. The museum was inaugurated on 13 November of the same year by the then Governor of Bengal, Carmichael. The foundation stone of Lord Carmichael was laid in 1911. The Calcutta Museum suddenly demanded all the artefacts preserved in it. At the initiative of the then Governor Carmichael, the Barind Museum was given the authority to collect and preserve its artefacts through an official notification issued on 14 February 1913. In 1923, Calcutta University jointly with the museum authorities began excavations at the Paharpur Buddhist Monastery in Naogaon. Later, 258 specimens were discovered from Paharpur in a single effort of the Barind Research Society. After 1947, there was a crisis over the existence of the museum. From 1949 to 1961, half of the museum building was used as a medical school. When the museum was about to close in 1984, Rajshahi University acquired its movable and immovable property on October 10 of that year. Among the visitors of the museum are Mahatma Gandhi, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose and many other famous personalities.

review_text: The Varendra Research Museum, established in 1910 by the Varendra Investigation Society, is not only the oldest museum in Bangladesh but also the first museum to be established in erstwhile East Bengal.It got its current name in 1919.It stands as a contribution of some of the enlightened citizens like Kumar Sarat Kumar Ray of Dighapatia, Akshaya Kumar Maitreya, and Ramaprasad Chanda.The museum's collection contains eleven different galleries exhibiting various antique religious sculptures and archaeological finds.There are collections from the Indus Valley Civilization and 265 items from Sompur.Various domestic wares made of metal,alloys,terracotta and ceramic are exhibited there.There are archaeological relics from the Muslim period.Most of the galleries display the sculptures of Hindu and Buddhist gods and goddesses.Notable Hindu gods and goddesses are Brahma,Vishnu,Siva,Surya,Ganapati,Bhairava,Parvati,Uma,Kali,Ganga,Chamund,Manasa,Sarwashwati,Varah,Vaishnabi etc.Buddhist relics include the sculptures of Yamari,Buddha,Manjusri,Manjuvara etc.There are some galleries exhibiting Arabic,Persian,Sanskrit and old Bengali stone inscriptions.There is a collection of old coins and documents.There is a Mihrab representing the Muslim heritage.The pictures of Muslim emperors such as Bahadur Shah,Aurangzeb,Shahjahan,Jahangir,Akbar,Humayun,Babur and Muhammad Shah are displayed in a particular gallery.The war weapons of different times,masks,folk music instruments and dresses of renowned persons of the royal families are shown in a gallery.From 1964 until now the museum has remained a part of Rajshahi University.

review_text:
I Badh (or "I Bandh") is not a typical scenic ghat. It is an embankment—a long, rugged, earthen wall built to hold back the colossal might of the Padma River. Visiting here is less about tranquil sunsets and more about witnessing a stark, powerful dialogue between human endeavor and relentless nature. The scenery is dramatic, humbling, and deeply atmospheric.

The Scenic Character:

The view is dominated by the embankment itself, a raised roadway that acts as your stage. From this vantage point, you look down onto the vast, sandy chars and the distant river channel on one side, and over the protected, lower-lying land on the other. This unique perspective frames the landscape like a living map.

· The Monumental Scale: The true spectacle is the sheer expanse. During the dry season, the Padma retreats, revealing miles of golden, sculpted sandbanks (chars) that stretch towards the hazy horizon. The river itself becomes a shimmering silver thread in the distance. It’s a panorama of breathtaking, almost desert-like emptiness, conveying the scale of the force this badh must contain.
· The Seasonal Drama: This is where the scenery tells its most potent story.
· In the Dry Winter: The landscape is serene, almost melancholic. Local life spreads onto the chars for farming, fishing, and grazing. The air is clear, perfect for long, contemplative walks along the bund, watching kite flyers against the vast blue sky.
· In the Raging Monsoon: The mood transforms entirely. The Padma rises, angry and powerful, its turbulent, muddy waters beating against the very foot of the badh. The once-distant river is now a roaring, intimidating presence. Standing on the embankment, feeling the spray and wind, you viscerally understand its purpose—it is a frontline against the flood, a silent guardian.
· Life on the Line: The scenery is animated by the resilient communities that live in its shadow. You'll see fishermen launching boats from the sandy shores, farmers tending to crops on the chars, and children playing on slopes that become a barrier for survival in a few months. This human element adds a poignant, resilient layer to the vast natural canvas.

Ambiance: The atmosphere is one of solitude and raw power. It’s often quiet, save for the constant wind that sweeps across the open space. There’s a tangible sense of exposure to the elements—sun, wind, and the latent force of the river. It’s a place for introspection, for feeling small yet connected to a grand, cyclical struggle.

Verdict: I Badh offers a fundamentally different, more raw scenic experience than the typical riverfront. It is not conventionally pretty; it is impressive and sobering. It provides a profound lesson in geography, human resilience, and the untamed personality of the Padma. Come here not for leisure, but for perspective. Come to stand on the rampart, feel the wind, and watch a landscape that breathes with the seasons, all held in a tense, beautiful balance by the earth beneath your feet.

Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5) for its unique, powerful, and authentic landscape. A must-see for those interested in the true, unvarnished relationship between land, water, and life in riverine Bangladesh.

review_text:
I recently visited I-Bandh in Rajshahi, and I must say, it was a truly delightful experience. This picturesque spot offers a serene escape from the hustle and bustle of city life. The well-maintained pathways invite leisurely strolls, allowing you to soak in the tranquility of the surroundings.
The lush greenery and vibrant flowers create a refreshing ambiance. It's evident that the authorities take great care in maintaining the park's natural beauty. The gentle breeze coming off the nearby Padma River adds to the peaceful atmosphere, making it an ideal place to unwind and reconnect with nature.
I particularly enjoyed the scenic views of the river from various vantage points along the bandh. Watching the boats glide by and the sunset paint the sky with vibrant hues was simply mesmerizing. It's a perfect spot for photography enthusiasts or anyone looking for a moment of calm reflection.
While the natural beauty is the main draw, I also appreciated the cleanliness and the presence of basic amenities. There were benches to rest on and designated areas that seemed well-kept.
I-Bandh is a gem in Rajshahi, offering a peaceful and visually appealing environment for individuals, couples, and families alike. Whether you're looking for a morning walk, an evening relaxation spot, or simply a place to enjoy nature's beauty, I highly recommend a visit to I-Bandh. It’s a refreshing oasis that leaves you feeling rejuvenated.
