The Padma River, one of the largest rivers in Bangladesh, offers a serene and breathtaking experience for anyone who visits its banks. Nestled beside this mighty river is a beautiful place, known for its peaceful atmosphere and natural beauty. The location is a perfect escape for those who want to immerse themselves in the tranquil environment and witness the simple yet stunning beauty of nature.

In the morning, the place comes to life with a crisp, fresh air that fills your lungs with each breath. The calmness of the river combined with the soft glow of the early morning sun creates a picture-perfect scene. The gentle ripples of the Padma River reflect the clear sky, while the surrounding greenery adds to the charm of the place. You can hear the sound of birds chirping and leaves rustling in the breeze, enhancing the sense of calm.

This spot is not only known for its beauty but also for the connection it offers with nature. The refreshing air and the river’s constant flow create a sense of peace and clarity. Whether you are looking to start your day with a peaceful walk or simply want to enjoy the beauty of the river, this place promises an unforgettable experience.

"I Badh" is a riverside embankment built along the banks of the Padma River in Rajshahi. It's a blend of engineering and aesthetics — both a flood control measure and a tourist magnet.

It acts as a protective dam (embankment) to guard Rajshahi city from the unpredictable moods of the mighty Padma, but over the years, it has evolved into a cultural heart of the city.

---

✨ Key Attractions

1. 🌅 Breathtaking Sunsets:
Watching the sun melt into the Padma river — chef's kiss! A must-see for nature lovers and selfie enthusiasts.

2. 🚶‍♂️ Riverside Walks & Jogging Track:
Wide paved paths with benches where you can stroll, jog, or simply sit and watch life flow by like the river.

3. 🌸 Padma Garden (পদ্মা উদ্যান):
A lush, green park area with flowering trees, fountains, and sitting areas — perfect for families, friends, and secret lovers.

4. 🎡 Street Foods & Local Delights:
Fuchka, chotpoti, grilled corn (ভুট্টা), tea in clay cups — it's a festival for your tastebuds.

5. 🚣‍♀️ Boat Rides:
Local fishermen or boatmen offer boat rides on the Padma. Calm, breezy, and soul-healing.

6. 🎶 Occasional Events & Festivals:
During Pahela Baishakh and other cultural festivals, “I Badh” turns into a musical, colorful, lively mela.

---

📍 Location

It's located just a few kilometers from Rajshahi College and Shaheb Bazar. Easily reachable by rickshaw or CNG.

Nearby Landmarks:

Rajshahi College

Shaheb Bazar

Barendra Museum

Rajshahi University (a bit farther)

---

⚙️ Engineering Marvel

The embankment is part of a larger flood control and riverbank erosion protection project. Without it, large parts of Rajshahi might get submerged during the monsoon. It's made with:

Reinforced concrete structures

Geo-bags and boulder lining

Drainage canals to manage rainwater

Shaheed A.H.M Qamaruzzaman Central Park and Zoo: Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park and Zoo is a large public park and zoo located in Rajshahi, Bangladesh. Spread over 33 acres on the banks of the beautiful Padma River, this park serves as one of the city's most popular recreational centers for students and tourists, combining natural beauty, diverse species of wildlife, and modern entertainment facilities.

The park is named after A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman, a prominent national leader and one of the four prominent figures martyred in 1975.

During the British colonial period, the area where the park is now located, near the bend of the Padma River, was used as a horse racing ground. After the British left, the land remained abandoned for many years, until in the early 1970s, local political leader Abul Hasnat Muhammad Kamaruzzaman took the initiative to turn this abandoned site into a public park under the Rajshahi Zilla Parishad. The park was officially inaugurated in 1972, later a zoo was added inside the park in 1983, and in 1996, the Rajshahi City Corporation took over its management.

The park has a variety of attractions for visitors of all ages. The zoo section houses a variety of wildlife including Bengal tigers, chital deer, crocodiles, monkeys, pythons and numerous species of birds such as peacocks and pelicans, A central lake offers paddle boat rides,
A small lake shelters fish and aquatic birds, creating a peaceful natural habitat, A children's play area with a seesaw, swings and slides.

The park is known for its lush greenery, which includes walking paths surrounded by eucalyptus and fruit trees and various artistic sculptures, a butterfly garden and an artificial hill and a beautifully designed bridge from which a picturesque view of the Padma River can be seen.

There are also shaded picnic areas, an amphitheater and designated parking facilities near the main entrance.

Operating Hours: 8:00 AM – 6:00 PM daily.

I recently had the opportunity to visit the Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park & Zoo and I must say, I was thoroughly impressed. This park and zoo is a true gem in theess bustling city, offering a tranquil and educational escape for people of all ages.

The first thing that struck me upon entering the park was the well-maintained and lush greenery. The park is spread over a vast area and is filled with beautiful trees, flowers, and shrubs. It was a refreshing change from the concrete jungle of the city. The pathways are well-paved and easy to navigate, making it accessible for everyone.

The zoo is home to a diverse range of animals, from exotic birds to majestic tigers. I was amazed at how well-cared for and happy the animals seemed. The enclosures were spacious and looked natural, mimicking their natural habitat. It was heartwarming to see the efforts put in by the zookeepers to ensure the animals' well-being.

One of the highlights of the park was the butterfly garden. It was a delight to see so many colorful butterflies fluttering around, and I even got the chance to hold one on my finger. The park also has a lake where visitors can rent paddleboats and enjoy a relaxing ride while taking in the scenic beauty.

Apart from the zoo and park, there are also different activities and events organized regularly to educate and entertain visitors. During my visit, I attended a talk on wildlife conservation, which was informative and eye-opening. It is great to see the park taking an active role in spreading awareness about the importance of preserving our planet's biodiversity.

The park also has a small food court offering a variety of snacks and refreshments. I tried some local delicacies and was not disappointed. The prices were reasonable, and the food was delicious.

Overall, I had a fantastic experience at the Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park & Zoo. It offers a perfect balance of education, recreation, and relaxation. I highly recommend this park and zoo to anyone looking for a peaceful and educational day out with family and friends. It is a must-visit for tourists and locals alike. I will definitely be visiting again soon.

If you’re hanging out in Rajshahi and need a break from the hustle, Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park & Zoo is pretty much the go-to spot. It’s not just a park; it’s the city’s favorite backyard.

The Vibe
The first thing you’ll notice is the space. It’s huge (about 33 acres!), green, and surprisingly breezy. Whether you're there for a sweaty morning jog or a slow afternoon stroll by the lake, the vibe is super chill. It’s the kind of place where you’ll see students hanging out, families picnicking, and kids losing their minds with excitement over the mini-train and rides.

The Zoo
To be real, the zoo side is a bit modest. You’ll see spotted deer, few crocodiles and a variety of birds. It’s great for a quick look, though some of the enclosures feel a bit "old school" and could definitely use a glow-up. Still, for the price of a ticket, it’s a solid deal.

Why go?
* Budget-friendly: It won't break the bank.
* Insta-worthy: The lake and tall trees make for some great shots.
* Central: It’s easy to get to from anywhere in town.
It’s a classic Rajshahi landmark—a little bit nostalgic, very green, and always full of life.
*Parking: Available with charge

Shaheed A.H.M. Kamaruzzaman Central Park and Zoo is a popular public park and zoo located in Rajshahi, Bangladesh. Covering an area of 33 acres, it serves as a significant recreational spot for the city’s residents1.

History

British Colonial Period: Originally a horse racecourse by the Padma River.

Post-Independence: Transformed into a park in 1972, named after A.H.M. Qamaruzzaman, a national leader of Bangladesh1.

Zoo Addition: The zoo was established in 19831.

Features

Flora and Fauna: The park boasts a variety of trees and houses numerous animals, including tigers, deer, crocodiles, monkeys, and various bird species1.

Recreational Facilities: The park includes an amphitheater, picnic spots, and a Ferris wheel, making it a prime attraction for both locals and tourists2.

Ticket Price : 25৳ BDT Only.

Puthia Rajbari is an architecturally stunning and historically significant palace, but the current state of management leaves a lot to be desired.

​While the exterior is beautiful, the indoor gallery is quite disappointing. It lacks a proper collection of historical artifacts and mostly just features some framed photographs, which doesn't do justice to the rich history of the place.

​Additionally, the atmosphere inside the complex is heavily disrupted by beggars and self-proclaimed priests (purohits) who are constantly pestering visitors for money. What is most alarming and heartbreaking is that these individuals are actually causing physical damage to the heritage structures.

​The site has immense potential, but the authorities urgently need to step up their preservation efforts, improve the gallery collection, and properly secure the complex from those harming the property.

The Puthia Rajbari, also known as the Five-Anna Zamindar House, was the residence of Maharani Hemantakumari Devi. Among the archaeological heritage sites of Bengal, Puthia Rajbari in Rajshahi is one of the most notable. In 1895, Maharani Hemantakumari Devi constructed the present rectangular two-storied palace in an attractive Indo-European architectural style.

It is located about 32 km northeast of the Rajshahi district সদর, along the Natore highway beside the Bagha–Puthia district road. One can reach Puthia by bus from any part of the country, and also easily by road after getting down at Natore or Rajshahi via train.

In the 17th century, during the Mughal period, the Puthia zamindari was one of the oldest estates in Bengal. It is said that a man named Nilambar received the title of “Raja” from the Mughal emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605–1627), after which it became known as Puthia Rajbari. In 1744, the estate was divided—where the eldest son received five and a half annas of the property, and the other three sons received three and a half annas collectively. The zamindari system continued until 1950, when it was abolished, along with the Puthia estate. However, despite the abolition, the palaces, temples, and other structures built during that era still stand today. This palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemantakumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law, Maharani Sarat Sundari Devi.

The front portion of the building features beautifully crafted pillars, decorations, wooden works, and floral and vine motifs on the walls and above the doors, showcasing exquisite architectural artistry. The roof of the palace is flat, constructed with iron beams, wooden supports, and tiles. A moat was dug around the palace for security purposes.

There are six large royal ponds surrounding Puthia Rajbari, each covering about six acres. There are also six temples nearby, the largest being the Shiva Temple (Puthia). Other temples include the Radha Gobinda Temple, Gopal Temple, Govinda Temple, and Dol Mancha. Each temple is adorned with exquisite terracotta artwork on its walls. The complex also includes Jor-Bangla temples, bungalow-style temples, and Pancharatna (five-spired) temples—each representing different architectural styles of Bengal. Additionally, there are the queen’s bathing ghat and the inner quarters, making the entire palace complex vast and impressive.

Puthia Rajbari is surrounded on all sides by moats. These were either built to prevent enemy intrusion or created while raising the land, as the area was previously low-lying.

Puthia Rajbari: Puthia Rajbari (also known as Panchani Zamindar Bari) is one of the major archaeological and historical sites in Bangladesh. The palace is located 30 km east of the city on the Rajshahi-Natore highway and one km south of the Rajshahi-Natore highway in Puthia upazila. It is famous for its Indo-Saracenic revival architecture and the historic Hindu temple complex that surrounds it.

It was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in memory of her mother-in-law Maharani Saratsundari Devi. It was used as the headquarters of the Puthia Rajbari, one of the oldest and richest feudal families of Bengal. It now houses a museum showcasing the history of Puthia and its surrounding areas.

Panchani Palace is located at the southern end of an open field. The two-storey palace features a blend of Mughal and European architectural styles, including massive Corinthian columns, a grand central gateway, and florally decorated balconies. The palace was built on 4.31 acres of land. The complex is surrounded by a defensive moat and large reservoirs (dighi) such as the Sivasagar and the Shyamsagar.

Main attractions:
•	The Palace: A large structure managed by the Department of Archaeology.
•	Temple Complex: This area contains the largest number of historical temples in Bangladesh, including the Shiva Temple, Jagannath Temple, and Govinda Temple. Many of these are decorated with exquisite terracotta artwork.
•	Bara Shiva Temple: Built in 1823, it is one of the largest Shiva temples in the country and houses a huge Shiva linga.
•	Pancharatna Govinda Temple: It is famous for its exquisite terracotta panels depicting Hindu mythological stories such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
•	Dol Mancha: A four-story pyramid-shaped structure used during the Doljatra festival.
•	Bara Ahonika Mandir: Built in the Do-Chala style, which reflects the traditional Bengali hut-shaped architecture.

This place is a major destination for tourists interested in the zamindari history of Bengal and ancient temple architecture.

Visiting hours: Generally open to the public from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM daily.

Puthia Rajbari is a captivating historical palace located in Puthia Upazila, Rajshahi District, Bangladesh. Constructed in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in memory of her mother-in-law, Maharani Saratsundari Devi, the palace exemplifies Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture—a blend of European and Mughal styles.  ￼

🏰 Architectural Highlights

The two-story palace is surrounded by moats and features multiple courtyards:
•	Kachhari Angan: The administrative court with porticos supported by semi-Corinthian columns. ￼
•	Mandir Angan (Gobindabari): The temple courtyard housing the Pancha Ratna Govinda Temple, adorned with intricate terracotta carvings depicting scenes from Hindu epics.  ￼
•	Andar Mahal: The inner quarters, including the residence of Maharani Hemanta Kumari, featuring a central reception hall and nine surrounding rooms. ￼

⸻

🛕 Temple Complex

Adjacent to the Rajbari is the Puthia Temple Complex, renowned for its collection of historic Hindu temples: ￼
•	Pancha Ratna Govinda Temple: A 19th-century temple with five spires and terracotta panels illustrating scenes from the Ramayana and Krishna’s life.  ￼
•	Pancha Ratna Shiva Temple (Bhubaneswar Shiva Mandir): The largest Shiva temple in Bangladesh, built between 1823 and 1830 by Rani Bhuban Mayi Devi.  ￼
•	Bara Ahnik Mandir: A unique temple combining Do Chala and Char Chala architectural styles, rare in Bangladesh.  ￼

⸻

📍 Visiting Information
•	Location: Approximately 30 km east of Rajshahi city, accessible via the Rajshahi-Natore highway. ￼
•	Admission: Open to visitors; no entry fee is typically required.
•	Best Time to Visit: Winter months (November to February) offer pleasant weather for exploration.

⸻

⭐ Overall Impression

Puthia Rajbari, with its rich history and architectural grandeur, offers a glimpse into Bangladesh’s royal past. The adjoining temple complex enhances its cultural significance, making it a must-visit destination for history enthusiasts and travelers alike.

review_text: Puthia Rajbari, located in Rajshahi, Bangladesh, is a stunning example of Indo-European architecture and the rich cultural heritage of the Puthia zamindar dynasty. Founded during Emperor Akbar’s reign (1556–1605) by Pitambara, the dynasty left an enduring legacy through its majestic palace and numerous temples. The palace, renovated in 1895 by Rani Hemantakumari Devi, spans 4.31 acres and features intricate sculptural details, a pediment, and a blend of administrative and residential spaces. Surrounded by protective moats like Shivsagar Dighi and Radhasagar Dighi, the estate also boasts iconic temples such as the Pancharatna Shiva Temple, Jagannath Temple, and Dol Mandir, renowned for their terracotta designs. Declared protected antiquities by the Department of Archaeology, these structures reflect the zamindars’ dedication to religion, philanthropy, and architectural excellence. The Puthia dynasty’s contributions, especially by figures like Maharani Saratsundari Devi and Rani Hemantakumari Devi, continue to inspire admiration, preserving the grandeur and cultural essence of a bygone era.

Puthia Rajbari is a breathtaking historical palace that beautifully blends Indo-Saracenic and Palladian architecture. Built in 1895, it features grand columns, intricate designs, and peaceful surroundings, including the serene Shyamsagar pond. The nearby Puthia Temple Complex adds to its cultural significance, making it a great destination for history and architecture lovers. However, the palace requires better preservation to maintain its charm. If you're visiting Rajshahi, this place is a must-see for a glimpse into Bangladesh’s royal past!

Puthia Rajbari, an example of Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture, is a palace in Puthia Upazilla, Rajshahi, Bangladesh. It was constructed in 1895 for Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi. The palace is located one kilometer south of Rajshahi Natore highway and 30 kilometers to the east of the town.
About a one-hour drive from Rajshahi city. You must purchase a ticket to enter. Visitors are permitted inside after 10am. It features museums with historical photo frames and several Black Stone Statues that were handcrafted from the urban archaeological sites of Mahasthangarh.
Some of the most striking Terracotta in the nation may be seen in Puthia Rajbari. The sculptures from 60 AD to 1200 AD are on display.

The main building of the palace is a huge, two-story structure with magnificent Corinthian columns and hanging balconies. The exterior of the palace is artistically decorated with flowery patterns, statues, and colored tiles. A large entryway and two garages for the carriages of the royal family stand out at the palace's entrance. The servants' quarters, a barrack, a jail, and the estate's treasury office were all located in the palace's basement floor. There is a well on the lower level where death row convicts were thrown and put to death. Visitors ascend a wooden staircase to a sizable hall that once housed the king's court. The vast room had featured superb glazed tiles and chandeliers and a large window looking out over beautiful gardens.

review_text:
Initially, Puthia was a village of Laskarpur Pargana, named after Laskar Khan Nilamber, the brother of the first zamindar of Puthia, who was the first to receive the title of Raja from the Mughal emperor Jahangir. A partition of the estate took place in 1744 and the zamindari was divided among 4 co shares among whom the panch ani (five annas) and char ani (four annas) co-shares become famous in conducting jamindary.

Puthia Rajbari is surrounded by ditches. The south end of an open field is where panch ani palace is situated. 4.31 acres of land was used for the Rajbari. The once strong walls surrounding the place are now damaged in places. The rajbari is divided into 4 courts :

Kachhari (office) Angan (court)

Mandir angan or Gobindabari (temple court)

Andar Mahal (inner quarters)

Residence of Maharani Hemanti Kumari

The rooms are built around the courts in the palace, with the exception of the Kachari Angan, the courts are one storeyed. Kachari Angan has porticos on both the west and east ends which project in the Palladian manner. The west entrance gate leads to Kachari Angan while the other leads to Temple or Gobindabari courts. Each portico is supported by 4 semi-Corinthian columns rising the full height of the building. The porticos contain arcaded, semi-glazed loggias at the first floor level. The building's central portion, between the porticos, continues the columned theme and also has a loggia at first floor level. Also here the 4 semi Corinthian pillars cover the upper parts of the building. A wooden staircase leads to the upper floor on the east side. There are three rooms of different size, two of which were used as treasuries. The other side, (Western) has 4 rooms with two verandahs. Close to Govindabari, there are two small rooms with verandah. Now, most of the rooms built on the east and south of Kachari Angan are at ruins.

The northern block of the building with east–west axis is double storeyed and has a wide hall of 21.95m x 7.16m. The upper storeyed portion has six variously announced rooms. In front of the hall there is a wide verandah with balconies on either side. The Pancharatna Bara Gobinda temple is located at the Gobindabari of this palace. The temple is beautifully ornamented with terracotta carvings. There are two rooms and several bathrooms in the western part of Andar Mahal. Most of the rooms in the court in western part of Andar Mahal are in ruins. In the eastern part of Ander Mahal there is one storeyed residence of Rani Hemanta Kumari. It has a porch in front of it and a central reception hall with nine rooms. There are extended verandahs with arches in front and rear of the hall room. Iron and wooden beams have been used in the roof.

review_text: Puthia Rajbari is a palace in Puthia Upazila of Rajshahi, Bangladesh.  It is located 32 km northeast of Rajshahi district headquarters on Bagha-Puthia district road towards Natore highway.  Puthia Rajbari is the residence of Rani Hemanta Kumari Devi.  This palace was built in 1895 by Rani Hemanta Kumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law late Maharani Sharut Sundari Devi.  Pillars, ornamentation, woodwork, flower and leaf paintings on the walls and doors of the building bear the hallmark of exquisite architecture.  There are several small and big temples and dighis around it.  A museum has been set up on the 2nd floor of the building.  Tickets are required for museum entry only.  Everything else can be seen without a ticket.  The museum houses several idols of Gods and Goddesses with Lord Vishnu being the most prominent.

review_text:
Puthia Rajbari is an impressive historic palace complex located about 32 km from Rajshahi city, Bangladesh. Built mainly in the 19th century by the Puthia royal family, this palace showcases an extraordinary fusion of Bengali, Mughal, and European architectural elements.

The Rajbari is known for its large courtyard, beautifully carved wooden doors, and decorative terracotta panels that reflect the rich craftsmanship of that era. The palace area is surrounded by several notable temples, including the Govinda Temple, one of the largest Hindu temples in Bangladesh, and the striking Pancharatna Shiva Temple built in 1823.

Visitors can wander around the spacious grounds, admire the impressive structures, and feel transported back in time. The Rajbari compound also has large ponds and tranquil gardens that make it an excellent spot for photography and relaxation.

A small museum inside the palace displays artifacts and historical information about the Puthia zamindar family who contributed significantly to the cultural and social development of this region.

Entry is usually free, but sometimes a small maintenance fee is charged. It’s best to visit in winter when the weather is pleasant, and the surrounding fields are lush green.

If you are interested in heritage architecture, cultural history, or simply want to enjoy a peaceful day trip near Rajshahi, Puthia Rajbari is highly recommended.

review_text: During the seventeenth century, in the Mughal era, the Puthia Zamindari was one of the oldest among the various kingdoms of Bengal at that time. It is said that a man named Nilambar received the title of "Raja" from the Mughal Emperor Jahangir (1605–1627 AD), after which the estate became known as the Puthia Rajbari (Royal Palace). In 1744, the zamindari was divided — the eldest son of the zamindar received five and a half annas of the property, while the other three sons received three and a half annas. The zamindari system continued until 1950. When the system was abolished, the Puthia zamindari also came to an end. However, even though the zamindari system was abolished, the palace, temples, and other structures built during that era still remain intact. This palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law, Maharani Sarat Sundari Devi.

Puthia Rajbari is surrounded by ditches. The south end of an open field is where panch ani palace is situated. 4.31 acres of land was used for the Rajbari. The once strong walls surrounding the place are now damaged in places. The rajbari is divided into 4 courts :

Karchri (office) Angan (court)
Mandir angan or Gobindabari(temple court)
Andar Mahal (inner quarters)
Residence of Maharani Hemanti Kumari
The rooms are built around the courts in the palace, with the exception of the kachari angan, the courts are one storeyed. Kachari angan has porticos on both the west and east ends which project in the Palladian manner. The west entrance gate leads to kachari angan while the other leads to Temple or Govindabari courts. Each portico is supported by 4 semi-Corinthian columns rising the full height of the building. The porticos contain arcaded, semi-glazed loggias at the first floor level. The building's central portion, between the porticos, continues the columned theme and also has a loggia at first floor level. Also here the 4 semi Corinthian pillars covers the upper parts of the building. A wooden staircase leads to the upper floor on the east side. There are 3 rooms of different size, each 2 of which were used as treasuries. Other side, (Western) has 4 rooms with 2 verandahs. Close to Govindabari, there are two small rooms with verandah. Now, most of the rooms built on the east and south of kachari Angan are at ruins.

review_text:
Puthia Rajbari is not just a palace; it is the centerpiece of the most impressive collection of historic Hindu temples in Bangladesh. Located about 30 km east of Rajshahi city, this site is a masterclass in Indo-Saracenic Revival architecture and a must-visit for history buffs and photography enthusiasts.
🏛️ The Experience: What to Expect
Walking into the Puthia complex feels like stepping back into the late 19th century. The main palace was built in 1895 by Maharani Hemanta Kumari Devi in honor of her mother-in-law.
1. The Royal Palace (Rajbari)
The palace itself is a grand, two-story structure with a symmetrical facade and massive Corinthian columns.
* The Vibe: It’s a mix of colonial elegance and local decay. While the front facade is relatively well-maintained and houses a small museum, the back portions are in various states of ruin, which adds a haunting, "forgotten kingdom" atmosphere.
* Must-See: Look for the intricate floral plaster reliefs and the multicolored glass still clinging to some of the windows.
2. The Temple Complex (The Real Star)
The Rajbari is surrounded by several temples that are often more architecturally significant than the palace itself:
* Bhubaneshwar Shiva Temple: The largest Shiva temple in the country. Its five soaring spires (Pancha Ratna) and the massive black basalt Shiva Lingam inside are breathtaking.
* Govinda Temple: Located within the palace courtyard, this temple is famous for its terracotta carvings. The walls are covered in detailed scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata—think of it as a 19th-century comic book carved in clay.
* Dol Mandir: A towering, four-story white structure that dominates the entrance to the complex.
📋 Quick Travel Tips
| Location | Puthia Upazila, Rajshahi (on the Natore highway). |
| Getting There | 40–50 minutes from Rajshahi city via bus or private car. |
| Best Time | November to February (cooler weather) or May–July (mango season!). |
| Duration | 1 hour is enough to see the main buildings. |
| Photography | Excellent for architecture and portraits; no special permits usually needed for exteriors. |
⚖️ The Verdict
Pros: * The highest concentration of historic temples in one walkable area in Bangladesh.
* Incredible terracotta artistry that rivals the famous Kantajew Temple.
* Less crowded and more "authentic" than many global heritage sites.
Cons:
* Maintenance is inconsistent; some areas feel neglected.
* Limited tourist facilities (restaurants/restrooms) directly at the site.
> Pro Tip: If you find a temple door locked, don't walk away! Usually, a local caretaker is nearby with the keys and will happily open it for you for a small tip (20-50 BDT).

Natore Rajbari, also known as Rani Bhabani’s Palace, is a historical site in Natore. Built in the 18th century, this palace reflects a blend of Mughal and European architecture . It was the residence of the influential Rani Bhabani, sometimes called the "Queen of Half Bengal" due to her significant influence in the region. The estate is divided into two parts, the "Boro Taraf" and "Chhoto Taraf," each with distinct features and history.

The palace grounds include several temples and large ponds, like the notable Jol Tungi Pukur, Though some buildings have suffered damage over the years, including the earthquake of 1897, the site retains its majestic charm. Today, visitors can explore the preserved sections, enjoy the surrounding gardens, and learn about the Rajbari’s significant role in the history and culture of Bangladesh​​​​​​.

One of the oldest rajbaris in Bangladesh (1700s), the magnificent but dilapidated Natore Rajbari was once the nerve-centre of undivided Bengal's second-biggest zamindari (land revenue estate), which lost its sheen in the 19th century. The entire complex moated by ponds and lined by centuries-old shady trees is actually a series of seven rajbaris, four of which remain largely intact. One palace houses a police camp, another is a government office, while several others simply lie in ruins.

The famous queen Rani Bhabani lived here and after the death of her husband, expanded both the estate and the palace.

Natore Rajbari is on the northern edge of town. From the bus stand, you can walk to it in about half an hour (just keep asking for directions) or take a rickshaw (Tk 50-30).

In the mid seventeenth century one Kamadev Maitra served as tehsildar to the Puthia Raj family. Kamadev’s second son Raghunandan was selected by the Raja to be his agent at the court of Nawab Murshid Quli Khan, the overlord of all Bengal.[5] When the Nawab moved his court from Dhaka to what became known as Murshidabad he took Raghunandan with him and appointed him his Dewan or minister. The Nawab proceeded to confiscate the estates of zamindars who failed to conform to his new regulations, and a number of such estates were acquired by Ramjivan, the elder brother of his Dewan Raghunandan.[6] In due course Ramjivan was given the title of Raja and set up his headquarters in Natore. His estate was generally referred to as the "Rajshahi Zamindari". [5]

The estate had an area of nearly 13,000 square miles and included not only much of North Bengal but also large parts of the areas later comprising the administrative districts of Murshidabad, Nadia, Jessore, Birbhum and Burdwan.[7]

The first palace or Rajbari at Natore was built by Raja Ramjivan. The palace was surrounded by two sets of moats which are still extant.[5]After the division of the estate a separate palace was built for the junior branch of the dynasty. Many of the original buildings were destroyed by the earthquake of 1897 and subsequently rebuilt or replaced.[7]

Ramjivan's Dewan Doyaram was granted landed estates and the title of Ray Raiyan by Nawab Murshid Quli Khan in recognition of his service in apprehending a recalcitrant zamindar named Sitaram Roy.[5][6] In due course Doyaram established his own dynasty the Dighapatia Raj with its own palace Dighapatia Palace[6].

Raja Ramjivan was succeeded by his adopted son Ramkanta.[5] After Raja Ramkanta's early death the Natore estate was ably managed by his widow, known as Rani Bhabani, who became famous for her good works.[5]

One of the oldest Rajbaris in Bangladesh (early 1700s), the magnificent but dilapidated Natore Rajbari was once the nerve-centre of undivided Bengal's second-biggest zamindari, which lost its sheen in the 19th century. The entire complex – moated by ponds and lined by centuries-old shady trees is actually a series of seven Rajbaris, four of which remain largely intact. One palace houses a police camp, another is a government office, while several others simply lie in ruins.

The main palace block within the compound, called Boro Taraf ('big palace'; home of the elder patriarch of the family), is approached via a long avenue lined with impressively tall bottle palms, the white trunks of which resemble temple columns. To the rear of Boro Taraf are the crumbling walls of Rani Bhavani's Palace, which was the residence of the eponymous Rani Bhavani, the widowed wife of one of the Natore rajas who took up the reins of the estate and went on to become a very powerful administrator herself.

To the far end of the complex stands a second palace block called Chhoto Taraf ('small palace'; for the younger brother of the family), consisting of two Rajbaris. The principal one faces a pond and is one of the most beautifully proportioned buildings in Bangladesh, although its cavernous central hall is now in a complete shambles. Entry is restricted, but peering through the broken window slats is allowed.

The peaceful and idyllic gardens around the palaces are as much an attraction as the buildings themselves; bring a picnic to eat in the shade of a gnarled old tree. There are several large ponds here that form an interesting centrepiece, around which are a couple of Hindu temples, one dedicated to Kali and another to Shiva.
